records.title: fix(fleetaccounts): gate the probe-ledger rung on block-derivability, not on FLEET_REG_DIR being set (#5390 follow-on)
records.body:
## The finding

`ff5b1996d` (#5390) made `internal/accountprobe` resolve the fleet registry by
**block-derivability** — the per-user dir the prober actually writes `probe_ledger.jsonl`
into wins, a `sessions.json` with no ledger beside it grades `blocks-unknown` with
`BlocksDerivable() == false`, and a fork is reported on stderr.

That fixes the **writer/resolver**. On the **roster** path it is still masked, because the
consumer never asks:

- `shouldConsultProbeLedger()` (`internal/fleetaccounts/status.go:201`) gates the ledger rung
  on `FLEET_REG_DIR` being **set**. With it unset the rung never runs at all, so even a
  correct resolution is not consulted.

The two call sites that DO benefit today are the ungated ones that pass an empty `regDir`:
`cmd/fak/resume_resolve.go:163` and `cmd/fak/resume_sweep_cli.go:129`. The latter is the
sharpest witness of the original fork — it resolves *its own* ledger dir correctly via
`resolveSweepRegDir` and then asks for the probe verdict with `""`, which resolved somewhere
else entirely.

## Proposed shape

1. Gate on derivability rather than on the env var:
   `return accountprobe.ResolveRegDir().BlocksDerivable()`.
   Strictly **wider and safer**: true whenever `FLEET_REG_DIR` points at a ledger-bearing dir,
   true for the per-user registry the env var never named, and **false** when `FLEET_REG_DIR`
   names a ledger-less dir — which today wrongly turns the rung on.

2. `computeRuntimeStatus` initialises `Available = true` (`status.go:350`), so an
   **un-derivable** registry still publishes unblocked seats. That wants a distinct
   `StatusSource` (e.g. `registry-unknown`), **not** a block. Do not convert absence into
   blocked: stranding seats repeats a prior mistake here, where a removal froze the very probe
   that would have cleared it. Unknown-health must stay distinguishable from both OK and
   blocked.

3. `cmd/fak`'s `defaultFleetRegistryDir` remains a **second copy** of this resolution that
   picks by *existence* rather than derivability. #5390 matched its rung order so the two
   converge where they can, but collapsing it onto `accountprobe.ResolveRegDir` is the real
   cure for #5390's "two processes converge on one answer" acceptance line.

## Caveat for whoever takes this

Change 1 makes the predicate **filesystem-dependent**. Existing `fleetaccounts` tests that
flip behaviour by setting or clearing `FLEET_REG_DIR` alone will need to write a ledger file
to keep asserting what they mean to assert.

## Acceptance

- The ledger rung runs whenever blocks are derivable, regardless of whether `FLEET_REG_DIR`
  is set, and does **not** run when the named dir cannot derive blocks.
- An un-derivable registry publishes seats as unknown-health, not as available.
- Negative witness: reverting the predicate to the env-var gate reds the new test.

Follow-on to #5390 (`ff5b1996d`), which deliberately scoped itself to the resolver half.

records.title: fix(resume): supply witnessed driver-liveness at the resume-stopped seam so #5386 stops deferring every mid-tool row (#5386 follow-on)
records.body:
Follow-on to #5386, which landed as `1d4820b15`.

#5386 replaced a guess with an honest tri-state: a mid-tool tail with no driver-liveness
evidence now resolves to `MIDTOOL_UNKNOWN` instead of being asserted as
`STOPPED_MIDTOOL`. The vocabulary, the total mapping, and the deferral are all on trunk
and tested. **What is not on trunk is anything that produces the evidence.**

## The gap, witnessed at HEAD

`cmd/fak/resume_stopped.go:127` is the *only* production caller, and it goes through the
compatibility wrapper:

    internal/resume/stopped/stopped.go:251
      func Classify(...) Row { return ClassifyWithLiveness(..., LivenessUnknown) }

So in production `live` is always `LivenessUnknown`, `midtoolDisp` always returns
`DispMidtoolUnknown` (`stopped.go:266`), and `Decide`'s `case DispMidtoolUnknown:`
(`stopped.go:535`) always appends to `d.Defer` (`:544`). The `live` and `gone` arms are
reachable only from tests.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a note

This is not merely unrealized value — it is a **behavior change in the conservative
direction that is currently unconditional**. Before `1d4820b15`, a mid-tool row took the
`DispStoppedMidtool` branch (`:521`) and could reach `d.Resume` (`:533`). Now every
mid-tool row defers. That is the *right* default when nothing is known — resuming a
session that is still inside a live tool call is the worse error — but it means
`fak resume stopped` presently offers strictly fewer resumable sessions than it did, and
will keep doing so until a producer exists. The fix is not to relax the default; it is to
supply the evidence.

## What closing this requires

1. At the `cmd/fak` seam, observe whether the driver process for a transcript is still
   alive, and call `ClassifyWithLiveness` with `LivenessLive` / `LivenessGone` instead of
   going through `Classify`.
2. Only claim a non-empty `Liveness` when it is actually witnessed. The doc comment at
   `stopped.go:68` is explicit: *"a shell that cannot observe one says `LivenessUnknown`
   and means it."* A liveness value inferred from age or file size would reintroduce the
   guess this issue removed, in a form that is harder to see.
3. Acceptance: a session whose driver is gone appears under RESUME; a session whose
   driver is live stays deferred; a session with no observable driver still defers with
   the `MidtoolUnknownBlockedBy` reason. All three through the real argv path, not
   through `ClassifyWithLiveness` directly — the current tests already cover that rung.

Note there is an existing process-census primitive in `internal/procguard` worth checking
before writing a new one; also #5385 reports that package's POSIX census is empty on
macOS, which would make `gone` unwitnessable there. On a host where liveness cannot be
observed, `LivenessUnknown` is the correct output, not a fallback guess.

This is an instance of the pattern in #5435: a fully-tested `internal/` primitive whose
only referents outside its own package are tests.

records.title: fix(gateway): the compaction bail-reason HELP declares a closed set of 9 while the emitters produce 11 (decode_failed, no_stable_breakpoint missing)
records.body:
`internal/gateway/metrics_render.go:1186` writes the Prometheus HELP text for
`fak_gateway_compaction_bail_reason_total` and declares its own vocabulary **closed**:

    closed set: under_budget|non_json|no_messages_key|too_few_msgs|no_breakpoint|
                window_no_drop|splice_failed|redecode_failed|prefix_mismatch

That is 9 members. The emitters disagree. Distinct reason literals actually present at
`HEAD` across `internal/agent/anthropic_compact.go`, `anthropic_cachebp.go` and
`anthropic_elide.go`:

    decode_failed          <- MISSING from the declared set
    no_breakpoint
    no_messages_key
    no_stable_breakpoint   <- MISSING from the declared set
    non_json
    prefix_mismatch
    redecode_failed
    splice_failed
    too_few_msgs
    under_budget
    window_no_drop

At least 11 emitted against 9 declared. `decode_failed` was added today by #5387
(`547e44b70`); `no_stable_breakpoint` predates it, so this drifted before that change and
was not caused by it.

## Why it matters more than a stale comment

The string does not merely under-document — it makes a **falsifiable claim of
completeness** to whoever reads the metric. A reader who trusts "closed set" builds a
dashboard or alert over 9 label values and silently drops the rest. `decode_failed` is
precisely the member you least want dropped: #5387 split it out of `too_few_msgs`
*because* a structural decode failure is a bug signal and a short conversation is not.
The metric now distinguishes them and the HELP text says the distinction does not exist.

## Root cause, which is the part worth fixing

The declaration lives in `internal/gateway` and the emitters live in `internal/agent`.
Nothing binds them, so the two drift with no gate. Re-typing two members into the string
fixes today's instance and guarantees a recurrence — this is the second drift already.

Prefer deriving the rendered list from an exported vocabulary owned by the package that
emits it, so adding a reason without registering it fails to compile (or fails a test)
rather than silently under-reporting. If that coupling is unwanted, the honest cheap
alternative is to **stop claiming the set is closed** in the HELP text and say the label
is open-ended.

## Acceptance

- Adding a new bail reason without registering it reds a test — witness the red.
- The rendered HELP enumerates every reason the compaction path can emit, or makes no
  closedness claim at all.
- No behavior change to the counter itself.

Note `internal/gateway` had active concurrent work at the time of filing; whoever takes
this should re-check `git status` for that package first.

records.title: fix(promptmmu): ArraySplicePoints collapses a malformed-JSON failure with three benign non-candidates into one ok=false (#5387 sibling)
records.body:
Sibling of #5387 (landed `547e44b70`) and #5388, in a third package.

`internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:238` — `ArraySplicePoints` returns a bare
`ok bool`, and **four structurally different outcomes collapse into `false`**:

    if len(raw) == 0                              { return ..., false }   // empty input
    if json.Unmarshal(raw, &obj) != nil           { return ..., false }   // MALFORMED JSON
    arrRaw, has := obj[key]; if !has              { return ..., false }   // key absent
    elems, spans, decoded := decodeArrayElements(raw, arrRaw)
    if !decoded || len(elems) == 0                { return ..., false }   // array undecodable / empty
    last := lastToolBreakpoint(elems); if last < 0 { return ..., false }  // no cache_control anchor

Three of those are ordinary **non-candidates**: the key is not present, the array is
empty, nothing carries `cache_control`. Those are the normal shape of a request that
simply is not spliceable, and they are uninteresting.

One of them is a **structural failure**: `json.Unmarshal` rejected the body, or
`decodeArrayElements` could not decode an array the caller believed was there. That means
the input was malformed or the decoder is wrong — a bug signal, not a routine miss.

This is the identical defect #5387 fixed one package over: a structural decode failure
hidden inside a benign no-op verdict, where the caller cannot tell "not applicable" from
"something is broken." The consequence is the same too — a body that fails to parse is
counted as a request that simply had no breakpoint, so a decoder regression shows up as a
quiet drop in splice rate rather than as an error.

## What to do

Give the caller a reason alongside `ok`, following the vocabulary style #5387 established
in `internal/agent` (closed set, registered in every declaration site). At minimum,
separate the malformed-input arm from the not-applicable arms; the three non-candidate
arms may stay merged if no caller distinguishes them, but say so deliberately rather than
by omission.

## Acceptance

- A malformed body and a body with no `cache_control` anchor produce **different**
  observable outcomes at the real call site, not just inside the helper.
- The witness drives an actual caller of `ArraySplicePoints`, so removing the split reds
  the test. A test that calls the helper directly does not establish that any consumer
  benefits — that is the gap #5435 tracks.
- Every declaration site of the new vocabulary is updated together. #5387's own sibling
  drift is already filed separately, so the pattern of registering-in-one-place-only is
  known to recur here.

Not verified: whether any current caller would change behavior on the split, or whether
this is presently latent. Worth establishing first — if no caller can act on the
distinction, the right fix may be an error return used only for observability.

records.title: fix(gateway): observeCompaction books every non-fire as a bail, so the live /metrics compaction rate is still pinned near 1.0 (#5388 sibling)
records.body:
Sibling of #5388, one layer up, in the package that serves live `/metrics`.

`internal/gateway/metrics_observe.go` — `observeCompaction`:

    switch {
    case off:                                    m.compactAttempts["off"]++
    case out.Reason == agent.CompactReasonNone:  m.compactAttempts["fired"]++ ...
    default:
        m.compactAttempts["bailed"]++            // <- every non-fire, unconditionally
        m.compactBailReasons[out.Reason]++
    }

The `default` arm books **every** non-fired outcome as a bail, including the four that
were never compaction *candidates* — `too_few_msgs`, `non_json`, `no_messages_key`,
`decode_failed`. Those are decided at the eligibility gate before any compactible span
exists, so counting them as declines says nothing about compaction health, and because
they dominate mixed traffic they pin the derived rate near 1.0. A rate that always reads
~1.0 cannot be alerted on.

This is the same defect #5388 just fixed in `internal/gatewayusageledger`, but that fix
cured only the **ledger fold**. The in-process exposition served from here is still
pinned, so a dashboard reading live `/metrics` sees the uninformative number while the
ledger-derived view sees the corrected one — the two now disagree, which is its own
reason to close this promptly.

## Why the fix is cleaner here than it was in the ledger

`internal/gatewayusageledger` is tier 1 and cannot import `internal/agent`, so its
partition is coupled to the reason vocabulary **by convention**: a future reason silently
reads as a candidate (safe direction, but not enforced). `internal/gateway` already
imports `agent` — the `agent.CompactReasonNone` comparison above is right there — so the
partition can be expressed against the real constants and a new reason can be made to
fail the build or a test rather than be silently absorbed. Take that option; it is the
compiler-checked version of what #5388 could only document.

## Acceptance

- Non-candidate outcomes stop incrementing the denominator the alertable rate divides by.
  Keep the existing `bailed` counter's meaning for continuity and add the candidate-only
  series alongside, as #5388 did, rather than redefining a live gauge underneath running
  dashboards.
- Unknown/unrecognised reasons fail **open** to candidate, so the rate can only read
  conservatively high — never silently understate a real problem.
- A witness driving `observeCompaction` with a mixed population where the old rate cannot
  separate a healthy cell from a broken one and the new rate can. #5388's fixture is a
  working model: two cells carrying the same non-candidate flood read 0.9474 vs 0.9989
  old (unseparable) and 0.0000 vs 0.9800 new.
- Adding a new reason without classifying it reds a test.

`metrics_observe.go` was clean of peer edits at filing time, though `internal/gateway` as
a whole had active concurrent work — re-check `git status` for the package before
starting.

Related: #5441 (the rendered HELP for these same reasons declares a closed set of 9 while
the emitters produce 11).

records.title: feat(skill): one-way ratchet on the resident skill-description floor — #3234 measured it, then it grew 30% in 20 days (epic #3229)
records.body:
Part of epic **#3229** (shrink the always-sent token floor). Follow-on to **#3234**, which
shipped the *measurement* and closed — after which the thing the measurement exists to
prevent happened.

## The regression, in the tool of record's own numbers

`#3234` landed `fak skill footprint` in `a37b4f4fff` (2026-07-08) and closed. Its body pinned
the measured baseline at **47 skills · 36,237 B** of resident `description` frontmatter.

Today (2026-07-28), the same verb reports:

```
$ fak skill footprint --top 8
skill footprint [interactive]: 58 skill(s); resident floor = 47236 bytes (~11809 tokens);
  description floor = 47236 B; name-only floor = 787 B; at-rest card floor = 51409 bytes
   1. study-repo               desc= 1877 B
   2. resume-watchdog-audit    desc= 1599 B
   3. scout-loop               desc= 1471 B
   4. super-loop               desc= 1359 B
   5. field-borrow             desc= 1332 B
   6. trajectory-control       desc= 1270 B
   7. disambiguation-score     desc= 1231 B
   8. stability-score          desc= 1223 B
```

| | #3234 landed (2026-07-08) | HEAD (2026-07-28) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | 47 | 58 | +11 |
| resident description floor | 36,237 B | **47,236 B** | **+10,999 B / +30.4%** |
| est. tokens (4 B/tok) | ~9,059 | **~11,809** | **+2,750** |

**Twenty days, +30.4%, entirely unopposed.** `name-only floor = 787 B` shows the size of the
headroom: 46.4 kB of the 47.2 kB resident floor is description prose.

## Why it happened: the userland half of the epic got a scorecard and no gate

The MCP half of this same epic has **two** one-way ratchets; the userland half has none.

| | measurement | growth gate | banked-win gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| MCP tool schemas | `fak footprint` (#3230) | `floorgate.go` — `FLOOR_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` | `FLOOR_BUDGET_STALE` |
| MCP descriptions | same | `descbudget.go` — `DESC_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` | `DESC_BUDGET_STALE` |
| **`.claude/skills` descriptions** | **`fak skill footprint` (#3234)** | **none** | **none** |

`internal/mcpfootprint/floorgate.go:20-26` states the failure mode this issue is reporting,
in advance:

> A BANKED WIN is required (FLOOR_BUDGET_STALE). [...] Otherwise the slack silently becomes
> headroom for future bloat and the ratchet stops ratcheting.

That is exactly what the table above records. Measurement without refusal is taste, and taste
lost 30% in three weeks.

## Compounding: #3234 closed with 1 of its 3 in-scope items delivered

`git show a37b4f4fff --numstat` is 3 files, +185 lines, all scorecard:

```
7    0  cmd/fak/skill.go
121  0  cmd/fak/skill_footprint.go
57   0  cmd/fak/skill_test.go
```

#3234's in-scope items **2** ("split the at-rest card from the faulted body") and **3** (the
userland migration of the heaviest descriptions) never landed. `internal/capindex/skill_resolver.go:87,99`
still copies the **whole** `description` into both the at-rest `CardBytes` and the ranking `Trigger`:

```go
cardBytes, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
    "name":        e.name,
    "version":     e.fm.version,
    "description": e.fm.description,   // :87 — the full prose, not a one-line intent
    ...
})
...
Trigger:   e.fm.description,           // :99
```

So the "name+one-line-intent" index #3234 promised does not exist, and nothing stops the next
skill from adding another 1.9 kB.

## Step 0 — confirm the residency premise before pinning the number

#3234 asserts the harness renders each `SKILL.md` `description` into always-resident context.
That should be re-confirmed against the current harness before a ceiling is pinned to it:
in this session's skill listing, **project skills appear as bare names while built-in skills
carry full descriptions**, which would mean the 47,236 B is fak's *model* of the resident floor
rather than bytes currently on the wire. The ratchet is worth landing either way — it is fak's
own committed scorecard and #3234's own done-condition — but the issue must not overclaim a
provider-billed saving it has not witnessed (Law A2: every value carries its provenance).

## In scope

1. **`SkillDescriptionBudgetBytes`** — a committed ceiling in a new `internal/skillfootprint`
   (or alongside `cmd/fak/skill_footprint.go`), pinned at the measured HEAD floor, mirroring
   `descbudget.go:DescriptionBudgetTokens` exactly: raising it is the reviewable diff line that
   binds the new tax to the change that caused it.
2. **The two-sided ratchet**, mirroring `descbudget.go`:
   - growth → `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`
   - slack after a trim → `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_STALE` (re-pin down or stay red)
3. **Register both refusal tokens in `dos.toml [reasons]`** with the structural drift gate
   (#3980's rule), so they are not free-text.
4. **A test that enforces it** over the real `.claude/skills` tree — the userland analog of
   `internal/mcpfootprint.TestRealFakMCPFloor`.
5. **A committed baseline doc** `docs/context-budget/skill-description-floor.md`, the sibling of
   `docs/context-budget/mcp-tool-floor.md`, carrying the number + provenance + regeneration command.

## Out of scope

- The `capindex` card split and the userland description migration — those are #3234's undelivered
  items 2 and 3 and deserve their own issue; **this one only stops the bleeding.** A ratchet pinned
  at today's floor is what makes that later trim a *bankable* win instead of headroom.
- The systemic MCP/built-in tool slices (#3231 / #3232) — already gated.
- Body payload compression (#3064 / #3204) — different axis.

## Done condition

- Adding a skill whose `description` pushes the sum past the pin reds the gate with
  `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`, and the only way through is raising the constant in the same commit.
- Trimming materially below the pin reds `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_STALE` until the ceiling is re-pinned down.
- `docs/context-budget/skill-description-floor.md` carries the measured number with its estimator
  provenance and the exact command that regenerates it.

## Witness

- `fak skill footprint --json` before/after, plus a test transcript showing a deliberately fattened
  fixture description refused with `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` and a trimmed one refused with
  `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_STALE`.
- `dos_check_reason` resolving both new tokens against `dos.toml`.

records.title: feat(context-budget): AGENTS.md is a ~16.7k-token per-agent floor invisible to fak footprint — serve its 25 kB refusal cookbook by query (epic #3229)
records.body:
Part of epic **#3229** (shrink the always-sent token floor).

## The slice the epic's own floor table misses

#3229 opens with a `/context` breakdown of what a fresh session pays before any work, and
prices the userland row as:

| Slice | Tokens | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Memory / CLAUDE.md | 0.4k (0.2%) | user (**already lean**) |

`CLAUDE.md` *is* lean — 2,227 B. But its third line is an instruction:

> Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) first for workspace-wide guidance.

`AGENTS.md` is **66,904 B ≈ 16,726 est. tokens** (4 B/tok, the same house estimator
`agent.RequestFootprint` uses). Every agent that obeys that instruction pays it as a turn-1
`Read`. It is therefore a **floor in effect but not in form**: because it is *pulled by an
instruction* rather than *resident in the system prompt*, it shows up in neither `/context`
nor `fak footprint` — the two surfaces this epic built to make the floor visible.

It is larger than every gated slice it sits beside:

| Slice | est. tokens | gated? |
|---|---|---|
| **AGENTS.md (turn-1 Read)** | **~16,726** | **no — and unmeasured** |
| `.claude/skills` resident descriptions | ~11,809 | no (see #5444) |
| fak MCP tool schemas | 5,888 | yes — `floorgate.go` |
| ‣ of which description prose | 1,966 | yes — `descbudget.go` |

The epic ratchets the 5,888 and misses the 16,726.

## Where the bytes are

```
66,904 B  AGENTS.md (12 top-level sections)
 42,677 B   ## Hard rules (these WILL bite an agent…)          64% of file
  25,010 B    ### If the kernel refuses you (recover, don't fight it)   37% of file
  5,370 B   ## Build / test / run
  4,401 B   ## New work defaults: spine first, then fan out
  2,774 B   ## Planning: two kinds of work
  … 7 more sections, all < 2.1 kB
```

One subsection — `### If the kernel refuses you` — is **25,010 B (~6,250 est. tok), 37% of the
whole file**. It is a flat cookbook: **zero `####` subheadings, 95 distinct refusal tokens**.
An agent that trips `BARE_COMMIT_SWEEP` needs one entry and reads ninety-five.

## It duplicates a store that is already machine-queryable

The recovery vocabulary already has a structured home, and fak already ships the readers:

- `dos.toml` carries **68 `[reasons…]` sections**.
- `dos_check_reason` and `dos_refuse_reasons` serve them over MCP today.
- #3980 exists precisely to register every fak-emitted refusal token there with a structural
  drift gate.

Measured overlap between the cookbook's tokens and `dos.toml`:

```
AGENTS.md refusal tokens in that section : 95
  also present in dos.toml               : 80  (84%)
  not present in dos.toml                : 15
```

**84% of the 25 kB is prose duplicating a store that is already queryable by token.** This is the
exact anti-pattern the epic's thesis names — *"do the shared setup once; query, don't survey"* —
applied against the repo's own contributor doc.

## Why this matters more under ultracode than the numbers suggest

`fak footprint` and `/context` both price **one** context. An ultracode/`Workflow` run pays the
per-agent floor **once per subagent**, so the bill is `floor × N`. At the medium workflow
guideline (≤15 agents), the AGENTS.md turn-1 Read alone is **~250k tokens** of fan-out tax, of
which ~94k is a refusal cookbook nobody reads 99% of. (The general fan-out axis is worth its own
issue; this one is about the single largest term in it.)

## In scope

1. **Measure it.** Extend the `docs/context-budget/` family with `agents-md-floor.md`: the
   per-section byte/token inventory above, with provenance and a regeneration command. The
   *instruction-pulled* floor is a distinct, currently-unnamed category from the *resident* floor —
   name it, so it stops being invisible to both existing surfaces.
2. **Serve the cookbook by query.** Replace the 25,010 B inline section with a short pointer
   ("you were refused `X` → `fak refuse explain X`, or `dos_check_reason`") plus the handful of
   rules that must be known *before* a refusal happens rather than after. Recovery text moves into
   the `dos.toml [reasons]` records that already exist for 80 of the 95 tokens; the remaining 15
   get registered (which #3980 wants anyway).
3. **Backfill the 15 unregistered tokens** into `dos.toml [reasons]` — an independent win for
   #3980's drift gate regardless of what happens to AGENTS.md.

## Out of scope

- A ratchet on AGENTS.md bytes. Worth doing, but pin the number only after the trim — pinning a
  ceiling at today's bloated floor banks the bloat (the `FLOOR_BUDGET_STALE` lesson in
  `internal/mcpfootprint/floorgate.go:20-26`).
- The `.claude/skills` description floor — that is #5444.
- The systemic MCP/built-in tool slices — #3231 / #3232, already gated.

## Risks to check before trimming

- **Do not trade context for round-trips.** If an agent must now make 3 extra tool calls to
  recover from a routine refusal, the lever loses. Mitigation: keep the *most frequent* refusals
  (the commit-lane family) inline and page out the long tail. Rank by observed refusal frequency
  before choosing the cut line, rather than by byte size.
- **Structural gates pin doc layout.** This repo reds on `INDEX_SYNC`, `CONCEPT_FRESHNESS`,
  frozen `File:`-pinned path inventories, and the `llms-full` mirror. A restructure of AGENTS.md
  must be checked against all of them first.
- **AGENTS.md is the contract.** Anything moved must stay reachable in one obvious hop; the goal
  is relocating reference material, never dropping a rule.

## Done condition

- `docs/context-budget/agents-md-floor.md` carries the measured per-section inventory with
  estimator provenance and a regeneration command.
- The refusal-recovery cookbook is reachable by token through an existing queryable surface, and
  AGENTS.md links to it instead of inlining it.
- All 95 tokens resolve via `dos_check_reason` (up from 80).

## Witness

- Before/after byte counts for AGENTS.md and for the section, from the regeneration command.
- A transcript showing recovery-by-token for a refusal whose text now lives only in the store.
- A green `make ci` proving no structural doc gate reds on the restructure.

records.title: fix(promptmmu+gateway): the system[] prune reports a structural splice failure as benign, and the gateway discards its result entirely (#5442 sibling)
records.body:
`CompactInboundTools` and `CompactInboundSystem` are documented twins ("the system[]
twin of CompactInboundTools", `internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:33`). #5442 split the
structural-vs-benign reasons on the tools side of the house. The system side still
collapses them — and, separately, the gateway throws away everything the system path
produces, so the split would be unobservable if made alone. Both halves are needed or
this lands as another helper nothing consumes.

## 1. The spine collapses a structural failure into the benign reason

`internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:45-48`:

```go
elems, spans, ok := decodeArrayElements(raw, systemRaw)
if !ok || len(elems) == 0 {
	return identity(raw, SkipNoSystem)
}
```

`!ok` means "the system[] element spans could not be recovered exactly" — the splice
machinery failed on a value that *is* an array. `len(elems) == 0` means the array was
simply empty. These are not the same event, and the tools twin already separates them
(`internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:158-164`):

```go
elems, spans, ok := decodeArrayElements(raw, toolsRaw)
if !ok {
	return identity(raw, SkipUndecodableTools)   // structural
}
if len(elems) == 0 {
	return identity(raw, SkipNoTools)            // benign
}
```

There is no `SkipUndecodableSystem` in the closed reason set at
`internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:10-20`. So an undecodable `system[]` is reported as
`no-system` — "no system[] array, or system is a bare string" per its own doc comment,
which is a *false* description of what happened. That is precisely the false-benign
reading #5442 and #5387 filed.

It matters beyond legibility: `ExplainToolSchemaStrategy`
(`internal/promptmmu/config.go:136-141`) routes the structural reasons to the defensive
`ToolSchemaMask` strategy —

```go
case SkipNoBreakpoint, SkipNothingAfter, SkipUndecodableTools, SkipSpliceUnproven:
	dec.Strategy = ToolSchemaMask
```

— and a system-side structural failure, reported as `SkipNoSystem`, is not in that set.
It falls through to `ToolSchemaUnchanged`, the "nothing needed doing" verdict.

## 2. The gateway consumer discards the system path's output entirely

This is why a reason-split alone would be unobservable. Compare the two call sites,
adjacent lines in `internal/gateway/messages_transform.go`:

```go
s.recordInboundPrunedToolDefinitions(reqTrace, s.maybeCompactInboundTools(req))  // :133
s.maybeCompactInboundSystem(req)                                                 // :134
```

Line 134 drops the return value. `maybeCompactInboundSystem`
(`internal/gateway/messages.go:1114-1136`) carefully builds a qualified name list —
`pruned = append(pruned, plan.Block+":"+name)` at :1132 — and nothing reads it.

And inside the loop, `internal/gateway/messages.go:1127`:

```go
if !res.Changed {
	continue
}
```

The `SkipReason` is dropped on the floor. The tools path does not do this: it builds a
`ToolSchemaDecision` (`messages.go:1071`), logs it via `logInboundToolSchemaDecision`
(:1073, :1083), and counts the prune via `s.metrics.observeInboundToolPrune`
(:1082, `internal/gateway/metrics_observe.go:383-389`).

There is no `observeInboundSystemPrune` anywhere in `internal/gateway`. So today a turn
that pruned three system blocks and a turn that pruned zero because the splice machinery
failed are indistinguishable from outside the process — no metric, no log line, no skip
reason. That is the same is-our-thing-ENABLED-and-USED gap #1089 covers, and the same
ships-unwired shape #5435 tracks.

## Acceptance

Both halves, in one change, or it is a helper with no consumer:

1. Add `SkipUndecodableSystem` to the closed set and split
   `internal/promptmmu/promptmmu.go:45-48` the way :158-164 already splits. Include it
   in the `ExplainToolSchemaStrategy` mask case at `config.go:137` alongside
   `SkipUndecodableTools`, since it means exactly the same thing: not safe to cut.
2. Give the system path the legibility the tools path already has — the returned
   `pruned` names consumed at `messages_transform.go:134` rather than discarded, and a
   witnessed prune count on `/metrics`. Whatever shape it takes, an operator must be
   able to tell "pruned nothing because there was no system array" from "pruned nothing
   because the splice machinery could not recover the spans".
3. A gateway-level witness driving the real `maybeCompactInboundSystem` seam with a
   body whose `system` value opens with `[` and still fails to decode, asserting the
   structural reason reaches the observable surface. A promptmmu-only unit test does not
   discharge this — that is the consumer-less shape this ticket exists to avoid.

## Provenance

Found while verifying #5442's landed fix. Every file/line reference above was read at
the HEAD that carries `0f9512c4b`.

Refs #5442, #5387, #5435, #1089

records.title: epic(docs): make fak legible and usable to people who do not already work on fak
records.body:
# Epic: make fak legible and usable to people who do not already work on fak

## Why

Every reader-facing surface in this repository was written by people who already have the
shared checkout, the tailnet, the internal box names, and the fleet vocabulary. That is
invisible from the inside and immediately blocking from the outside.

Concrete, verified examples from the current tip:

- **The contributor route cannot be followed without write access.** `CONTRIBUTING.md`
  documents commit-to-`main` only and never says *fork* or *pull request*, while
  `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` clearly expects PRs.
- **The advertised newcomer on-ramp is empty.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the PR template both
  route new contributors to the `good first issue` label. That label has **0** open issues
  against **5446** open issues total.
- **The Mac showcase only works for us.** `README.md` bills `fak mac` as a one-command
  showcase; `docs/fak/mac-agent-ui.md` opens with "Use this when `node-macos-a` is already
  running the always-on Qwen3.6 stack" and depends on our launchd labels, our tailnet host,
  and an SSH key named `id_ed25519_prod_to_laptop`. There is no zero-to-working path.
- **The front-page proof is a hidden dev verb.** `README.md` leads with `fak agent --offline`,
  but `fak agent` is absent from `fak help` and `fak help agent` prints `fak dev agent — …`.
- **The corpus is enormous and unranked for a newcomer.** 31 tracked markdown files at the
  repository root and 1219 under `docs/`, with at least five documents competing to be the
  entry point (`README.md`, `START-HERE.md`, `GETTING-STARTED.md`, `LEARNING-PATH.md`,
  `INDEX.md`).
- **There is nowhere to ask a question.** GitHub Discussions is disabled and
  `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` declares no `contact_links`.

## Scope

Children of this epic each fix one specific newcomer-blocking surface. The standard for a
child is: *a competent person who has never seen this repository can follow the surface end
to end and reach the stated result, without needing our hosts, our checkout, or our
vocabulary.*

Work is grouped as:

1. Contributor path — fork/PR route, scoping the internal fleet contract, a real
   good-first-issue queue, a place to ask questions.
2. The Mac / local-model showcase — a genuine zero-to-working path, and honest framing of
   what `fak mac` requires.
3. Entry-point sprawl — one obvious front door, internal governance docs demoted out of the
   newcomer path.
4. CLI first contact — `fak help` matching what the README tells people to run.
5. Accuracy defects a cold reader actually hits.

## Non-goals

Not a rewrite of the technical documentation, and not a change to the internal fleet rules
themselves — those rules stay, they just need to be *scoped* as internal rather than
presented as the only path.

records.title: docs(contributing): the advertised good-first-issue on-ramp has zero open issues
records.body:
## Problem

`CONTRIBUTING.md` names the `good first issue` label as the primary on-ramp twice — in
"New here and want a bounded first change?" and again under "Good first issues — where to
start" — and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` welcomes first-time PRs.

That label currently has **0 open issues**, against **5446 open issues** in the repository:

```
gh issue list --repo anthony-chaudhary/fak --label "good first issue" --state open --jq length
# 0
```

So the single most-advertised path for a new contributor dead-ends on an empty list. With
5446 open issues there is no shortage of candidate work — it has simply never been triaged
for newcomer suitability.

## Likely files

- `docs/adoption/good-first-tasks.md` — the standing on-ramp list that exists but is not a live queue
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the section pointing at the label

## Expected steps

1 Triage a first batch of genuinely bounded, self-contained issues and apply the
  `good first issue` label — target at least 10 so the list is not empty again after two
  contributors.
2 For each, ensure the body states the file to touch, the expected result, and how to verify,
  without requiring the shared checkout or fleet tooling.
3 Add a short maintainer note on keeping the queue non-empty.

## Acceptance

`gh issue list --label "good first issue" --state open` returns a non-empty list of issues an
outside contributor can complete with a fork and a PR.

## Batch policy

Not a bulk sweep: one specific, reproducible newcomer-blocking defect, filed once with
verified evidence.

## Parent context

Child of the public-onboarding epic #5447.

## Work estimate
Estimate: 3 points. Uncertainty: operator-supplied estimate; revise through the parent denominator when evidence changes.

## Overall completion contribution
Contribution: 3/100 points.

records.title: docs(contributing): PR template asks outside contributors for internal lane trailers they cannot resolve
records.body:
## Problem

`.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` presents a "Ship-discipline checklist" that every PR
author is asked to satisfy. Two of its items are internal fleet mechanics that an outside
contributor has no way to satisfy or even decode:

- "Conventional-Commits subject ending in a `(fak <leaf>)` stamp" — the leaf names are the
  `[lanes]` in `dos.toml`, an internal dispatch config. Nothing reader-facing explains
  which leaf a given diff belongs to.
- "Staged by explicit path (`git commit -s -- <paths>`, never `git add -A`)" — this rule
  exists because *our* checkout is a shared multi-session tree. In a contributor's own fork
  it is meaningless.

The template's own header is welcoming ("First PR? Welcome — don't sweat the checklist"),
which makes the mismatch more confusing rather than less: the reader is told both to relax
and to satisfy five unexplained gates.

## Likely files

- `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` — split contributor-facing from maintainer-facing items
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the authority the template defers to

## Expected steps

1 Reduce the contributor-facing checklist to what an outside PR author can actually do:
  DCO sign-off, a description, and evidence that a relevant check was run.
2 Move the lane-trailer and explicit-path items into a clearly-marked maintainer/in-repo-agent
  section, stating they apply to direct-to-trunk commits, not forked PRs.
3 If the `(fak <leaf>)` stamp is genuinely required on squash-merge, say so and explain how a
  maintainer applies it, rather than asking the contributor to guess.

A first-time external contributor can complete every unchecked box in the contributor section

records.title: docs(contributing): scope trunk-guard and ci-preflight setup steps to maintainers, not first-time contributors
records.body:
## Problem

`CONTRIBUTING.md` "Set up and verify the checkout" presents four numbered steps as the
required path, several of which assume maintainer context:

- Step 1 requires `python tools/install_trunk_guard.py` to arm the trunk guard and
  public-leak scan. The trunk guard exists to police direct commits to `main` in the shared
  tree; it has no function in a contributor's fork, but the guide presents installing it as
  mandatory setup.
- Step 4 makes `fak ci-preflight` a "**required committed-tip gate**" run "after the
  explicit-path commit and before push" — a sequence that only exists if you are pushing to
  this repository's `main`.
- Step 3 makes `make ci` "the required pre-commit green gate", with no statement of how long
  it takes or that CI will also run it, so a newcomer cannot tell whether a focused package
  test is acceptable for a small PR.

The net effect is a setup list that reads as heavyweight and partly inapplicable, with no
signal about which parts a first-time contributor genuinely needs.

## Likely files

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the setup and workflow sections
- `docs/dev-tooling.md` — where build-profile detail already lives

## Expected steps

1 Mark each setup step with who it applies to: everyone, or maintainers/in-repo agents only.
2 Give a minimal contributor path — clone the fork, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, run the
  tests for the package you touched — and say plainly that CI runs the full gate on the PR.
3 Keep the full internal gate sequence, but under a heading that scopes it to direct-to-trunk work.
4 State the approximate runtime of `make ci` so a reader can plan.

## Acceptance

A newcomer can identify, in under a minute, the shortest set of checks their PR needs, and is
not told to install a guard that governs a tree they do not have.

## Batch policy

Not a bulk sweep: one specific, reproducible newcomer-blocking defect, filed once with
verified evidence.

Child of the public-onboarding epic #5447.

records.title: docs(contributing): Windows test command uses a .\fak\ path that only resolves from outside the clone
records.body:
## Problem

`CONTRIBUTING.md` tells Windows contributors:

> **Tests run through WSL, not native Windows** — `.\fak\test.ps1` (whole suite) or
> `.\fak\test.ps1 ./internal/<pkg>/`.

The path `.\fak\test.ps1` only resolves from the *parent* of the clone — it is the shape of

is `.\test.ps1`.

`GETTING-STARTED.md` gets this right (`./test.ps1`), so the two documents disagree.

## Likely files

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the Windows testing bullet
- `GETTING-STARTED.md` — already correct; use as the reference

1 Correct the paths to `.\test.ps1` and `.\test.ps1 ./internal/<pkg>/`, relative to the
  repository root the same document already tells the reader to work from.
2 Sweep `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `AGENTS.md` for other `.\fak\`-prefixed paths that assume the
  parent-directory workspace layout.

## Acceptance

Every command in `CONTRIBUTING.md` runs as written from the repository root of a fresh clone.

records.title: docs(github): no route for questions — Discussions disabled and issue chooser has no contact links
records.body:
## Problem

A newcomer with a *question* — not a bug — has nowhere to go.

- GitHub Discussions is disabled (`hasDiscussionsEnabled: false`).
- `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` is a single line, `blank_issues_enabled: true`, with
  no `contact_links` block. So the "New issue" chooser offers only bug report, feature
  request, and three internal fixture templates, with no route to docs, security, or Q&A.
- `SECURITY.md` correctly asks for private reporting, but nothing in the issue chooser tells
  a reporter that before they open a public issue.

The practical result is that usage questions land as bug reports, or are not asked at all —
and the repository loses the earliest and cheapest signal about what confuses new users.

## Likely files

- `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` — add `contact_links`
- `README.md` — surface where to ask

## Expected steps

1 Add `contact_links` to the issue chooser pointing at: the documentation front door, the
  private security-reporting route in `SECURITY.md`, and a question venue.
2 Decide the question venue — enabling GitHub Discussions is the low-cost option; otherwise
  designate a labelled "question" issue type and say so.
3 Add a one-line "Questions / support" pointer near the end of `README.md`.

## Acceptance

From the "New issue" chooser, a newcomer can see where to ask a usage question and where to
report a vulnerability privately, without opening a misfiled public issue.

## Problem

`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yml` is well-written, but its worked example is drawn

```
placeholder: "Example: \`fak commit --path docs/x.md -m \\"...\\"\` refused with PATHSPEC_RACE
even though the tree was clean."
```

`fak commit` is one of the 241 dev/repo verbs used to develop *this repository*;
`PATHSPEC_RACE` is a shared-checkout refusal. An external user who installed the binary to

friendly intent.

gives `fak v0.9.3` as the example, while the current release is 0.41.0.

1 Replace the reproduction placeholder with a product-path example, e.g. a `fak guard` or
  `fak serve` invocation and the unexpected verdict or error it produced.
2 Refresh the version placeholder to a current release string.
3 Review the other issue templates for internal-only vocabulary in reader-facing text.

Every example in the public issue templates uses a command an external user of the released
binary could plausibly have run.

records.title: docs(mac): the flagship Mac showcase walkthrough assumes our internal always-on gateway and has no zero-to-working path
records.body:
## Problem

`docs/fak/mac-agent-ui.md` is presented in `README.md` as the walkthrough for the flagship

records.title: feat(wipref): C8 — refs/fak/wip/* fleet visibility: ride git fetch/push like leaseref, plus a garden-tick class
records.body:
## Parent context

Child **C8** of epic #3871, which specifies it as:

> **C8** — `refs/fak/wip/*` fleet visibility: the WIP refs ride `git fetch`/`push` like leaseref;
> `fak wip status --fleet` folds a peer host's crashed-session WIP.

Filing it as its own issue — the roadmap line exists but I could not find a child issue for it, and
#3873 (C1) explicitly lists "fleet sync (C8)" as out of its scope, so the durability work that
*has* landed is local-only by design rather than by omission. This adds field evidence for
prioritising it, plus two things the roadmap line does not cover (§3, §4).

## 1. Current state: the sibling namespaces have diverged exactly where C8 would close the gap

`cmd/fak/wip.go:5` calls the checkpoint ref "a sibling of the lease refs, `refs/fak/locks/*`", and
#3873 sets the goal as "a robust ref namespace **on par with leaseref**". Measured against that bar:

| | `refs/fak/locks/*` (leases) | `refs/fak/wip/*` (checkpoints) |
|---|---|---|
| replication engine | `internal/leaseref/sync.go:90` — `Sync(ctx, remote, doPush, doFetch)`, push-then-fetch with a documented ordering rationale | **none** |
| publish path | `cmd/fak/leasewrite_endpoint.go:121` — `publishAcceptedLease` pushes the namespace to origin | **none** |
| operator verb | `cmd/fak/leaseref.go:202` — "CONVERGE the `refs/fak/locks/*` namespace with a remote (default origin)" | **none** |
| expiry delete-push | `internal/leaseref/drain.go:15,109` — one-sided `:refs/fak/locks/session-<id>` refspec | **none** |
| periodic tending | `cmd/fak/garden.go:129-131` — "stale_leases (expired `refs/fak/locks/*`) → reap the expired records in-process" | **none** |

Two greps state the position precisely:

```
grep -rn "refs/fak/wip" --include="*.go" .        ->  35 hits
  ... of those, co-occurring with "push"          ->   0 hits
grep -rlin "wip" cmd/fak/garden*.go               ->  (no files)
```

The only `push` in `cmd/fak/wip.go` is `wip land --push` (`cmd/fak/wip.go:1250`, "push after a
verified commit"): it pushes the resulting **commit** once `land` has materialised and committed the
delta. That is the success path, not replication of the checkpoint, and it is unavailable in exactly
the case that motivates C8 — when the delta *cannot* be landed yet.

Net effect today: the ephemeral thing is durable across machines, the valuable thing is not. A lease
is worthless the moment its session dies and it is engineered to survive; the uncommitted delta is
reachable from no branch and lives on exactly one disk. Epic #3871's own thesis names this — "the one
thing no durable store holds is the actual code a session wrote but has not committed" — and C8 is
the last step of it.

## 2. The hazard model already assumes these refs are on a remote

`internal/gitgate/gitgate.go:164-169` refuses `git push --prune` because it was "the converge that
emptied the fleet's `refs/fak/locks/*` **and `refs/fak/wip/*`** from a stale clone (#5360)", and the
deny text warns it "mass-deletes peers' branches, lock leases, **and WIP checkpoint refs**". #5360
puts that at ~8400 lock/wip refs. So a shipped guard already protects remote wip refs that no shipped
path publishes — C8 is the half that makes the guard's premise true.

## 3. Not in the C8 line: the garden tick has no wip class

`fak garden tick` already reaps five classes — `reaped_leases`, `reaped_sessions`,
`reaped_lock_files`, `reaped_intents`, `reaped_growth_logs` (`cmd/fak/garden.go:199-203`) — including
the sibling lease namespace in-process. The checkpoint namespace is absent from all of them. C8 as
written covers `fetch`/`push` and `status --fleet`; **replicated refs also need tending on a clock**,
or fleet visibility turns a local-only pile into a shared one. Worth folding into C8's scope or
splitting out.

## 4. Not in the C8 line: in C8's absence, a workaround convention grows

In one private fleet repo I can only describe in aggregate, an ad-hoc parking convention — a commit
parented on trunk, pushed to a ref outside `refs/heads/` so neither a branch nor a lease is involved —
has accumulated **528 refs on the shared remote** (40 under `refs/hold/*`, 488 under
`refs/tags/hold/*`). No `fak` verb creates, lists, lands, or ages one; each is hand-built from
`write-tree` / `commit-tree` / `git tag` plumbing.

I built one of those myself, before finding `fak wip` — which is the report worth having here. The two
mechanisms have exactly complementary holes: `wip` has the lifecycle (`checkpoint` / `status` /
`restore` / `land` / `attribute` / `blocked` / `sweep-guard` / `reconcile` / `selfcheck`) and no
durability past the disk; the ad-hoc route has durability and no lifecycle at all. An agent needing
both picks by whichever gap it notices first, and the one it notices is *durability*, because that is
the one that loses work. So the cost of C8 staying open is not only unreplicated refs — it is a second
convention accreting outside the tool's lifecycle entirely.

That count is one repo's snapshot and nothing in the ask depends on it; the reproducible part is §1.

## Done condition

- `refs/fak/wip/*` rides `git fetch` / `push` on an opt-in basis, reusing the `leaseref.Sync` shape
  rather than a new ref writer (per #3873's "reuse that discipline" constraint).
- `fak wip status` distinguishes **replicated** from **local-only**. Today "checkpointed" and "safe"
  are the same word, and that is the part that bites: the failure `autocheckpoint` (C5) protects
  against — *this session is about to die* — is correlated with the one it does not — *this checkout or
  machine goes away* — and a compaction boundary is precisely when you cannot tell which you are at.
- `fak wip status --fleet` folds a peer host's crashed-session WIP (the epic's wording).
- A wip class in the garden tick, so replicated refs are tended on the same clock as the sibling (§3).

Opt-in rather than default for the push: replicating a dirty working tree off-machine is a real
privacy and bandwidth decision an operator should make deliberately, not inherit.

## Related

#3871 (epic, C8), #3873 (C1 — local durability, fleet sync out of scope), #5340 (the collection half
of retention), #5336 (read-path scaling), #5360 (the prune loophole that deleted wip refs), #5337
(`--file-ticket`). Filed separately: the RECLAIM recovery driver, and a one-line
`fak recover COLLISION_RISK` wording fix (`cmd/fak/recover.go:210-219`).

records.title: feat(wip): RECLAIM decays into QUARANTINE by construction — the recovery half of wip reconcile has no driver (complement to #5340)
records.body:
## RECLAIM decays into QUARANTINE by construction, and the recovery half of `wip reconcile` has no driver — the complement to #5340

## Parent context

Epic #3871 ships both halves of recovery as separate children, and both have landed:

- **C3** — orphan reconciliation, the closed vocab `RECLAIM | QUARANTINE | DISCARD_WITNESSED`. The
  *classifier*.
- **C4** — `fak wip land <session>` drives a restored delta to a stamped commit. The *lander*.

What no child covers is the thing that **connects them**: nothing runs the classifier and hands its
RECLAIM rows to the lander while they are still RECLAIM. The classifier is advisory ("prints
decisions, mutates nothing", `cmd/fak/wip.go:150`) and the lander is per-session and manual. So the
pipeline is complete except for the pump, and §1 is why that specific gap has a deadline the rest of
the epic does not.

**Scope, so this is not read as a duplicate.** #5340 fixes *collection*: making `reap` able to delete
dead-session checkpoints whose deltas are subsumed or empty. It deliberately routes the rest to KEEP,
and says so in its own words:

> A non-empty, unlanded, still-recoverable delta from a dead session is `OwnerClosedDirty` → KEEP
> (that is exactly what `wip restore` / `reconcile --file-ticket` exist to recover).

That is the right call. This issue is about the sentence's second half: **nothing drives that
recovery.** #5340 makes the store stop growing; it does not make the kept work land. Those are
different asks, and the recovery one has a deadline the collection one does not.

### 1. RECLAIM is a decaying state — from the classifier's own definition

`internal/wiprecon/recon.go:44-49`:

```go
type Candidate struct {
	Session string
	Owner   Owner
	Landed  bool // the delta is already present in HEAD (git-witnessed)
	Applies bool // the delta applies cleanly to the current working tree (git apply --check)
}
```

`recon.go:60-72` folds it: crashed + `Landed` → `DISCARD_WITNESSED`, crashed + `Applies` → `RECLAIM`,
else → `QUARANTINE`. The discriminator is `cmd/fak/wip.go:1061`.

`Applies` is `git apply --check` against **the current working tree**. So a fixed checkpoint's verdict
is a function of a tree that keeps moving: the same ref is RECLAIM early and QUARANTINE later with no
change to the ref itself. That is decay in the classifier's own terms — not something I inferred from a
before/after observation. The tool only ever reports a snapshot verdict, never a transition, which is
part of the problem: the expiry is invisible.

Because capture is automatic and instant (`autocheckpoint` at every risky boundary) while triage is
manual and eventual, the race is lost by default. In one private fleet repo, `reconcile` returned
**131 QUARANTINE to 2 RECLAIM**. By the time anyone looks, the cheap window has shut on essentially
everything.

Two honest qualifications: `git apply --check` failure includes plain *file already exists* collisions
from independent parallel creation, not only line-level conflicts, so "conflicts" is a gloss; and at
least one ref in that count is not a normal crashed-session checkpoint.

### 2. "Garbage collection" is the wrong frame for what is in the store

Same repo, read-only forms only:

```
fak wip reap --census --json  ->  total 134  landed 0  live 0
                                  closed_clean_estimate 1
                                  closed_dirty_recoverable 133  unknown 0
```

`landed: 0`, `unknown: 0`, `closed_dirty_recoverable: 133`. **There is no garbage in this store.**
There are 133 unlanded deliverables from dead sessions, each classified *recoverable* by the tool
itself (`cmd/fak/wip.go:128-130`). A collector's job is to remove what nobody wants; every ref here is
something someone wanted and nobody landed. Calling the activity collection hides that, because a
collector reporting `0 reapable` reads like a *clean* store rather than a *full* one.

*On the numbers:* they are volatile and I would rather say so loudly than caveat it quietly. The same
read-only census across one working session gave **131 → 133 → 134**. The drift is the finding, not
noise to apologise for: the store grew three times while I watched it and shrank zero times. Treat any
total as illustrative; the monotonicity is the point.

### 3. There is a clock, and the checkpoint namespace is not on it

`fak garden tick` already reaps five classes — `reaped_leases`, `reaped_sessions`,
`reaped_lock_files`, `reaped_intents`, `reaped_growth_logs` (`cmd/fak/garden.go:199-203`) — including
the sibling lease namespace in-process (`cmd/fak/garden.go:129-131`). It has no wip class:

```
grep -rlin "wip" cmd/fak/garden*.go   ->  (no files)
```

So the scheduler exists, the drain verbs exist, and they have never been introduced. I have raised the
missing wip class as part of C8 (fleet visibility) separately; noted here because the garden tick is
the natural home for the driver this issue asks for.

### 4. Base drift is the mechanism and is surfaced nowhere

Nothing reports a checkpoint's parent age or distance from trunk, so RECLAIM's remaining life cannot
be seen before it expires — only inferred after. I hit this by hand on the ad-hoc parking route: a
parked commit whose parent was 7 hours old against a trunk that had moved ~300 files. It still
applied, but only because every path in it was a pure add. The generic shortcut for recovering parked
work — diff it against current `HEAD` — had by then become a ~300-file revert of everyone else's
afternoon.

### 5. `--file-ticket` fans out where it should roll up

`cmd/fak/wip_ticket.go:11` — "It acts ONLY on QUARANTINE verdicts; DISCARD_WITNESSED/RECLAIM are
untouched." One idempotent ticket per orphan is reasonable for hand-made checkpoints and does not
survive contact with `autocheckpoint`, which makes them automatically, per session, at every risky
boundary. At the distribution in §1 a single invocation files ~131 tickets. #5340's own batch policy
already states the principle — "Not a spam batch; do not fan this out into per-ref tickets" — so this
is asking for `--file-ticket` (#5337) to honour the same rule.

### Ask, in the order I would do it

1. **Act on RECLAIM while it is still RECLAIM.** A `reconcile --reclaim` that lands cleanly-applying
   dead-session deltas through the normal commit gates — or, if auto-landing is too strong, surfaces
   them as a ranked worklist with exit 3, the shape `wip blocked --landable` already uses
   (`cmd/fak/wip.go:137-144`). This is the whole lever; the rest is cleanup.
2. **Put that driver on the garden tick**, next to the sibling namespace's reaper.
3. **Surface base drift** in `wip status` / `reconcile` — parent age and distance from trunk — so
   RECLAIM's remaining life is visible before it expires.
4. **Roll up `--file-ticket`** into one tracking issue with an inventory, per-orphan tickets opt-in for
   small sets (#5337).
5. **Re-describe the collector.** `reap --census` is genuinely good reporting; it is calling the
   activity garbage collection that makes `0 reapable` sound like good news.

**Related:** #3871 (epic — C3 ships the classifier, C4 ships the lander, nothing pumps between them),
#5340 (collection half — this is its recovery complement), #5337 (`--file-ticket`), #5336 (read-path
scaling), #3873 (C1, local durability).

records.title: fix(recover): COLLISION_RISK's two routes both discard finished work — fak wip checkpoint is the missing third
records.body:
## `fak recover COLLISION_RISK` offers two routes and both discard finished work — `wip checkpoint` is the missing third

Small, self-contained fix with a suggested patch. Filed separately from the two design issues it is
adjacent to, because it should not block behind them.

`cmd/fak/recover.go:210-219` is the whole recovery record:

```go
"COLLISION_RISK": {
	Reason:     "COLLISION_RISK",
	Summary:    "wait for the live lease or choose a disjoint lane/region",
	Executable: false,
	Steps: []recoveryStep{
		{Argv: []string{"dos", "top"}, Summary: "inspect live leases and workers"},
		{Argv: []string{"dos", "arbitrate"}, Summary: "retry arbitration with a disjoint region"},
	},
	Notes: []string{"do not bypass the lease; repartition or wait"},
},
```

Both routes assume the work is not finished yet. Neither is right when it is.

The case: a change was written, built, vetted and green, and blocked only because the lanes covering
its paths were held by live peers. **"Wait for the live lease"** leaves finished work sitting
uncommitted in a shared checkout, where peers sweep it into their own commits — a hazard `fak wip
sweep-guard` exists specifically to warn about (`cmd/fak/wip.go:156-159`), so the kernel already knows
that waiting-while-dirty is dangerous. **"Choose a disjoint lane/region"** is advice for work not yet
started; you cannot re-aim a change that is already written at a different lane.

The route that actually applies is the one not listed: **check the work into something durable,
release the lane, land it when the lane frees.** `fak wip checkpoint` is exactly that. I did not find
it from this message — I found it hours later while reading the verb catalogue, having hand-rolled a
worse equivalent in the meantime.

`fak recover` is where an agent arrives *at the moment it is blocked*, which makes it the
highest-leverage place in the tool to name a capability. A capability that exists but is not named at
the point of need is, for an agent, indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

### Suggested patch

```diff
 		"COLLISION_RISK": {
 			Reason:     "COLLISION_RISK",
-			Summary:    "wait for the live lease or choose a disjoint lane/region",
+			Summary:    "checkpoint finished work, or wait for the live lease, or choose a disjoint lane/region",
 			Executable: false,
 			Steps: []recoveryStep{
+				{Argv: []string{"fak", "wip", "checkpoint"}, Summary: "park a FINISHED delta durably so the lane can be released"},
 				{Argv: []string{"dos", "top"}, Summary: "inspect live leases and workers"},
 				{Argv: []string{"dos", "arbitrate"}, Summary: "retry arbitration with a disjoint region"},
 			},
-			Notes: []string{"do not bypass the lease; repartition or wait"},
+			Notes: []string{
+				"do not bypass the lease; repartition, park, or wait",
+				"if the change is already written and green, checkpoint it — waiting while dirty exposes it to a peer's sweep (see `fak wip sweep-guard`)",
+			},
 		},
```

Checkpoint is listed first deliberately: it is the only one of the three that is safe to do
*immediately* and loses nothing if the operator then also waits or repartitions.

### One open question for the maintainer

Two other reason tokens (`MERGE_IN_PROGRESS`, `STALE_BASE_DELETION`) carry concrete executable
guidance, so there is precedent for flipping `Executable: true` here — `fak wip checkpoint` is a
concrete command. I have deliberately left it `false` in the patch above, because I do not know
whether an executable reason's steps are ever auto-run, and a recovery route that silently
checkpoints on every collision is a behaviour change rather than a doc fix. Your call; the wording
change stands either way.

**Related:** #5085 (a lease whose holder is 4h-stalled wedges the lane — same "blocked by a live-looking
lease" family, from the admission side rather than the recovery side). I checked the five issues whose
bodies mention `COLLISION_RISK` (#5116, #5089, #5085, #5059, #5056); none is about this recovery
record's text, so as far as I can tell this is unfiled.

records.title: fix(guard): Apple Terminal companion overlay window outlives its process — `; exit` assumes a close-on-clean-exit profile that is not the stock default; make auto-close the default
records.body:
## Problem

On Apple Terminal, `fak guard --split` (the `auto` default for an attended launch) opens the
`fak info` overlay as a companion **window**, spawned in `cmd/fak/guard_split.go`:

```go
// The trailing `; exit` lets the window close itself when the overlay ends (with the
// default close-on-clean-exit profile) instead of lingering as a dead shell.
plan.Spawn = []string{"osascript",
    "-e", `tell application "Terminal"`,
    "-e", `set agentWindow to front window`,
    "-e", `do script "` + appleScriptQuote(shellJoin(overlayCmd)+"; exit") + `"`,
    ...
```

That parenthetical is the bug. Apple Terminal's stock **Basic** profile ships
`When the shell exits: Don't close the window`. There is no close-on-clean-exit default to
rely on, so the documented intent does not hold on an unconfigured Mac:

1. the overlay exits (correctly — see #2340's `--max-idle` backstop),
2. `; exit` exits the shell,
3. Terminal keeps the window, parked on `[Process completed]`.

**One dead window per guarded session, accumulating monotonically** for as long as the
operator's Terminal stays open. Nothing ever reaps them, and the only signal that a window
is dead is reading its last line.

## Observed

An attended Apple Terminal kept open across roughly two days of `fak guard -- claude` runs
accumulated **~100 dead overlay windows — about 84% of every window open in the app**; the
rest belonged to live sessions. They were uniform: scrollback ends with the overlay
dashboard, then

```
fak info: no gateway answering at http://127.0.0.1:<port> — is `fak guard` running? ...
fak info: gateway closed — guarded session ended
[Process completed]
```

The `--max-idle` backstop had fired exactly as designed in every one of them. The *process*
was gone; only the window remained. Recovering the window list meant closing them by hand.

## Why #2340 does not already cover this

#2340 ("`fak info` dashboard panes never exit, so they accumulate") was measured on Windows
Terminal and fixed by making the overlay process self-exit — the `--max-idle` flag help says
the point is that a pane "cannot poll a dead URL forever and leak a terminal pane".

On Apple Terminal that process exit is **necessary but not sufficient**, because the window
is not the process. #2340's acceptance criterion —

> After a guarded session ends, its info pane exits within ~30 s; pane count returns to
> interactive baseline instead of growing monotonically.

— is therefore still unmet on Apple Terminal: the window count grows monotonically even
though every overlay process exits on time. This is the Apple Terminal residue of #2340,
not a regression in it.

## Fix (proposed default: auto-close)

Close the companion window on clean overlay exit, by default, without depending on a profile
setting the operator never chose:

1. **Preferred — the overlay closes its own window.** `fak info` already resolves whether it
   is on a tty; on a clean exit in the guard-spawned case, have it close its own window by
   that identity:
   `tell application "Terminal" to close (every window whose tty of tab 1 is "/dev/ttysNNN")`.
   This keys on something the overlay owns, works regardless of profile, and leaves a
   non-clean exit (crash, operator Ctrl-C) on screen for debugging.
2. **Alternative — pin the spawned tab's exit action.** Apply a settings set whose
   `shell exit action` is `close always` to the tab `do script` returns, instead of assuming
   the operator's default profile does it.
3. **Escape hatch.** `--split-close-on-exit` (default **true**), so an operator who wants the
   dead window for post-mortem reading can opt out, and so the behavior is documented rather
   than implicit in a profile.

### Guard rail for whoever implements this

The closer must key on the overlay's **own** window/tty identity — never a global predicate
like "close every Terminal window with no running process". Operators legitimately keep
exited-shell windows around, and a global sweep would collect their scrollback too. A global
predicate is defensible for a one-off manual cleanup; it is not acceptable behavior to ship.

## Acceptance

- On Apple Terminal with `--split=auto`, after a guarded session ends the companion overlay
  window is **gone**, within about one `--interval` of the overlay process exiting.
- Across a multi-session run, Terminal window count returns to the live-session baseline
  instead of growing by one per session — the #2340 criterion, met on Apple Terminal.
- `--split-close-on-exit=false` reproduces today's lingering-window behavior.
- A non-clean overlay exit still leaves its window open and readable.
- iTerm2's inline split path is unaffected — its pane already closes with its process.

records.title: feat(cost): make the guard dollar estimate VISIBLE and basis-stamped — four rate cards disagree 3x on the Opus-class base, and no surface prints which one it used
records.body:
## Outcome

`fak guard` can already price a served turn, but an operator never sees a dollar figure for the
session in front of them, and the four price books in the tree disagree by up to 3x on the same
model class. Make cost a first-class, visible, deliberately-**ESTIMATED** output of a guarded
session: one canonical rate card, a printed *basis* line naming every assumption behind the number,
and a **modifier axis** for the provider settings that change the rate for the same tokens (premium
"fast" output mode, long-context tier, batch tier, seat-vs-metered). Give a self-hosted upstream an
optional cost basis too, so "load" is legible in the same currency instead of being dollar-blind.

Estimated is fine. A stamped estimate is worth more than a hidden exact number. What is not fine is
a bare `$` with no basis, or four numbers that cannot all be right.

## Problem

### A. Four rate cards, three different Opus-class bases

| site | Opus-class base, $/MTok in / out |
| --- | --- |
| `internal/sessionaudit/sessionaudit.go:28` (`Pricing["opus"]`) | **15 / 75** |
| `internal/gateway/cache_pricing.go:59,61` (`ClaudeOpus48*PerMTokUSD`) | **5 / 25** |
| `internal/modelroute/cost.go:53,80` (`FrontierAnchor`, `"frontier"`) | **3 / 15** |
| `cmd/fak/guard_resume.go:107` (inline fallback) | **5 / 25** |

Each site documents its own number as authoritative: `cost.go:49-52` calls 3/15 "the repo's
published $3 in / $15 out convention"; `cache_pricing.go:58-59` calls 5/25 "the default
guarded-Claude base input price" with source label `default:anthropic/claude-opus-4-8`;
`internal/sessionaudit/sessionaudit.go:17` says "The Claude tiers use Anthropic's published rates".
At most one of
these can be the published Opus list price.

The *multipliers* agree everywhere — `internal/cacheprice/cacheprice.go:34-38` (0.1x read,
1.25x/2.0x write) is the one canonical rate, and `sessionaudit.Pricing["opus"]`'s cache rows are
exactly 1.25x/0.1x of its own base. Only the base diverges. Some of the spread may be deliberate
(a discounted effective rate, a rough routing ladder vs a billing card) — nothing says which, and
that is precisely the defect: the disagreement is undocumented and unlabelled.

#3927 reconciled the *fable* row's role/price contradiction across four seams; the Opus-class base
was not in its scope, and `internal/modelroute/cost.go:69-75` still names the sessionaudit fable row
as unreconciled residue.

### B. The live meter resolves a basis and throws it away

- Guard boot arms the served-spend meter at `cmd/fak/guard_child.go:219`
  (`armServedSpendPricing(up, agentName)`), re-armed with a statically-known model at
  `cmd/fak/guard_upstream_posture.go:115`. **Both call sites discard the `(source string, ok bool)`
  return** (`cmd/fak/session_spend.go:67`), so the basis — `default:anthropic/claude-opus-4-8`,
  `env:FAK_SPEND_*`, or dollar-blind — is resolved once per process and never rendered anywhere.
- The live table knows exactly two Claude rows (`cache_pricing.go:129-159`): opus-4-8 and fable-5.
  Every other Claude tier misses and falls back to the agent-name context, i.e. the Opus row —
  `cmd/fak/session_spend.go:77-79` states this in its own doc comment ("prices every Claude tier as
  the Opus 4.8 default"). So a `--model claude-sonnet-4-6` guarded session meters at the Opus row,
  while an offline audit of that same session prices it from `sessionaudit.Pricing["sonnet"]`
  (3/15). The two surfaces disagree on one session *by construction*, and #4635's canonical-ID +
  fail-closed-on-unknown discipline landed only on the audit side.
- **The exit summary prints token-equivalents, never dollars.**
  `cmd/fak/guard_format.go:308-343` renders "avoided-spend attribution" entirely in token-equiv.
  The only `$` guard emits is the resume projection at `cmd/fak/guard_resume.go:354`, whose price is
  either operator flags or the inline `{5, 25}` fallback at `:105-107` — an *unpriced* input
  silently becomes a *priced* number, with no marker that a default was substituted.
- Dollars are computed for the opt-in ceiling only: `--budget-envelope ... spend=$25`
  (`cmd/fak/guard.go:150`) to `internal/session/budget_envelope.go:124`, debited via
  `servedTurnSpendMicroCents`. Set no ceiling and the pricing still runs — nothing surfaces.

### C. There is no rate-modifier axis

`gateway.CachePricing` is two scalars (`cache_pricing.go:120-123`), and the only modifiers in the
model are the three cache-TTL constants. Nothing can express a provider setting that changes the
**rate** for the same tokens:

- **Premium / "fast" output mode.** Claude Code exposes a fast output mode that bills the same
  model at a premium over its base rate (the multiplier is the provider's to cite). The string
  `fast` appears nowhere in the pricing path — only as a test tier, e.g. `cmd/fak/test.go:81`. A
  session run that way is under-booked by the whole multiplier, silently.
- **Long-context tier.** Guard *already detects* the `[1m]` variant marker —
  `guardClaudeOneMillionModel`, `cmd/fak/guard_provider.go:403-405` — and uses it for the
  auto-compact window. The verdict never reaches the pricer: `normalizedPricingContext`
  (`cache_pricing.go:162-170`) does not strip the suffix, and the
  `strings.Contains(c, "claude-opus-4-8")` branch at `:146` therefore prices
  `claude-opus-4-8[1m]` at the standard-window rate. Providers charge a premium above the standard
  window, and the information needed to price it is already in the process.
- **Batch / off-peak tiers** and **seat-vs-metered billing.** A subscription seat's *marginal*
  dollars per turn are ~0 while its load is real; a metered key's are not. Same tokens, different
  money, no axis to say so.

Reasoning **effort** is the one modifier already modeled, and modeled correctly — as an
expected-output-token *volume* multiplier, explicitly never a rate
(`internal/modelroute/effortcost.go:12`, "WHY EFFORT IS A SEPARATE LENS, NEVER A RATE MULTIPLIER";
the ladder at `:37-53`, medium=1.0 ... xhigh/ultracode=2.4). But that lens lives in the routing
forward-estimate only. The posture it prices is chosen at launch — `effortcost.go:43-45` points at
the launcher's `--settings '{"ultracode":true}'` in `cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go` — and a guarded
session launched that way carries a ~2.4x expected-output-volume prior that no guard-side cost
surface ever applies. Fast mode is the complementary case: a genuine *rate* modifier with no home at
all.

### D. Self-hosted is dollar-blind by design, which hides load

`cmd/fak/session_spend.go:12-22`, resolution step 3: a `fak serve` local model "stays dollar-blind
by default because a local turn costs no provider dollars", and #5115's scope deliberately keeps
qwen/local UNPRICED. That is right for *billing* and wrong for *load*: a local GPU-hour has a real
price, and an operator comparing a local run against a metered one has no shared currency.
`FAK_SPEND_*_PER_MTOK_USD` already lets one be hand-set — the mechanism exists, it just is not
first-class, not derived from anything measurable, and not labelled as an estimate.

## Impact

- A dollar figure's meaning depends on which surface printed it, and no surface prints which card it
  used — so two honest fak outputs can differ 3x on the same session with no way to tell why.
- Live metering over-books cheap Claude tiers (Sonnet/Haiku priced at the Opus row) and under-books
  premium output modes and long-context variants. The errors do not cancel.
- The #1573 spend ceiling inherits the same basis, so `spend=$25` means different things depending
  on which resolver armed it, and a breach is `BUDGET_SPEND_EXHAUSTED` either way.
- Self-hosted work is invisible in the only currency that compares it against a metered run.

## Done when

- [ ] One canonical per-model rate card; other sites read from it, or document in-file why they
      deliberately differ (rough routing ladder vs billing card is a fine reason — an unstated
      3x is not).
- [ ] Every operator-facing dollar figure carries a **basis stamp**: raw + canonical model id, which
      card, which modifiers were applied, ESTIMATED vs OBSERVED, and an explicit `dollar-blind` when
      unpriced. The `(source, ok)` returns at `guard_child.go:219` and
      `guard_upstream_posture.go:115` stop being discarded.
- [ ] `fak guard`'s exit summary prints an estimated session cost beside the token-equiv attribution
      it already prints (`guard_format.go:308-343`), unconditionally — no `--budget-envelope`
      required — and marked as an estimate.
- [ ] A modifier axis alongside `CachePricing` for rate-changing settings, with rows for premium/fast
      output, long-context (`[1m]`), batch, and seat-vs-metered. Defaults may be rough and
      overridable in the existing `--prices` / `ParseEffortCosts` idiom; each ships with its source
      cited or is marked ASSUMED.
- [ ] `guardClaudeOneMillionModel`'s verdict reaches the pricer: a `[1m]` id cannot resolve to the
      standard-window rate.
- [ ] A non-default Claude tier declared via `--model` meters at its own row or is dollar-blind —
      never silently at the Opus row.
- [ ] An unpriced input to the resume projection reports unpriced rather than falling back to the
      inline `{5, 25}` at `guard_resume.go:107`.
- [ ] An optional local cost basis (e.g. `$/GPU-hour / measured throughput -> $/MTok`) so a
      self-hosted session reports estimated cost and load in the same units — labelled ESTIMATED,
      off by default, never conflated with a billed figure.

## Out of scope

- **Which absolute price is correct.** That is a published-rate question and the maintainer's call;
  this issue asks for one card and a printed basis, not a specific number.
- The fable role/price reconciliation (#3927) and the gpt/gemini rows (#5115).
- Any per-account or private billing data. Published rates plus declared assumptions only.

## Prior art

rate rows) - #3927 (fable taxonomy contradiction, same shape one model over) - #1573 (the spend
axis this would make legible) - #4488 (provider-cost KPI).
