records.title: [feature] leaseref: a typed EvidenceKind beside the Evidence sentence, so a caller can route on the remedy
records.body:
## The problem

`ClassifyLiveness` (`internal/leaseref/liveness.go:79`) returns `(class, evidence string)`, and
`ClassifiedLease` surfaces them as `liveness` / `reclaimable` / `evidence` (lines 69–71). Two of
those three are machine-routable. The one that carries *which comparison decided* is an English
sentence.

That matters most for `peer-unknown`, which has **two causes with opposite remedies**:

- **`liveness.go:81`** — `rec.SessionID == ""`: *"lease carries no session_id (legacy/unbound
  record)"*. The **acquirer** never bound a session. The remedy is at the acquire call site
  (`--session`); waiting changes nothing, ever.
- **`liveness.go:89`** — no descriptor for the bound id: *"no session descriptor at
  refs/fak/locks/session-…"*. The acquirer did bind; the **publisher** is missing or died before
  its first publish. The remedy is to start/repair `fak leaseref session-publish`.

Both correctly classify not-reclaimable, so **admission is unaffected and the fail-closed rule
should not change** — that rule is the right posture and this issue does not touch it. The gap is
one level up: a supervising loop that wants to *repair* the condition rather than merely avoid the
lane has to pattern-match prose to tell "fix the acquire call site" from "fix the publisher". Those
are different owners and different fixes, and today they are the same `{liveness: "peer-unknown",
reclaimable: false}` object.

`peer-dead` has the same shape, less urgently: terminal `STOPPED` (`liveness.go:94`) and a lapsed
heartbeat (`liveness.go:99`) are one class, and a reaper may reasonably want to log or rate-limit
them differently — a session that announced its own exit is not the same event as one that stopped
answering.

So the closed vocabulary the package doc is careful to establish for `liveness` (lines 39–51,
"the `--json` contract a calling loop routes on") stops one level short of the field that actually
explains the verdict.

## Proposed solution (optional)

A closed `EvidenceKind` family in the same shape as the existing `Liveness*` constants — one per
`return` in `ClassifyLiveness` (there are exactly six: lines 81, 85, 89, 94, 99, 103):

```go
// EvidenceKind is the machine-routable companion to the Evidence sentence: WHICH
// comparison decided the class, so a caller can select a REMEDY without parsing prose.
// The sentence stays authoritative for humans; this is the routing key.
const (
    EvidenceSelfSession     = "self-session"       // liveness.go:85
    EvidenceNoBinding       = "no-session-binding" // :81 — fix the ACQUIRER
    EvidenceNoDescriptor    = "no-descriptor"      // :89 — fix the PUBLISHER
    EvidenceTerminalStopped = "terminal-stopped"   // :94
    EvidenceHeartbeatLapsed = "heartbeat-lapsed"   // :99
    EvidenceHeartbeating    = "heartbeating"       // :103
)
```

`ClassifiedLease` gains `evidence_kind`; `ClassifyLiveness` returns it alongside the sentence.
Strictly additive — no change to `liveness`, `reclaimable`, or the existing sentences, so nothing
that routes on today's contract breaks. Because the function is already pure ("it reads only its
inputs — no I/O — so a test drives every branch with literal values"), the test burden is one
table case per kind, asserting **every kind is reachable**.

One open question I'd rather you decide than guess: a third return value on `ClassifyLiveness`
(mechanical, but it is a signature change to an exported function), a small returned struct, or a
parallel `ClassifyLivenessKind` wrapper that leaves the current signature alone. Happy to send a PR
in whichever shape you prefer — say the word and I'll match your call.

Context: the four-state classification and its fail-closed rule are #2164; the fenced acquire this
sits beside is #906-C1.

records.title: [feature] leaseref liveness: report how much of the live set has POSITIVE liveness evidence
records.body:
## The problem

`fak leaseref liveness` classifies each live lease and fails closed: a lease with no `session_id`,
or one whose bound session has no descriptor, comes back `peer-unknown` / not-reclaimable
(`internal/leaseref/liveness.go:81` and `:89`). That is the correct posture and this issue does not
propose changing it.

The consequence appears one level up, in aggregate. Consider a set of holders where **none** passes
`--session` at acquire, or none runs `fak leaseref session-publish`. Then by those two branches
every live lease classifies `peer-unknown`, and `ClassifyLive` returns a complete, well-formed,
correctly-computed array in which **every row is an absence of evidence**. Nothing in the output
distinguishes that from a healthy read: there is no field that says *the liveness signal is
installed and inert*.

So the two situations a reader most needs to tell apart produce the same-shaped answer:

- "I looked at every live lease and their owners are genuinely unclassifiable right now."
- "I have no way to look at all, because nothing on the write path publishes the input this
  classification consumes."

The first is a fleet state. The second is a **wiring defect in the observer**, and it is the one
that quietly invalidates every downstream verdict. A caller reading only `liveness` values cannot
see it, and a human skimming a list of `peer-unknown` rows reads them as data rather than as a
missing feed.

This is the package's own fail-closed reasoning applied to the classifier itself: `ClassifyLiveness`
is careful that absence of evidence never reads as death per-lease, but the *view* lets absence of
evidence across the whole set read as a clean answer.

## Proposed solution (optional)

Emit a summary alongside the array, e.g.:

```json
{
  "total": 12,
  "by_class": { "self": 1, "peer-live": 0, "peer-dead": 0, "peer-unknown": 11 },
  "liveness_coverage": 0.083
}
```

where `liveness_coverage` is the fraction of live leases whose class rests on **positive** evidence
(`self`, `peer-live`, `peer-dead`) rather than on absence (`peer-unknown`). A `liveness_coverage`
near `0.0` is then a one-glance statement that the `session-publish` side is unwired, rather than
something a reader has to infer by noticing that every row says the same thing.

Two notes on fit:

- `fak leaseref audit` already emits the garden control-pane envelope (`ok`/`verdict`/`reason`).
  A coverage floor is a natural `verdict` input there — an all-absence read arguably deserves
  `ACTION` (fix the publisher) rather than a clean `ok`, since the report cannot support any
  conclusion about reclaimability.
- If the typed-evidence-kind proposal in #5484 lands, `by_evidence_kind` makes the
  summary directly actionable — it separates "acquirers are not binding sessions" from "the
  publisher is down", which are different fixes. But `by_class` + `liveness_coverage` stand alone
  and do not depend on it.

Happy to send a PR if you like the shape.

Context: the four-state classification and its fail-closed rule are #2164.

records.title: fix(agent): the stream-stall deadline re-arms on `ping`, so the stalled-but-warm upstream it exists to catch never trips it
records.body:
## What happened

`internal/agent/stream_stall.go` guards the streaming upstream paths (`StreamAnthropicRaw`,
`CompleteStream`) with an inter-byte idle deadline: `stallReader.Read` resets a one-shot timer
before every underlying `Read` and stops it after (`internal/agent/stream_stall.go:111`), so **any**
read that returns bytes re-arms the window. The default window is 60 s
(`internal/agent/stream_stall.go:152`, `FAK_STREAM_STALL_TIMEOUT_S`, clamped to [5 s, 600 s]).

The file states the case it exists to catch (`:8`) — an upstream that

> sent headers and some frames, then went silent (a transient overload / "API issue")

and it also states, as intended behavior (`:15`), that

> a stream emitting steady deltas / `ping` events / SSE keepalives never trips

Those two are in tension. On the Anthropic SSE wire a keepalive `ping` is a frame like any other: it
returns bytes, so it re-arms the deadline. An upstream that has wedged the generation but is still
emitting keepalives is therefore indistinguishable from a healthy stream, for as long as it keeps
pinging — and a loaded server emitting keepalives while making no progress is precisely the
transient-overload shape named in the purpose statement.

So the detector separates *socket alive* from *socket dead*, not *turn progressing* from *turn
wedged*. The consequence is that the hang it was written to prevent is still reachable whenever the
upstream keeps the connection warm: since `fak guard` raises the whole-request ceiling to 600 s so a
long-but-healthy extended-thinking turn is not cut off (`:5-8`), a wedged-and-pinging turn blocks
for that full ceiling rather than failing in ≤60 s. And because `ErrUpstreamStalled` is never
raised, the stall accounting reads clean for the very turn that failed, so the metric points away
from the cause.

## What you expected

Either the deadline catches a stream that goes quiet *in content* while staying warm, or the doc
comment stops claiming to catch "went silent" when what it detects is "socket dead".

## Suggestion

Two deadlines answering two different questions, instead of one answering neither fully:

- **Liveness (bytes)** — keep `stallReader` exactly as it is. It correctly detects a dead socket,
  and `ping` *should* re-arm that one.
- **Progress (content)** — arm a second, longer deadline in the SSE scanner, reset only by frames
  that advance the turn (`content_block_start` / `content_block_delta` / `message_delta`) and
  explicitly **not** by `ping`. That is the one that separates wedged from warm.

If a second window is more than the case warrants, a cheaper first step: count consecutive
`ping`-only reads and treat "N pings with no intervening content frame" as the stall condition.

Related but distinct: #5415 and #5399 are SSE flush / buffered-decode stalls on the in-kernel and EP
paths; this is the inter-byte detector in `internal/agent`.

## Version / environment

`internal/agent/stream_stall.go` as introduced in 0af3daf, unchanged at `origin/main` (affbb1c7).
Platform independent — pure Go logic, no OS-specific path.

records.title: fix(gateway): the durable usage ledger drops the "stalled" upstream-error kind, so the failure stream_stall.go exists to detect cannot be attributed after the fact
records.body:
## What happened

The gateway classifies an upstream failure into a coarse KIND
(`internal/gateway/metrics.go:504`, `upstreamErrorKind`), and `"stalled"` is one of them — the kind
produced by `agent.UpstreamStalledError`, i.e. by the idle-deadline detector in
`internal/agent/stream_stall.go`. Per the comment at `metrics.go:501`, that kind feeds

> the upstream-error counter and the `fak-turn … FAILED` debug line

Both are process-local. The counter lives in the in-memory metrics surface served on `/metrics`, and
the debug line goes to stderr. Under `fak guard` the gateway is a per-invocation process, so both
disappear when the wrapped command exits.

The durable sink is `.fak/nightrun/gateway-usage.jsonl` (`internal/gatewayusageledger`), and it
exists for precisely this reason — `cmd/fak/serve.go:203` describes the snapshot as being written

> so a crash before a clean exit still leaves a trail (#1610)

But its counter struct has no stall field. It carries `Quarantined`
(`internal/gatewayusageledger/ledger.go:50`), `Errored` (`:53`), and even a dedicated `DenyAllStops`
(`:136`) — while every distinct upstream failure kind collapses into the one `errored` total.
`grep -i stall internal/gatewayusageledger/` returns nothing.

So deny-all earned its own durable counter, and `stalled` — the kind an entire file exists to produce
— does not survive into the only record that outlives the process. After the fact you can see that N
turns errored; you cannot see that any of them stalled, which is the one thing the idle deadline was
added to tell you.

## What you expected

The kind the classifier already computes is preserved in the durable snapshot, so a stall is
attributable after the process is gone.

## Suggestion

Either a `stalled` counter alongside `deny_all_stops`, or — cheaper to extend — a small
`upstream_error_kinds` map keyed by the string `upstreamErrorKind` already returns, so a future kind
(`oom`, `unreachable`, …) needs no new field and no schema bump.

Complements #5486, which is about the detector's trigger condition rather than the record it leaves.

## Version / environment

`origin/main` (affbb1c7). Platform independent — pure Go logic, no OS-specific path.

records.title: [bug] streaming passthrough: an in-band Anthropic `error` frame on a 200 is never retried and becomes an opaque 502
records.body:
## What happened

`fak guard -- claude` intermittently dies mid-session with a `502` from the gateway instead of riding out a transient upstream refusal. The retry that the code is clearly designed to do never happens — one upstream attempt, then the turn ends.

The cause is that **Anthropic has two ways to refuse a streamed turn**, and the streaming passthrough only retries one of them.

1. **HTTP-status refusal** — `429` / `503` / `529` / `5xx`. `retryableStatus` covers this correctly (`internal/agent/retry.go`, which lists `408/429/500/502/503/504/529`), and `StreamAnthropicRaw`'s loop retries it with backoff before any byte reaches the client. This path works.

2. **In-band refusal** — the upstream answers `HTTP 200` + `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, then sends an SSE `error` frame *as its first event*, before any `message_start`:

   ```
   event: error
   data: {"type":"error","error":{"type":"overloaded_error","message":"Overloaded"}}
   ```

   The retry loop in `StreamAnthropicRaw` decides purely on `r.StatusCode`, so a `200` breaks out of it and the refusal is only discovered later, inside the SSE reader. It lands in the event callback at `internal/gateway/messages_stream_passthrough.go`:

   ```go
   case "error":
       if p.started {
           p.send("error", ev.Data)
           return nil
       }
       p.s.logf("gateway: upstream error before stream start (messages)")
       writeErr(p.w, http.StatusBadGateway, "upstream model error")
       p.wroteError = true
       return errPassthroughResponded
   ```

   Three things go wrong there, and all of them are one-way:

   - **No retry.** The loop has already been exited, so nothing re-sends — even though an in-band `overloaded_error` is exactly as transient as the HTTP `529` that path 1 retries eight times by default.
   - **No fallback.** `p.wroteError = true` makes the caller take `case p.wroteError: return true`, which also skips the buffered fallback. So the turn has no second chance of any kind.
   - **The signal is destroyed.** The response is a hardcoded `502`, and `errType(502)` in `internal/gateway/http.go` is `server_error`. The upstream said `overloaded_error`; the client is told the gateway crashed. A wrapped client that would have backed off on an overload has nothing to branch on. The existing code already knows this matters — `upstreamErrorStatus` deliberately maps a real `529` to `upstream_overloaded`/`overloaded_error` with the comment that flattening it to a 502 "strips the client's ability to apply the right posture" — but the in-band path never reaches that mapper.

This is why the failure is *intermittent* rather than reproducible: whether a given overloaded moment surfaces as an HTTP status (retried invisibly, session survives) or as an in-band frame on a 200 (dies immediately) is the upstream's choice and varies between attempts.

## Reproduction

A gateway-level test with a fake upstream that always refuses in-band. `FAK_PLANNER_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3` pins the budget, so a retried transient must produce 3 upstream hits:

```go
upstream := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    atomic.AddInt32(&hits, 1)
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    io.WriteString(w, "event: error\ndata: {\"type\":\"error\",\"error\":{\"type\":\"overloaded_error\",\"message\":\"Overloaded\"}}\n\n")
    w.(http.Flusher).Flush()
}))
```

POST a `"stream":true` request to `/v1/messages` through the gateway:

```
upstream hit 1 times, want 3
error type = "server_error", want overloaded_error
```

The same fixture returning a real `502` status instead of the in-band frame **does** hit 3 times — confirming the retry machinery is healthy and only this entry path bypasses it.

## What I expected

An in-band `error` frame arriving before `message_start` is not terminal — nothing has been relayed to the client yet, so the response status is still fak's to choose. It should be treated as the same class of event as the equivalent HTTP status:

- a transient one (`overloaded_error`, `api_error`, `rate_limit_error`, `timeout_error`) gets re-sent under the existing backoff budget, invisibly;
- a request error (`invalid_request_error`, `authentication_error`, …) surfaces immediately with the upstream's real status, not a 502 and not a retry burst;
- once the budget is genuinely spent, the client sees the upstream's own status and type (`529` / `overloaded_error`), so its own backoff can work.

An `error` frame arriving **after** `message_start` is a different case and should keep its current behavior — the client already owns a live 200 stream, so it can only be forwarded as a terminal SSE error, not retried.

## Version / environment

`fak` built from source at `8119c5e0`, macOS / arm64, Go 1.26.

PR to follow.

records.title: The three biggest prompt-shrink levers are Anthropic-passthrough-only, so a self-hosted local model gets none of them — silently
records.body:
**Title:** `feat(gateway): the three biggest prompt-shrink levers are Anthropic-passthrough-only, so a self-hosted local model gets none of them`

**Labels:** `enhancement`, `agentic-serving`, `track/B-performance`, `class:dev`

## The claim

Three of the gateway's largest prompt-shrink levers are documented as working **only** on the
Anthropic passthrough. Their own flag help says so:

- `--defer-cold-tools` — "Anthropic passthrough only."
- `--compact-history-budget` — "on the Anthropic PASSTHROUGH (an upstream `--base-url` anthropic) … No effect on non-passthrough wires."
- `--elide-stale-reads` — "No effect on non-passthrough wires."

An agent whose upstream is a **self-hosted OpenAI-wire model** (`--provider openai --base-url
http://127.0.0.1:PORT`) is not on that path. Inbound `/v1/messages` is served
(`internal/gateway/http.go:74`), but a non-Anthropic upstream falls to the **generic planner**
(`internal/gateway/messages.go:222`, `:226`) rather than the byte-for-byte passthrough — so all
three levers are inert by construction.

## Why this is the wrong way round

Those three levers matter *most* where there is no provider bill. On a metered API an unshrunk
prefix costs money. On a single-GPU self-hosted deployment it costs **GPU-seconds of prefill** —
recomputed every turn, by every concurrent agent, on the same card that is running another resident
workload. A tool-schema floor and a sprawling history are exactly the two things a coding-agent-shaped
prompt has too much of, and `--defer-cold-tools` / `--compact-history-budget` are the levers for them.

## The second-order harm: a false null

Anyone A/B-testing "does the kernel help a local model?" on this wire measures **≈0 savings** and
writes it up as *"fak's cache levers buy nothing for a self-hosted model."* That conclusion would be
about an unwired lever, not about the kernel. The gap is currently silent — nothing at request time
tells the operator that the levers they enabled are inert on the wire they chose.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Each of the three either (a) works on the generic-planner path, or (b) **refuses by name** at
      startup/first request with a typed error that names the lever *and* the wire, so "enabled but
      inert" is not reachable.
- [ ] `--debug-stats` (or `/debug/vars`) reports, per turn, which shrink levers were **live** —
      not merely configured.
- [ ] `fak ablate` arms record the live-lever set, so an arm can never be quoted as a lever result
      when that lever was inert.
- [ ] A test asserts a non-passthrough wire with all three enabled produces either the shrink or the
      typed refusal, never a silent identity.

records.title: applyGemma4Config never reads the MoE expert axes, so a 128-expert top-8 gemma4 checkpoint loads as dense
records.body:
**Title:** `bug(ggufload): applyGemma4Config never reads the MoE expert axes, so a 128-expert top-8 gemma4 checkpoint loads as dense`

**Labels:** `bug`, `model-arch`, `track/A-model-support`, `class:dev`

## The claim

`applyMoEExpertCounts` (`internal/ggufload/gguf_config.go:291`) reads the shared MoE expert-axis GGUF
scalars — expert count, expert-used count, expert FFN width — into `model.Config`. It is called from
exactly two places:

- `applyQwen3MoEConfig` (`:303`) → call at `:304`
- `applyGLMMoeDsaConfig` (`:486`) → call at `:488`

It is **not** called from `applyGemma4Config` (`:317`), which builds the per-layer
`LayerTypes` / `HeadDimPerLayer` / `RopeDimPerLayer` / `Window` slices and then sets representative
scalars — but never touches the expert axes.

So a gemma4 checkpoint that is a sparse MoE resolves with `NumExperts == 0`: the loader concludes it
is dense.

## Reproduction

`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` (Apache-2.0, public) declares in its own `config.json`:

```json
"model_type": "gemma4",
"text_config": { "enable_moe_block": true, "num_experts": 128,
                 "top_k_experts": 8, "moe_intermediate_size": 704,
                 "num_hidden_layers": 30 }
```

Load a GGUF conversion of it and inspect the resolved `model.Config`: the expert axes are zero.

## Consequence

- `internal/ggufload/estimate.go` documents `ExpertsUsed` as "0 when the header omits it
  (active-*/token pending)" — but here the header does **not** omit it; the gemma4 path just never
  looks. So `--plan-json` sizes this checkpoint as if the expert FFN weren't there, and the expert
  FFN is where the great majority of a 26B/A4B model's parameters live.
- Any expert-aware lever (`--cpu-offload-experts`, `--expert-parallel`, expert prefetch/coalescing)
  has no axis to dispatch on for this family.
- The misreport is **silent** — nothing refuses, and the resolved numbers look plausible.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `applyGemma4Config` calls `applyMoEExpertCounts` (or the equivalent), so the expert axes land
      in `Config`.
- [ ] A header-fixture test asserts 128 / 8 for a MoE gemma4 header, **and** asserts a dense gemma4
      header still resolves to `NumExperts == 0` (the flag `enable_moe_block` exists, so both shapes
      are real).
- [ ] `--plan-json` reports a non-zero expert band for a MoE gemma4 header.

records.title: Wire the dedicated gemma4 forward onto the resident-quant path — f32-only makes the arch unservable at any real size
records.body:
**Title:** `feat(model): wire the dedicated gemma4 forward onto the resident-quant path — f32-only makes the arch unservable at any real size`

**Labels:** `enhancement`, `model-arch`, `track/A-model-support`, `class:dev`

## The claim

`internal/model/arch_support_gemma4.go` ships a typed refusal — `ResidentQuantUnsupportedError` —
whose message ends: *"the dedicated gemma4 forward is not wired on the resident-quant path
(issue #4274). Serve this architecture on the f32 (non-quant) forward."*

That refusal was the right call for #4274: the alternative was a panic deep in the shared qk-norm
band, because gemma4 interleaves two attention regimes with **different per-layer `head_dim`** and
the generic band passes the scalar `cfg.HeadDim` to `applyQKNormCfg`. #4274 is closed, and the
refusal is what shipped.

But the capability gap it names is still open, and it is load-bearing: **f32-only means gemma4 is
supported only at sizes nobody serves.** A 26B-class checkpoint at f32 is ~100 GB of weights. On any
single card in the ≤48 GB class the arch is, in practice, unsupported — the dedicated forward exists
and cannot be reached by a real checkpoint.

## What "wired" has to mean

The refusal's own comment states the acceptance bar: *"real work that needs a correctness witness
(logit cosine vs a reference run) before it can be trusted."* That bar should stay.

## Definition of done

- [ ] The resident-quant CPU forward dispatches to the gemma4 path (`ForwardGemma4`,
      `arch_support.go:97`) instead of running the shared uniform-geometry block code.
- [ ] `applyQKNormCfg` receives the **per-layer** `head_dim` (`headDimForLayer`), not the scalar.
- [ ] Correctness witness: logit cosine of the resident-quant forward vs the f32 reference on the
      same prompt, recorded in the issue.
- [ ] `ResidentQuantUnsupportedError` is **kept** for geometries still genuinely unsupported — the
      fix is to shrink its domain, never to delete the refusal.
- [ ] A test asserts a gemma4-geometry resident-quant session now prefills instead of refusing, and
      that a still-unsupported geometry refuses by name.

records.title: A cached Session/KV path for gemma4 — the forward is cacheless, so every turn re-prefills the whole prompt
records.body:
**Title:** `feat(model): a cached Session/KV path for gemma4 — the forward is cacheless, so every turn re-prefills the whole prompt`

**Labels:** `enhancement`, `model-arch`, `pagedattention`, `track/A-model-support`, `class:dev`

## The claim

The gemma4 forward has **no cached Session path**. The diagnostic flag that exists to work around
that says so in its own help text — `cmd/diagtok/main.go:26`:

> `--cacheless` … "greedy-decode via repeated cacheless Forward (for arches without a cached Session
> path yet, e.g. gemma4)"

Consequences, in order of cost:

1. **Decode re-runs the sequence forward per token** instead of extending a cache.
2. **There is no prefix cache**, so none of the reuse machinery (`internal/radixkv`,
   `internal/l3kv`, `internal/kvmmu`, `internal/cachemeta`) can engage for this family. A
   shared-prefix or multi-agent story is unavailable on this arch by construction.
3. An agent loop re-prefills its entire standing head (system prompt + tool schemas + context)
   **every turn, for every concurrent session** — which on a self-hosted single-GPU deployment is
   the dominant cost of a turn, ahead of decode.

## ⭐ Why this arch is an unusually good target, not a hard one

From the public `config.json` of `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` (Apache-2.0), verifiable by anyone:

- `text_config.num_hidden_layers: 30`, and `layer_types` is a repeating **five `sliding_attention`
  then one `full_attention`** pattern ⇒ **25 sliding + 5 global**.
- `text_config.sliding_window: 1024` — a hard cap, not a hint.
- `head_dim: 256` but `global_head_dim: 512` — the two regimes have **different per-layer geometry**,
  which is why a dedicated gemma4 forward exists at all.

A sliding layer at position *t* never attends further back than 1024 tokens. So the state sufficient
to resume **any** continuation of a cached prefix is exactly:

```
5 global layers  × full prefix depth
+ 25 sliding layers × the last 1024 tokens
```

**The sliding tier stops growing at the window.** Five-sixths of the layers contribute a *constant*
to a persisted prefix regardless of how long that prefix is — so a cached prefix on this family is a
**bounded object**, where a uniformly-global model's grows with context. That is an unusually cheap
target for prefix persistence and reuse.

The information the cache needs is already parsed: `applyGemma4Config`
(`internal/ggufload/gguf_config.go:317`) fills `Config.Window` per layer from the header's
`attention.sliding_window_pattern`, alongside `HeadDimPerLayer` and `NumKVHeadsPerLayer`.

## Definition of done

- [ ] A cached `Session` for heterogeneous window/global geometry: per-layer KV extents driven by
      `Config.Window`, not one uniform buffer.
- [ ] Window-capped layers **bound** their KV allocation at the window rather than at the context
      length.
- [ ] A prefix-reuse test: a second turn over the same prefix prefills only the delta, and its logits
      match the cacheless forward within tolerance.
- [ ] `--cacheless` stops being the only way to decode this arch (keep the flag as a reference-path
      diagnostic).

records.title: Direct-resident native q4_0 load — the default Q4→f32→Q8 round-trip makes a q4_0 checkpoint bigger than its own file
records.body:
**Title:** `feat(ggufload): direct-resident native q4_0 load — the default Q4→f32→Q8 round-trip makes a q4_0 checkpoint bigger than its own file`

**Labels:** `enhancement`, `model-arch`, `track/A-model-support`, `performance`, `class:dev`

## The claim

`fak serve --gguf` documents its own load path, verbatim:

> "load these GGUF weights into the in-kernel engine at boot … **Default path is lean-Q8
> (Q4→f32→Q8 round-trip); set `FAK_Q4K=1` for the direct-resident-Q4_K path** (Qwen3.6-27B q4_k_m,
> the P1/P2 decode lever)"

So there is a direct-resident path for **Q4_K** and none for **q4_0**. `internal/model/quant_q4.go`
is the resident int4 ("Q4_0-style") weight path, but `internal/model/quant_q4k.go` records why it is
not the same thing:

> "The Q4_0-from-q8w path (quant_q4.go) re-quants from q8w, so it STILL pays the Q4→f32→Q8 load
> round-trip **AND keeps q8w (~30 GB) resident next to q4w (~17 GB)** — measured: ~11 GB of swap on
> the 36 GB box. It also uses Q4_0, not the GGUF's Q4_K, so it does not remove the Q8 quantization
> error that drifts the greedy continuation"

— i.e. the resident Q4_0 copy is *derived from* the Q8 round-trip, not read from the file's native
q4_0 blocks, and the round-trip's **peak** holds both copies at once. So the transient, not just the
steady state, is what breaks the fit.

## Why that inverts the reason q4_0 was shipped

A checkpoint distributed as native q4_0 is chosen because it is small. Loading it through Q8 lands it
at Q8_0's ~1.125 bytes/weight resident (`quant_q4k.go` states the three densities: Q4_K 0.5625,
Q4_0 0.625, Q8_0 1.125). For a 26B-class model that is ~29 GB resident from a file that is roughly
half that on disk — so the lean-Q8 default turns the *smallest available* artifact into one that no
longer fits a 24 GB card, let alone one shared with another resident process.

This is not hypothetical: a q4_0 quantization-aware-training GGUF is the vendor-published artifact
for a current public MoE release (`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it`, Apache-2.0 — `num_experts: 128`,
`top_k_experts: 8`), and the expert FFN bands, where most of its parameters live, are exactly what
the round-trip inflates.

## Definition of done

- [ ] A direct-resident q4_0 load that never materializes f32 or Q8 for the weight bands, mirroring
      what `FAK_Q4K=1` does for Q4_K.
- [ ] A byte-accounting test: resident bytes for a q4_0 header track ~0.625 B/weight, not ~1.125.
- [ ] The **peak transient** during load is asserted too — a direct path that still spikes through
      f32 has not fixed the fit problem.
- [ ] `--plan-json` reports the resident demand for the *selected* path, so a would-be fit refusal is
      visible before anything is allocated.

records.title: kvbudget.Shape has no per-layer window, so KVGiBPerStream over-counts a window-capped arch — MaxStreams under-reports and Admit refuses streams that fit
records.body:
**Title:** `feat(kvbudget): Shape has no per-layer window, so KVGiBPerStream over-counts a window-capped arch — MaxStreams under-reports and Admit refuses streams that fit`

**Labels:** `enhancement`, `track/A-model-support`, `pagedattention`, `class:dev`

## What the package does today

`internal/kvbudget` is a pure, GPU-free KV-cache VRAM calculator, scoped by its own package doc to
"concurrent GLM-5.2 (`glm_moe_dsa`) decode streams", with an MHA/GQA branch alongside the MLA+DSA
one. Its admission half (`admit.go`) reserves the worst case before letting a stream in —
`Stream.WorstCaseBlocks()`, `ReserveBlocks()`, `Reservation.Admit()`, `AdmitAll()`. That contract is
right: reserve first, so an admitted stream can never starve a neighbour mid-flight.

## The claim

`Shape` carries a **scalar** `Layers` and no per-layer attention extent. So every per-token figure is
uniform across layers:

- `MHAElemsPerToken()` = per-head K+V summed over `Layers`
- `KVElemsPerToken()` branches between MLA and MHA, both scalar-`Layers`
- `KVGiBPerStream(ctx, q)` scales that by `ctx` — i.e. **linear in context, for every layer**

That is exact for a uniformly-global model. It **over-counts** any architecture whose layers do not
all attend over the whole context, because it charges a window-capped layer for the full `ctx` it
will never hold.

Downstream, the over-count propagates: `MaxStreams(budgetGiB, perStreamGiB)` under-reports how many
streams fit, and `Reservation.Admit()` refuses streams that would actually have fit. For an
admission gate, over-reservation is the failure mode that matters — the whole point is to admit
everything admissible and refuse only what would starve a neighbour.

## The counter-example, verifiable from a public config

`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` (Apache-2.0). From its own `config.json`:

- `text_config.num_hidden_layers: 30`, `layer_types` = a repeating five `sliding_attention` then one
  `full_attention` ⇒ **25 sliding, 5 global**
- `text_config.sliding_window: 1024` — a hard cap
- `head_dim: 256`, `global_head_dim: 512` — the two regimes differ in width as well as extent

So its true worst case is **`constant + linear`**: 25 layers contribute a fixed amount bounded by the
1024-token window (flat in `ctx`), and only 5 layers grow with `ctx`. A scalar-`Layers` model
calibrated on the sliding tier's per-token cost predicts several times the real figure at long
context.

⭐ The needed inputs are already parsed elsewhere in the tree: `applyGemma4Config`
(`internal/ggufload/gguf_config.go:317`) fills `Config.Window`, `HeadDimPerLayer` and
`NumKVHeadsPerLayer` per layer.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `Shape` can express per-layer `(window, kv_heads, head_dim)`; the scalar form stays valid as
      the uniform case.
- [ ] A window-capped layer's worst case is bounded at `min(window, ctx)`.
- [ ] Table test over both shapes: a uniform arch stays **byte-identical** to today's answer, and a
      window/global arch yields `const + linear`.
- [ ] `MaxStreams` and `Admit` consume the corrected figure.
- [ ] The refusal names which term ran out, so an operator can tell a context problem from a
      concurrency problem.

⛔ Scope note: this is about the *geometry* the calculator can express. It does not change the
reserve-before-admit contract, which is already correct.

records.title: fix(accounts): a seat cannot front a third-party Anthropic-compatible endpoint — the #2358 secret floor strips the credential its own launch argv references
records.body:
## Summary

A `fak accounts` seat cannot currently front a **third-party Anthropic-compatible endpoint**
(a cloud vendor's model-serving gateway that speaks the Messages API). Three independent
things break, and the first one is a genuine footgun that affects more than this use case:
**the always-on #2358 secret floor deletes the exact environment variable that the launch's
own `fak guard` argv references via `--api-key-env`.**

I hit all three while wiring a vendor endpoint as a reserved (never-auto-rotated) seat, and
have a working, tested fix. Filing as an issue first because the central change relaxes a
security floor and deserves design review before a patch lands.

Line numbers below are against `origin/main` as of filing.

---

## Bug 1 — the launch argv references a variable the broker has already deleted

Two call sites, ~10 lines apart, disagree:

```go
// cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:386 — resolve --api-key-env NAME into the guard argv
guardCacheArgs := guardCachePostureArgs(mcMode, launchSeatAPIKeyEnv(home))

// cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:397 — ...then broker the spawn, which strips that variable
grant := launchSpawnBroker(newLaunchBrokerAttempt("accounts_launch", guardAgentBaseName(command), argv, envMap(env), home.Dir))
```

`newLaunchBrokerAttempt` (`cmd/fak/dispatch_tick_broker.go:122`) immediately calls
`sanitizeLaunchEnv` (`:337`), which applies `policy.StripInheritedSecrets`
(`internal/policy/inherited.go:364`). That floor matches variable names by **substring**
(`internal/policy/inherited.go:315-325`):

```go
for _, needle := range []string{
    "TOKEN", "SECRET", "PASSWORD", "PASSWD", "CREDENTIAL", "COOKIE",
    "PRIVATE_KEY", "PRIVATEKEY", "AUTHORIZATION", "SESSION_KEY",
    "UPSTREAM_API_KEY",
} {
    if strings.Contains(up, needle) { return true }
}
```

`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` contains `TOKEN`. So a seat whose credential is the bearer variable
gets `--api-key-env ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` spliced into its argv, and then has that variable
removed from the child's environment before exec. The child reports **"Not logged in"**
against a perfectly valid credential, with nothing in the error pointing at the floor.

Note this is **not** specific to third-party endpoints — any seat whose `--api-key-env`
names a variable containing one of those substrings hits it. `providerAPIKeyNames`
(`internal/policy/inherited.go:340`) already exists as an escape hatch, but it only spares
such variables from the *value* check, not the *name* check, and it is a fixed
`{ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY}` set rather than something a launch can extend.

### Why the floor is still right

Substring matching is the correct default — it is what makes the floor catch
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, `NPM_TOKEN`, and every variable nobody enumerated. The bug is not the
breadth of the match; it is that **a launch has no way to declare the one variable it
legitimately depends on.**

## Bug 2 — the first-party default model is pinned into a vendor argv

`cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:127` pins `defaultLaunchModel = "claude-opus-5"` (plus a
fallback chain) into every account-switched launch. That id does not exist in a third-party
vendor's namespace, so the launch fails at the model layer even once auth works:

```
"result": "There's an issue with the selected model (claude-opus-5)...", "is_error": true
```

The pin is deliberate and correct for first-party seats. It just needs to not apply when
the seat is pointed somewhere the id is meaningless.

## Bug 3 — "available, but never auto-selected" is inexpressible at the provider layer

`accounts.Home.Reserved` + `RotationPolicy.AvoidReserved` already gives this at the
**config-home seat** layer: a reserved seat is excluded from the rotation pool while
staying launchable by name. There is no equivalent at the **provider-credential** layer
(`internal/modelroute`'s `Roster`/`placementCandidates`), so an account that should only
ever serve on explicit request can still be picked by automatic placement.

This matters for a vendor rung specifically: you want it reachable when a task genuinely
needs it, and never reachable by accident.

---

## Reproduction

```bash
# any Anthropic-compatible endpoint; the failure is in fak, not the endpoint
fak accounts add vendor \
  --base-url https://gateway.example.com/serving-endpoints/anthropic \
  --seat-env ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=... \
  --reserved

fak accounts launch vendor --guard=false -- -p "say OK"
# -> "Not logged in", despite a valid credential in the seat env
```

`--guard=false` is required and worth documenting on its own: `fak guard` injects its own
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` at a loopback gateway and proxies with guard's credential, which
overrides the seat's endpoint.

---

## Proposed fix

**1. Let a launch declare, by name, the credential it depends on.**

```go
// internal/policy/inherited.go
func StripInheritedSecrets(ambient []string) (kept, stripped []string) {
    return StripInheritedSecretsExcept(ambient, nil)
}

// StripInheritedSecretsExcept is StripInheritedSecrets with an explicit, caller-DECLARED
// keep-set of variable NAMES that survive the floor.
func StripInheritedSecretsExcept(ambient []string, declared []string) (kept, stripped []string)
```

with these properties, each pinned by a test:

- **Exact-match, case-sensitive** name comparison — no case-folding, so a declaration
  cannot accidentally cover a neighbouring variable.
- **Non-transitive** — the exemption applies to one spawn. A child that spawns its own
  child re-strips.
- **Narrow** — declaring one variable does not widen the floor for any other; every other
  ambient secret is still removed *and* still recorded in the audit's
  `StrippedSecretEnv`.
- **Visible** — a surviving credential changes the env shape `EnvDigest` is computed over,
  so a declaring launch is distinguishable from a strict one in the audit trail.
- **Default-unchanged** — `nil`/empty/whitespace declarations are byte-identical to the
  historical floor.

Exposed as a *separate entry point* (`newLaunchBrokerAttemptDeclaring`) rather than a
variadic on the existing one, so that exempting anything from the floor is visible at the
call site rather than an easily-missed extra argument.

The declaration is then derived from the seat — the same `launchSeatAPIKeyEnv(home)`
resolution that produced the `--api-key-env` reference in the first place — so the two
cannot drift apart. That is the actual invariant: **whatever the argv references, the floor
must keep.**

**2. Defer to the seat's own model when it is third-party.** Leave `--model` empty (which
also disables the first-party fallback chain, so one substitution covers both and they
cannot disagree) and print a one-line notice saying why. An explicit `--model` still wins,
so probing what a vendor endpoint serves stays possible.

**3. Add a `manual_only` account posture to `internal/modelroute`** — excluded from
`placementCandidates`, plus a validation rule that a `manual_only` account cannot be the
`Roster.Default`. Complements `accounts.Reserved` at the other layer.

---

## Open design question (worth resolving before merge)

An adversarial review of my own patch flagged one thing I have not fixed, and I think it
should be settled in review rather than by me unilaterally:

`seatDeclaredCredentialEnv` derives the declaration from `home.APIKeyEnv`, which is read
from the on-disk seat registry — a plaintext file an operator can hand-edit. Its only
validation is `ValidAPIKeyEnvName` (POSIX identifier syntax). So a registry entry can name
*any* ambient variable as a seat's `api_key_env` and have it exempted from the floor on
every launch of that seat.

That is a smaller hole than it first looks — it requires write access to the seat registry,
which is already a trusted input, and the exemption is per-launch and non-transitive. But
it is strictly wider than it needs to be. Options:

- (a) cross-check the declared name against a known-vendor credential allowlist, mirroring
  `providerAPIKeyNames`;
- (b) require the declared name to match a documented Anthropic-compatible variable
  (`ANTHROPIC_*`);
- (c) accept it as within the registry's existing trust boundary and document it.

I lean (b) — it closes the "name an arbitrary AWS/GitHub secret" case without needing a
list that goes stale every time a vendor appears. Happy to implement whichever the
maintainers prefer.

---

## Status

Implemented with 12 new tests covering the boundary (declaration passes; strict default
unchanged; case-sensitivity; non-transitivity; one declaration does not widen the floor;
the audit records what was stripped). Verified end-to-end against a live Anthropic-compatible
third-party gateway: a headless run returns a real completion with `provider: gateway` and
the vendor model id in `modelUsage`.

Happy to open a PR. Flagging the security-floor relaxation for review first, since it is the
kind of change that should not land quietly.

## Related

- #2358 — the closed issue that introduced the always-on inherited-env secret floor this
  change extends.
- #5416 — `epic(modelroute): three-zone model placement`. This is the **vendor** rung of
  that ladder: a seat pointed at a third-party frontier endpoint, reachable on request and
  never by automatic placement. `manual_only` is the complement of that epic's "nothing
  chooses a zone" gap — it makes an account *unchooseable* automatically.
- #2354 — `epic(security): first-class agent-spawn leak prevention across every descendant`.
  The non-transitivity property above is deliberately aligned with that epic.

records.title: feat(leasequeue): a refused lease evaporates, so a busy fleet schedules the claim plane by lottery — the waiter plane is written and imported by nothing
records.body:
**Ask: help wanted on lane/lease contention under load.** When the fleet is busy, *taking* a claim
costs more than doing the work — and the failure is structural, not a bug: **a refused acquire returns
a verdict and no object**. There is no line to stand in, so every retry re-races from scratch and
whoever polls first after a release wins. A caller that has waited four hours has exactly the same
chance as one that arrived 200 ms ago.

The uncomfortable part, and the reason this is filed here: **the priority-ordered queue that fixes it
is already in this tree, tested, and imported by nothing.**

---

## 1. What hurts, in three shapes

**(a) You often can't even ask.** `dos lease-lane acquire` serializes every lane's lease traffic
through one global lock file — the journal append happens under it — and the default retry budget is
about a second (5 retries × 0.2 s). Under a live fleet that budget loses almost every time, so the
answer is `lock-busy`, which says nothing about the lane: you never got as far as the question.
Measured, 20 sequential acquires across two lanes: **19 of 20 came back `lock-busy`**, all naming the
same peer as lock owner. Re-running a single call with `--retries 200 --retry-interval 0.5` returned
the real verdict immediately (`refuse — already held by a live loop`). `release` has no `--retries`
flag at all, so a busy mutex surfaces there as an unhandled traceback instead of a clean refusal —
measured, **17 tries at 3 s spacing (~51 s)** to win the mutex, and the caller keeps holding the lane
until it does.

**(b) When you do get to ask, the refusal is terminal and carries nothing.** No queue position, no
depth, no ETA, no "3rd in line behind a lease that expires in 6 min". And the two obvious escape
hatches fail closed: against a lane held `exclusive`, with the caller's writes in a provably disjoint
subtree, **both `--mode shared` and `--tree <narrowed glob>`** still returned `refuse` /
`journaled: false`. The lock is on the lane *name*; `tree` is descriptive. So "my files don't actually
collide" is a true statement that changes nothing — the only doors are a different lane, the holder
releasing, or an evidence ladder proving the lease orphaned.

**(c) Nothing computes demand, so nothing can be scheduled.** A holder cannot see that anyone is
waiting, so there is no pressure to release early and a lease strands for its whole TTL. Nobody can
answer "what is the oldest wait on this lane?" — which is exactly what #3603 asks for. And a unit can
be picked every tick and refused at the lease every tick, forever: `internal/dispatchaging` bounds how
long a READY unit waits to be *picked*, and **that guarantee does not survive the lease hop.**

## 2. Evidence

Publicly checkable, from this repo — `internal/leasequeue/doc.go` already records the load from #4324:
`LANE_LEASE_HELD` is the **#2 refusal class, ~1,273 events, ~58% of the collision plane, a large share
of them phantom collisions against finished workers.** #5085 is the wedge that produces those phantoms
(admission honoring a lease whose holder stopped heartbeating hours ago), and #4324 is the strand that
feeds it (a lease held for its whole TTL instead of released on worker exit).

Corroborating shape from a busy multi-agent workspace, stated as ratios — the absolute volumes are not
mine to publish, and the ratios are what matter:

- Over a lane WAL on the order of 10^5 records, **~95% of acquire attempts that got far enough to be
  judged were refused** — roughly **20 refusals per successful grant**. A later window of the same
  workspace was worse, not better (~40 refusals per grant).
- **Saturation is reachable, and not rare.** In the newest lease snapshot, **every declared lane in
  the taxonomy was held at once** — so an arriving worker had no free lane to be auto-assigned to, and
  every request it could have made would have been refused.
- Of those live holders, **about two-thirds carried no heartbeat timestamp since acquire**; the oldest
  such holder had held for **over an hour** and was still counted live. The record does carry a `pid`,
  but a pid check is not usable for liveness here — a lease minted through a subprocess reads dead even
  for a live owner — so the heartbeat is the only liveness evidence, and most holders have none. That
  is the mechanism behind the phantom-collision share above.
- In the agents' own logs, contention messages (`lock-busy` plus `held by a live loop`) run at roughly
  **40% of the volume of acquire attempts**, and git `index.lock` contention at about **1.4×** it.
  Caveat: those are raw string occurrences (a command and its echoed output both match, and resumed
  sessions duplicate), so read them as a load indicator, not a deduplicated event count.

Scope note: the acquire path and the WAL live in the kernel CLI outside this repo. The **queue**, the
conflict predicate, the aging law and the poll schedule are all in *this* repo — which is why the fix
belongs here.

## 3. The fix is already written, and wired to nothing

`internal/leasequeue` (landed `dd27b113`, 471 LOC + 500 LOC of tests + an 84-line doc) is precisely the
priority-ordered waiter plane this issue asks for: lapsed tickets abandoned, survivors ranked by
`dispatchaging`'s aging law **over their enqueue clock** (so the anti-starvation guarantee crosses the
lease hop), each tested by `regionadmit`'s one conflict predicate against live holders + this pass's
grants + **every higher-ranked waiter's reservation** (HPC conservative backfill — cheap here because
the conflict test is static tree geometry, so no runtime duration estimate is needed), each queued
waiter handed `seatpark`'s poll schedule plus its blocker, rung, place in line and observed ETA. One
waiter list serves both shapes, because a named lane is a mutex (one line) while a tree is a conflict
graph (overlap is not transitive), and both fall out of the same predicate.

Census, re-runnable by anyone with the repo:

```sh
# importers of leasequeue, module-wide, production and test → both empty
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} -> {{join .Imports " "}}' ./... | grep internal/leasequeue
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} TEST-> {{join .TestImports " "}} {{join .XTestImports " "}}' ./... \
  | grep internal/leasequeue

# every neighbour it composes IS in the shipped binary; the queue alone is not
for p in leasequeue seatpark dispatchaging regionadmit leaseref; do
  printf '%s: %s\n' "$p" "$(go list -deps ./cmd/fak | grep -c "internal/$p\$")"
done
# leasequeue: 0   seatpark: 1   dispatchaging: 1   regionadmit: 1   leaseref: 1

fak leasequeue      # → fak: unknown verb "leasequeue"
```

The landing commit's own subject advertises a verb — `feat(leasequeue): ... (fak leasequeue)` — and
that verb does not exist. So this is `unwired-debt` in its purest form: the design and the tests are
done, the wire and the surface are missing, and until they land the queue cannot make a single
scheduling decision.

## 4. What I'd like help with

**W1 — a refused acquire must mint a ticket instead of evaporating.** At the acquire refusal site,
enqueue the waiter and return the object: blocker, place in line, poll schedule, observed ETA. Safe to
land incrementally, because `Plan` reads no clock (`NowUnix` is data) and does no I/O, and a zero-value
aging policy leaves the order at *arrival* semantics — so wiring it changes **no existing decision**
until the knobs are turned on.

**W2 — ship `fak leasequeue`,** the verb the landing commit already names: per-lane queue depth and
oldest wait, my place in line, who blocks me and for how long. The same fold feeds #3603's fleet
aggregate.

**W3 — priority classes, which is the part I actually want.** An interactive operator should not queue
behind twenty background loops. The class already exists *in the refusal text* — admission says "you
are an interactive operator (not a dispatch loop)" — but not in the order. Map class → base weight in
the aging fold, and keep the hard starvation deadline so no class can be starved by a hotter one.

**W4 — `--wait` on acquire, with the precedent already set in this repo.** `fak memgate` admits a load
and offers `--wait N --interval S` to poll until RAM frees; lane admission offers no equivalent, so
every caller reinvents a retry loop. Poll on the schedule the queue hands back instead. And make
"didn't get to ask" (`lock-busy`) distinguishable from "no" (`refuse`) by exit code — conflating them
makes a caller either park work that could have landed, or retry work that never can.

**W5 — then, and only then, the two things the queue explicitly cannot fix.** Its own doc is honest
about this: it holds nothing, acquires nothing, reaps nothing, and never infers holder liveness. So
release-on-exit (#4324) and the stalled-holder reap (#5085) stay separate issues. But W1 makes both
*legible* and supplies the evidence a reap gate needs — how many live waiters are stacked behind a
holder that stopped heartbeating. W1 first, then those.

## 5. Non-goals

- **No second scheduler.** The value of `leasequeue` is that it calls `regionadmit.Decide` for every
  conflict test and ranks with `dispatchaging.Fold` — one predicate, one aging law. A private twin of
  either is the failure mode, not the feature.
- **Do not relax exclusion.** `--mode shared` and `--tree` narrowing refusing to yield to a live
  exclusive holder is correct behavior; the fix is *fairness and legibility*, not weaker locks.
- **Do not make the hot path pay.** The queue is off the hot path by construction (pure, no I/O). Keep
  it there.

---

records.title: [bug] guard: an inline `--settings '{"ultracode":true}'` silently discards guard's ENTIRE hook stack (Claude's `--settings` is last-wins, not merged)
records.body:
## What happens

Claude Code's `--settings` flag is **last-wins, not merged**: when an argv carries two
`--settings` occurrences, the keys of the earlier one are dropped wholesale.

`fak guard` installs its own hook-settings FILE onto the child argv via
`appendClaudeSettingsArg` (`cmd/fak/guard_precompact.go:309`), inserted right after the
child's `argv[0]`. Any launcher that then appends an inline
`--settings '{"ultracode":true}'` LATER on that same argv silently discards guard's whole
file.

## Why it matters

Everything guard installs through that one file disappears:

- the deny-all auto-continue `Stop` hook and the task-handoff gate
  (`guardStopHookMatchers`, `cmd/fak/guard_stophook.go:1100`)
- the `PreToolUse` commit-boundary lint gate
  (`guardCommitGateMatchers`, `cmd/fak/guard_stophook.go:1086`)
- the toolproc journal on `PreToolUse` / `PostToolUse` / `SessionEnd`
  (`guardToolprocSetHooks`, `cmd/fak/guard_toolproc_hooks.go:162`)
- the `SessionStart` affordance (`cmd/fak/guard_sessionstart.go:279`)
- the `PreCompact` coherence gate (`cmd/fak/guard_precompact.go:283`)

The session still *looks* correctly guarded — the guard process is there, the argv even
mentions `--settings` — but none of those hooks fire. It fails silently and in the
safe-looking direction, which is why it has gone unnoticed.

Scope, so this triages accurately: the tool-call policy floor is **not** affected. Those
denials are adjudicated in-process and are not installed as hooks by this file, so they
survive. What is lost here is observability and session-lifecycle behaviour, and the
commit-boundary lint gate (which defaults to shadow mode anyway). Filing as an ordinary
defect, not a security report.

It lands on exactly the highest-tier work, because ultracode is what the top rungs ask for:

- the interactive launcher under `--ultracode=on`, which appends
  `ultracodeSettingsArg` (`cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:58`)
- `tier/T0` and `tier/ultra` fleet workers, whose launch profile carries
  `UltracodeSettingsArg` (`internal/dispatchtick/launchprofile.go:49`)

## Repro sketch

Launch a Claude child through `fak guard` with any hook installer enabled AND an inline
ultracode `--settings` later on the argv, then observe that none of the hooks listed above
run. Comparing the child's effective settings against guard's own settings file shows the
guard file's keys absent.

## What I expected

One `--settings` on the child argv, carrying both guard's hooks and the requested
reasoning posture — so asking for a higher reasoning tier does not silently cost you the
hook stack.

## Version / environment

Reproduced by reading `origin/main` at `13f5f1a6`. Platform-independent: the defect is in
argv construction, not in any host behaviour.

## Suggested fix

Keep exactly **one** `--settings` on the argv:

- ultracode has no `--effort` level of its own (it is a settings key only), so it has to be
  folded into the file the hook installers already wrote — and must run *after* them, since
  every installer round-trips the settings struct.
- Callers that used to append the inline payload should relay the posture to guard instead
  of handing the child a second `--settings`.

A per-message reasoning posture also cannot live in `~/.claude/settings.json`, because that
one file is shared by every session on the host: `"ultracode": true` there would leak the
orchestration cost into every headless fleet worker, and `false` would deny it to an
attended human. Guard is the only seam that knows which kind of session it is launching, so
resolving the posture by attendance (interactive vs headless `-p`) belongs there.

## Proposed fix

A fix is up as #5509 (14 files, +944/-99), which keeps exactly one `--settings` on the
child argv and merges the posture key into it.

records.title: fix(gateway): /v1/completions still stalls the stream preamble that #5399 fixed for chat
records.body:
## The gap

`#5399` / `#4855` fixed the streaming-stall preamble for the **chat** surface: `internal/gateway/http.go` now calls `stream.open()` before `completeServed`, so a `stream:true` chat request emits its status line and headers immediately instead of after the whole decode (`affbb1c70`, `internal/gateway/chat_stream_preamble.go`).

`POST /v1/completions` was not covered and still has the identical stall:

- `internal/gateway/completions.go:82` — blocks in `completeServed`
- `internal/gateway/completions.go:113` — calls `writeCompletionStream(w, resp)` only after that returns, and that function is what writes the headers and the `200`

So for the full duration of a multi-rank decode a legacy-completions client cannot distinguish an accepted streaming request from a dead socket — the same failure mode, on the same in-kernel path, that the chat fix removed. On the original [redacted:public-corpus] 8-rank GLM-5.2 EP report that window was 1120+ seconds.

Explicitly **not** a gap: the Anthropic `/v1/messages` fall-through already opens early (`internal/gateway/messages.go:1557-1571` writes 200 + headers + `message_start`, then pings on a ticker).

## Why it is not a one-line flush

It inherits the same three decisions `#5399` flagged, which is why it wants its own ticket rather than a drive-by:

1. what the preamble emits before any model byte exists (headers only, or a first frame);
2. how an upstream error *after* the preamble is surfaced, given the status line is already committed and cannot become a 4xx/5xx — the chat side answers this with an SSE `error` event and asserts no raw-body leak;
3. whether the follower ranks mirror the leader's preamble.

## Acceptance

- A legacy-completions sibling of `internal/gateway/ep_stream_stall_test.go`: assert the status line + headers land **before** the modeled EP collective join, not after.
- A named post-preamble upstream-error test for the completions surface, asserting the error reaches the client as a stream event and no raw body leaks.
- `go test ./internal/gateway/... -count=1` green.
- The test must be witnessed non-vacuous against pre-fix source (the chat fix used `go test -overlay`, which works here too and mutates nothing in the tree).

## Provenance

Found while verifying `#5399` in a dispatch wave; the chat half was confirmed already-shipped and the residual split out here so it does not ride a closed ticket.

**Summary**

Agentic vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave textual reasoning with explicit tool calls such as cropping and code-based image manipulation, have emerged as a compelling paradigm for reliable and interpretable multimodal reasoning. However, recent studies have revealed that such models often use tools unfaithfully. Many process images are irrelevant to the question (e.g., the tool crops the wrong region or misses the queried target), yet the call still receives full credit and the model still answers correctly. Such decorative or misaligned tool calls waste computation and reveal that the model leans on prior knowledge or the original image rather than the evidence it retrieves.…

records.title: ci: two cmd/fak handoff tests are permanently skipped — ci.yml installs dos-kernel 730 lines after the go test step that needs it
records.body:
## What

Two `cmd/fak` tests have not actually executed in CI since the `dos`-on-PATH skip guards were added. They skip on every run, and they fail on every box where they do run — so the pair is dead weight that reads as green.

- `cmd/fak/handoff_chain_smoke_test.go:36` — `t.Skip("dos not on PATH")` (`TestHandoffToWitnessedCloseChain`)
- `cmd/fak/relay_handoff_rotate_close_test.go:49` — `t.Skip("dos not on PATH")` (`TestRelayHandoffRotateClose`)

## Why CI never notices

Both steps live in the **same** job, `build-vet-test` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 27-890):

- line 122 — `run: go test -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...`
- line 852 — `run: python -m pip install --quiet --disable-pip-version-check dos-kernel`

The install is 730 lines *after* the test step. So at the moment `go test ./...` runs, `dos` is not on PATH, both guards fire, both tests skip, and the job stays green. The dependency is real but the ordering makes it unsatisfiable.

## Why they fail when they do run

Verified locally: the underlying cause is in `tools/issue_resolve_witnessed.py`.

- `latest_reopen_ts` (~L427) shells out to `gh api .../timeline`.
- On rc != 0 it returns `read_ok=False` (~L443).
- `reopen_blocks_close` (~L461) turns that into a fail-closed `REOPEN_UNKNOWN` (~L476).

The gate cannot distinguish *"the timeline showed no reopen"* from *"there was no repo or remote to ask."* Both collapse to the same fail-closed verdict, so the close is blocked in any environment without a live remote.

## Suggested fix

Two separable pieces — worth doing both, and they can land independently:

1. **Ordering** — move the `dos-kernel` install ahead of the `go test ./...` step (or into the job's setup block) so the guards can actually be satisfied. If `dos` is genuinely not wanted for the main test step, the honest alternative is to delete the two tests rather than keep them permanently skipped.
2. **Fail-closed conflation** — teach `reopen_blocks_close` to separate "asked and got a clean no" from "could not ask." Only the former should be treated as evidence; the latter is an unknown and should be reported as such rather than silently reused as a refusal.

Note that fixing (2) alone still leaves the tests skipped in CI, and fixing (1) alone will turn the job red until (2) lands — so land (2) first, then (1).

## Evidence

Line numbers above are at `dc5c911916083c5a5d2f5938f6398a9253259f62`. The job-boundary claim is checkable with a grep for top-level job keys in `ci.yml`: `build-vet-test:` at 27, `race-detector:` at 891, `head-snapshot-build:` at 947.

records.title: flake: dos commit-audit reports CLAIM_UNWITNESSED 'commit is EMPTY' under contention, reddening the handoff smoke that #5518 is about to un-skip
records.body:
## What

`TestHandoffToWitnessedCloseChain` (`cmd/fak/handoff_chain_smoke_test.go`) failed once at **step 8** under heavy fleet contention, then passed on both re-runs.

The failing step calls `dos commit-audit`, which returned after ~36s with:

```
CLAIM_UNWITNESSED ... "the commit is EMPTY (touched no files)"
```

At the time, peers were concurrently running `go build ./...` and `go test ./internal/model/...` on the same box.

## Evidence strength — read this before acting

This is **one observation, with two clean re-runs after it** (24.8s, then 8.65s). That is enough to record, not enough to diagnose. I am filing it deliberately *ahead* of the fix in #5518 rather than after, for the reason below.

The step that failed precedes the `tools/issue_resolve_witnessed.py` gate logic entirely, so it is not related to the no-repo-context fix landing for #5518. The ~36s duration alongside a "commit is EMPTY" verdict is the interesting part: it suggests `dos commit-audit` may be reading commit state before it has settled, or timing out internally and reporting the timeout as an empty commit rather than as a timeout. If so, the defect is the *misreport*, not the slowness — an audit that cannot read the commit should say it could not read it.

## Why this is urgent-ish rather than routine

#5518 fixes the CI ordering that currently keeps this exact test permanently skipped. **Once #5518 lands, this test starts running in CI for the first time.** If the flake is real, it will show up as an unexplained intermittent red in `build-vet-test` and will look like #5518 broke CI, when in fact #5518 merely made a pre-existing flake visible.

So the honest sequencing is: record this now, and if a red appears after #5518, check here first.

## Next checkable step

Not yet diagnosed. The cheap witness would be to run the smoke in a loop under deliberate CPU contention and capture whether the "EMPTY" verdict correlates with elapsed time crossing a threshold:

```
go test ./cmd/fak/ -run TestHandoffToWitnessedCloseChain -count=20 -v
```

with a parallel `go build ./...` loop running. If the failures cluster at the long-duration end, it is a timeout being mis-surfaced.

Requires `dos` on PATH, or the test skips and proves nothing.

records.title: feat(serve): nothing consumes KVCacheShape, so a window-capped gemma4 is still charged ~4.5x its real KV cost at stream admission
records.body:
## What

`Config.KVCacheShape()` now computes a correct per-layer KV budget (#5498, landed), but **nothing in production reads it.** The corrected number exists only at the seam.

Checkable right now — every importer of the package:

```
$ grep -rn 'internal/kvbudget"' --include='*.go'
internal/model/kvbudget_perlayer_test.go
internal/model/kvbudget_shape.go
internal/model/kvbudget_shape_test.go
```

Three files: one producer and two test files. No planner, no serve path, no admission gate.

`KVCacheShape`'s own doc comment has said *"nothing in the decode path consumes the Shape yet"* since it was introduced, so this is a known and honestly-documented gap rather than a regression — but #5498 closing makes it worth tracking on its own.

## Why it matters concretely

For a gemma-4 cadence (30 layers, 5-sliding-then-1-global, window 1024) at ctx=16384, F16, measured through `FitRow`/`MaxStreams` at `kvbudget.FreeVRAMGiB`:

| | uniform (what the planner effectively assumes) | per-layer (what the Shape now computes) |
|---|---|---|
| KVGiBPerStream | 1.875 | 0.41015625 |
| MaxStreamsRaw | 109 | **502** |

So a window-capped architecture is being charged roughly 4.5x its real KV cost. Until something consumes the Shape, the serve path keeps refusing streams it could comfortably serve.

Those two figures are reproduced exactly by `TestKVCacheShapePerLayerShrinksPerStreamBudget` in `internal/model/kvbudget_perlayer_test.go`.

## Next checkable step

Wire the stream-admission decision to `Config.KVCacheShape().FitRow(...)` / `MaxStreams`, then assert that a gemma-4 session at 16k admits more than 109 streams.

## Care required

This is the point where the number stops being cosmetic and starts gating real capacity, so it deserves more caution than the seam work did:

- Under-charging KV is far worse than over-charging: over-charging refuses serviceable streams, under-charging admits streams that then OOM mid-decode. The current conservatism is a safe failure mode and the wiring must not lose that asymmetry.
- `Shape.uniform()` deliberately keeps the untouched `ctx x bytes/token` expression bit-identical for architectures that declare no per-layer window, so wiring must not accidentally route uniform architectures through the summed path — algebraically equal is not the same as bit-identical at every quant.
- `kvbudget.GLM52DSA` (`internal/kvbudget/kvbudget.go:121`) is the only other `Shape` literal in the module and leaves `PerLayer` nil. That is correct (GLM-5.2 is uniformly global), but a consumer must handle a nil profile rather than assume one.

## Related, not blocking

`internal/model/kvquant.go:185` carries its own independent `VHeadDim`-vs-`HeadDim` fallback plus per-layer/hybrid logic. Whether it needs the same window refinement was not audited. Flagging only — it is a separate question from the wiring above.

records.title: fix(dos): dos_commit_audit silently ignores its commit argument and audits HEAD, so a witness verdict can be attributed to the wrong sha
records.body:
## What happens

The `dos` MCP tool `dos_commit_audit` accepts a `commit` argument and **silently ignores it**, auditing `HEAD` instead. It reports the HEAD sha in its own `sha` field, so the response looks well-formed and authoritative — it is simply about a different commit than the one asked about.

Three calls, three different `commit` values, one workspace (`C:\work\fak`):

| `commit` passed | `sha` returned | `source_files` returned |
|---|---|---|
| `bc0988c11` | `b66a2dba5` | `internal/agent/stream_stall.go`, … |
| `affbb1c70` | `b66a2dba5` | `internal/agent/stream_stall.go`, … |
| `059d561a7` | `b66a2dba5` | `internal/agent/stream_stall.go`, … |

`b66a2dba5` was `HEAD` at the time. The three requested commits are unrelated to it and touch `internal/toolprocgate/`, `internal/gateway/`, and `internal/superloop/` respectively — none touches `internal/agent/`.

The argument is *declared*: passing it raises no validation error. It is accepted and dropped.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than documenting

The verdict is a **witness**. Its whole purpose is to answer "does commit X's diff do the kind of thing commit X's message claims". Auditing a different commit does not weaken that answer — it inverts it, because:

- The failure is **silent and directional**. A caller auditing an old, genuinely-unwitnessed commit gets `verdict: OK` whenever HEAD happens to be well-formed. The tool fails toward "witnessed", which is the unsafe direction for a gate.
- The response **self-reports a sha**, so a caller that logs the result records a true-looking statement about the wrong commit. Any downstream record built from this is mis-attributed at the source.
- Anything that closes issues on a commit-audit verdict is affected. The close-resolved arm's comments cite a resolving commit and say the close was "witnessed via `dos commit-audit` (verdict OK / diff-witnessed)". If the audit graded HEAD rather than the cited commit, the citation is not evidence for what it appears to attest.

Found while auditing a backlog of tickets that were fixed on trunk but never auto-closed, so the practical impact is not hypothetical — this is exactly the path that decides whether a fix is credited to its ticket.

## Note on the CLI

The installed `dos` CLI does not accept `--commit` at all (`dos: error: unrecognized arguments: --commit`), so the CLI and the MCP surface disagree about whether targeting a specific commit is even expressible. Worth settling both ways at once.

## Suggested resolution

Either honour `commit`, or reject it explicitly. A hard error on an argument that cannot be honoured is strictly better than a confident answer about the wrong object. If the audit is intentionally HEAD-only, the parameter should be removed from the schema and the tool should say so in its description.

Upstream note: the audit implementation lives in `dos-kernel`, so the fix likely belongs there; filing here because the close-resolved arm that consumes it operates on this repo's issues.

records.title: chore(triage): the backlog holds a dense population of already-fixed tickets — 15 of 23 examined were landed on trunk, and the close-resolved arm skipped 5 that named their issue correctly
records.body:
## The backlog contains a substantial population of tickets that are already fixed on trunk

An audit of the newest 400 open issues found **15 whose fix is already landed and witnessable by sha**. Eight of them were still open at audit time and have now been closed with the resolving commit cited:

| # | resolved by | note |
|---|---|---|
| 5399 | `affbb1c70` | SSE preamble opened before decode completes |
| 5415 | `affbb1c70` | duplicate of #5399, same commit |
| 5401 | `b74671ffc` | commit subject cites `(#3622)`, **not** #5401 |
| 5446 | `9640b729a` | structural `system[]` read failure named |
| 5407 | `bc0988c11` | reuse verdict pairs registered |
| 5111 | `dbcd6ac29` | resident-CUDA routed-expert path reachable |
| 5039 | `059d561a7` | steerpr overlay registered |
| 4989 | `89b47d6a3` | fired-but-no-ledger-row surfaced |

Each was verified by reading the commit and its file list directly, not from a self-report.

Scale context: ~**1316 open issues**. The sample was the newest 400; 64 of those were `idea-scout:` entries and excluded, leaving 336 actionable, of which only 23 were examined closely enough to reach a verdict. **The 15 come out of 23 examined** — so the density is high and the remaining ~1293 unexamined issues almost certainly hide more.

## Why they stayed open — it is not simply "no closing keyword"

The obvious theory is that the fix commits lack a `Fixes #N` trailer. That is true but insufficient, and worth stating precisely because it changes the remedy.

Measured over the 9,999 commits since 2026-06-01:

- **56.4%** (5,644) reference an issue as a bare `#NNNN`
- **9.3%** (930) use a closing keyword GitHub acts on

So ~47% of commits name their ticket in a form GitHub ignores. That is the headline gap.

But the repo does not rely on GitHub's native auto-close — there is a close-resolved arm that comments *"Resolved by `<sha>` … Closed by the DOS dispatch loop's close-resolved arm, witnessed via `dos commit-audit`"*. That arm demonstrably works: it has closed 30+ issues between 2026-07-21 and 2026-08-02, including three today.

**And yet 5 of the 8 commits above named the correct issue number in the subject and were still not closed.** So the arm reaches back through history, works, and skipped these. The gap is in the arm's *selection*, not only in commit-message hygiene.

One likely contributor, filed separately as #5521: `dos_commit_audit` silently ignores its `commit` argument and audits `HEAD` instead. Since the arm's own comment says its close is "witnessed via `dos commit-audit`", a mis-targeted audit would decide the wrong commit's witness status. That is a hypothesis about the arm, not a verified read of its source — worth confirming before designing a fix.

Two further causes observed:

1. **Wrong issue number in the trailer.** `b74671ffc` resolves #5401 while citing `(#3622)`. A wrong number is worse than none: it looks handled.
2. **Wrong-repo filing.** #5505's entire evidence base (`internal/leasequeue`, commit `dd27b113`) exists in neither `origin/main` nor the object DB; its own body concedes the code "lives in the kernel CLI outside this repo." A one-line `git cat-file -t <sha>` premise check catches this class.

## Cheap mitigation available today

Fix subjects are frequently near-verbatim restatements of the ticket title. One command surfaced 11 of the 15 verdicts with no source reading at all: dump `git log --since=<d> --format='%s'`, extract `#\d{3,5}`, intersect with the open-issue list. Worth running as a pre-dispatch filter so workers stop being spent on already-fixed tickets — that is the concrete cost here, and it was being paid.

Caveat: epics (#5170, #5015, #5315, #5289) are referenced by many commits and legitimately stay open, so the intersection is a triage queue, not an auto-close list.

## Not verified

- #5254 has a landed, witnessed fold (`2ab350829`) but is a measurement-style ticket rather than a named defect, so "fully discharged" is a judgement call. Left open deliberately.
- The remaining ~1293 unexamined open issues. The 15/23 density is from a sample deliberately weighted toward recent, symbol-naming tickets and should not be extrapolated linearly.

records.title: fix(gateway): /v1/completions never starts EP followers, so a legacy request enters a multi-rank collective no follower was released into
records.body:
## What

EP follower fanout is wired to the chat route only. `/v1/completions` never starts followers, so on a multi-rank EP deployment a legacy-completions request enters a multi-rank decode that its follower ranks were never told about.

Two independent reasons, both structural:

1. **The only production call site is the chat handler.** `startEPFanoutFollowers` is invoked at `internal/gateway/http.go:485`, on the chat path. Every other reference in the package is in `ep_fanout_test.go`. `handleCompletions` (`internal/gateway/completions.go:26`) never calls it.

2. **The endpoint list is hardcoded to the chat suffix.** `epFanoutURLsFromEnv` (`internal/gateway/http_epfanout.go:162`) builds each follower URL as:

   ```go
   urls = append(urls, strings.TrimRight(part, "/")+"/v1/chat/completions")
   ```

   So even if the legacy handler did call it, every follower would be asked for `/v1/chat/completions` — a different route with a different request schema than the one the front rank is serving.

## Why it matters

`startEPFanoutFollowers`' own doc comment states the constraint plainly (`http_epfanout.go:27-35`): rank-local expert parallelism reduces the routed-expert delta through a process-group AllReduce, and *"that collective makes progress only if every process reaches it."*

The legacy route does reach a multi-rank decode — `completions.go:85-90` describes `completeServed` as blocking "for the WHOLE decode" and names the "multi-rank decode" explicitly. So the front rank enters a collective that no follower has been released into.

This is the same failure class as #5514, which is why it surfaced while fixing it: #5514 was the *preamble* not being flushed before the collective join. This is the *followers* never joining at all. Fixing the first makes the second observable, because the client now gets its 200 and headers promptly and then waits.

## Confidence

**Verified by reading:** the single call site, the hardcoded suffix, and that `handleCompletions` does not call the fanout starter. These are direct reads of trunk at `b32ab0586`.

**Not verified:** the runtime consequence on real multi-rank hardware. I did not run a multi-rank EP deployment, so whether this manifests as a hang, a timeout, or a silently degraded single-rank result is inferred from the AllReduce contract in the doc comment rather than observed. Someone with the bridge live should confirm which before assuming severity.
