```
fatal: the remote end hung up unexpectedly
No refs in common and none specified; doing nothing.
```

and **exit 1** (observed on git 2.51.0).

## Why it matters

The empty namespace is not an exotic state — it is the state of every fresh clone, and of any host that has not yet taken a lease. So `fak leaseref sync` fails on exactly the machines most likely to run it first, with an error that reads like a network or remote-permission problem rather than "there was nothing to send".

## How this was found

Building the checkpoint-replication path for #5479, which reuses leaseref's ordering. The new code inherited the same assumption from the comment above, and its own `TestWipSyncEmptyNamespaceIsACleanNoOp` caught it on the first run:

```
--- FAIL: TestWipSyncEmptyNamespaceIsACleanNoOp (0.94s)
    wip_sync_test.go:215: sync of an empty namespace: git push origin +refs/fak/wip/*:refs/fak/wip/* exited 1
```

`wipref.wipSync` short-circuits an empty push for this reason. `leaseref` was deliberately not touched in that change — it was out of that lane — so the bug is still live here.

## The fix

Same shape as the one already in `internal/wipref/sync.go`: count the local refs in the namespace before pushing, and skip the push (reporting a clean no-op) when there are none. Correct the comment at `sync.go:53-55` while you are there — the fetch half of its claim is right and worth keeping, the push half is what misled.

## Verify

A test that runs `leaseref sync` against a throwaway `git init --bare` remote from a clone holding zero `refs/fak/locks/*`, asserting a clean exit. `internal/wipref/sync_test.go`'s `TestWipSyncEmptyNamespaceIsACleanNoOp` is a working model to copy — it builds the bare remote in a temp dir and never touches a real origin.

Found while landing #5479.

records.title: docs(config): FAK_USAGE_LOG is on by default and documented in zero markdown files
records.body:
`FAK_USAGE_LOG` is on by default, writes to the user config dir on nearly every invocation, and appears in zero markdown files.

## The gap

`grep -rn FAK_USAGE_LOG` hits **8 Go files and 0 documentation files.**

What it does, from the source rather than from docs:

- `usagelog.Enabled()` is **on by default**; `FAK_USAGE_LOG=off` disables it.
- `FAK_USAGE_LOG_PATH` overrides the destination.
- The default destination is `<user-config-dir>/fak/usage.jsonl`.
- It is written on essentially every invocation of the binary.

An on-by-default journal that writes to a user's home directory, with an opt-out that is only discoverable by reading Go source, is a front-door defect in the same class as #5465 — the binary does something an adopter would want to know about, and nothing tells them.

To be clear about scope: `internal/usagelog` imports no `net/http`. This is a **local** journal, not telemetry that leaves the machine. That is precisely why it should be easy to document plainly and put to rest.

## What to do

Give it a real home in the configuration reference: what is recorded, where it lands, that it is local-only, and how to turn it off. `INSTALL.md`'s "What's in the binary" section currently mentions it in passing and is, as of #5465, the **only** place it is described anywhere — that is a stopgap, not the right home.

## Verify

`grep -rn FAK_USAGE_LOG docs/ *.md` returns the new documentation, and the page states the default state, the default path, the opt-out spelling, and the local-only property.

Good first issue: it is a documentation change, the facts are all in `internal/usagelog`, and it needs no shared checkout or fleet tooling.

Found while landing #5465.

records.title: docs(scorecard): 13 docs still name the retired tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py, and fak score seo emits it in its own report
records.body:
`python tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py` is still the documented verification command in 13 live docs — and the Go tool that replaced it emits the dead command in its own output.

## The script does not exist

```
$ ls tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py
ls: cannot access 'tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py': No such file or directory

$ git log --oneline -1 -- tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py
16be4d9d9e chore(scorecard): retire the seo-aeo python tool, wire callers to Go (#4205) (fak score)
```

It was ported to the `fak score seo` verb (`cmd/fak/seoaeoscore.go` over `internal/seoaeoscore`). The port landed; the callers named in prose did not all move with it.

## Two halves

### 1. Thirteen docs still tell a reader to run it

Each of these carries `python tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py` as a **verification step** — the "run this to prove your change is good" line at the bottom of the page:

- `docs/adoption/casts/README.md`
- `docs/adoption/compare/matrix.md`
- `docs/adoption/compare/vs-firewall.md`
- `docs/adoption/compare/vs-guardrails.md`
- `docs/adoption/compare/vs-routers.md`
- `docs/adoption/compare/vs-serving-engines.md`
- `docs/adoption/concept-card.md`
- `docs/adoption/launch-kit.md`
- `docs/adoption/naming.md`
- `docs/adoption/objections.md`
- `docs/adoption/signals.md` (two places — a table row and a command block)
- `docs/adoption/social-storyboard.md`
- `docs/enterprise-positioning.md`

Replacement spelling is `fak score seo` (add `--scope core` where the original passed a scope). `CONTRIBUTING.md` was already corrected in #5450 and is **not** part of this.

### 2. The replacement tool emits the retired command in its own report

This is the sharper half. `internal/seoaeoscore/render.go` generates the scorecard body, and three of its strings still name the script it replaced:

- `~line 112` — "The measuring TOOL is public (`tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py`)"
- `~line 116` — the HTML provenance comment: `process: tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py`
- `~line 118` — the regenerate instruction: ``Regenerate + transfer: `python tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py --scope %s --transfer --stamp DATE` ``

So running `fak score seo --markdown` today produces a document instructing the reader to run a script that was deleted in order to regenerate it. The provenance comment also misattributes the artifact to a process that did not produce it.

The regenerate line has a second defect: **`fak score seo` has no `--transfer` flag.** Its full flag set is `--workspace --scope --json --markdown --stamp --compare`. So that instruction names a dead script *and* a flag that does not exist in the replacement — copying it and substituting the verb still fails.

Whoever fixes this needs to decide what the transfer step actually is now, or drop the claim. Do not invent a `--transfer` flag to make the sentence true.

## Verify

```
grep -rn "tools/seo_aeo_scorecard.py" --include=*.md --include=*.go . \
  | grep -v docs/notes/ \
  | grep -v concept-disambiguation-scorecard \
  | grep -v _scratch/
```

should return nothing. Then `fak score seo --markdown --scope core` and confirm the emitted body names only commands that exist.

Out of scope deliberately: dated records under `docs/notes/` (historical, correct as written for their date) and the generated `docs/concept-disambiguation-scorecard/README.md` row, which regenerates from its own corpus.

Found while landing #5450.

records.title: feat(gateway): wire the EP decode coordinator into serve and retire the request mirror for in-kernel decode (#5532 follow-on)
records.body:
Wire `model.EPDecodeCoordinator` / `RunEPFollower` into the serve path, and retire the HTTP request mirror for in-kernel decode.

## Where this comes from

#5532 asked for an in-loop rank barrier so the EP fanout could cover `/v1/fak/agent/sessions`. Settling it produced three results:

1. **The barrier already exists.** `model.EPDecodeCoordinator` / `model.RunEPFollower` (#4835, `internal/model/ep_decode_coord.go`) is announced from `Session.Prefill` and `Session.Step` (`internal/model/kv.go`). Its unit is finer than a turn, so it covers an owned loop's N forward passes route-agnostically, and a parked follower never tokenizes, never samples, and structurally cannot execute a tool.
2. **It has zero non-test callers.** On the tracked tree the only references are the definition, the `epCoord` field in `internal/model/weights.go`, and a comment. Its own doc names the gap: "the cmd/fak + internal/gateway serve wiring that parks follower ranks in RunEPFollower".
3. **A second route had the same defect and it was worse.** Under `fak serve --native`, `/v1/messages` drives the same owned loop via `agent.RunArm(fak=true)`, on a pattern the coverage gate classified COVERED. With one follower configured, a two-turn native request drove **4 forward passes and 2 tool-result turns** instead of 2 and 1 — the follower re-ran the whole governed loop and dispatched the tool a second time.

(3) is fixed: `handleAnthropicMessages` now skips the fanout when `s.native` is set. That trades an unrecoverable duplicated side effect for a loud stall, which is the same judgement #5528 made for agent-sessions. **This ticket is the real fix** — the stall.

## The work

Rank 0 installs the coordinator, rank > 0 parks in `RunEPFollower`, and the per-request HTTP mirror is retired for in-kernel decode. The mirror is a per-request stand-in for a barrier that now exists at a better layer.

## The blocker to settle first

**Prefix reuse and the coordinator currently contradict each other.** `epCheckMirror` fails closed on a position mismatch, and `internal/agent/inkernel_decode.go` does prefix reuse (`ids[prefillAt:checkpoint]`) — the exact desync it refuses. So wiring the coordinator requires one of:

- disable prefix reuse on the coordinated path (costs the prefill saving on multi-rank), or
- teach `epCheckMirror` about prefix reuse (keeps the saving, more subtle).

Decide this explicitly and record why. Do not wire the coordinator without resolving it — it will fail closed at the first reused prefix.

## Also worth doing here

The #5528 coverage gate classifies by route **pattern** only, and `/v1/messages` proved a pattern can be covered in one server mode and owned-loop in another. Consider keying the classification on **(pattern, mode)** so a future `--native`-only branch on `/v1/responses` or `/v1/chat/completions` cannot repeat this silently. Today `s.native` appears in exactly three places, all in `messages.go`, plus the `ownsSessionLoop()` accessor — so the blast radius of getting this wrong is currently one route, and that will not stay true.

## Honest constraint

**Nothing here is witnessable without real multi-rank hardware.** The existing suite models all of this in-process with no weights and no device; the hardware consequence is inferred from the AllReduce contract, not measured. Anyone taking this should say up front whether they have a multi-rank target, because the interesting failure modes (hang vs timeout vs silently degraded single-rank answer) are exactly the ones a single-process model cannot show.

Follow-on to #5532 and #4835.

records.title: fak node install owns com.fak.serve-gateway and hardcodes the Anthropic upstream, so a local-model gateway cannot be installed
records.body:
`fak node install` owns the launchd label `com.fak.serve-gateway` and hardcodes the Anthropic upstream into it, so a local-model gateway cannot be installed by the sanctioned installer.

## The collision

`cmd/fak/node.go:122` fixes one label for the installed unit:

```go
// nodeGatewayLabel is the launchd / systemd service name.
const nodeGatewayLabel = "com.fak.serve-gateway"
```

`tools/install-mac-node.sh` uses the same label, and so does the local-model gateway recipe in `docs/fak/mac-agent-ui.md`. One label means one loaded unit, so the adjudication proxy and the local-model gateway cannot coexist on a Mac. #5458 documented this as a warning ("settle this before you install") because the doc lane could not fix the code; this is the code half.

## Why the installer cannot just be used for both

The plist template at `cmd/fak/node.go:306-307` pins the upstream:

```go
<string>--provider</string><string>anthropic</string>
<string>--base-url</string><string>https://api.anthropic.com</string>
```

and `fak node install`'s flag set is `--addr --port --remote --key-env --rotate-key --uninstall` — there is no way to set `--base-url`, `--model`, or the environment variables a local-model unit needs. So the installer can only ever produce the Anthropic unit, and anyone wanting the other one must hand-write a plist that then collides with it.

## What to settle

Two defensible shapes; pick one and record why:

1. **Derive the label from what is installed** — e.g. `com.fak.serve-gateway` for the default and a suffixed label when a non-default upstream is configured, so both units can be loaded at once. Needs `--uninstall` and `status` to learn which labels exist rather than assuming the constant.
2. **Keep one label and teach the installer the other upstream** — add `--base-url` / `--model` (and a way to pass `EnvironmentVariables`), so there is exactly one installer and the label genuinely names one thing.

(1) is more useful if anyone actually runs both; (2) is smaller and keeps `launchctl list` legible. Do not do half of each — the failure mode being fixed is precisely that the label does not identify the unit.

## Verify

Whichever shape: installing the local-model gateway and the adjudication proxy on the same Mac must not require uninstalling one, OR `fak node install --help` must be able to produce both. Then drop the collision warning at `docs/fak/mac-agent-ui.md:236` and the `--uninstall`-first workaround it prescribes.

Found while landing #5458.

records.title: fak wip has no remote-deletion path, and the leaseref drain shape is unsafe to copy verbatim for checkpoints
records.body:
`fak wip` can now publish checkpoints to a remote but has no way to delete them, and the obvious drainer can destroy a peer's only copy of uncommitted work.

## Where this comes from

#5479 added the publish half: `fak wip sync` pushes `refs/fak/wip/*` to a remote and fetches peers' checkpoints into a read-only per-remote mirror at `refs/fak/remotewip/<remote>/*`. Deletion was deliberately left out and named rather than half-built.

## Why it is not just "copy leaseref drain"

`fak leaseref drain` (`cmd/fak/leaseref.go:74`, `:785`, #5358) is the working model for the mechanics — it delete-pushes proven-expired ids, opts into the pre-push bulk-deletion gate the hook reserves for exactly this drainer, and has a report mode that mutates nothing before `--apply` does the live drain. Copy that shape.

What does **not** carry over is the safety argument. A lease ref is a *claim*; deleting an expired one destroys nothing, which is why "proven expired from the LOCAL ref view" is a sufficient target rule there. A checkpoint ref is *the work itself* — a `commit-tree` snapshot of an uncommitted delta. On a remote, it may be the **only surviving copy** of a peer's work if that peer's machine is the thing that died, which is the entire scenario the mirror was built for. So a drainer that reuses leaseref's expiry rule would delete precisely the checkpoints the feature exists to preserve.

## What to settle before writing the delete path

1. **What makes a remote checkpoint safe to delete?** Candidate: its delta is provably contained in a commit reachable from the remote's default branch — i.e. the same question `wip reap` already answers locally, but asked against the remote rather than this HEAD. "Old" is not an answer; an old checkpoint of unlanded work is the most valuable one.
2. **Who is allowed to delete whose?** Draining only your OWN sessions' refs is defensible without further argument. Draining a peer's needs a stated rule and probably an explicit opt-in flag.
3. **Report mode must come first and be genuinely read-only** — including on the remote.

## Also deferred from #5479, and cheaper

`fak wip status --fleet`: today `status` grades replication for one remote from the local mirror (`--remote`, a local ref read, never a network probe). A fleet view needs a **stamped mirror listing** — when each remote's mirror was last fetched — so the report can distinguish "this peer has no checkpoints" from "this clone has not fetched that peer since Tuesday". Without the stamp the fleet column would silently present staleness as absence, which is the same class of overstatement `ClassifyReplication` was careful to avoid. That stamp is the shared prerequisite for any garden-tick consumer of wip state too, so it is worth landing on its own before either reader is written.

## Verify

For the drainer: a test against a throwaway `git init --bare` remote (`internal/wipref/sync_test.go` builds one and never touches a real origin) showing report mode deletes nothing, and that a checkpoint whose delta is NOT reachable from the remote's branch survives `--apply`.

Deferred from #5479. Related: #5358.

records.title: SessionStart driver-pid witness is prospective-only and misses a node-wrapped driver, so two first-generation shapes still defer forever
records.body:
The SessionStart driver-pid witness is prospective-only and matches one process image stem, so two real first-generation session shapes still defer forever.

## Where this comes from

#5542 (`e029f0513`) closed the leak where a session never launched through `fak` had no launch-ledger row, so the stopped-driver liveness probe could not answer "is this driver alive?" and deferred on every tick. SessionStart now walks up to eight ancestor hops and records a witnessed driver pid.

That fix is real and lands the common case. Two gaps were named at the time rather than papered over, and both are still open.

## 1. It only helps sessions started AFTER it was installed

SessionStart runs at session start. A first-generation session that is **already running** never gets a row — the one hook that could witness its pid has already fired. So the population the fix was written for (sessions started by hand, before `fak` was in the picture) is exactly the population that keeps deferring until it exits.

Worth deciding: is a backfill possible at all? A later hook in the same process tree — the Stop hook, or any guard invocation — could run the same ancestor walk and write the same row, which would close this without a new mechanism. The reason not to do it in #5542 was scope, not impossibility. If the answer is "no backfill, the session must restart", say so in the docs so an operator stops waiting for a reclaim that will never come.

## 2. The walk matches a process image stem, and a node-wrapped driver has a different one

`guardSessionStartDriverPIDIn` (`cmd/fak/guard_sessionstart.go:252`) returns the first ancestor where:

```go
if dispatchProcessImageMatchesProduct(p.Name, "claude") {
```

Matching on the image stem rather than the cmdline is deliberate and correct for the case it was built against — it is what stops `fak guard -- claude ...` from being mistaken for the driver it wraps, since the wrapper's stem is `fak`. But it also means a driver launched through a Node wrapper (`node .../cli.js`) presents the stem `node` and is never recognized, so the walk runs out of hops and returns 0 — correctly reported as "not witnessed" rather than "gone", but still a permanent defer for that install shape.

Fixing this needs a rule that admits the wrapper without re-admitting `fak guard`. Cmdline inspection is the obvious lever and the one the current code deliberately avoids; if it is used here it should be narrow (a `node` stem whose argv names the driver entrypoint) and it must keep the `fak guard --` case failing to match. Add a test for both directions — the wrapper matching, and `fak guard -- claude` still not matching — because that pair is the whole contract.

## Verify

For (2): a table test over synthetic `procguard.Proc` chains, which is how `guardSessionStartDriverPIDIn` is already tested — it is the pure half and takes the snapshot as an argument, so neither gap needs a live process tree to witness.

Deferred from #5542.

records.title: fix(cmd): `fak capabilities` is implemented, tested and advertised by fak guard, but has no dispatch arm
records.body:
`fak capabilities` is fully implemented and tested, has no dispatch arm, and `fak guard`'s own help tells you to run it.

This is the same defect #5546 closed for `fak idea-scout`, in a second verb. The comment that landed with that fix (`cmd/fak/main.go:547-552`) describes the shape exactly: a verb shipped with an implementation, a doc page, and skill lines pointing agents at it — "but never a dispatch arm, so the advertised verb" is unreachable.

## Witness

```
$ fak capabilities
fak: unknown verb "capabilities"
  'fak help' shows the overview; 'fak help --all' lists every verb.

$ fak dev capabilities
fak dev: unknown verb "capabilities"
```

Yet the implementation is right there, complete with usage text and flag parsing:

- `cmd/fak/capabilities.go:22` — `func runCapabilities(stdout, stderr io.Writer, argv []string) int`
- `cmd/fak/capabilities.go:23` — `flag.NewFlagSet("capabilities", ...)`, supporting `--root`, `--json`, `--limit`, and a free-text intent
- `cmd/fak/capabilities.go:68` — `writeCapabilitiesUsage`
- `cmd/fak/capabilities_test.go` — three passing tests covering `--json`, an intent query, and the `--limit -1` refusal

`runCapabilities` has **zero** production callers. Grep it and every hit outside its own definition is in `capabilities_test.go`. The tests are green, which is why nothing has flagged it: the code is exercised, just never reachable from a command line.

## The binary advertises it

`cmd/fak/guard_capabilities.go:22` prints, verbatim:

```
fak guard: self-describe — `fak capabilities [<intent>]` or the fak_capabilities MCP tool
lists the memory-forward toolbelt (memq drivers, fak index * verbs, fak_changes/dos_arbitrate),
each card carrying the exact call to make
```

So an operator who reads fak's own output is told to run a verb fak refuses. The MCP half of that sentence (`mcp__fak__fak_capabilities`) does work — only the CLI half is missing.

## Three more sites point agents at it

- `.claude/skills/field-borrow/SKILL.md:3` — in the skill's `description`, i.e. the line that decides whether the skill gets invoked at all: "DOGFOODS fak's own self-query surface (`fak_feature_query` / `fak capabilities` / `fak index docs|leaves|verbs|claims`)"
- `.claude/skills/field-borrow/SKILL.md:58` — "**`fak_feature_query`** (MCP) / `fak capabilities <intent>` — intent → ranked capability"
- `.claude/skills/study-repo/SKILL.md:219` — "Dogfood `fak_feature_query` / `fak capabilities` / `fak index docs|leaves|verbs|claims`"

Both skills present the MCP tool and the CLI verb as interchangeable. An agent running the CLI half gets `unknown verb` and has no way to tell that it was told to run something that never existed, versus something that broke.

`INDEX.md:364` also describes a past field-borrow pass as having dogfooded "`fak capabilities`/`fak index`".

## Expected fix

Add the dispatch arm next to its siblings in `cmd/fak/main.go` — `idea-scout` is at `:547` and shows the pattern, including a comment recording why the arm was missing:

```go
case "capabilities":
    os.Exit(runCapabilities(os.Stdout, os.Stderr, os.Args[2:]))
```

Note `runCapabilities` returns an `int` rather than taking `os.Args[2:]` and exiting itself, so match whatever convention the neighbouring int-returning verbs use rather than copying `cmdPolicy`'s shape blindly.

## Done when

1. `fak capabilities` runs and prints the toolbelt; `fak capabilities --json` parses; `fak capabilities compact my context` returns ranked cards.
2. A test asserts the verb is *reachable*, not merely that `runCapabilities` works — the three existing tests already pass today with the verb unreachable, so extending them proves nothing. Assert against the dispatch path.
3. `fak help --all` lists it, so the next audit of docs-vs-verbs sees it.

## Related sighting, not part of this

`docs/integrations/codex-memories.md:20` has a surface-map row formatted as a command, `` `fak memq` | Query/inspection boundary ``, and `fak memq` does not exist in either namespace. Unlike `capabilities` there is no implementation behind it — the nearest real verbs are `fak dev memory` and `fak dev memory-read`. That one is a docs decision (name the real verb, or say the surface is not built), not a wiring fix, so it should be its own issue if someone wants it.

Found by auditing every backticked `fak <verb>` in tracked docs against the live verb table. Most other misses were honest: `fak perf`, `fak checkpoint` and `fak elide-witness` are each described in place as a named follow-on that does not exist yet, and `CLAIMS.md:188` says so in as many words.

records.title: docs(integrations): codex-memories lists `fak memq` as a command and no such verb exists in either namespace
records.body:
`docs/integrations/codex-memories.md:20` lists `fak memq` in a surface-map table formatted as commands, and no such verb exists.

## Witness

```
$ fak memq
fak: unknown verb "memq"
  did you mean 'fak dev demo'?

$ fak dev memq
fak dev: unknown verb "memq"
```

The row:

```
| `fak memq` | Query/inspection boundary | Read-back aid, not proof by itself |
```

Every other row in that table names something you can actually run, so a reader has no way to tell this one is different. The backtick-plus-`fak`-prefix formatting is what makes it a defect rather than a naming choice.

## This is a docs fix, not a wiring fix

Unlike [#5558](https://github.com/anthony-chaudhary/fak/issues/5558) — where `fak capabilities` is fully implemented and merely undispatched — there is no CLI implementation behind `memq`. `internal/memq` is a real package, but it is a **subsystem**, not a verb. The nearest things an operator can actually run are:

```
fak memory drivers [--json]
fak memory recall ...
```

(`fak memory <subcommand>` — confirmed from its usage output.)

## Every other `memq` mention in the docs is already honest

Worth stating so nobody sweeps them:

- `docs/integrations/agent-memory.md:213` — "Store as a `memq` backend … `internal/memq`" — names it as the package it is.
- `docs/notes/CONCEPT-MEMORY-VIEW-FORMATS-2026-07-03.md:86` — "Not wired into `memq`'s driver-level renderer yet" — explicitly describes it as internal and unwired.
- `docs/notes/O1-TURN-CONTEXT-PLANNER-2026-06-23.md:68` — "`memq` already gives a memory **query language**" — subsystem, no `fak ` prefix.
- `docs/concept-disambiguation-scorecard/INDEX.md:1639` — a bare `memq` cell in the concept scorecard, correctly unprefixed.

Only the `codex-memories.md` row prefixes it with `fak ` and puts it in a command column.

## Expected fix

One of:

1. Name the real verb — replace with `fak memory` / `fak memory recall` if that is what the boundary actually is. Check what the surrounding rows describe before substituting; the row's job is "query/inspection boundary" and `fak memory recall` may or may not be it.
2. Drop the `fak ` prefix and the command formatting, so the row reads as the subsystem `memq` like every other mention in the tree.

Option 2 is the safe default if the mapping in option 1 is not obvious from the page's context.

## Done when

`fak memq` appears in no tracked doc as a runnable command, and `docs/integrations/codex-memories.md`'s surface map either names a verb that resolves or stops formatting a subsystem as a verb.

Found by auditing every backticked `fak <verb>` in tracked docs against the live verb table. Note for whoever picks this up: the verb index is not the whole table — `fak dev` dispatches a further ~240 verbs and `fak mac` sits outside both, so check a candidate against `fak <v> --help` **and** `fak dev <v> --help` before calling it missing.

records.title: perf(capindex): the skill card carries the full description twice, so 98% of the resident skill floor is prose (epic #3229)
records.body:
Epic **#3229** wants the always-sent token floor smaller. For `.claude/skills` the measurement
landed (#3234) and the ratchet landed (#5444), but the **trim** — the part that actually returns
tokens — has never had an issue of its own. #5444 scoped itself to "stopping the bleeding" and
named this as out of scope, so it would otherwise survive only as a sentence inside a closed
ticket.

## The headroom, measured

`go test ./internal/skillfootprint/ -run TestSkillDescriptionBudgetPassesAtHEAD -v` prints the
current floor:

```
resident description floor: 47236 bytes (~11809 est. tokens) across 58 skills (budget 47236, slack 2000)
  top 1:  1877 B  study-repo
  top 2:  1599 B  resume-watchdog-audit
  top 3:  1471 B  scout-loop
  top 4:  1359 B  super-loop
  top 5:  1332 B  field-borrow
  top 6:  1270 B  trajectory-control
```

`fak skill footprint` reports `name-only floor = 787 B` against that 47,236 B. So **~98% of the
resident skill index is description prose**, and every skill stays invocable by name without a
byte of it. That ratio is the whole opportunity.

## Why it is still all resident: one field, copied into two places

`internal/capindex/skill_resolver.go:80-102` puts the **entire** `description` into both the
at-rest card and the ranking key:

```go
cardBytes, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
    "name":        e.name,
    "version":     e.fm.version,
    "description": e.fm.description,   // :87 — full prose in the at-rest card
    "tags":        e.fm.tags,
})
...
Trigger:   e.fm.description,           // :99 — the same full prose as the ranking key
```

There is no "one-line intent" anywhere in the type. #3234's promise of a `name + one-line-intent`
index does not exist in the code, which is why the floor could grow 30% in 20 days unopposed.

## What this issue is

The two undelivered items from #3234, restated with today's line numbers:

1. **Split the at-rest card from the faulted body.** `CardBytes` should carry what is needed to
   *decide whether to load a skill* — name, version, tags, and a short intent line — not the
   full description. The full prose becomes fault-in-on-selection.
2. **Migrate the heaviest descriptions.** The six above are ~8.9 kB between them. A one-line
   intent per skill plus a faulted body is where the banked win comes from.

## Design questions to settle first

- **Is `Trigger` allowed to shrink?** It is the ranking key. If selection quality depends on the
  full prose, then shrinking `Trigger` trades tokens for worse skill selection, which is a real
  cost and not obviously the right trade. Measure before assuming; a shrunk `Trigger` that picks
  the wrong skill costs far more than 11.8k tokens.
- **Where does the one-line intent come from?** A new frontmatter field is honest but requires
  touching 58 `SKILL.md` files. Deriving it (first sentence of `description`) needs no migration
  but silently degrades for any skill whose first sentence is not self-contained. Deriving-with-an-
  override is the likely answer; pick deliberately.
- **What does the ratchet do when the win lands?** By design, trimming materially below the pin
  reds `SKILL_DESC_BUDGET_STALE` until `SkillDescriptionBudgetBytes` is re-pinned down in the same
  commit. That is the intended flow, not a problem — but whoever does the trim should expect it
  and bank the win rather than being surprised by a red.

## Done when

- The resident skill index prices materially below 47,236 B with every skill still invocable and
  still selected correctly.
- `SkillDescriptionBudgetBytes` is re-pinned down in the same commit as the trim, so the win is
  banked rather than left as headroom.
- Skill-selection quality is shown not to regress — whatever the existing evidence for selection
  quality is, it must still hold with the shrunk `Trigger`.

## Not in scope

- The ratchet itself (#5444, shipped).
- The measurement verb (#3234, shipped).
- MCP tool schema / description slices (#3230, #3231, #3232) — different axis, already gated.

Follow-on to #3234 (items 2 and 3) and #5444. Part of epic #3229.

records.title: fix(cmd): the ambient lease-ref sync passes context.Background() to a network git push, so a slow remote hangs the loop-drive tick forever
records.body:
Found while landing #4324. This is the root cause of a test hang that has been reading as an unrelated flake for a while, so it is worth its own ticket.

## The defect

`cmd/fak/leaseref_sync_ambient.go:82`:

```go
if _, err := store.Sync(context.Background(), step.Remote, push, fetch); err != nil {
```

`store.Sync` shells out to `git push` / `git fetch` against a real remote. `context.Background()` never cancels, and `internal/leaseref/runner.go` has no independent deadline of its own, so there is no upper bound on how long that call can block. A slow, hanging, or auth-stalled remote blocks the loop-drive tick indefinitely.

## Evidence

Captured stack from the hang:

```
leaseref.gitRunner … exec.Cmd.Run → WaitForSingleObject   (internal/leaseref/runner.go:25)
  ← Store.runSyncDirection "push" origin <refspec>        (internal/leaseref/sync.go:125, :104)
  ← ambientLeaseRefSyncImpl: store.Sync(context.Background(), …)  (cmd/fak/leaseref_sync_ambient.go:82)
  ← syncLoopDriveTickLeaseRefs                            (cmd/fak/leaseref_sync_ambient.go:96)
  ← (*loopDriveRegionHold).ensure                         (cmd/fak/loop_drive_region.go:202)
  ← superloopDriveRegionAdmit                             (cmd/fak/superloop_drive.go:90)
```

## Why it matters beyond production

`TestSuperloopDriveEnvBatchRaisesDefaultThroughput` has been hanging until the test timeout and reading as an environment flake. It is not. `newLoopDriveRegionHold` binds to the process cwd, so running the `cmd/fak` suite from a real checkout makes that test issue a live `git push` against the real remote and block in `WaitForSingleObject`.

Two independent confirmations that the lease-ref count is NOT the cause (an earlier hypothesis, since refuted): it still hung with only 3 lock refs; and with `FAK_LEASEREF_SYNC=off` the whole `TestSuperloopDrive*` family passes, the previously-hanging test in **2.33s**.

So this one unbounded context is why the `cmd/fak` package suite is not cleanly runnable unmodified. Fixing it has leverage well beyond the hang itself.

## Suggested shape

Give the ambient sync a bounded context — a deadline appropriate for a best-effort convergence step, not an unbounded one. The sync is already advisory at this call site: every error is collected into `LeaseRefSyncAttempt{Err: …}` and reported rather than propagated, so a deadline expiry has a natural, already-implemented home. Consider whether the bound belongs at this call site or lower, in `leaseref.Store` itself, so every ambient caller inherits it — there is at least one other `Sync` caller worth auditing at the same time.

## Done when

- No ambient lease-ref sync call passes a context that cannot expire.
- A test pins that a stalled git runner causes the sync to give up and report, rather than block — the injected-runner seam in `internal/leaseref` can simulate it without a real remote.
- `go test ./cmd/fak/ -run TestSuperloopDrive -count=1` completes without needing `FAK_LEASEREF_SYNC=off`.

Refs #4324

records.title: fix(dispatch): three spawn-failure returns strand the lane lease for the full TTL — two of them are unreachable by any releaser
records.body:
`dispatchTickLiveSpawn` acquires the lane lease at its top and returns on three failure paths without ever handing it back, so a lane that never ran a worker is held for the full TTL.

## What is there now

`acquireDispatchLaneLease` is called first thing in `dispatchTickLiveSpawn` (`cmd/fak/dispatch_tick.go`). Three paths then return early:

| path | verdict | fence sidecar written? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| broker refused the launch | `SPAWN_BROKER_DENIED` | no |
| the spawner itself errored | `SPAWN_FAILED` | no |
| the process exited immediately after spawn | `SPAWN_FAILED` | yes |

Each does `payload["ok"] = false`, `recordDispatchPayload(...)`, `return finish(payload), nil`. None releases the lease. Nothing else in the tick will: the witness sweep is the only releaser (`9657fa05d`, #4324) and it is keyed on a spawned worker's log stem.

## Why the first two are the worse pair

`writeDispatchLeaseFenceSidecar(spawned.Log, lease)` runs *after* the spawner returns, so on the broker-denied and spawner-errored paths there is no `spawned.Log` and no sidecar at all. The #4324 releaser refuses without one — correctly, it cannot prove the lease is ours — so those two lanes are unreachable by any releaser and are pinned for `WorkerTimeoutS + LeaseTTLMarginS`, roughly forty minutes, having done no work.

The third path already writes the sidecar, so a sweep could in principle reach it; whether it does depends on the dead-pid gate seeing a pid that exited before the sweep ran. That one is worth confirming rather than assuming.

## Shape of a fix

The lease is in scope at all three returns and the fencing token is in hand at the acquire, so a released-on-the-way-out helper can present `{holder, generation}` to `leaseref.ReleaseFenced` directly, without a sidecar round trip. It must keep #4324's guard: a **zero generation is refused outright**, because `ReleaseFenced` skips its generation comparison when either side is 0 (see the doc comment on `internal/leaseref/release.go`), which degrades the fence to a holder-string match — and holders collide, since a reused daemon presents the same `host:pid`. A release that ignores that could free a lane out from under the peer that now owns it.

A failed hand-back must stay non-fatal: degrade to today's behaviour, keep the TTL, record the reason on the payload.

## Adjacent, smaller

`#4324`'s graded row records `lease_released` or `lease_release_refused` but has no `lease_release_retried` rung, so a transient `LEASE_CONTENDED` (the ref advanced between the read and the CAS delete — the one outcome that *is* worth retrying) is indistinguishable in the ledger from a permanent refusal.

Found while verifying #4324; not in that unit's scope.

records.title: fix(dispatch): lane leases carry no SessionID, so every one classifies peer-unknown and the reclaim path can never fire
records.body:
Every lane lease the Go dispatcher takes classifies `peer-unknown`, so the reclaim path that exists for exactly this case can never fire on one and the only way a dispatch lane comes back is the TTL.

## The gap

`leaseref.ClassifyLive` sorts a live lease into `self | peer-live | peer-dead | peer-unknown` keyed on the session descriptor, and `peer-unknown` fails closed to not-reclaimable — deliberately, per `internal/leaseref/leaseref.go` and `internal/leaseref/cascade.go`: *"an absent descriptor is peer-unknown, never proof of death."*

`acquireDispatchLaneLease` (`cmd/fak/dispatch_tick.go`) never populates `Record.SessionID`. `git grep -n SessionID -- cmd/fak/dispatch_tick.go` returns nothing. So the classifier has no descriptor to key on, every dispatch lane lease lands in `peer-unknown`, and a lease whose owning session is provably gone is retained anyway until it ages out.

The reclaim machinery is built and tested; dispatch simply never hands it the one field it needs.

## The constraint any fix has to respect

There is a deliberate, load-bearing decision immediately adjacent, and it is not the same field:

```go
// SelfID stays empty on purpose: a live lease under this very id (a previous
// worker on this lane, still running) must refuse here exactly as it always
// has — with a pinned FAK_LEASE_OWNER the fence would otherwise read the new
// tick as the SAME holder and silently renew, double-spawning the lane.
```

That is about `regionadmit.Request` **at admission** — it keeps a new tick from recognising itself as the incumbent. Stamping `Record.SessionID` on the lease **being written** is a different seam: it is evidence for a later reader about who owned this, not an identity the acquire compares against. A fix should say which of the two it is touching and show that the double-spawn refusal still holds, because the two are one screen apart and easy to conflate.

## Checkable end state

A dispatch-acquired lease whose session has published a terminal STOPPED state classifies `peer-dead` and is reclaimable; a lease whose session is still live classifies `peer-live` and is not; and the existing "previous worker on this lane, still running" case still refuses at acquire.

Found while verifying #4324 (landed `9657fa05d`), which hands a lane back when a worker exits *normally*. This is the other half: the lane whose owner died without exiting.

records.title: fix(cmd): fak wip sync reports Pushed=true for a push it never ran, and disagrees with its leaseref sibling
records.body:
`fak wip sync` reports `Pushed: true` for a push it deliberately never ran, and two of its comments cite a sentence that is being corrected out of existence.

## The dishonest field

`cmd/fak/wip_sync.go` short-circuits an empty checkpoint namespace — correctly, and for exactly the right reason (a zero-match push refspec can exit 1; see #5550). But the skip records itself as a success:

```go
if len(local) == 0 {
    res.Pushed = true
} else {
    ...actually push...
}
```

`Pushed` is the field a reader consults to answer "did this clone publish?", and here it answers yes for a subprocess that never started. `SyncResult.Published` separately reads 0, so the information is recoverable by someone who knows to cross-check — but that is a workaround for the field, not a defence of it.

`internal/leaseref` grew the same short-circuit for the same reason and chose the opposite shape deliberately: `Pushed` stays **false** and a separate `PushSkippedEmpty bool` carries the no-op, so a ledger can tell "published my leases" from "had none to publish". Two sibling substrates now disagree about what `Pushed` means, which is worse than either choice alone.

## The stale citations

Both of these quote `internal/leaseref/sync.go:53-55` as a *live wrong claim* to argue against:

- `cmd/fak/wip_sync.go` (~86): *leaseref/sync.go states that "a wildcard refspec matching ZERO refs is a successful no-op in git" — that holds for fetch, but NOT for push*
- `cmd/fak/wip_sync_test.go` (~209): the same sentence, quoted in full

The quoted sentence is being corrected in the #5550 fix — the file now says the asymmetry outright. Once that lands, both comments argue with a strawman that no longer exists in the tree, and a reader following the citation finds text that already agrees with them.

## Suggested end state

- `Pushed` false + a `PushSkippedEmpty`-shaped field, matching `internal/leaseref.SyncResult`, so the two substrates agree.
- Both comments repointed at what `internal/leaseref/sync.go` says now, keeping the reasoning and dropping the disagreement.
- Whatever reads `SyncResult` (the `--json` surface, any ledger row) checked for a consumer that treats `Pushed` as "a push happened" and would flip behaviour. That check is the part worth doing carefully; the field change itself is small.

Found by the worker on #5550 while deciding which shape to give the new field; outside that ticket's fence.

records.title: fix(cmd): fak session ls --fleet fetches peer refs with context.Background(), so a stalled remote hangs the command
records.body:
`fak session ls --fleet` fetches peer session refs with `context.Background()`, so a stalled remote hangs the command with no deadline anywhere below it.

## The gap

`cmd/fak/session_inventory.go:131-135`:

```go
ctx := context.Background()
// Best-effort fetch: a fleet view of peers' sessions needs the remote refs, but a
// missing remote / no network must degrade to "the C2 refs this clone already has",
// never fail the whole listing (the same fail-open posture as leaseref publish).
if _, ferr := store.Sync(ctx, remote, false, true); ferr != nil {
```

The fail-open posture is right and is not what this ticket disputes. The gap is that fail-open only covers **cannot reach** the remote, not **cannot finish reaching** it. `store.Sync` shells out to a real `git fetch`; `internal/leaseref` carries no deadline of its own; so an auth-stalled or black-holed remote parks the command inside `exec.Cmd.Run` indefinitely and the stderr degradation line is never printed.

`store.LiveSessions(ctx, now)` on the next line inherits the same unbounded context.

## Why this is filed separately rather than fixed in #5564

#5564 bounded the **ambient** lease-ref sync — the one on the loop-drive tick, where an unbounded wait wedges an automated loop. This site is different in kind and was deliberately left alone there: `fak session ls --fleet` is foreground, operator-invoked, one-shot, Ctrl-C-able, and on no tick, so it cannot wedge a loop. It is a worse *interactive* experience, not a stalled fleet.

That also means the fix is not simply copying `ambientLeaseRefSyncBudget`. An operator who typed `--fleet` asked for the remote view and may reasonably wait longer than a tick may; the right bound here is probably wider, and probably wants to say so in stderr when it expires ("showing already-fetched C2 refs only" is already the right sentence, it just needs to fire on timeout too).

## Constraint

Do not put the bound inside `leaseref.Store.Sync`. `Sync` takes a `context.Context`, so it must honour its caller's deadline rather than impose one — `cmd/fak/leasewrite_endpoint.go` deliberately wraps it in a *wider* 30s `leasePublishTimeout` and documents why, and a floor inside `Sync` would make that constant a lie. #5564 established this; keep to it.

Also out of scope on purpose: `cmd/fak/leaseref.go:777`, the explicit `fak leaseref sync` verb. A hidden cap on the command whose entire job is to sync would be wrong.

## Checkable end state

`fak session ls --fleet` against a remote that never answers returns within a stated bound, prints the existing degradation line naming the timeout, and lists the C2 refs this clone already has. A test can pin it with `leaseref.NewWithRunner` and a transport verb that blocks on `<-ctx.Done()`, as `TestAmbientLeaseRefSyncGivesUpOnAStalledGitRunner` does — no remote is contacted.

Found during the `Sync` caller audit for #5564.

records.title: feat(cmd): ambient lease-ref sync re-pays its full budget every tick on a node with wedged credentials
records.body:
On a node with genuinely wedged git credentials, the loop-drive tick now pays the full ambient lease-ref sync budget on *every* turn — bounded, but repeated, and the node has already learned the answer.

## Where this comes from

#5564 gave `ambientLeaseRefSyncImpl` a convergence budget (`ambientLeaseRefSyncBudget`, 10s) covering the whole sync plan, so a stalled `git push` can no longer hang the tick forever. That fixed the unbounded hang and is not in dispute here.

What it does not do is remember. `loopDriveRegionHold.ensure` runs the sync boundary **twice a turn** (fetch-before-decide, push-after-write), so a node whose credential helper is stalled spends up to ~2x10s per turn, every turn, re-learning that the remote is unreachable. Every one of those attempts is nonfatal and every one is discarded.

## Suggested shape

A circuit breaker: after a budget expiry, skip ambient sync for N ticks, then let exactly one probe through; a success closes the breaker. The report already carries enough to drive this — `ambientLeaseRefSyncStepErr` marks a spent budget distinctly from an ordinary transport failure, which is exactly the signal a breaker should trip on and an ordinary "no remote configured" degradation should not.

Open questions a fix should answer rather than assume:

- **Trip on a spent budget only, or on any transport failure?** They are different: a spent budget means the remote is answering slowly or not at all, while a missing remote already degrades cheaply and instantly and needs no breaker.
- **Where does the breaker's state live?** In-process is simplest and is probably enough, since the thing being protected is a long-running loop's tick. Persisting it across processes would make a fresh `fak` invocation inherit a peer's verdict about the network, which is a bigger claim than this ticket needs.
- **Is the skip visible?** A silently-skipped sync is how a node ends up quietly isolated from the fleet for an hour. The skip should surface in the same `LeaseRefSyncReport` the caller may already print, distinguishable from "synced fine".

## Constraint

Whatever lands must keep the property #5564 established: the surface is explicitly nonfatal, so the breaker may cost cross-node visibility until it closes, and must never turn into a verdict the tick acts on.

## Checkable end state

A node whose transport blocks pays the budget once, then skips for N ticks with the skip visible in the report, and resumes syncing within one tick of the transport recovering. Pinnable with the same `leaseref.NewWithRunner` stalled-runner harness `TestAmbientLeaseRefSyncGivesUpOnAStalledGitRunner` uses, with no remote contacted.

Filed as the natural sequel to #5564, which does not ask for it.

records.title: fix(dispatch): the stranded-revert rung attributes dirty files by lease tree, not by who holds the lane, so it can stash a live worker's mid-edit files
records.body:
The sweep's stranded-revert rung decides which dirty files belong to a dead worker by matching the **lease tree globs**, never by asking who currently holds that lane. A live worker editing inside the same globs is therefore indistinguishable from the dead worker's strand, and can have its mid-edit files archived and stashed out from under it.

## The gap

`dispatchWitnessRevertStranded` (`cmd/fak/dispatch_tick_witness.go:550`) attributes with:

```go
if !dispatchPathInLeaseTree(f.Path, tree) {
    continue // a peer's WIP outside the dead worker's lane: never touched
}
```

The comment states the actual guarantee precisely, and it is narrower than it first reads: peers **outside** the lane are safe. A peer **inside** the lane is not distinguished from the dead worker at all — `tree` is the dead worker's declared `.tree` sidecar, and the rung never consults the lease to ask whether that lane has since been re-acquired by someone else.

The five fire conditions do a lot of work and this is not a claim that the rung is reckless. But none of them is an authorship check:

1. non-empty declared lease tree — the *dead* worker's;
2. dirty files exist and root is toplevel;
3. at least one dirty file under the lease tree globs — the ambiguous step;
4. at least one match is a tracked `.go` file;
5. a scoped `go build` of those package dirs **fails**.

Condition 5 is the strongest guard and it is also the one a live worker trips routinely: a worker mid-edit is very often at a non-compiling intermediate state. That is the overlap. Files are archived under `<runs>/<stem>.stranded` first and reverted with `git stash push -- <paths>` (recoverable via `git stash pop`), so the bytes are not destroyed — but a worker whose files silently revert underneath it is going to report nonsense, and recovering by hand means knowing which of several stashes is yours.

## Why now

This is pre-existing — it applies whenever a lease TTL expires before its sweep. But #5565 (landed `4e6431726`) now hands a lane back **in-tick** on five spawn-failure paths instead of waiting out the full TTL, and #5566 proposes making dead-owner lanes reclaimable rather than TTL-bound. Both are correct and both make lanes turn over faster, which widens the window in which the previous holder is dead, a new holder is live, and this rung is looking at the new holder's files.

## Suggested end state

The rung consults the lease before it attributes: if the lane the `.tree` describes is currently held by a **live** lease that is not the dead worker's, it returns nil and touches nothing. The lease record is the authorship evidence the rung is currently missing; `leaseref.ClassifyLive` already sorts exactly this question, and #5566 is about giving dispatch leases the descriptor that makes it answerable.

Worth deciding explicitly, not by default: what to do when the lane is held but classification is `peer-unknown`. Given the rung's own archive-before-destroy posture, failing closed (touch nothing) is the shape that matches the rest of the file.

Found by the worker on #5565 while wiring the in-tick hand-back; flagged as an adjacent seam rather than pulled into that diff.

records.title: loop-drive tick discards every lease-ref sync report, so no degradation is ever printed
records.body:
All three `syncLoopDriveTickLeaseRefs` call sites in `cmd/fak/loop_drive_region.go` (lines 137, 152, 202) discard the returned `loopdrive.LeaseRefSyncReport` entirely.

That makes the report's whole degradation vocabulary unobservable in practice:

- #5564 added a 10s convergence budget and a give-up path that attributes a failure to the deadline (`ambientLeaseRefSyncStepErr`).
- #5569 added a convergence breaker whose skip is deliberately reported as `Outcome: degraded` with a stable token, explicitly so a skipped sync is never mistaken for a clean one.

Both are correct at the producing end and both are dropped on the floor at the consuming end. A node whose lease-ref transport is wedged converges with no peer visibility and prints nothing at all, which is exactly the silent-isolation failure the breaker's visibility guarantee was written to prevent.

**Why it was not fixed in #5569:** the fix means editing `loop_drive_region.go`, which was out of that ticket's scope, and it is a real decision rather than a mechanical wiring — printing on every tick risks per-tick stderr noise on a loop that runs continuously. Plausible shapes: print only on a transition (clean -> degraded and back), print only the first skip of a breaker-open run, or route it to the tick payload instead of stderr.

**Verify:** a loop tick whose lease-ref sync is degraded (or skipped by an open breaker) surfaces that fact somewhere an operator or the tick payload can see, and a healthy tick stays quiet.

Found by the #5569 worker while wiring the breaker; the report shape it depends on is already in place.

records.title: fix(tools): loops_inventory's $TaskName parser is unguarded, so a reintroduced interpolated name lands silently in committed docs
records.body:
## What

`tools/loops_inventory.py:138` parses the scheduled-task name out of each `register_*.ps1` with:

```python
_TASKNAME = re.compile(r"\\s*=\s*['\"]([^'\"]+)['\"]")
```

and consumes it at `:285` with `mname = _TASKNAME.search(text)` — **first match anywhere in the file**, no anchoring to a param block, and **no rejection of an interpolated value**. The captured name is written into the committed `docs/loops-inventory.md`.

## Why it matters

This is the same value `#5409` just hardened at the *installer* end (`a7478b3f8` pinned `tools/register_worktree_doctor.ps1:41` to a literal `'FleetWorktreeDoctor'` so a reinstall updates the live task in place instead of orphaning it). That fix guarded the **write** end. This is a **second, independent reader** of the same value, and it is unguarded:

- `search` takes the first hit, so a `$TaskName = '...'` appearing earlier in a `<# ... #>` header block or a comment wins over the real parameter default.
- The character class `[^'\"]+` happily matches an interpolated body like `"Fleet$($Suffix)Doctor"` — it captures the literal text `Fleet$($Suffix)Doctor`, which names no real task.

So if any registrar reintroduces exactly the drift #5409 removed, the inventory does not refuse and does not warn — it writes a task name that matches nothing on the host into a doc the fleet reads as ground truth.

Not currently mis-parsing: all 12 `register_*.ps1` files carry literal defaults today (verified by grep). This is a **latent** defect — the guard is missing, not yet tripped.

## Done when

- The parser rejects (or loudly refuses) a captured value containing `$`, backtick, or `$(` rather than emitting it.
- The match is anchored to the param/assignment site rather than `search`-anywhere, so a header-block mention cannot win.
- A refusal is visible in the generated doc or the exit code — a silently wrong name is the failure mode being closed.
- A test pins both: an interpolated `$TaskName` refuses, and a header-block decoy does not shadow the real default.

## Notes

`tools/*_test.py` in CI runs **without pytest**, so keep any `__main__` block last, and prefer extending a test file already listed in `internal/pythongate/baseline.go` over adding a new one.

Found while verifying #5409 (which needed a zero-line diff — its fix was already pushed).

records.title: fix(tools): account_probe's select_targets has an anti-spam ceiling and no coverage floor, so an available-looking seat is never probed again
records.body:
## What

`tools/account_probe.py` `select_targets` (~:643) bounds probe frequency from ABOVE only. `min_interval_min` (:675-682) stops a seat being re-probed too often. Nothing forces a seat to be probed at all.

The selectors close the loop:

- CLI default `blocked` → `not row["available"]` (`_should_probe`, :618-640)
- the recurring cadence — `tools/fleet_resume_watchdog.ps1:69-81`, `-Probe auto` → `stale` → `blocked or not (active_sessions or live_sessions)`

So a seat that reads *available* and carries session evidence is **never selected**. Available → not probed → no row → still available. It never re-enters the probe population on its own.

The one caller that does probe every seat, `tools/resume_sweep.py:180-184`, passes `--all --no-ledger` and so deliberately records nothing.

## Why this is the open half of #5391

The read side is now fixed on both folds — `433ad9c3a0eb` (Go) and its Python mirror gave the roster a per-seat unknown-health trigger, so a seat the ledger never measured stops publishing a confident `registry` status source and hedges instead.

But **no read-side change can invent a verdict that was never recorded.** The folds now say "this seat is unmeasured" accurately; they do not make it measured. #5391's acceptance line 1 — *every enrolled seat has a probe row within a stated freshness budget* — is still **not yet**, and it is not reachable from the read side at all.

## Done when

- `select_targets` takes a `max_coverage_age_min` floor: force-include any enrolled worker whose newest ledger row is older than N minutes, **regardless of availability** — the dual of the existing `min_interval_min` ceiling.
- The floor is wired from the recurring cadence, i.e. `fleet_resume_watchdog.ps1`'s `-Probe auto` path, not just available as a manual flag. A floor nothing calls changes nothing.
- `tools/account_probe_test.py` pins both directions: an available seat with a stale/absent row IS selected, and the ceiling still suppresses a seat probed moments ago (the floor must not defeat the anti-spam bound).
- After a cadence cycle, `accountprobe.GradeSeats` reports coverage sufficient for the enrolled set — i.e. the read-side hedge added by `433ad9c3a0eb` stops firing because the seats are genuinely measured, not because the check was relaxed.

## Notes / hazards

- Do **not** discharge this by loosening the read-side gate. The hedge is correct; the missing measurement is the defect.
- The busy-ledger precondition (`CoverageReport.Sufficient`) exists to keep #5439's boundary — a host with no ledger at all does not probe and must not have every seat relabelled. A coverage floor must not change that.
- `internal/accountprobe/coverage.go` (`GradeSeat`/`GradeSeats`/`SeatCoverage`/`SeatCoverageMaxAgeMin`) is the grading substrate and now has exactly one consumer; it is the natural oracle for the acceptance check above.
- `CoverageReport.Note()` still has **no caller** — the gap is graded but surfaced in no operator view. Natural home is the `fak fleet-accounts list` footer via `fleetaccounts.RenderList`. Could be folded in here or split.
- CI runs `tools/*_test.py` **without pytest** — keep any `__main__` block last, and extend a test file already in `internal/pythongate/baseline.go` rather than adding a new one.
- `tools/fleet_accounts_test.py` has 4 pre-existing failures + 1 error in `WaveAllocationTest`/`IdentityReconciliationTest`, unrelated to this area.

Split out of #5391, whose read-side half landed as `433ad9c3a0eb`.

records.title: feat(gitdaily): add witnessed daily lock cleanup and object maintenance
records.body:
## Summary

Add a once-per-local-day `fak git-daily` tick that an OS scheduler can fire to keep a hot shared clone healthy. The tick must reclaim only evidence-proven orphan locks before running the existing guarded object-database maintenance tiers, record a bounded JSONL witness, and emit reboot-surviving launchd/systemd/Task Scheduler units.

This is a scheduled hygiene sibling of #5084, not a replacement for its high-water dispatch trigger. It must not close #5084 unless that issue's threshold gate and no-progress incident are separately satisfied.

## Done when

- `fak git-daily` reaps stale lease, index/next-index, dead-owner commit, residue, and ref locks through existing safety decisions before object maintenance.
- The unattended default never prunes unreachable objects or worktrees; grace-prune and worktree pruning remain explicit opt-ins.
- Mutating ticks serialize and dedupe per local calendar day; `--force`, `--dry-run`, JSON, and ledger status are witnessed.
- Emitted launchd, systemd, and Windows Task Scheduler units carry the absolute repo root; Windows uses S4U, Limited, and StartWhenAvailable.
- A logic witness fails if lock cleanup does not precede maintenance, if dry-run mutates, if same-day dedupe repeats work, or if advisory/failed actions are counted as cleared locks.
- A captured live run proves stale locks are reclaimed and the loose-object count falls in one tick.

## Parent context

Parent: #4602. Related remaining trigger contract: #5084.

## Work estimate

8 points.

## Overall completion contribution

8/21 points of #4602: this ships a periodic serialized host, stale-lock preflight, and live fold witness. #5084's high-water gate and no-progress incident remain separate open acceptance criteria.

## Completion standard

development

records.title: perf(gateway): give the toolproc reuse seam an operator arming path and a dogfood measurement (#5119 follow-on)
records.body:
## Parent
#5119 (shipped 71ac557634) wired the live toolproc reuse cache onto the gateway
seam: serve in `adjudicateProposedServed`, deposit in `admitInboundResults`.
Grandparent #4764. Sibling vocabulary rung #5407.

## Why
The seam is live but **no operator can turn it on**. Arming is a wiring-time
method, `(*gateway.Server).SetToolprocReuse(cfg, digest)`, and it has no call
site outside its own tests -- the same host-set posture `SetToolMaxAge` (#1349)
has carried since it landed. Consequence: the cache is armed nowhere, so the
perf this family exists for is measured nowhere. The default-off posture is
correct and should stay; what is missing is the operator-facing way to flip it
where the gateway can witness the same filesystem the tool executor reads
(fak's own guard/native path).

This is deliberately NOT folded into #5119: flipping a saver knob on is its own
coordinated change in this repo (the token-saver default-flip ritual -- flag,
default, docs, cli-reference, claims, witness), and half-doing it inside a seam
commit is how a knob ends up undocumented.

## Spine
- `internal/gateway/toolproc_reuse.go` -- `SetToolprocReuse` / `DisarmToolprocReuse`
  already exist and are the arming surface; nothing here needs redesign.
- `cmd/fak/serve.go` -- the live `fak serve` construction site, where a flag
  would call it. Note this file is a shared-trunk hot spot with concurrent
  editors; land the call in the smallest possible hunk.
- `toolproc.FileDigest(root)` is the digest witness; root must be the tree the
  executor actually reads, or every read refuses (fail-closed, not stale).

## Steps
1. Add one operator knob (flag or `FAK_*` env, default OFF) that calls
   `SetToolprocReuse`, with the digest rooted at the served repo.
2. Decide and document the coalescing sub-opt-in (`ArmedConfig.CoalesceQueries`)
   -- it must stay separately opt-in from immutable-read serving.
3. Document it in `docs/cli-reference.md` alongside the other served-read knobs.
4. Dogfood: run a real session armed, and report `BodyHits` / `ServedBytes` from
   `ArmedCache` as the net-true avoided-spawn number. This is the measurement
   #5119 could not produce, because nothing could arm it.

## Acceptance
An operator can arm the seam on a live `fak serve` without editing Go, the
default stays inert (the pre-#5119 path byte-identical), and one dogfood run
reports non-zero `BodyHits` with the digest key on the receipt.

## Closure
A commit citing this issue that adds the arming call site + doc, plus a comment
carrying the dogfood numbers.

## Lane
gateway (`internal/gateway/**`, `cmd/fak/serve.go`).

## Non-goals
Changing the default to ON; widening what is servable (writes/unknowns stay
fail-closed); replacing the vDSO name probe, which is complementary.

records.title: feat(operator): subtract parked/blocked emissions before the ORPHANED-FOLLOWON verdict judges
records.body:
Part of #4954. Follow-on from #4957 (the orphaned-follow-on witness), raised by its **first armed run**, not by reasoning.

## Why

#4957's witness fires correctly: it separates "not recently touched" from "carried". It does **not** separate **blocked** from **orphaned**. On the first armed run (`7d8b4ecfa4`, recorded in `docs/super-loops.md`) all seven emitted refs flagged, and at least one — #4835 — is **operator-gated**: it waits on a live [redacted:public-corpus] 8-GPU witness nobody can produce on demand. That is parked work, not unowned work, and it inflated the orphan count.

This is exactly what keeps `FAK_SUPERLOOP_FOLLOWON` gated OFF. The promotion bar in `docs/super-loops.md` is "a gated run where the orphan count tracks a real backlog — every flagged orphan is one an operator agrees is genuinely unowned". A backlog of legitimately-parked work cannot clear that bar, so **this leaf is what unblocks promotion of #4957's axis to on-by-default.**

## Spine

`superloop.ClassifyFollowon` (`internal/superloop/superloop.go`) already takes a pure `FollowonRead` of `FollowonEmission{Ref, Resolved, Open, Advanced}`. The fold does not need to change shape — the *shell* needs to mark a parked emission, and the fold needs to not count it.

- `cmd/fak/superloop_followon.go` — `resolveFollowonEmission` reads `state,updatedAt`; widen the live read to carry the park signal.
- `internal/superloop/superloop.go` — a `Parked` bit on `FollowonEmission`; a parked emission is neither orphaned nor a fabricated clean.

## Nuance — keep the fail-closed asymmetry

The existing direction is to **under**-report orphans, never to slander live work. Subtracting parked emissions moves the same way, so it is safe. But the park signal must be **durable issue state** (a label, a blocked/gated marker, a linked open blocker), never a worker's self-report — the #4957 rule that the verdict is assembled only from re-verifiable ground truth. An *unreadable* park signal must fail closed to the existing behavior, not silently un-park.

Open question the implementer should settle from ground truth, not guess: whether "parked" is best read from a label (`blocked`, `operator-gated`), from an open blocking link, or from a declared park in the issue contract. Pick the one the repo actually maintains.

## Acceptance / Done when

- An emitted ref that is durably parked/blocked does **not** count toward `FollowonOrphaned`, and the walk's `orphaned` count drops accordingly.
- An emitted ref that is genuinely open-and-unowned still flags, with `RELAY_ORPHANED_FOLLOWON` unchanged.
- An unreadable park signal fails closed to today's behavior (never un-parks an orphan on an absence).
- A re-run of the #4957 armed-run table with the park subtraction applied, recorded next to the first one in `docs/super-loops.md`.

## Closure

Contract test in `internal/superloop` for the parked-emission fold + a `cmd/fak` test binding a hermetic park signal, plus the re-run evidence above. Promotion of `FAK_SUPERLOOP_FOLLOWON` to on-by-default is a **separate** decision this leaf only unblocks.

## Out of scope

Re-filing or re-dispatching orphaned work (#4958 owns the front door). Promoting the gate.

## Lane

`internal/superloop` + `cmd/fak` — stamp resolves per `fak index lane` on the touched paths.
