affect other generators, extend item 1's test to cover them rather than opening one per file.

## Lane

`docs`

## Path hints

- `tools/concept_disambiguation_scorecard.py` (line 2112 — the `As of` row)
- `docs/concept-disambiguation-scorecard/README.md` (line 23 — the blank row)
- `docs/fak/concept-glossary.md` (the entry rule and anchors)
- `docs/industry-scorecard/README.md` (line 31 — a correct sibling to match)

## Hot-tree landing plan

**Owning lane(s)**
- `tools` — `tools/concept_disambiguation_scorecard.py` — the generator fix — usually clean
- `docs` — `docs/concept-disambiguation-scorecard/**`, `docs/fak/concept-glossary.md` — regenerated output plus ids

**Contention check**
`dos arbitrate --workspace . --lane docs && git status -sb -- docs/fak/concept-glossary.md tools/concept_disambiguation_scorecard.py`

**Partition plan (clean-now vs hot-later)**
- **CLEAN NOW:** item 1 — the generator's refuse-on-empty behaviour and its test, in
  `tools/**`. Self-contained, no doc churn beyond the regenerated `As of` row.
- **HOT LATER:** items 2 and 3 — the id allocation touches every glossary entry, so it is a
  large single-file diff that should not sit unmerged next to peer doc edits. Land it in one
  pass once the `docs` lane is quiet.

**Commit recipe**
`fak commit --path tools/concept_disambiguation_scorecard.py -m "fix(tools): refuse an empty scorecard provenance row (fak tools)"`

## Boundary notes

Public issue. Every path, line number and quoted string is from the public tree.

## Closure binding

Resolving commit must cite this issue number (`#N`) and carry a matching `(fak tools)` or
`(fak docs)` trailer so the close arm can witness the diff.

records.title: feat(hooks): give the explainer description a checked shape contract (fak hooks)
records.body:
**Parent context:** #5601 (grounding epic) · `docs/explainers/`

**Generation:** next · **Work unit:** leaf · **Expected steps:** 3

## Current state

`docs/explainers/` holds **53** pages and **all 53 carry YAML frontmatter with a `description`
field** — coverage is already 100%, which is the unusual and good part. What the field has no
contract for is its **shape**, and the drift is visible across the directory:

| page | `description` length |
|---|---|
| `awq-quantization.md` | 174 chars |
| `agent-runtime.md` | 193 |
| `addressable-kv-cache-in-5-min.md` | 231 |
| `addressable-kv-cache.md` | 444 |
| `agent-virtual-filesystem.md` | 552 |

The long ones are single sentences carrying four or five clauses joined by colons, em-dashes
and vendor lists — for example one opens by naming four external products before it says what
the page is about, and another spends its first clause on an analogy before the noun. They are
well-written prose; they are not a description a newcomer can hold in one breath, and they are
not what the field is consumed as (a summary, a search snippet, a hover card).

The failure mode is quiet: a drifted description still *reads* well. Nothing flags it, because
nothing states what "right" is. Any count of how many pages have drifted would be a hand-typed
number that decays the day after — which is why this issue asks for the check, not the tally.

## Why this is next

Marked `next`, not `now`: unlike the other leaves under #5601 this one has no correctness
defect behind it. Nothing is silently green; the pages are honest, just uneven. It earns its
place in the epic because it is the same shape of fix — replace a discipline held by authors
by hand with one a program states — applied to the one surface where fak's coverage is already
complete and only the contract is missing.

Landing it after the correctness leaves also means the lint pattern they establish can be
reused here rather than invented twice.

## Working spine

Every explainer's `description` satisfies a stated, machine-checked shape contract, so a page
that drifts fails a lint instead of reading fine.

## Priority context

- **Working path:** newcomer lands on an explainer → reads the description → decides to stay.
- **Current blocker:** no stated shape, so quality varies 3× in length and structure.
- **Unblocks:** the field becomes reliable enough to reuse as a search snippet or index line.
- **Not polish first:** it *is* polish relative to the correctness leaves, hence `next`.

## In scope

1. **State the contract** in `docs/explainers/README.md`: a small number of bounded rules —
   a length ceiling, a sentence-count ceiling, one idea per sentence, no unexpanded acronym,
   and no leading vendor list. Exact thresholds are the implementer's call; the constraint is
   that each rule is mechanically checkable, not a matter of taste.
2. **Add the lint** as a hygiene gate alongside the existing ones in `internal/hooks`, or as a
   `tools/` checker if a doc lint fits better there. It must report its denominator — *"N of
   53 pages checked"* — per the exemplar leaf under #5601, so a run that scanned nothing is
   distinguishable from a clean one.
3. **Bring the existing pages into contract** in a separate commit from the lint, so the lint's
   own diff stays reviewable.

## Out of scope

- Rewriting explainer *bodies*. This issue governs the frontmatter `description` only.
- Any claim about whether a description is *true*. The contract is about shape; truth stays the
  author's and review's job, and the gate should say so explicitly so nobody reads a green lint
  as a fact-check.
- The other frontmatter keys (`title`, `slug`, `keywords`, `date`).

## Done condition

A lint states the description contract, reports how many pages it checked, and fails on a page
that violates it; the 53 existing pages pass.

**Witness:** `go test ./internal/hooks -run 'Explainer|Description'`

**Acceptance gate:** `go test ./internal/hooks` plus a `fak hygiene` run that names the gate.

## Assumptions

- The `description` field is consumed as a standalone summary (search, index, hover), which is
  what makes a shape contract worth enforcing; if it is only ever read inline, the value drops
  and the thresholds should loosen accordingly.
- 100% frontmatter coverage holds — measured now, and worth re-measuring in the lint rather
  than trusting this issue.

## Confusion risks

- **Shape ≠ truth.** A green lint means the description is well-formed, not accurate. State
  this in the gate's own message so the verdict cannot be over-read.
- **Not a coverage gap.** All 53 pages already have the field; do not "fix" this by adding
  descriptions.
- The length figures above are a sample of five pages, not a survey of all 53 — they show the
  spread exists, not how many pages violate a contract that does not exist yet.

## Coordination notes

- If the exemplar leaf under #5601 lands first, reuse its denominator-reporting shape rather
  than adding a second convention.
- `docs/explainers/**` is touched by doc work regularly; land the lint before the content pass
  so the content pass has something to verify against.

## Trigger

Filed from a review of the explainer frontmatter surface for the class in #5601.

## Batch policy

One issue for the directory. Do not open one per page; the content pass is one commit.

## Lane

`docs`

## Path hints

- `docs/explainers/README.md` (where the contract belongs)
- `docs/explainers/*.md` (53 pages, all with frontmatter)
- `internal/hooks/` (the hygiene gate registry, if the lint lands as a gate)

## Hot-tree landing plan

**Owning lane(s)**
- `hooks` — `internal/hooks/**` — the lint itself — usually clean
- `docs` — `docs/explainers/**` — the contract statement and the content pass

**Contention check**
`dos arbitrate --workspace . --lane docs && git status -sb -- docs/explainers internal/hooks`

**Partition plan (clean-now vs hot-later)**
- **CLEAN NOW:** the lint plus its unit tests in `internal/hooks/**`, defaulting to advisory so
  it cannot red a shared trunk on arrival — the same `DefaultMode: "warn"` treatment the
  existing advisory gates get in `internal/hooks/hooks.go`.
- **HOT LATER:** the contract text and the 53-page content pass in `docs/explainers/**`, which
  is a wide diff and should wait for a quiet `docs` lane. Promote the gate from warn to block
  only after that pass lands.

**Commit recipe**
`fak commit --path internal/hooks -m "feat(hooks): lint the explainer description shape (fak hooks)"`

## Boundary notes

Public issue. All cited paths and measurements are from the public tree.

## Closure binding

Resolving commit must cite this issue number (`#N`) and carry a matching `(fak hooks)` or
`(fak docs)` trailer so the close arm can witness the diff.

records.title: feat(moe): bound the activated expert set — wire the paged residency ring under the expert weight HAL (epic #5606 R0)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R0, the keystone rung). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap

On the resident-quant device path, routed MoE expert weights stage through
`Session.expertSwiGLUHAL` (`internal/model/hal.go:248-284`) into `Session.weightHALStaged`
(`internal/model/hal.go:170-181`):

```go
func (s *Session) weightHALStaged(key string, mk func() compute.Tensor, dtype compute.Dtype) compute.Tensor {
	if s.halW != nil {
		if t, ok := s.halW[key]; ok {
			return t
		}
	}
	t := s.Backend.Upload(mk(), dtype)
	if s.halW != nil {
		s.halW[key] = t
	}
	return t
}
```

`s.halW` is **never evicted** — it is torn down only at session close
(`internal/model/hal.go:83-103`). So device weight residency equals *the union of every expert
activated since the session started*, growing monotonically toward the full expert bulk. That
is a memoizer, not a cache: no budget, no victim, no accounting, and no seam a residency
policy could attach to.

The alternative placement is no better for this: `--cpu-offload-experts` (`splitKernel`,
`internal/model/moe_offload.go:132-142`) is a static name predicate that keeps *all* experts
host-resident forever — "the floor, not a cache", in the file's own words.

So fak has no bounded activated working set on any live path.

## What already exists

`internal/model/paging_ring.go` is exactly the missing object: a bounded per-weight device ring
with a byte budget, LRU victim selection, pinned-exemption, and `pageIn`/`hit`/`evict` counters,
reusing `polymodel.Pool`'s proven policy so `used()<=budget()` and pinned-never-evicted hold by
construction. Its correctness contract is already pinned by `paging_ring_test.go` (a ring
`matMul` is bit-equal to a resident `MatMul` on both hit and miss; an evicted weight pages back
in on next use).

Its sole constructor today is `internal/model/v4_expert_runtime.go:67` — the DeepSeek-V4 live
expert runtime. Every other architecture gets the unbounded memoizer. The ring's own header
(`:38-44`) names this rung explicitly: *"wiring it into the session weight HAL as the paged
twin of weightHALQ4K/weightHALQ8 ... is still the follow-on rung"*. #2726 was closed COMPLETED
on the primitive; this is the rung it left open.

## The work

1. Give `Session` an optional expert ring (budget-configured; nil ring = today's behaviour,
   byte-for-byte).
2. In `weightHALStaged` (or a routed-expert wrapper above it), dispatch to the ring when the
   canonical name satisfies `isRoutedExpertWeight` (`internal/model/moe_offload.go:92-94`) —
   dense projections, attention, router and LM head keep their permanent `halW` residency,
   since they are touched every token and are small.
3. Free the device handle on eviction through the existing ring lifecycle (no new lifecycle).
4. Keep `s.halW` as the residency map for the non-routed classes; the ring owns routed experts
   only, so the shared-vs-routed distinction #3212 landed is preserved (shared experts are
   always-hot ⇒ pinned or `halW`).

Scope fence: this rung changes *where a routed expert's device handle lives and when it is
freed*. It introduces **no new arithmetic** — the ring's `matMulStaged` computes what the
resident HAL computes.

## Witness

- **Bit-exactness** — a ring-served decode is byte-identical to the resident-HAL decode over a
  fixed prompt on the cpu-ref backend (the ring's existing hit/miss bit-equality test extended
  to the session seam).
- **Boundedness** — over a decode window that activates more distinct experts than the budget
  holds, peak device weight bytes stay `<= budget`, and `evict > 0` proves the bound was
  actually exercised rather than trivially satisfied.
- **Recovery** — an evicted expert pages back in on its next activation (output unchanged,
  `pageIn` increments).
- **Default-unchanged** — with the ring unconfigured, `halW` behaviour and byte output are
  identical to HEAD.

## Why this is P0

R2 (pin-set), R3 (prefetch), R4 (evictor policy), R5 (checkpoint tier) and R7 (cross-agent
coalescing, #5243 L2) are all policies or observers **on this object**. None of them can land
while routed-expert residency is an unbounded map. This is the single wiring that turns eight
finished-but-inert components into a path.

records.title: feat(moe): ship the graded --n-cpu-moe N knob and admit on the activated working set (epic #5606 R1)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R1). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap — the sizing math shipped, the knob did not

#5281 closed as *"graded expert-spill knob (`--n-cpu-moe N`) + auto-fit N to a measured device
budget"*. What actually landed is `internal/model/expert_spill_fit.go`: the pure sizing math —
`ExpertSpillBudget`, `fitAt`, `AutoFitExpertSpill`, `ResolveExpertSpill`, with an out-of-range
refusal type. It is correct, tested, exported.

It has **no caller.** A tree-wide grep for `ResolveExpertSpill|AutoFitExpertSpill|ExpertSpillFit`
outside `internal/model` and outside `_test.go` returns nothing, and no CLI flag exposes N:
`cmd/fak/serve.go:221` still offers only the boolean `--cpu-offload-experts`, whose own help
text describes the `--n-cpu-moe` hybrid it cannot actually grade.

So the operator's only choice is still binary: **all** expert layers on host, or **none**.

## The second half — preflight admits on the wrong quantity

`internal/ggufload/estimate.go` has `EstimateCPUOffloadExpertsMemoryPlan` (:332) and
`FitCPUOffloadExpertsOnDevice` (:491), and `internal/ggufload/preflight.go:172-190` calls them.
Both reason about the **full expert bulk** under the all-or-nothing predicate
(`model.CPUOffloadExpertWeight`, `estimate.go:461`). `cmd/fak/serve.go:924-956`
(`refuseEPPlanIfUnfit`) likewise sizes against `model.MoEResidentWeightBytes()` in full.

That is the right question for a *static* placement and the wrong one once R0 (#5606) gives the
session a bounded activated working set: a model can be servable with a ring budget far below
its expert bulk, and today preflight refuses it before decode ever starts.

## The work

1. **Expose the knob.** `--n-cpu-moe N` (integer, llama.cpp semantics: the FIRST N MoE layers'
   experts go to host, the last `MoELayers-N` stay device-resident — the semantics
   `expert_spill_fit.go:19` already implements) plus `auto`, which calls `AutoFitExpertSpill`
   against measured device headroom. Keep `--cpu-offload-experts` working as the `N = all`
   alias so no existing invocation changes meaning.
2. **Wire the placement.** The spill count must reach the runtime predicate: `splitKernel`'s
   `onHost` (`internal/model/moe_offload.go:139`) becomes layer-aware for the graded case
   rather than the all-experts `isExpertWeight`.
3. **Admit on the working set.** Preflight sizes device residency as
   `dense base + non-spilled expert layers + ring budget` instead of the full expert bulk, and
   reports the sized split in the plan JSON. The refusal path stays fail-closed: refuse when
   even the dense base plus a minimum viable ring does not fit.

## Witness

- A checkpoint whose full expert bulk exceeds the measured device budget is **admitted** at a
  chosen N and decodes, where HEAD refuses.
- `--n-cpu-moe N` for each N in `{0, mid, all}` produces the documented residency split, and
  `auto` picks the largest N that fits the measured budget.
- Refusal still fires (with the typed reason) when the dense base plus the minimum ring does
  not fit — no OOM-minutes-later regression.
- Output is byte-identical across N: the spill is a placement decision over the same math,
  exactly as the existing placement-invariance witness asserts for the binary split.

## Dependency

Independent of R0 for the knob and the placement; the *admission* half wants R0's ring budget
to size against. Land the knob first if R0 is still in flight — it is a strict improvement over
the binary flag on its own.

records.title: feat(moe): consult the warm-start pin-set and persist the usage histogram on the live ring (epic #5606 R2)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R2). Depends on R0 (the live ring). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap

#4358 landed the whole warm-start machine in `internal/model/expert_warmpins.go` (421 lines):
a durable per-`(layer, expert)` usage histogram with crash-safe per-turn dump and summed load
at boot (`ExpertUsageHistogramSchema`, `Persist`/`Load`/`Sum`), pin selection
(`WarmStartExpertPins`), and a between-turns quiescent actuator (`RepinPass`) that swaps the
coldest pinned experts for the hottest recent ones under a bounded swaps-per-pass cap and a
decaying heat model.

None of it is consulted. `pagedRing.pins` is documented as inert at
`internal/model/paging_ring.go:56-61`:

> `pins` ... nil until `WarmStartPins` seeds it — a ring that was never warm-started has no
> pin-set, so `isExpertPinned` reports false and `RepinPass` is a no-op. Off the live serve
> path today (`matMulStaged` still takes a static `pinned` per call; consulting the set is the
> #2726 follow-on).

So every process start faces a cold activated set and re-pays every page-in, even for a
workload whose hot experts were measured yesterday. The file's own scope note names this rung.

## The work

1. **Consult, don't pass.** `matMulStaged` (`paging_ring.go:104`) takes `pinned bool` from the
   caller; for routed experts it should consult `isExpertPinned(layer, expert)`
   (`expert_warmpins.go:419`) on the seeded set instead. Keep the parameter for the non-expert
   callers so the ring stays general.
2. **Lifecycle.** Dump the per-turn histogram (crash-safe, already implemented), sum the
   persisted histograms at boot, and call `WarmStartExpertPins` to seed the ring's pin-set
   before the first decode.
3. **Actuate between turns.** Run `RepinPass` at the quiescent point between turns under its
   existing bounded swaps cap, so the pinned hot-set drifts with the workload instead of
   freezing at boot.
4. **Emit the drift signal** `RepinPass` already returns (`[]ExpertPinSwap`) — #3902 consumes
   it, and R6 surfaces it.

## Witness

- **Warm-start pays.** For a repeated workload, turn-2 cold page-ins fall measurably against
  turn-1, and against a control run with the histogram deleted.
- **Persistence.** The pinned set survives a process restart (histogram summed at boot
  reproduces the same seed set for the same trace).
- **Bounded actuation.** `RepinPass` performs at most the configured swaps per pass, and every
  swap is reported.
- **Invariant preserved.** Pinned experts are never evicted under budget pressure
  (`polymodel.Pool`'s existing invariant, now exercised through a live pin-set) and
  `used() <= budget()` still holds.

## Note on the shared/routed split

Shared experts (`isSharedExpertWeight`, `moe_offload.go:82-84`) fire for **every** token — they
are always-hot by construction, not by measurement, so they should be pinned structurally
rather than competing for histogram-earned pin slots. #3212 already landed that distinction;
this rung must not undo it.

records.title: feat(moe): overlap expert page-in with compute via next-layer router lookahead (epic #5606 R3)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R3). Depends on R0 (the live ring). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The idea — the deterministic floor, before any prediction

Layer `L+1`'s router input is available before layer `L`'s expert GEMMs retire. So the *next*
layer's activated expert set is not a prediction problem at all — it is **known** slightly
early. Issue the page-in for those experts against the ring while the current layer's GEMMs
compute, so the fetch latency overlaps compute instead of stalling decode.

This is strictly weaker — and strictly more certain — than #4300 / #4318, and that is the
point: it is the floor those rungs stand on.

## Relation to the tracked prefetch issues (compose, do not fork)

- **#4300** (predictive router-driven prefetch) owns the *speculative* policy layer: rank
  experts by predicted near-future use across **tokens**, prefetch above a probability
  threshold, tolerate mispredictions. It needs a residency object with an async page-in seam to
  attach to.
- **#4318** (small-model expert prediction) approximates the big router locally — a longer
  horizon on the same seam.
- **R3** is the same-step, zero-misprediction case: the routing is computed, not guessed.

Land R3 first; #4300 then raises the lookahead horizon on the seam R3 builds, and its
misprediction-cost accounting has a zero-error baseline to be measured against.

## What already exists

- `route` / `glmRoute` (`internal/model/moe.go:357`, `:659`) produce the per-layer
  `[]routePick` — the exact activated set, already materialized.
- `emitExpertRoute` (`internal/model/expert_replay.go:29-37`) is a live observer seam on that
  set (currently used only by the off-path trace recorder).
- `willneedExpertSlice` (`internal/model/expert_readahead.go`, #4359) is the host-side
  `MADV_WILLNEED` hint half — built, off-path, and explicitly designed for exactly this
  overlap ("issue a best-effort `MADV_WILLNEED` over the NEXT picked expert's sub-range while
  the caller computes the CURRENT expert's GEMM").

## The work

1. Add an async page-in / prefetch entry point on the ring (admit-without-compute), so a
   prefetch cannot perturb the resident set's correctness — a prefetched expert is an ordinary
   resident, a dropped prefetch is an ordinary miss later.
2. Drive it from the next layer's computed route at the point the current layer's GEMMs are
   dispatched.
3. On the host tier, fire `willneedExpertSlice` for the same set (#4359's promotion path).
4. Account it: prefetch issued / prefetch hit (arrived before demand) / prefetch wasted
   (evicted before use).

## Witness

- **Overlap fraction** — share of activated-expert page-in latency overlapped with compute,
  prefetch on vs off, at a fixed ring budget.
- **Decode step time** — per-step decode time with prefetch on vs off, same budget, same
  prompt.
- **No correctness delta** — output byte-identical with prefetch on and off (prefetch changes
  *when* bytes move, never *which* bytes are computed).
- **No thrash** — prefetch must not increase evictions of experts that are then re-demanded in
  the same step; report prefetch-wasted so a regression is visible rather than hidden in an
  aggregate hit-rate.

## Honest caveat

The literature warns that prefetch *accuracy* does not equate to cache *performance* — a
prefetch that evicts a hotter resident is a net loss even at 100% accuracy. R3's zero-error
routing makes accuracy a non-issue but not the eviction interaction, so the prefetch-wasted
counter is load-bearing, not decorative, and R4's regret gauge is the arbiter if the two
interact badly.

records.title: feat(moe): choose the ring evictor on measured Belady regret instead of inherited LRU (epic #5606 R4)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R4). Depends on R0 (the live ring). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap — LRU is a default here, not a finding

`pagedRing` evicts by pure recency: the byte budget, the LRU victim choice and the
pinned-exemption are all inherited from `polymodel.Pool` (`internal/model/paging_ring.go:22-27`).
That inheritance was the right call for the primitive — reuse a proven policy rather than
invent one — but it means the eviction policy for **expert** residency was never chosen on
evidence about expert access.

And the evidence is contested. The dedicated-MoE-caching survey in
[`docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-DEDICATED-MOE-CACHING-2026-07-10.md`](../blob/main/docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-DEDICATED-MOE-CACHING-2026-07-10.md)
records three independent systems converging on the claim that **temporal-locality is the wrong
prior for MoE expert access** — access is layer-sequential/deterministic rather than
recency-driven — and that *prefetch prediction accuracy does not equate to cache performance*.
Whether that holds for fak's traces is an open, measurable question, not something to assume in
either direction.

## What already exists — both halves

- **A candidate policy.** `internal/model/expert_residency_lfu.go` (#4357) simulates a
  value-aware policy: routing-heat **hysteresis** (admit a newcomer only if
  `hot > victim + victim/4 + 4`, so a one-off cold expert cannot evict a hot resident) plus
  **LFU-decay** (periodic `heat >>= 1`, so the resident set follows phase drift). It already
  reports `EvictionDelta` and `HitDelta` against the LRU baseline over the same event stream.
- **A referee.** #4233 pointed the KV Belady replay oracle at the expert-access surface:
  `BeladyKVReplayOracle` + `ReplayKVCacheMulti` + `GoodDecisionRatio` (realized/oracle), i.e. a
  policy-**regret** gauge rather than a bare hit-rate.

Both are off the live path, and the live ring is still LRU. The measurement exists; the
promotion never happened.

## The work

1. **A policy seam on the ring.** Make the victim rule pluggable (LRU today, so the default is
   byte-for-byte unchanged) rather than hard-inherited.
2. **Feed the referee real traces.** Capture live routed-expert access via the existing
   observer (`SetExpertRouteObserver`, `expert_replay.go`) into the replay corpus, so policies
   are scored on observed routing, not only on the synthetic hot-set/jitter fixture.
3. **Promote on the gauge, not on the story.** Score LRU, hysteresis+LFU-decay, and (if the
   layer-sequential finding reproduces on fak traces) a staleness-ordered rule, and ship the
   winner behind the same measurement.

## Witness

- `GoodDecisionRatio` (realized/oracle hit tokens) of the shipped policy vs LRU **on the same
  real routing trace**, plus the eviction delta.
- **Promotion gate:** ship a non-LRU policy only on a positive eviction delta *with no hit
  regression* (`HitDelta >= 0`) — the demotion condition #4357 already states.
- **A locality diagnostic** reported alongside: does recency predict next-use on fak's traces,
  or is access layer-sequential? This is the finding that decides whether the whole axis is
  worth further investment — a negative result here is a publishable outcome for this rung, not
  a failure.
- Output byte-identical under every policy (eviction changes residency lifetime, never math).

## Sequencing note

R4 deliberately follows R0 and R2. Tuning an evictor before the ring is live, and before the
pin-set removes the structurally-hot experts from the eviction contest, would measure the wrong
distribution.

records.title: feat(moe): serve a ring miss from a per-expert checkpoint read instead of the fused slab (epic #5606 R5)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R5). Depends on R0 (the live ring). Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap — a ring miss has nowhere cheap to fall to

R0 bounds device residency, but the tier *below* the ring is still "the whole model, resident
in host RAM". A GGUF MoE checkpoint stores each layer's routed experts as one fused
`[E, out, in]` tensor; the loader materializes the entire `E`-expert slab before splitting, so a
top-k route pays `E*stride` bytes of residency for the `k*stride` it activates. On a checkpoint
whose expert bulk exceeds host RAM, that is the wall — the ring cannot help, because the miss
path has no way to read one expert.

## What already exists — both halves, both unwired

- **`internal/model/gguf_expert_source.go`** — `ggufExpertSource`, the lazy per-expert
  range-read source for fused GGUF slabs. It indexes `{offset, [E,out,in], quant-block
  geometry}` per fused tensor at construction (no payload IO) and reads exactly one expert's
  sub-range `[offset + e*stride, offset + (e+1)*stride)` through a caller-supplied
  `io.ReaderAt`. Its test already proves streamed-expert bytes are bit-identical to the
  fully-resident slab slice, and that a read moves exactly `stride` bytes, never `E*stride`.
  Its header states the promotion condition plainly: wire it under the `ggufload` expert split
  behind a measured bytes/token witness, *with `pagedRing` as the residency tier above it*.
- **`internal/model/expert_readahead.go`** (#4359) — the safetensors twin (`readExpertSlice`)
  plus the `MADV_WILLNEED` overlap hint.

The `io.ReaderAt` parameter is the composition seam: it already accepts a plain file, the
mmap/`ReadAt` seam, or an `internal/stripeload.StripedReaderAt` that fans one expert read
across byte-identical mirrors by bandwidth.

## The work

1. Construct a `ggufExpertSource` on the loader path for fused routed-expert tensors instead of
   materializing the whole slab (the `ggufload` GLM expert-split seam).
2. Serve a ring **miss** from it: read that expert's stride, stage, admit. Device / host /
   checkpoint becomes a real ladder rather than a two-rung one.
3. Keep the fully-resident path as the default until the witness clears — this is an added
   tier, not a replacement.

## Witness

- **Bytes scale with k, not E.** Bytes read per decode step at a fixed ring budget scale with
  the activated count, not the expert count — measured, not asserted.
- **Bit-identical output** vs the fully-resident slab path over a fixed prompt (the source's
  existing byte-identity test lifted to the decode seam).
- **Residency ceiling.** Host resident bytes for expert weights stay bounded by the configured
  tier size rather than the checkpoint's expert bulk.
- **Honest regression check.** Report decode step time alongside — a per-expert read has more
  syscall overhead than one big sequential read, so the win is a *residency* win that must not
  silently cost more than it saves on a host where the slab already fit.

## Invalidating assumption (stated, per the source's own frame)

That experts are contiguous, equal-stride, unpadded segments of the fused tensor. If a
checkpoint family violates that, the source must refuse rather than read misaligned bytes.

records.title: feat(moe): expose activated-expert residency as an operator surface — serve telemetry + a fak verb (epic #5606 R6)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R6). Depends on R0. Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap — none of this is visible to an operator

There is **no `fak` verb for MoE residency**. A grep of `cmd/fak/main.go` for a `moe` or
`expert` verb returns nothing. Serve exposes expert *placement* flags
(`--cpu-offload-experts`, `--expert-parallel`) but reports no residency telemetry: no activated
set size, no hit / page-in / evict counts, no bytes per token, no pinned set. The ring's
counters (`pageIn`, `hit`, `evict` — `internal/model/paging_ring.go:52-54`) are unexported and
reach no surface; the only place ring-shaped numbers are printed today is the standalone
simulator `cmd/coalescebench`.

Two finished gauges are also stranded with no consumer:

- `ScoreExpertPlacement` (`internal/model/expert_placement_drift.go`, #3902) — coverage
  (fraction of observed touches served by a planned-resident expert) and drift (how far the
  resident set has moved from the observed top-k hot set). It exists precisely to answer "is
  the residency plan still right?" and has no caller.
- The eviction-regret gauge from #4233 (`GoodDecisionRatio`), reachable only through the
  replay harness.

By this repo's own standard — an operator can turn it on and inspect it through a `fak` verb —
R0 through R5 are not first-class until this rung lands. It is also the rung that makes every
other rung's witness *reproducible by someone else*, rather than a number in a PR body.

## The work

1. **Serve telemetry.** Expose per-window ring counters and derived rates: activated distinct
   experts, hit / page-in / evict, resident bytes vs budget, bytes moved per token, pinned-set
   size. Wire into the existing plan/stats JSON surface rather than inventing a new channel.
2. **A `fak` verb.** Report the same view for a live or just-completed serve, plus the two
   stranded gauges: placement coverage/drift against observed routing, and eviction regret vs
   the Belady ceiling.
3. **Reconciliation.** The reported numbers must be the ring's own accounting, not a parallel
   estimate — one source of truth, so telemetry cannot drift from behaviour.

## Witness

- The verb reports a live ring's counters over a decode window, and the numbers reconcile
  exactly with the ring's internal accounting (`hit + pageIn` equals activated-weight lookups;
  `resident bytes <= budget`).
- Coverage/drift is reported for a run whose planned pin-set is deliberately stale, and the
  drift number moves in the expected direction — proving the gauge is live, not a constant.
- Zero-overhead-when-off: with telemetry disabled, decode step time and byte output are
  unchanged.

## Why P2 and not P0

It measures the object R0 creates; it cannot precede it. But it should not slip past R2/R3 —
every rung after R0 is *tuning*, and tuning without an operator-visible meter is how the nine
existing off-path components got built without anyone noticing they were never turned on.

records.title: feat(moe): share the expert residency ring across agents to coalesce page-ins (epic #5606 R7, unblocks #5243 L2)
records.body:
Child of epic #5606 (R7), and the missing mechanism under epic #5243's **L2** lever. Depends on
R0. Plan: [`docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`](../blob/main/docs/MOE-ACTIVATED-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md).

## The gap — #5243's central lever has no object to act on

Epic #5243's thesis: with **B** concurrent agents, their per-step top-K expert selections
**coalesce** — the union `U(B)` of experts a batch touches is far smaller than `B*K`, so one
streamed expert serves many agents at once, and aggregate net tokens/sec scales with B. The
epic itself labels L2 (cross-agent expert coalescing) **NOT BUILT**.

The reason it is not built is structural: coalescing requires a **shared, bounded residency
object** that multiple agents' activated sets can hit. fak has no such object on the live path.
Today each session gets its own unbounded `halW` memoizer (`internal/model/hal.go:170-181`),
which is per-session state that never evicts — so there is nothing for B agents to share, and
no accounting that could report a coalescing ratio even if they did.

The children #5246 (coalescing ratio + effective-bytes/token telemetry), #5247 (fused grouped
GEMM over the coalesced union), #5249 (routing-skew model) and #5251 (witness on real GLM-5.2
traces) all describe measurements and optimizations **over a coalesced union that does not yet
exist as a runtime object**. R0 creates it; this rung makes it shared and measured.

## The work

1. **Share the ring across sessions on one device.** Routed-expert residency is a property of
   the (model, device) pair, not of a conversation — the same expert weight is the same bytes
   for every agent. Lift the ring to that scope with the lifetime and concurrency discipline
   that implies.
2. **Coalesce the demand.** Within a decode step, admit the *union* of the batch's activated
   experts once, so a page-in is charged once and served B times.
3. **Account it.** Report the coalescing ratio `B*K / |U(B)|` and effective bytes per
   agent-token — feeding #5246 directly, with real numbers instead of simulated ones.

## Witness

- **Coalescing is real, not assumed.** For B in a sweep, measured `|U(B)|` against the `B*K`
  upper bound and the modelled curve from #5249 — on real routing, which is what #5251 asks
  for.
- **Bytes per agent-token fall as B grows** at a fixed ring budget, while per-agent output stays
  byte-identical to a single-agent run (coalescing changes *who pays* for a page-in, never
  what is computed).
- **No cross-agent leakage.** Sharing weight residency must not share anything else: weights
  are model-constant bytes, KV and conversation state remain per-session. This is the load-bearing
  safety property of the rung and needs its own test, not a comment.

## Sequencing

Strictly after R0. Best after R6, so the coalescing ratio lands on an existing telemetry
surface rather than growing a private one — but R7 can precede R6 if #5243's bench schedule
demands it, at the cost of a temporary private meter.

records.title: epic(gitbroker): stop spawning a git process per question — resident git query broker
records.body:
## Why

Ablating the "ghost slowdown" on the reference Windows agent host (note:
`docs/notes/RESEARCH-GHOST-SLOWDOWN-BASELINE-ABLATION-2026-08-05.md`, landed `559cddf4a5`)
found the box sustains **25.8 process births/sec**, that **87.2 % of page faults are charged
to no live process** (the processes are dead before any per-process counter is read), and
that one process creation costs a measured floor of **~8,166 page faults / ~2,203 context
switches / ~12,981 syscalls**. Process creation is the dominant term in the host's fault load
— **≥37 %** of it by an arithmetic that uses an undercounted birth rate and a cheapest-process
cost, so the true share is higher.

A follow-up cost ladder (10 calls each, same session, warm) locates the cost precisely:

| invocation | cost |
|---|---|
| `/usr/bin/true` (32 KB, does nothing) | **26 ms** |
| `git --version` | 35 ms |
| `git rev-parse HEAD` | 38 ms |
| `git diff-index --cached --name-only HEAD` | 39 ms |
| `git status --porcelain` | 78 ms |
| `fak.exe version` (65.5 MB Go binary) | **172 ms** |

`/usr/bin/true` does nothing and costs 26 ms: that is the Windows `CreateProcess` floor, paid
before any program runs an instruction. So `git rev-parse HEAD` is 26 ms of Windows and 12 ms
of git — **the small, frequent git calls that make up the churn are ~2/3 pure spawn overhead.**

**Tuning git therefore attacks the wrong half of the bill.** The reducible cost is not what git
does; it is that a process was created to ask. The direct demonstration:

```
200 x `git cat-file -t <oid>`         6,408 ms   (200 processes)
1  x `git cat-file --batch-check`        82 ms   (1 process)
```

**78x, and 200 processes become 1.**

Scale of the surface in-tree: **152 `exec.Command` git sites in Go** (of 400 total, non-test)
and **107 `subprocess` git sites in Python** (of 554) — 259 call sites.

## Why NOT a git server

The obvious reading of "front it with a git server" does not work, and this epic explicitly
rejects it so nobody re-proposes it. `git daemon` and `git http-backend` speak the **wire
protocol** — `upload-pack` / `receive-pack`, i.e. clone, fetch, push. They answer "give me
these objects to transfer." Every hot query in the ablation is a **local working-tree or index
question** — is this path dirty, what is HEAD, what does this checkpoint's delta touch — and
the wire protocol has no verb for any of them. Fronting one adds a network hop and answers
nothing we actually ask.

The right shape is the same instinct with the right protocol: a **local query broker**.

## Design: `fak gitd`, a resident git query broker

**Transport.** One Unix-domain socket per repo, token-authed. Precedent already works in this
tree on Windows: `cmd/fak/guard_lifecycle_ipc.go:51` does `net.Listen("unix", path)` and Go
supports AF_UNIX on Windows 10+. Go clients dial in-process; Python gets a ~40-line stdlib
`socket` client with no new dependency.

**Backend: a warm git pool, never a fresh spawn.** One long-lived `git cat-file --batch` and
one `git cat-file --batch-check` per repo, fed on stdin, plus `git update-index --index-info`
for index writes. This is git's *designed* interface for exactly this access pattern — it is
what `fast-export` and every serious git tool uses. The broker multiplexes every caller onto
these; they become the only git processes on the hot path.

**Query surface split by consequence.** This split *is* the correctness argument:

- **Class A — content-addressed reads** (object type/size, blob bytes, tree entries, commit
  metadata, by OID). A git object is immutable by construction, so these cache **forever with
  no invalidation problem at all**. Large fraction of all traffic, free to cache correctly.
- **Class B — working-tree state** (is-dirty, status, index contents). Mutable and shared with
  peers. Cached against an invalidation key of (`.git/index` mtime+size, HEAD OID, refs mtime)
  with single-flight coalescing. A wrong answer here is advisory.
- **Class C — decision-bearing** (anything feeding a commit gate, a mutation, or a refusal).
  **Never cached, ever.** The broker still pays off via a warm index and serialization, but
  every answer is freshly computed. Enforced by test, not by discipline.

**Single-flight coalescing is the biggest win and the least obvious.** 8 resident sessions run
per-turn hooks and N python dispatchers run on timers, all independently asking the same
question of the same tree. Collapsing concurrent identical queries into one execution is an
~8x cut *before* any caching, and it needs no invalidation reasoning.

**Fail-open, always.** Broker down, unreachable, or slow => the client spawns git exactly as it
does today. Non-negotiable: #4603 (`core.fsmonitor=true` + dead daemon) is the standing lesson
that a resident thing which dies must not take the fleet with it. It also makes rollout safe —
the broker can be adopted one call site at a time with no flag day.

**Arming readout.** Per the rule this repo just learned the hard way in `internal/stallscan`:
never spell "unmeasured" the same way as "healthy". Every response carries its provenance
(`broker` / `cache` / `fallback-spawn`), so "the broker is down" can never be read as "the tree
is clean".

## Migration: do not touch 259 sites

Route through the wrappers that already exist rather than editing call sites. Go already has
~7 (`gitOut` `cmd/fak/affected.go:647`, `gitWipOut` `cmd/fak/wip.go:272`, `runGitOutput`
`cmd/fak/concept.go:207`, `gitOutput` `cmd/fak/llms_full.go:176`, `gitRunner`
`cmd/fak/treedoctor.go:313`, plus `internal/gitgate`). Consolidate to one runner interface,
then swap its implementation. Python gets one `tools/fak_git.py` and migrates incrementally.

## Definition of Done

The epic is done when **all** of these hold, each with a committed witness:

1. **A benchmark exists in-tree** that reports git *process spawns* (not wall-clock) per unit of
   work for the three hot paths — Stop hook, dispatch tick, `fak commit` gate — and it is
   runnable by anyone on any host. Every claim below cites it. No claim without a witness.
2. **>=80 % fewer git process spawns** on those three hot paths, measured by (1) before and
   after, with the raw before/after numbers recorded in the issue.
3. **Fail-open is proven, not asserted**: a test kills the broker and asserts every call site
   produces byte-identical output to the pre-broker behaviour. A broker that is down costs
   latency, never correctness.
4. **No cached answer can reach a commit decision.** An architest or source-scan test fails the
   build if a Class C query is served from cache.
5. **Provenance on every response** (`broker` / `cache` / `fallback-spawn`), surfaced far enough
   that an operator can tell an unavailable broker from a calm tree.
6. **Both languages routed**: the Go runner interface and `tools/fak_git.py` both go through the
   broker, with the remaining unmigrated call sites counted and listed (a number, not "most").
7. **Cache invalidation has a negative test**: a peer commit / index write during a cached
   window must invalidate, proven by test, not by argument.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Replacing git with an in-process git library for **write** paths. Index semantics, hooks, and
  refs locking are not worth reimplementing; read paths only, and only after the broker lands.
- Enabling `core.fsmonitor`. It is `false` in `.git/config` deliberately (#4603 dead-daemon
  drift; `fak git-maint --repair-fsmonitor` exists for it) and the ceiling is ~40 ms on a
  ~110 ms `status` because `core.untrackedCache` and `core.fscache` are already on. Wrong
  target: it optimizes git's work, not the spawn.

## Rungs

Spine first, then fan out. The spine is rung 1 — a batch pool behind the existing Go wrapper,
no protocol, no daemon — because it delivers most of the win with none of the lifecycle risk.

## Parent context

Parent: #3153 (the low-usage stall). #3153 established that the freeze is `CreateProcess` cost
plus soft-fault contention, invisible to CPU/RAM/disk meters by construction. This epic is the
reduction half: #3153 says process creation is the mechanism, this says stop creating them.

## Work estimate

21 points.

## Overall completion contribution

21/30 points of #3153: this is the reduction arm. Rungs land against it and each names the fraction it
closes. The epic stays open until every Definition-of-Done item above carries a committed
witness.

## Completion standard

development

records.title: feat(gitbroker): benchmark git process spawns per unit of work on the three hot paths
records.body:
## Why Every claim in #5619 is a spawn-count claim, and right now nothing in the tree counts spawns. Wall-clock is the wrong unit: it moves with host load, and the whole point of the parent epic is that the cost is *per process created*, not per millisecond elapsed. This rung is first because Definition-of-Done item 1 of #5619 says no later claim may land without citing it. ## Scope A benchmark that reports **git process spawns** (a count, with the window it was counted over) per unit of work for the three hot paths: - the Stop hook (`cmd/fak/guard_stophook.go` -> `runWipAutoCheckpoint`) - one dispatch tick - one `fak commit` gate run Counting method must survive short-lived processes. A PID-diff poll sampler measured a **20x undercount** against a known ground truth of 200 injected ~40 ms spawns (it caught 10), so do NOT count by polling `Get-Process`. Count at the source: instrument the runner/wrapper that issues the exec, or use an event-driven source. If you use a sampling method anyway, you must report its measured undercount alongside the number. ## Work unit leaf -- one commit adding a spawn-counting benchmark verb plus its baseline fixture. No behaviour change to any existing path. ## Done condition A single in-tree verb reports git process spawns, with the window they were counted over, for the Stop hook, one dispatch tick, and one `fak commit` gate run, and its before-baseline is committed as a fixture. ## Acceptance gate - `fak bench gitspawn` (or equivalent in-tree verb) reports spawns per hot path, runnable on any host with no scheduled-task or admin prerequisite. - The count carries its window; a bare count with an implicit interval is rejected in review (see `internal/stallscan` `SpawnWindowSeconds` for why this repo now treats that as a defect). - A committed before-baseline for all three paths, in the issue and in a test fixture. - The counting method is stated, and if it can undercount, the measured undercount is stated with it. ## Current state Nothing in the tree counts git process spawns. `internal/stallscan` counts process births host-wide but does not attribute them to git or to a caller, and every existing perf claim in this area is wall-clock, which moves with host load and hides the per-spawn cost that #5619 is about. ## Witness `go test ./cmd/fak -run GitSpawnBench` passes, and the new verb prints a spawn count plus the window it was counted over for each of the three hot paths, on a host with no admin rights and no scheduled task. A committed fixture records the before-baseline so a later rung's improvement claim has something to subtract from. ## Likely files - `cmd/fak/guard_stophook.go` - `cmd/fak/benchmarks.go` - `cmd/fak/commit.go` - `internal/stallscan/stallscan.go` ## Why now Every later rung in #5619 states a spawn-count improvement, and none of them can be checked without this. Filing it after the optimizations would mean measuring the improvement with an instrument built by the person claiming it. ## Working spine Add a spawn-counting benchmark verb under `cmd/fak`, wired to count at the exec seam rather than by polling the process table, and commit its baseline output as a fixture. ## In scope A new benchmark verb that counts git process spawns for the Stop hook, one dispatch tick, and one `fak commit` gate run; the window each count covers; a committed baseline fixture. ## Out of scope Any change to how those three paths call git. This rung only measures. Reducing the count is #5621 and later. ## Expected steps 4 ## Assumptions - The three hot paths can be invoked in-process or as a subcommand from a test, without a live fleet. - Counting at the exec seam is sufficient; git subprocesses that git itself spawns internally are out of scope for the count and should be stated as such. ## Confusion risks - Do NOT count by polling `Get-Process` / the process table. That method was measured at a 20x undercount (10 of 200 injected ~40ms spawns caught), and the bias grows as processes get shorter -- worst exactly where churn is worst. - A count without its window is not a measurement. `internal/stallscan` shipped that defect once already. - Wall-clock is not the unit. The whole premise of #5619 is that cost is per-spawn. ## Coordination - Work directly on trunk (`main`); the trunk guard refuses off-trunk commits (`OFF_TRUNK`). - Commit by explicit path (`fak commit --path

-F `), never `git add -A` -- this is a shared multi-session checkout and a peer's uncommitted work sits in the same tree. - End the subject with a `(fak )` trailer or the ship stays NOT_SHIPPED. ## Trigger Definition-of-Done item 1 of epic #5619 requires it before any other rung's claim can land. ## Batch policy One issue, one benchmark verb. Do not fan out per hot path. ## Closure binding Closes when the verb is committed, its baseline fixture is in the tree, and the numbers are pasted into this issue. ## Parent context Parent: #5619. ## Work estimate 3 points. ## Overall completion contribution 3/21 points of #5619: the witness every later rung cites. ## Completion standard development

records.title: feat(gitbroker): one git runner interface with a warm cat-file --batch pool behind it
records.body:
## Why This is the **spine** of #5619 and deliberately ships before any daemon, socket, or cache. It delivers the measured 78x on batchable queries with no new process to supervise, no IPC, and no cache-invalidation reasoning â€” so if the rest of the epic stalls, the box still gets faster. Measured: `200 x git cat-file -t ` = 6,408 ms across 200 processes; one `git cat-file --batch-check` fed the same 200 OIDs on stdin = 82 ms in 1 process. ## Scope 1. **Consolidate the wrappers.** Go currently has at least 7 near-duplicate git exec helpers: `gitOut` (`cmd/fak/affected.go:647`), `gitWipOut` (the `wip` verb's copy -- DEFERRED, see Out of scope), `runGitOutput` (`cmd/fak/concept.go:207`), `gitOutput` (`cmd/fak/llms_full.go:176`), `gitRunner` (`cmd/fak/treedoctor.go:313`), plus `internal/gitgate`. Land ONE runner interface they all route through. This is a mechanical refactor and must not change any behaviour. 2. **Add a warm pool behind it**, in-process: a long-lived `git cat-file --batch` and `git cat-file --batch-check` per repo, lazily started, reaped on exit. Object reads go through the pool; everything else still spawns as today. 152 `exec.Command` git sites exist in Go (non-test) â€” do NOT edit them. Route through the wrapper. ## Work unit leaf -- one refactor commit consolidating the git exec helpers behind a single runner, with the batch pool added behind that seam. ## Done condition Every Go git call reaches git through ONE runner interface, and object reads on that interface are served by a warm `git cat-file --batch` pool that falls back to spawning when it is unavailable. ## Acceptance gate - One runner interface; the 7 helpers are gone or are thin shims over it. - Object reads (`cat-file -t/-s/-p`, `rev-parse ^{...}`) go through the batch pool. - The pool is reaped: no orphaned `git cat-file` survives process exit, proven by test. An orphan here is worse than the churn it fixes. - A crashed/hung pool falls back to spawning, transparently â€” proven by a test that kills it. - The #5619 benchmark shows the spawn drop, before and after, in the issue. - `make ci` green; no behaviour change on any existing call site. ## Current state Go has at least 7 near-duplicate git exec helpers and 152 non-test `exec.Command` git sites. Every git question spawns a fresh process; nothing is batched. `git cat-file --batch` is not used anywhere on a hot path. ## Witness `go test ./cmd/fak ./internal/gitbroker` passes, including a test that kills the pool and asserts the caller still returns byte-identical output, and a test that asserts no `git cat-file` process survives exit. The #5620 benchmark shows the object-read spawn count drop, before and after, pasted into this issue. ## Likely files - `cmd/fak/affected.go` - `cmd/fak/buildcheck.go` - `cmd/fak/concept.go` - `cmd/fak/llms_full.go` - `cmd/fak/treedoctor.go` - `internal/gitgate/gitgate.go` ## Why now It is the largest win available with no new process to supervise: 200 x `git cat-file -t` costs 6,408ms across 200 processes, one `git cat-file --batch-check` on the same 200 OIDs costs 82ms in one. It also creates the seam every later rung needs, so nothing after it has to touch call sites. ## Working spine Consolidate the ~7 duplicate Go git exec helpers onto one runner interface (pure refactor, no behaviour change), then add a lazily-started `git cat-file --batch` / `--batch-check` pool behind that interface for object reads only. ## In scope One runner interface; the existing helpers reduced to shims or removed; a per-repo batch pool serving object reads; reaping on exit; transparent fallback to spawning. ## Out of scope - The seventh duplicate, `gitWipOut` in the `wip` verb, is explicitly NOT converted here. That file is mid-refactor by a peer -- ~304 lines are moving out of it into a new sibling that is not in HEAD yet -- so a conversion would land on top of an in-flight move, and the dispatcher refuses to spawn onto it (DIRTY_PATH_COLLISION) for the same reason. Convert it in a one-line follow-up once that move commits; the interface this rung lands is what makes that follow-up a one-liner. Any daemon, socket, cross-process sharing, or cache. Those are #5622 and #5623. Also out: the 152 `exec.Command` call sites -- route through the wrapper, do not edit them. ## Expected steps 6 ## Assumptions - The 7 helpers differ only in error handling and output trimming, so one interface can cover them without changing any caller's observable behaviour. - `git cat-file --batch` is available in the pinned Git for Windows version. ## Confusion risks - An orphaned `git cat-file` process is WORSE than the churn this fixes. Reaping is not optional and needs its own test. - The refactor must be behaviour-preserving. If a helper's error handling differs meaningfully, preserve the difference rather than normalizing it silently. - `cmd/fak/buildcheck.go` is frequently co-occupied by peers; check `git status` before assuming a hunk there is yours. ## Coordination - Work directly on trunk (`main`); the trunk guard refuses off-trunk commits (`OFF_TRUNK`). - Commit by explicit path (`fak commit --path

-F `), never `git add -A` -- this is a shared multi-session checkout and a peer's uncommitted work sits in the same tree. - End the subject with a `(fak )` trailer or the ship stays NOT_SHIPPED. ## Trigger Rung 2 of epic #5619; the spine the rest of the epic builds on. ## Batch policy One issue, one runner interface and one warm pool -- do not split them, an interface with no consumer is dead code. Port only the call sites named under Likely files, enough to prove the interface carries real traffic. The bulk conversion of the remaining Go call sites is NOT in this rung and gets no ticket per site: it rides on top of a landed interface as one follow-up, capped at one. ## Closure binding Closes when object reads go through the pool, the #5620 benchmark shows the spawn drop before/after in this issue, and `make ci` is green with no behaviour change at any call site. ## Parent context Parent: #5619. ## Work estimate 5 points. ## Overall completion contribution 5/21 points of #5619: the spine â€” most of the win, none of the daemon lifecycle risk. ## Completion standard development

records.title: feat(gitbroker): fak gitd resident broker over a per-repo unix socket, with content-addressed cache
records.body:
## Why The spine (#5619 rung 2) batches *within* one process. But the churn is generated by MANY short-lived processes â€” 8 resident sessions running per-turn hooks plus N python dispatchers on timers. Nothing is reused across them. A resident broker is the only way to share a warm git backend across separate client processes. ## Scope - `fak gitd`: resident per-repo broker over a Unix-domain socket, token-authed. Precedent that already works on Windows in this tree: `cmd/fak/guard_lifecycle_ipc.go:51` uses `net.Listen("unix", path)`; Go supports AF_UNIX on Windows 10+. - Backend is the rung-2 pool. The broker multiplexes all clients onto it. - **Class A cache only** in this rung: content-addressed reads (object type/size, blob bytes, tree entries, commit metadata, keyed by OID). Git objects are immutable, so this cache needs **no invalidation at all** â€” that is why it comes first. Working-tree state is the NEXT rung. - **Provenance on every response**: `broker` / `cache` / `fallback-spawn`. Per the `internal/stallscan` lesson, "the broker is down" must never be spelled the same way as "the tree is clean". ## Work unit leaf -- one commit adding the broker command and its socket transport over the pool from #5621. ## Done condition `fak gitd` serves content-addressed git reads to separate client processes over a per-repo Unix socket, tagging every response with its provenance, and a client whose broker is dead or slow produces the same answer by spawning. ## Acceptance gate - `fak gitd` starts, serves, and is discoverable by a client with no env hand-wiring. - Class A queries are served from cache across separate client processes (proven by two distinct client invocations, second one cache-hit). - **Fail-open proven by test**: kill the broker mid-run, assert every client produces byte-identical output to the pre-broker path. Only latency may change. - No Class B or C query is cached in this rung. If it is not content-addressed, it is not cached here. - Provenance is on every response and surfaced where an operator can see it. - The broker cannot wedge a client: every client call is deadlined, and blowing the deadline falls back to spawning. ## Current state #5621 batches within one process. But the churn comes from many short-lived processes -- 8 resident sessions running per-turn hooks plus timer-driven python dispatchers -- and nothing is shared across them. There is no resident git backend. AF_UNIX on Windows is already proven in this tree by the guard lifecycle socket. ## Witness `go test ./cmd/fak -run Gitd` passes, including: two separate client processes where the second is a cache hit; a test that kills the broker mid-run and asserts byte-identical client output; and a test that asserts a hung broker is cut off by the client deadline rather than wedging the caller. Provenance (`broker`/`cache`/`fallback-spawn`) appears on every response. ## Likely files - `cmd/fak/guard_lifecycle_ipc.go` - `cmd/fak/serve.go` - `internal/gitgate/gitgate.go` ## Why now #5621 batches within one process, but the churn comes from many short-lived ones: 8 resident sessions running per-turn hooks plus timer-driven python dispatchers, none of which share anything. Cross-process reuse needs a resident backend, and this is the smallest thing that provides one. ## Working spine Add `fak gitd`: a per-repo Unix-socket broker whose backend is the #5621 pool, serving content-addressed reads with an in-memory cache and a provenance tag on every response. ## In scope The broker command; the socket transport with token auth; Class A (content-addressed, keyed by OID) caching only; provenance on every response; a client-side deadline with spawn fallback. ## Out of scope Working-tree state, single-flight, and any mutable cache -- all #5623. The python client is #5624. No write paths at all. ## Expected steps 7 ## Assumptions - AF_UNIX works on this Windows host: `cmd/fak/guard_lifecycle_ipc.go:51` already does `net.Listen("unix", path)` in production. - Git objects are immutable, so Class A entries never need invalidation. ## Confusion risks - Fail-open is the whole safety argument. #4603 (`core.fsmonitor=true` plus a dead daemon) is the standing lesson that a resident thing which dies must not take the fleet down with it. - 'Unmeasured' must never be spelled the same way as 'healthy' -- a broker that is down must not read as a clean tree. That is why provenance is a done-condition and not a nice-to-have. - Only content-addressed queries are cacheable here. If it is not keyed by an OID, it does not belong in this rung. ## Coordination - Work directly on trunk (`main`); the trunk guard refuses off-trunk commits (`OFF_TRUNK`). - Commit by explicit path (`fak commit --path

-F `), never `git add -A` -- this is a shared multi-session checkout and a peer's uncommitted work sits in the same tree. - End the subject with a `(fak )` trailer or the ship stays NOT_SHIPPED. ## Trigger Rung 3 of epic #5619, unblocked once #5621 lands the pool. ## Batch policy One issue, one broker commit. Do not add cache classes beyond A. ## Closure binding Closes when two separate client processes share the cache (second is a hit), a test kills the broker and asserts byte-identical client output, and provenance is visible to an operator. ## Parent context Parent: #5619. ## Work estimate 5 points. ## Overall completion contribution 5/21 points of #5619: cross-process reuse, which in-process batching cannot give. ## Completion standard development

records.title: feat(gitbroker): single-flight coalescing and working-tree state cache with a proven invalidation
records.body:
## Why Two separate wins, in dependency order. **Single-flight is the bigger one and needs no cache.** 8 sessions and N dispatchers ask the same question of the same tree concurrently. Collapsing concurrent identical in-flight queries into one execution is an ~8x cut with **no invalidation reasoning at all** â€” the answer is computed fresh, it is just computed once. Land this first and independently. **Then Class B**: working-tree state (is-dirty, status, index contents), which is genuinely mutable and shared with peers committing into the same checkout. ## Scope - Single-flight over the broker: concurrent identical queries share one execution. - Class B cache keyed on (`.git/index` mtime+size, HEAD OID, refs mtime). - **Class C stays uncached, enforced by test**: anything feeding a commit gate, a mutation, or a refusal is always freshly computed. This is the correctness line of the whole epic. ## Work unit leaf -- one commit adding single-flight and the keyed working-tree cache to the existing broker. ## Done condition Concurrent identical broker queries execute once, and working-tree state is cached against an invalidation key that a peer's commit provably busts, while decision-bearing queries are never cached at all. ## Acceptance gate - Single-flight lands and is measured **separately** from the cache, so its contribution is attributable rather than bundled. - A **negative test**: a peer commit / index write during a cached window invalidates. Proven by test, not by argument. This is the test that decides whether the cache is safe. - A source-scan test inside `internal/gitbroker` fails the build if a Class C query reaches the cache. - Stale-read budget stated explicitly: what is the worst-case staleness a Class B reader can observe, and why is that acceptable for every current Class B caller? ## Current state The broker from #5622 caches only content-addressed reads, which need no invalidation. Working-tree state -- the actually-hot query -- is still computed per caller, and concurrent identical queries from 8 sessions each execute separately. ## Witness `go test ./cmd/fak ./internal/gitbroker` passes, including a NEGATIVE test where a peer commit / index write during a cached window forces an invalidation, and a source-scan test in `internal/gitbroker` that fails the build if a decision-bearing (Class C) query reaches the cache. Single-flight is benchmarked SEPARATELY from the cache so its contribution is attributable. ## Likely files - `internal/gitbroker/singleflight.go` (new) -- the coalescer itself, and the file that binds this rung to the `gitbroker` lane. Without a path under `internal/gitbroker/**` the rung routes to no lane at all and cannot be dispatched. - `internal/gitbroker/treestate.go` (new) -- the Class B working-tree state cache and its invalidation key (`.git/index` mtime+size, HEAD OID, refs mtime). - `cmd/fak/guard_lifecycle_ipc.go` - `cmd/fak/commit.go` - `internal/commitlane/status.go` - `internal/gitgate/gitgate.go` ## Why now Single-flight is the biggest remaining win and needs no cache at all: 8 sessions asking the same question concurrently collapse to one execution, computed fresh. Class B follows because working-tree state is the actually-hot query and the only one whose caching needs a real argument. ## Working spine Add single-flight coalescing to the broker and measure it alone; then add a working-tree cache keyed on (`.git/index` mtime+size, HEAD OID, refs mtime), with decision-bearing queries excluded by a test. ## In scope Single-flight over the broker; the keyed Class B cache; a source-scan test in `internal/gitbroker` that fails the build if a Class C query reaches the cache; a stated worst-case staleness budget. ## Out of scope Any caching of a query that feeds a commit gate, a mutation, or a refusal. Those stay freshly computed, permanently. ## Expected steps 7 ## Assumptions - `.git/index` mtime+size plus HEAD and refs mtimes are sufficient to detect any peer mutation that matters to a Class B reader on this filesystem. - Every current Class B caller can tolerate the stated staleness; if one cannot, it is Class C. ## Confusion risks - Measure single-flight SEPARATELY from the cache. Bundled, neither contribution is attributable and a later regression cannot be localized. - The invalidation test must be NEGATIVE -- a peer writes, and the cache must be shown to miss. A positive test proves nothing about correctness here. - This is a shared checkout: peers commit into the same tree continuously, so 'nobody else writes during the window' is never a safe assumption. ## Coordination - Work directly on trunk (`main`); the trunk guard refuses off-trunk commits (`OFF_TRUNK`). - Commit by explicit path (`fak commit --path

-F `), never `git add -A` -- this is a shared multi-session checkout and a peer's uncommitted work sits in the same tree. - End the subject with a `(fak )` trailer or the ship stays NOT_SHIPPED. ## Trigger Rung 4 of epic #5619, unblocked once #5622 lands the broker. ## Batch policy One issue. Land single-flight first and independently; if Class B proves contentious, single-flight still stands alone. ## Closure binding Closes when single-flight is benchmarked separately from the cache, a peer commit during a cached window provably busts it, and the Class C exclusion is enforced by a failing-build test. ## Parent context Parent: #5619. ## Work estimate 4 points. ## Overall completion contribution 4/21 points of #5619: the 8x that needs no cache, plus the cache that needs real invalidation. ## Completion standard development **Why the enforcement test lives in the broker package, not architest.** The rule -- no decision-bearing query may be answered from cache -- is enforced by a source-scan test inside `internal/gitbroker`, deliberately not by an architest. Same teeth, and it keeps the constraint next to the code it constrains; architest is fak's shared witness machinery and a guarded worker may not ship into it.

records.title: feat(gitbroker): tools/fak_git.py — route the 107 python git call sites through the broker

## Why Python is the largest non-shadow spawner in the ablation (525 births, 20.1 %), and it is the thing *driving* most of the git spawns â€” the dispatchers shell out to git in a loop. 107 `subprocess` git sites exist across `tools/*.py` (of 554 subprocess sites total).
