An audit of its six acceptance criteria against trunk (`dc971c2c3c`) found **four fully met and two blocked on the same two missing seams**. The issue stays open not because the work is hard but because its remaining scope was never stated as a checkable unit, so each dispatch re-derives the audit and lands nothing.

This issue is that unit. It does not restate #4746; it names only what is left.

## Already landed (do not redo)

- `internal/model/loadprovenance.go` — artifact, digest, validation, `DiffLoadProvenance` routing.
- `internal/ggufload/gguf_load_provenance.go` — header-only producer; `(*File).LoadProvenance`.
- `internal/ggufload/gguf_transform_contract.go` — arch-keyed semantic contracts (#4744).
- `internal/provenance/runmanifest.go` — `load_provenance` field, `sha256:<hex>` shape check, fingerprint ordering.
- `docs/model-load-provenance-troubleshooting.md` — the routing guide (#4746 criterion 6).

## What is actually missing

**1. No operator-facing surface.** Nothing under `cmd/` references `LoadProvenance` or `DiffLoadProvenance`. `fak info` has no provenance mode. #4746's "operators can compare two runs and immediately see transform/path differences" is satisfied as a **Go API only** — an operator with two run directories has no command to run. Steps 1 and 2 of the troubleshooting guide are code samples, not CLI invocations.

**2. No production `RunManifest` producer.** `provenance.RunManifest` is constructed **nowhere** in non-test code. The `load_provenance` field is therefore *enforced but unpopulated*: `Validate` refuses a malformed digest, but nothing supplies a correct one. #4746's "run/readiness evidence records the artifact digest" holds at the schema and seam level (`TestLoadProvenanceDigestIsAcceptedByRunEvidence`, `TestRunEvidenceDivergesOnRealLoaderSemantics`) but no live run emits a manifest carrying it.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A `fak` command renders one artifact and diffs two, printing each `ProvenanceDelta` with its `InvestigationArea`, and emits nothing that could carry a prompt, a path, or a weight.
- [ ] At least one production code path constructs a `provenance.RunManifest` with `LoadProvenance` populated from `(*ggufload.File).LoadProvenance(scope).Digest()`.
- [ ] A test proves a run whose loader semantics changed fails its baseline comparison **through the production path**, not only through a hand-built manifest.

## Note on #4746 criterion 1

"A Qwen3.6 load reports the `ssm_a: negative-decay -> A_log` transform and how many layers/tensors used it" is **met** by `TestLoadProvenanceReportsQwen36SSMADecayInversion`, against a synthetic header-only GGUF fixture. This is not a mock: the producer is **header-only by construction**, so the criterion never required model weights — a real checkpoint exercises the identical code path with a larger tensor directory. Dispatch hosts without a `.gguf` on disk are **not** blocked on it. What a real checkpoint would add is confirmation of a *shipped release's* actual tensor/layer counts, which needs only that file's header. See "What the Qwen3.6 witness does and does not prove" in the troubleshooting guide.

records.title: CORE_SELF_MODIFY: ancestor:<ref> is constant-true for anything already on the trunk — 13/50 clearances used it, two of them citing each other
records.body:
## Claim

`ancestor:<ref>` is the second-most-used maintenance witness for `CORE_SELF_MODIFY` — **13 of the 50** `corelock-maintenance` records in `refs/notes/fak/decisions` — and it is **true by construction for every ref that is already on the trunk**. A claim that cannot be false is not a witness.

This is the sibling of #5871 (`committed:`/`path:` prove only existence). #5871's measurement and the follow-on correlation work (bf988ce33ba8, `witness_correlation`) both classify `ancestor:` as *indeterminate* — "cannot name a change at all" — which is accurate but understates it: the claim is not merely unrelated to the change, it is unfalsifiable.

## Verified

The rung (`internal/witness/witness.go`, case `"ancestor"`) is `git merge-base --is-ancestor <arg> HEAD`. Run in this checkout:

```
git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD HEAD          # exit 0  -- a commit is its own ancestor
git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD   # exit 0  -- the trunk is an ancestor of the trunk tip
```

Both CONFIRM. Any SHA already on `main` CONFIRMs for the same reason.

## What the record actually contains

All 13 `ancestor:` clearances, from the notes ref:

| claim | shape |
|---|---|
| `ancestor:HEAD` (78ce42d121) | the degenerate case, verbatim |
| `ancestor:origin/main` (165b9e5c61) | the degenerate case, spelled differently |
| 11 x `ancestor:<sha>` | a commit that had already landed |

The 11 SHA-shaped claims are not obviously degenerate until you resolve them, and two of them form a **self-referential chain of core-lock clearances**:

- `c8e0ac780c` (a `corelock-maintenance` record) cleared the lock with `ancestor:40988d01c` — itself a commit that appears in this same corpus.
- `a8b9082858` (also a `corelock-maintenance` record) cleared the lock with `ancestor:c8e0ac780` — i.e. it cited the commit immediately above.

Verified: `git merge-base --is-ancestor c8e0ac780 a8b9082858` exits 0, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor 40988d01c c8e0ac780c` exits 0. Each core-lock edit was cleared by pointing at the previous core-lock edit, which was itself cleared the same way. Nothing outside the chain was ever consulted.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

`internal/witness` is a SHARED resolver. `ancestor:` is the correct and load-bearing rung for its original purpose — "did this phase actually ship?" — where the ref names a *prerequisite* the caller could not have created (`internal/hooks/gate_fileadmission.go`, `cmd/fak/dispatch_tick_witness.go`, `internal/agent/turn.go`, `internal/workflow/journal.go`). Refuting `ancestor:HEAD` in the resolver would break rungs that are behaving correctly, for a defect that belongs to one consumer.

The asymmetry is the point: for the core-lock gate the claim is offered *about the change now being made*, and that change is not yet a commit, so **no** history-shaped claim can name it even in principle. `internal/corelockgate/correlate.go` already records this ("claim kind %q names no repository path; it resolves against commit history, which cannot contain the change because this gate runs before that change is a commit").

## Directions a maintainer might weigh

1. **Refuse history-shaped claims at the core-lock consult point only.** `corelockgate.CheckCoreLockHardSelf` owns a changed pathset; a claim kind that cannot possibly correlate with it could be refused there without touching the shared resolver or any other producer.
2. **Point the 13 at the grammar that now exists.** `changed:<path>` (ffc676b46b69) is confirmed only for a path the change actually carries, and `committed:<path>` works for any already-tracked file in the change — so an `ancestor:` claimant at this gate always has a checkable alternative. That was NOT true before ffc676b46b69 for a purely additive change, which is why closing the grammar gap came first.
3. **Leave it, and downgrade the audit language.** A `hard-self-maintenance-witness-confirmed` note whose witness is `ancestor:HEAD` currently reads as an independent corroboration and is not one.

## Not proposing a fix

Changing a core-lock clearance is a policy decision and the recorded distribution has not accumulated since the correlation observation landed. Filed for triage. Enforcement of any kind here should follow the same order the grammar work did: measure first, and make sure an honest maintainer always has a claim they can truthfully make before any shape is refused.

## Reproduction

```
git grep -l corelock-maintenance refs/notes/fak/decisions \
  | sed 's|refs/notes/fak/decisions:||; s|/||' \
  | while read s; do git notes --ref=refs/notes/fak/decisions show $s \
      | sed -n 's/.*"witness":"\(ancestor[^"]*\)".*/'"$s"' \1/p'; done
git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD HEAD; echo $?          # 0
git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD; echo $?   # 0
```

records.title: fix(closureaudit): a shipped+witnessed issue outside the dispatcher's 600-commit scan window is re-dispatched forever (135 runs burned)
records.body:
## The state that has no name

A dispatcher that re-selects an open issue until it closes has **no nameable state for
"the work already landed but nothing will ever close it."** It just re-dispatches. Each
new worker arrives, finds the feature built, has nothing to add, and exits
`CLAIM_NO_COMMIT` with `reason: unknown` — an invisible loop that burns one seat per
turn, forever, with zero issue-side activity to show for it.

## Census (2026-08-07, this repo's own ledger)

Denominators, so no subset is read as a total:

| population | count |
|---|---|
| open issues in repo | 1373 |
| recorded dispatch runs (`.dispatch-runs/*.witness`) | 2403 over 316 distinct issues |
| open issues with >= 1 run | 118 (785 runs) |
| closed issues that had runs | 198 (1618 runs) |
| open issues never dispatched | 1255 |

Grading every open issue against the **real** closure oracle — a resolving cite
(`closureaudit.ClassifyRefs`) + `dos commit-audit` `OK`/`diff-witnessed` + a
resolution-binding `claim_kind` (#2998):

- **47 OPEN issues already carry a binding, diff-witnessed commit on trunk.** They are
  `OPEN_WITNESSED`: closable right now, and re-dispatching any of them cannot produce a
  close.
- 20 of those 47 have dispatch runs — **292 runs total**, of which **135 were spent
  AFTER the witnessed commit had already landed.** That 135 is pure waste.
- The other 98 open-with-runs issues (490 runs) have no witnessed resolving commit;
  their run outcomes are dominated by `restart_exhausted` (251) and `unknown` (214) —
  worker mortality, a different defect.

## Root cause: a scan WINDOW, not a missing stamp

`tools/issue_resolve_dispatch.py:open_witnessed_dispositions` is the pre-dispatch
`OPEN_WITNESSED` guard added by #5071. It reads only the most recent
`scan_limit = 600` commits.

This repo lands **229 commits on its busiest day** and 466 in the trailing 7 days, so
600 commits reaches back **9.5 days at the mean and under 3 days at peak**. A binding
commit older than the window is **permanently invisible** to the guard. The issue is
provably shipped, provably witnessed, and will still be re-selected forever.

Measured: **15 of the 47** have their *newest* binding commit deeper than 600; **24**
have their *oldest* one deeper. Worst case is #2728 — binding commit `edcace6bde` sits
**1269 commits back**, and 33 of its 41 dispatch runs post-date it.

## What this is NOT

A widely-circulated theory tonight held that these issues fail to close because the
commit's `(fak <leaf>)` trailer does not match the issue's registered lane. **That is
false, and I checked it against the code and against #5027 specifically.**

The `(fak <leaf>)` trailer is matched against **touched paths**
(`internal/hooks/commitstamp.go:402-476`), never against an issue. The strings
`leaf` / `lane` / `fak ` appear nowhere in the decision path of
`tools/issue_closure_audit.py`, `internal/closureaudit/`,
`cmd/fak/dispatch_closure_audit.go`, or `tools/issue_resolve_witnessed.py`.
"Resolving commit cites `#N` and carries a matching `(fak <leaf>)` trailer" is
**authored prose in an issue-body template** (`internal/checkpointscore/dispatch.go:81`,
`internal/dogfoodissues/dogfoodissues.go:591`); only its non-emptiness is ever checked
(`internal/issuecontract/contract.go:1237`). Its content has drifted from the enforced
rule.

Concretely for #5027: `e68be47327` — *"test(cmd): add the steer-prs partial-state
operator gate (#5027) **(fak cmd)**"* — cites `#5027` in the subject and audits
`verdict=OK claim_kind=test witness=diff-witnessed`. It is a **fully binding, fully
witnessed** commit *with the "wrong" leaf*. It landed 2026-08-04; the issue is still
open on 2026-08-07.

## Shipped here

`internal/closureaudit/bindprobe.go` — `Probe(issue, candidates, audits, scanLimit)`, a
pure read-only fold returning one of `BOUND` / `BOUND_OUT_OF_SCAN_WINDOW` / `UNBOUND`,
plus per-commit near-misses named `mention_only` / `unwitnessed` /
`nonbinding_claim_kind` / `out_of_scan_window`, and a checkable `Next`. `Shipped()` is
the predicate a dispatcher should consult before re-selecting.

It also ports `commit_binds_resolution` / `_issue_is_docs_rung` to Go as
`ClaimKindBinds` / `IssueIsDocsRung` — the #2998 claim-kind gate that existed only on
the Python side, so `closureaudit.Grade` currently over-credits a doc-kind claim as
resolving a feature issue.

## Follow-ons (deliberately NOT done here — they change live dispatch)

1. Wire `Probe` into the pre-dispatch selector so an issue whose work demonstrably
   landed is surfaced to a human instead of re-selected.
2. Fix the window itself: `open_witnessed_dispositions` should scan by DATE or by
   `--grep "#<N>"` over full history, not by a fixed 600-commit count. The count is a
   function of fleet velocity, which is exactly the thing that grows.
3. Fold the missing #2998 claim-kind gate into `closureaudit.Grade`.

records.title: fix(accounts): Claude 5-hour vs weekly caps are misclassified — the 5-hour rolling window has no cap kind, and 4 of 8 real banners are undetected
records.body:
## Problem

fak cannot reliably tell a Claude **5-hour rolling cap** from a **weekly limit**, and in the most
common modern banner phrasings it does not detect the cap at all. The cap-kind vocabulary is
`{session, weekly}` with `session` as the default — there is no `5-hour rolling` kind anywhere —
so the 5-hour window has no home and lands in a bucket whose hold is clamped to 90 minutes.

`internal/fleetaccounts/capstate.go` opens with "the cap-disambiguation core: it resolves a carried
throttle's *5-hour rolling cap vs weekly limit* question ONCE into a canonical CapState". That core
is sound. The defect is entirely **upstream of it**: the classifier that decides which leg
(`reset` vs `weekly`) a throttle is written into is a two-regex string match that defaults to
`session`, and it is fed by a banner detector that misses the exact phrasings Claude emits today.

### Measured behavior (run against the live classifier, `tools/issue_resolve_dispatch.py`)

`_cap_hit_from_text` + `_write_cap_hold`, `fallback_min=60`:

| worker-log banner | detected | kind | reset_text | hold written |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Claude usage limit reached. Your limit will reset at 3pm (America/Los_Angeles).` | **no** | — | — | **none** |
| `You've hit your 5-hour limit. Your limit will reset at 3pm (America/Los_Angeles).` | **no** | — | — | **none** |
| `You've hit your usage limit; resets 3pm (America/Los_Angeles)` | yes | `session` | `3pm` | **1.50h** (clamped) |
| `Claude usage limit reached. Your weekly limit will reset on Nov 3 at 9am (…).` | **no** | — | — | **none** |
| `You've hit your weekly limit. Your limit will reset at Nov 3, 9am (…).` | yes | `weekly` | `''` | **1.00h** (blind fallback) |
| `You've hit your Opus weekly limit. Your limit will reset on Monday at 9am.` | yes | `weekly` | `''` | **1.00h** |
| `You've hit your limit for the week. Try again Nov 3.` | yes | **`session`** | `''` | ≤1.50h |
| `kind=weekly_limit announced_wait=1h7m0s` (gateway) | yes | `weekly` | `1h7m0s` | 1.12h ✔ |

Only the gateway's own `announced_wait` line — the one path #2610 already fixed — produces a
correct hold. Every Claude-emitted banner is either invisible or held for the wrong duration.

## Systemic cause

1. **A hyphen defeats the banner detector.** `_CAP_BANNER_RE = r"hit your[\w\s]*limit|…"`
   (`tools/issue_resolve_dispatch.py:2802`). `[\w\s]` excludes `-`, so `hit your 5-hour limit`
   does **not** match while `hit your 5 hour limit` does. The one banner that names the 5-hour cap
   explicitly is the one the detector cannot see.
2. **The "Claude usage limit reached" phrasing matches no branch at all** — it carries none of
   `hit your … limit`, `limit exhausted`, `rate limited`, `HTTP 429`. No hold is written, so the
   dispatcher keeps spawning workers into the wall for the entire window.
3. **The reset parsers only accept "resets <when>".** Claude's modern phrasing is "your limit
   will **reset at/on** <when>". `_CAP_RESET_RE` / `_CAP_RESET_FALLBACK_RE` require the literal
   `resets`; `_RESET_AT_RE` accepts `reset at` but only followed by an **ISO** date, so `3pm` and
   `Nov 3, 9am` are both dropped → `reset_text=''` → blind `fallback_min` hold.
4. **Classification is a default-to-session coin flip.** `_CAP_WEEKLY_RE = r"weekly[\w/\s]*limit"`
   requires the literal word `weekly` *before* `limit`. `limit for the week`, `resets Monday`,
   `7-day limit` all fall through to `session`.
5. **The 90-minute clamp over-fires on the 5-hour cap.** `_SESSION_HOLD_MAX_MIN = 90` guards the
   `session` bucket against a stale bare time-of-day, but the 5-hour rolling cap lives in that
   bucket by default and its real reset is up to 5h out — the seat is re-offered up to **3.5h
   early** and respawns into the same wall.
6. **The misclassification is then laundered into the wrong leg.**
   `fleet_accounts.active_account_cap_throttles` (`tools/fleet_accounts.py:628`) sets
   `throttle["weekly"]` **only** when `kind == "weekly"`; otherwise the reset lands in the daily
   `reset` slot. So `DisambiguateCap`'s `CapWeekly` / `CapDaily` verdict — and every predicate
   reading it — is only as good as that upstream default.
7. **The Go store has no weekly/5-hour distinction either.**
   `internal/accounts/cooldown.go` has one `CooldownUsageLimit` kind and one
   `DefaultCooldownWindow = time.Hour`, whose own comment reads "Sized to a rolling 5-hour cap's
   typical near-term reset". The repo's own `TestResolveResetNoWindowIsZero`
   (`internal/accounts/cooldown_test.go:413`) pins `"weekly limit reached; resets at 15:00"` →
   zero → the 1-hour default. A weekly-capped account is therefore re-admitted to the pool
   ~168 times before its real reset unless the message happens to carry an `announced_wait`.
8. **The launch classifier discards the distinction it already has.**
   `launchModelUsageLimitSignals` (`cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:732`) lists both `"5-hour limit"`
   and `"weekly limit"`, but both collapse into a single `launchModelUsageLimit` before reaching
   the store, so the information is thrown away at the seam where it would matter.

The through-line: **three independent classifiers** (Python dispatcher gate, Python fleet-accounts
fold, Go launch/cooldown) each re-derive "what kind of cap is this?" from raw text with different
regexes and different defaults, and none of them models the 5-hour rolling window as its own kind.

## Proposed fix

1. Introduce one shared cap-kind vocabulary — `rolling_5h`, `weekly`, `session`, `rate` — and make
   `rolling_5h`, not `session`, the default for an unqualified Claude usage-limit banner.
2. Extract ONE banner detector + ONE reset parser used by both the Python dispatcher gate and the
   Go cooldown writer (mirroring how `accounts.ResolveReset` is already the single reset resolver
   shared by both Go writers). Cover the hyphenated `5-hour`, the `Claude usage limit reached`
   phrasing, and the `will reset at/on <wall-clock|dated>` clause.
3. Give each kind its own default window and its own clamp: a `rolling_5h` hold runs to its named
   reset (bounded by 5h, not 90m); a `weekly` hold runs to the named weekday/dated reset and never
   falls back to a 1-hour window.
4. Add `CooldownWeeklyLimit` (or a `CapKind` field on `CooldownEntry`) so the Go store can hold the
   two windows independently as separate signals on the same account, and plumb the kind through
   `classifyLaunchModelUnavailable` → `recordLaunchCooldown` instead of collapsing it.
5. Write `throttle["weekly"]` from the typed kind rather than from a substring match, so
   `DisambiguateCap` receives a real classification.

## Acceptance criteria

- A fixture corpus of the eight banners in the table above classifies to the correct cap kind at
  the real seam, with the currently-undetected four detected.
- A 5-hour cap whose banner names a reset 4h out is held ~4h, not 1.5h; a behavioral test asserts
  the seat is still cooled at now+1.5h.
- A weekly cap whose banner names a dated or weekday reset is held to that reset; a behavioral test
  asserts the seat is still cooled at now+1h (today it is re-admitted there).
- The Go and Python classifiers agree on all eight fixtures — one parity test pins them together.
- `DisambiguateCap` reports `CapWeekly` for the weekly fixtures and `CapDaily` for the 5-hour
  fixtures, driven by the typed kind rather than a substring match.
- Proof includes the failing-before/passing-after behavioral tests plus one scrubbed captured
  worker-log tail for each of the two cap kinds.

## Relationship

- #2610 fixed the gateway `announced_wait` path only — the one row in the table that is correct
  today. This issue covers the Claude-emitted banners that path never sees.
- #4998 (org auth walls) is a different, non-self-recovering wall class; it shares the cooldown
  store but not the cap-kind question.
- #5573 (`account_probe` coverage floor) governs when a capped-looking seat is re-probed; a correct
  hold length is the input that gate assumes.

## Work estimate
Estimate: 3 points. Uncertainty: scoped from the measured fixture table; revise if the shared
classifier has to absorb the codex banner family too.

## Overall completion contribution
Contribution: 3/3 points.

## Completion standard
production

## Target operating envelope
- cap_kind_recall: >= 8/8 fixture banners classified to the correct cap kind
- five_hour_hold_error: <= 15 min vs the banner-named reset
- weekly_hold_underruns: 0 re-admissions before the banner-named weekly reset

## Witnessed operating envelope
- cap_kind_recall: n/a (no shared classifier landed yet; measured today is 4/8 detected, 3/8 correctly kinded)
- five_hour_hold_error: n/a (no rolling_5h kind exists yet; measured today is -2.5h at a 4h reset)
- weekly_hold_underruns: n/a (no typed weekly window yet; measured today is a 1h hold on a multi-day cap)

## Notes

Evidence in this issue was produced by calling `_cap_hit_from_text` / `_write_cap_hold` directly
against the listed banner strings; the Go-side claim is pinned by the existing
`TestResolveResetNoWindowIsZero` and `TestCoolWeeklyLimitHonorsAnnouncedWait`.

records.title: feat(idea_scout): substance gate — a repo-size admission floor so scaffold repos cannot ride the fresh/trending lane
records.body:
## Parent context

`/scout-loop` pass 2026-08-08 over the open `idea-scout` queue. Study note:
`docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-SENTRYLLM-2026-08-08.md`. Lead studied and closed
not-planned: #5596. Nearest open neighbour: #4075 (see Confusion risks).

## Generation

now (`gen/now`)

## Current state

`idea_scout` rewards freshness and star-velocity but scores nothing about whether the
surfaced repo contains implementing code.

- `tools/idea_scout.py:322-396` — `score_candidate()` sums exactly six things: term hits
  (`W_TITLE_HIT`/`W_BODY_HIT`), recency (`W_RECENT_180` + `W_RECENT_30`), stars
  (`stars // STAR_DIVISOR`), HN/Reddit points, push-freshness
  (`W_FRESH_PUSH`/`W_RECENT_PUSH`), and star velocity (`stars // age_days`, capped at
  `TRENDING_CAP`). No term reflects repo substance.
- `tools/idea_scout.py:824` and `:836` — `fetch_github()` and `fetch_github_fresh()` both
  request `fullName,description,url,stargazersCount,pushedAt,updatedAt,createdAt,language`.
  No size field is fetched. (`language` *is* fetched and stored at `:460`, but it is never
  read by `score_candidate()` — only rendered into the issue body at `:680-681` — and a
  null `language` would only catch a repo with no code files at all.)
- `tools/idea_scout.py:457-461` — `parse_github_repos()` copies exactly three keys into
  `extra` (`stars`, `pushed_at`, `language`), and `score_candidate()` reads only `extra`.
- The Go port is identical on all three counts: `internal/ideascout/fetch.go:57,67` (same
  `--json` list), `internal/ideascout/ideascout.go:151-162` (`type GitHubRepo`, no size
  field), `internal/ideascout/parse.go:88-91` (same three-key `Extra`),
  `internal/ideascout/score.go:12` (`ScoreCandidate`, same six summands).

**Witness — a real false positive, not a hypothetical.** The pass selected the
highest-scoring *repo-shaped* lead in the open triage queue (116 open `idea-scout` issues
at the time) and studied it: #5596 `Sentry-LLM/SentryLLM`, **score 75** —
`terms: prompt injection, defense; recent (0d); very fresh (≤30d); pushed ≤45d (actively
updated); trending (34★/day, +20)`. Read at pinned
`@1ac6b81bfa73be2237e6219e3155d47b74b2b7a2`, it implements none of what it advertises:

- README claims 10 detection categories, an SDK, and OWASP LLM Top-10 coverage, and marks
  `[x] Prompt injection detection (v1)` as shipped.
- The entire runtime is one handler — `artifacts/api-server/src/routes/health.ts:6@1ac6b81`
  (`router.get("/healthz", …)`, returning `{ status: "ok" }` at `:7`) — and
  `lib/api-spec/openapi.yaml:14@1ac6b81` is the only entry under `paths:` (`:13`).
- `lib/db/src/schema/index.ts:20@1ac6b81` is the unedited Drizzle template — `export {}`.
- `replit.md:1@1ac6b81` is still the scaffold header (`# [Project name]`).
- A grep for `injection|jailbreak|exfiltrat|threat` across every `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.yaml`
  matches **zero** source files (85 such files tracked).
- The README install line is uninstallable: `registry.npmjs.org/sentryllm` → **HTTP 404**.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:28,37@1ac6b81` runs `npm ci` / `npm test` in a pnpm workspace
  with no `package-lock.json`, and the root `package.json` has neither a `test` nor a
  `lint` script — plus a `preinstall` hook that exits 1 for any non-pnpm agent, so step
  `:28` fails before anything else runs. The CI is decorative.

For calibration, in the same queue `kvpress` (#5328, 1142 stars, real kernels) scored
**30**. The scaffold beat it by 45 points — 2.5x — and 69 of its 75 points came from
recency + push-freshness + velocity, 6 from term hits, and **0** from stars (34 stars
earn nothing: `34 // STAR_DIVISOR(100) == 0`).

**Sizes, from the same API surface the fix uses:**
`gh search repos --owner Sentry-LLM --json fullName,size,stargazersCount SentryLLM`
→ `[{"fullName":"Sentry-LLM/SentryLLM","size":135,"stargazersCount":35}]`;
`gh search repos "kvpress" --limit 1 --json fullName,size` → `[{"fullName":"…/kvpress","size":7455}]`.
A 55x gap on a field that is already free on the call the scout already makes.

## Why this is next

Every wasted `/scout-loop` cycle is a whole study pass — clone, read, note, close — spent
on a repo that a single already-fetched integer would have deprioritised. This is the
cheapest precision lever in the crawler, and it sits upstream of the entire triage-closure
family (#4072–#4076): accounting for a bad decision is worth less than not making it.

## Working spine

`/scout-loop` surfaces a lead → the lead has code behind its README, or it never reaches
the queue.

## Priority context

Working path: idea_scout gather → score → file → `/scout-loop` study → borrow-or-close.
Current blocker: the top of the repo-shaped queue can be a scaffold, so the study step
burns a cycle to discover there is nothing to read.
Unblocks: the #3947 accounting family becomes meaningful once the decisions being
accounted for are the right ones.
Not polish: this is one config floor and one comparison per lane on both implementations,
not a scorer redesign.

**Generation fit (`gen/now`).** The crawler is the current default path and the defect is
live today. *Promotion:* readiness is provable by the focused test below rather than by a
dogfood window, so nothing gates the move toward now. *Demotion / retirement:* if #4075's
two-stage file-evidence re-check lands first and subsumes an admission floor, retire this
leaf instead of duplicating the seam. *Invalidating assumption:* the floor assumes `size`
correlates with substance; that assumption could fail for a vendored-asset repo that is
large but hollow, or for a genuinely small dense library — recheck the floor against a
wider sample before widening it. *Orthogonality:* generation is a horizon, not a priority
ordering (`priority/P2` is set independently), not a branch strategy (this lands on the
shared trunk, `main`, with no branch of its own), and not a runtime feature gate — the
admission floor is always on and is never an exposure gate.

## Work unit

leaf

## Expected steps

5

## Assumptions

- `size` (KB) is returned by `gh search repos --json` for every repo and costs no extra
  round-trip. Verified:
  `gh search repos "prompt injection" --limit 2 --json fullName,size` → exit 0 with `size`
  populated. **`diskUsage` is NOT a `gh search repos` field** — it is the GitHub GraphQL
  `Repository.diskUsage` name, and `gh search repos --json diskUsage` exits with
  `Unknown JSON field: "diskUsage"` plus the legal field list. Do not use it; `gh_json()`
  at `tools/idea_scout.py:815` raises on a non-zero exit, which would kill both GitHub
  lanes.
- `tools/idea_scout_test.py` and `tools/idea_scout.py` are already listed in
  `internal/pythongate/baseline.go:334-335`, so extending that test file lands. A **new**
  `tools/*_test.py` would not clear the python gate — do not create one.
- `internal/ideascout/testdata/source_corpus.json` is read by both
  `tools/idea_scout_test.py:999` and `internal/ideascout/ideascout_test.go:1011`; a case
  added there must pass on both implementations.

## Confusion risks

- **This is not a scoring weight.** The obvious framing — a `W_THIN_REPO` negative term —
  does not work at any proportionate magnitude. To push the witness's 75 below `kvpress`'s
  30 needs a penalty of 46; to push it below `min_score` (25, `tools/idea_scout.py:249`)
  needs 51. Both are >2x the largest weight in the file (`W_RECENT_30 = 22`, `:280`) and
  larger than `TRENDING_CAP + W_FRESH_PUSH` combined, which would make a self-declared
  proxy the heaviest term in the scorer. Use a pre-score admission floor instead, mirroring
  the existing `fresh_min_stars` (`:258`, applied `:1073-1074`).
- **Not a fresh-lane-only floor.** The witness has 34 stars, which clears the stars-lane
  `min_stars: 25` (`:255`) too, and `extra["lane"]` (set at `:1077`) is never rendered so
  we cannot even prove which lane admitted it. The floor must apply to both GitHub lanes.
- **Nearest open neighbour is #4075**, not the epic. #4075 ("two-stage cheap→file-level
  re-triage with a real defer state") shares this exact seam and stage — its own body says
  "**Seam:** `tools/idea_scout.py` (`plan_issues` scoring)" and "add a per-candidate
  file-evidence re-check that can move include→defer". The whole #4072–#4076 family is
  **pre-file**, not post-file (#4073 names `tools/idea_scout.py:445`, the `max_issues` cap,
  now at `:753`; `plan_issues` runs strictly before `create_issue`). This leaf is narrower:
  a single already-fetched integer used as an admission floor, no `defer` state, no ledger
  transition. If #4075 lands first, fold this in as its GitHub-repo instantiation.
- Repo size is a proxy, not a substance oracle. The witness is not "README-only" — it has
  81 `.ts`/`.tsx` files and 7,088 lines — it is *scaffold-only*. A floor tuned to flag
  135 KB is therefore more aggressive than "catch a repo with no code," and a genuinely
  small, dense library will be swept up. That trade must be stated in the config comment,
  not discovered later.

## Coordination notes

- Two dos.toml lanes: `tools` and `ideascout`. Land in two commits, `tools` first (see
  Partition plan) — the Go commit carries the shared corpus case, so landing it first
  would red `tools/idea_scout_test.py` on the trunk between commits.
- Do not touch `plan_issues`, the ledger, or `max_issues`: that surface belongs to
  #4073/#4075.

- Required model tier: T1
- Optimal model tier: T0 — the cross-language cross-pin (Python + Go read one corpus) is
  the trap a lower tier misses.

## Trigger

A `/scout-loop` or `/study-repo` pass finds that the lead it studied has no implementing
code, i.e. the study produced zero borrows because there was nothing to borrow.

## Batch policy

One issue for this axis. Re-observations of the same defect append a witness bullet to
this issue rather than filing a new one; a *different* precision axis (e.g. archived
repos, forks, star-farming) gets its own leaf.

## In scope

- `tools/idea_scout.py`: add `size` to the `--json` list in `fetch_github()` (`:824`) and
  `fetch_github_fresh()` (`:836`); carry it through the `parse_github_repos()` `extra`
  allow-list (`:458-460`) as `"size": it.get("size", 0)`; add a
  `min_repo_size_kb` key to `DEFAULTS` (`:245-273`, alongside `min_stars`/`fresh_min_stars`)
  and apply it as a pre-score admission floor in **both** GitHub lanes (`:1061-1062` and
  `:1073-1074`), with a comment stating the proxy trade.
- `internal/ideascout`: the same four changes — `fetch.go:57,67`; a `Size int
  \`json:"size"\`` field on `GitHubRepo` (`ideascout.go:151-162`); the `Extra` map in
  `parse.go:88-91`; `MinRepoSizeKB` in `Config`/`DefaultConfig`/the config-key switch
  (`ideascout.go`, `config.go:25-27,235-239`) and the floor in `gather.go:87,96`.
- Tests: extend `tools/idea_scout_test.py` (`GithubParseTest.test_maps_fields` for the new
  `extra["size"]` mapping; a gather case for the floor) and
  `internal/ideascout/ideascout_test.go`, plus one shared case in
  `internal/ideascout/testdata/source_corpus.json`.

## Out of scope

- Any negative scoring weight (`W_THIN_REPO`) — see Confusion risks for the arithmetic.
- Reading repo contents, trees, or languages via extra API calls. The whole point is that
  `size` is free on the call already being made.
- The `defer`/skip-audit ledger (#4073, #4075) and the `max_issues` cap.
- Filters on archived / fork / star-velocity abuse — separate axes, separate leaves.
- Tuning the floor against anything beyond the two witnessed points; pick a conservative
  default and record the rationale in the config comment.

## Done condition

`gh search repos --json size` is requested and carried into `extra`/`Extra` on both
implementations, and a GitHub repo candidate whose `size` is below `min_repo_size_kb` is
dropped before scoring in **both** the stars lane and the fresh lane, on both
implementations, with the default value and its proxy trade documented inline. A
`size: 135` candidate is not admitted; a `size: 7455` candidate is admitted and its score
is byte-identical to today's.

## Witness

`python tools/idea_scout_test.py && go test ./internal/ideascout`

## Acceptance gate

`python tools/idea_scout_test.py && go test ./internal/ideascout && go build ./...`

## Lane

tools

## Path hints

- `tools/idea_scout.py`
- `tools/idea_scout_test.py`
- `internal/ideascout/fetch.go`
- `internal/ideascout/parse.go`
- `internal/ideascout/gather.go`
- `internal/ideascout/config.go`
- `internal/ideascout/ideascout.go`
- `internal/ideascout/ideascout_test.go`
- `internal/ideascout/testdata/source_corpus.json`

## Owning lane(s)

- `tools` — `dos.toml:1063` `tools = ["tools/**", "scripts/**"]` — covers
  `tools/idea_scout.py`, `tools/idea_scout_test.py`
- `ideascout` — `dos.toml:852` `ideascout = ["internal/ideascout/**"]` — covers all Go
  files above including `testdata/source_corpus.json`

## Contention check

`dos arbitrate --workspace . --lane tools && dos arbitrate --workspace . --lane ideascout && git status -sb -- tools/idea_scout.py tools/idea_scout_test.py internal/ideascout/`

## Partition plan (clean-now vs hot-later)

Two clean lanes at filing time (`git status --porcelain` over all nine paths was empty).
Both halves are independently landable and independently green — land in this order:

- **PART 1 (`tools`, land first):** the Python `size` fetch + `extra` mapping + floor, with
  its unit tests in `tools/idea_scout_test.py`. Self-contained; green alone.
- **PART 2 (`ideascout`, land second):** the Go mirror **plus** the shared
  `testdata/source_corpus.json` case. The corpus is read by both test files, so it must
  land with the Go half, after the Python half already implements the behaviour — landing
  the corpus case first would red `tools/idea_scout_test.py` on the trunk.

If `ideascout` is hot when you pick this up, PART 1 still lands; the corpus case then
covers only the already-landed Python behaviour once PART 2 follows.

## Commit recipe

`fak commit --path tools/idea_scout.py --path tools/idea_scout_test.py -m "feat(idea_scout): add a repo-size admission floor so scaffold repos cannot ride freshness (fak tools)"`

then

`fak commit --path internal/ideascout/fetch.go --path internal/ideascout/parse.go --path internal/ideascout/gather.go --path internal/ideascout/config.go --path internal/ideascout/ideascout.go --path internal/ideascout/ideascout_test.go --path internal/ideascout/testdata/source_corpus.json -m "feat(ideascout): mirror the repo-size admission floor in the Go scout (fak ideascout)"`

Never `git add -A`; no worktrees (`OFF_TRUNK`). The trailer binds the **path lane**, so it
is `(fak tools)` for the Python commit and `(fak ideascout)` for the Go commit — not
`(fak idea_scout)`.

## Boundary notes

Public issue only. No credentials, no private lab or accelerator evidence, no operator
paths. All foreign-repo evidence is from a public MIT repo read at a pinned public sha;
all API evidence is from unauthenticated-equivalent public endpoints.

## Closure binding

Resolving commits must cite `#5891` and carry matching `(fak tools)` / `(fak ideascout)`
trailers so the close arm can witness the diff. Close only when the Witness command above
is green on the trunk with both commits landed.

## Final checks

- [x] This is a leaf, not an epic or research placeholder.
- [x] The generation horizon is selected, or this issue is explicitly marked needs-triage.
- [x] The in-scope work can be verified by the witness above.
- [x] I have not included secrets, private lab/operator evidence, credentials, or
      proprietary data.

---

**Dogfood witness — ABSENT on axis.** Axis: does a surfaced lead contain implementing
code, or only a README?

- `fak_feature_query` "idea-scout crawler substance gate: filter README-only repos with no
  implementing code from surfaced leads" → no card on the axis.
- Re-witnessed with "score a GitHub repo lead by repository size or code volume, not just
  stars and freshness" → no card on the axis.
- In-repo control (reproducible from a clean checkout):
  `grep -niE "diskusage|substance|scaffold|vaporware|readme.only|hollow" tools/idea_scout.py internal/ideascout/*.go`
  → no hits, while
  `grep -c "score" tools/idea_scout.py` and
  `grep -n "min_stars\|fresh_min_stars\|min_score\|min_points" tools/idea_scout.py`
  → `:249`, `:255`, `:256`, `:258` — i.e. the file is full of admission floors and every
  one of them is a popularity floor. No archived filter, no fork filter, no denylist, no
  size or content check exists on either implementation.

Verdict: **ABSENT-on-axis.** fak has the crawler and a transparent scorer; it has nothing
that asks whether the thing it surfaced is real.

records.title: fix(safecommit): bind lock-holder identity to process start time so a recycled PID cannot wedge the lane forever
records.body:
## Problem

`safecommit`'s PID-reuse guard (#2339) decides "is the recorded lock holder still the
original process?" with an **image-name heuristic**, and the allowlist is biased against
exactly the host fak runs on.

`internal/safecommit/lockprobe.go:117` declares:

```go
var committerImageTokens = []string{
	"fak", "git", "go", "dlv", ".test",
	"claude", "node", "pwsh", "powershell", "cmd", "bash", "sh", "zsh",
}
```

and `looksLikeCommitterImage` (`internal/safecommit/lockprobe.go:125`) returns true for
any image containing one of those substrings, which makes the lock **not reapable**
(`ProbeLock`, `internal/safecommit/lockprobe.go:177-183`).

On a fleet host the running process set is overwhelmingly `pwsh`, `node`, `claude`,
`git`, `bash`, `cmd` — the allowlist *is* the ambient process population. So when the
original holder dies and the OS recycles its PID onto any ordinary fleet process, the
probe reports `Alive=true`, `Foreign=false`, `Reason=""`, and the lock is judged
permanently un-reapable. `holder_dead` never fires (the PID *is* alive) and
`holder_foreign` never fires (the image looks committer-like). The lane stays wedged
until a human intervenes.

The broad allowlist is deliberate and correct as a *fail-safe* — #2339's acceptance
forbids breaking a live committer's lock. The defect is that image name is too weak a
discriminator to be the only identity signal.

## The borrow

Bind lock/lease ownership to **`pid` + the process start time**, not to `pid` + a name
guess. Start time makes identity *provable*: if the process at that PID started after
the lock was recorded, the original holder is gone, whatever its image is now called.

Source: `PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent@a18809e0`, MIT.

- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-lease.ts:140` — `getProcessStartId(pid)`,
  a three-platform start-time probe: Windows `Process.StartTime.ToUniversalTime().Ticks`,
  Linux field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat`, macOS/BSD `ps -p <pid> -o lstart=`.
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-lease.ts:177` — `isLeaseOwnerAlive` requires
  both `isProcessAlive(pid)` **and** a start-id match, and treats an *unreadable*
  start-id as alive (same fail-safe direction fak already takes).
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-lease.ts:249-257` — the recorded owner
  persists `processStartId` alongside `pid` at acquisition time.

Their axis is identical to fak's: never break a live holder's lease, never wedge on a
dead one. They reach it with proof; fak reaches it with a name heuristic.

## Why they built it this way

prime-agent runs daemon-backed sessions that outlive the terminal and get reattached
(`packages/coding-agent/docs/long-running-agents.md`); a session lease that wedged after
a crash would strand the saved session behind a lock forever. They pay a subprocess
(PowerShell / `ps`) per liveness check to buy that. fak's fleet has the same
crash-then-reclaim shape, so the tradeoff transfers.

## Scope (ship-alone)

Add the start-time identity to `safecommit` only. `Foreign` gains a second, stronger
trigger; the image allowlist stays as the fallback for records with no recorded
start-id, so existing lockfiles keep today's behavior.

Not in scope here: `internal/procguard` (`deadowner.go`) applies the same bare-PID
liveness before killing, and is a plausible second site for the same primitive — it
needs its own witness and its own leaf, not a speculative expansion of this one.

## First checkable step

Add `internal/safecommit.processStartID(pid int) (string, bool)` behind the existing
`//go:build windows` / unix split (mirroring `alive_image_windows.go`), and a unit test
that proves the discriminator the image check cannot make: a lockfile recording
`{pid: P, startID: S_old}` where PID `P` is alive with start-id `S_new` and image `pwsh`
must probe `Reapable() == true` with `Reason == ReapReasonHolderForeign`, whereas today
`internal/safecommit/lockprobe.go:179` returns not-reapable. Use the existing
`processImageNameFn` package-var seam for injection.

## License

**INSPIRE.** prime-agent is MIT and fak is Apache-2.0, so vendoring would be permitted
with attribution — but this is TypeScript and the borrow is the technique (which
per-platform syscall yields a stable start id), not the bytes. Reimplement clean-room in
Go, citing the source above.

---
Studied via `.claude/skills/study-repo`; trail in `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-PRIME-AGENT-2026-08-08.md`.

records.title: feat(gateway): add a worktree-effect no-progress verdict so a varying-output zero-diff loop is caught
records.body:
## Problem

fak's structural no-progress detection reads the **output stream**, never the
**artifact**. `internal/gateway/noprogress.go:47-57` defines exactly two closed verdicts:

- `NO_PROGRESS` — K consecutive turns of *byte-identical planner output digests*
  ("the model is emitting byte-identical work", `internal/gateway/noprogress.go:48-51`);
- `LIVELOCK_REFUSED_CALL` — the same call re-proposed until guardrsi's livelock detector
  trips, i.e. no effect-capable call is ever *admitted*
  (`internal/gateway/noprogress.go:53-56`).

Both miss the most expensive all-night failure mode: a worker whose output **varies**
every turn and whose calls are **admitted** every turn, but which changes nothing on
disk. It re-reads files, re-runs tests, rewrites the same explanation with different
wording, retries a gate. Planner digests differ, so `NO_PROGRESS` never latches. Calls
are admitted, so `LIVELOCK_REFUSED_CALL` never latches. The loop spends its full turn and
token budget looking busy and lands a zero-byte diff.

The file's own framing names the gap precisely — it distinguishes reading "what the model
said" from reading "what the loop did" (`internal/gateway/noprogress.go:8-16`) — but both
implemented verdicts still key off what the model *emitted*, not what the repository
*became*.

## The borrow

Fingerprint the **worktree** and treat a byte-identical fingerprint across a
failed-then-retried gate as futility.

Source: `PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent@a18809e0`, MIT.

- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/autonomous.ts:374` — `captureGitWorktreeSnapshot`
  builds a three-part fingerprint: `git status --porcelain=v1 -z -uall --no-renames`,
  `git diff --no-ext-diff --binary HEAD`, and a content hash of untracked files
  (`untrackedHash`, `autonomous.ts:421`). Both git reads pass `--no-optional-locks`
  (`autonomous.ts:394`, `autonomous.ts:407`) so fingerprinting never takes the index lock
  — a property fak already values (`internal/commitlane/status.go:316`).
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/autonomous.ts:296-311` — if the current fingerprint
  equals the snapshot taken after the last failure *of that same gate command*, the gate
  is **not rerun**; the attempt counter still increments and the agent is told exactly
  why: `"not rerun: workspace unchanged since previous failed gate"` /
  `"Edit source files, tests, or a blocker artifact before attempting to finish again."`
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/autonomous.ts:370` — `gitWorktreeSnapshotsEqual` is a
  plain three-field byte comparison.

Note the untracked-content hash rather than status alone: it counts a brand-new
untracked file as progress, and it does not trust stat-cache dirtiness.

## Why they built it this way

Their autonomous mode exists for long-horizon research evals with a hard budget
(`DEFAULT_AUTONOMOUS_LIMITS`, `packages/coding-agent/src/core/autonomous.ts:48` — 3
continuations / 12 turns / 80k tokens / 30 min) and the agent is explicitly forbidden to
declare itself done: *"Do not end the session yourself; the verifier/evaluator decides
completion when configured gates pass"* (`autonomous.ts:46`). Once you refuse the agent's
self-report, you need an independent progress oracle, and the artifact is the only thing
that cannot be narrated. fak takes the same "a green build is a self-report" stance
(`internal/orphanscan/orphanscan.go:11`), so the reasoning transfers directly.

## Scope (ship-alone)

One new closed verdict alongside the existing two — proposed `NO_EFFECT` (name to
settle in review; it must not collide with `NO_PROGRESS`'s output-digest meaning) —
latched when a turn completes with a worktree fingerprint byte-identical to the previous
turn's, for K consecutive turns. It reuses the existing plumbing wholesale: the closed
`dos.toml [reasons]` vocabulary, the `ArmMetrics.StoppedBySession` surface, and the
session-gate non-proceed path.

Deliberately excluded: reusing the fingerprint to *skip* re-running an expensive gate
(the `make ci` cost saving). Same primitive, separable value, its own leaf.

## First checkable step

Add `internal/gateway` (or a small sibling) helper `worktreeFingerprint(ctx, root)`
returning the status/diff/untracked-hash triple via `--no-optional-locks`, plus a test
that drives the detector with K turns of *differing* planner-output digests over an
unchanged tree and asserts the session gate returns non-proceed with the new reason —
the case `internal/gateway/noprogress.go`'s digest comparison provably lets through
today. Pair it with the inverse: one turn that writes a single untracked file must reset
the counter.

## License

**INSPIRE.** prime-agent is MIT, fak Apache-2.0, so vendoring is permitted with
attribution, but the borrow is the fingerprint recipe (which three git reads, why
untracked content is hashed, why `--no-optional-locks`) rather than TypeScript to
translate. Reimplement clean-room in Go, citing the source above.

---
Studied via `.claude/skills/study-repo`; trail in `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-PRIME-AGENT-2026-08-08.md`.

records.title: fix(accounts): 'fleet-accounts wave' allocates slots on cooled accounts, so every worker's guard rotates to one pool and the fan-out collapses
records.body:
## What

`fak fleet-accounts wave --count N` allocates session slots **without consulting the
cooldown store**, so it hands out slots on accounts it already knows are usage-limited.
Each worker's `fak guard` then independently discovers the cooldown at startup and
rotates to the same fallback account — collapsing the whole fan-out onto ONE rate-limit
pool.

This is precisely the failure `tools/launch_wave_detached.ps1` exists to prevent. Its
`.WHY` header states the problem it solves: *"all N workers share ONE usage pool and the
fan-out serializes"*. It fixes the switcher tie-break, but the cooldown blind spot
re-creates the identical outcome one layer down.

## Witness (wave of 12 requested, 9 spawned, 2026-08-08)

The plan printed 3 distinct pools:

```
WAVE PLAN  requested=30  allocation_requested=12  granted=12  distinct_pools=3  target_tier=t1
  (naive burst would give 1 pool; this wave uses 3 distinct pool(s) and 12 bounded session slot(s))
  lane 1: <acct-A>   t1  slot=1/6  pool=uuid:5586...cca2
  lane 2: <acct-B>   t1  slot=1/6  pool=uuid:06a1...860f
  lane 3: <acct-C>   t1  slot=1/6  pool=uuid:43df...fa7
  ...
```

Every spawned worker's guard log, line 1:

```
lane  1 :: account "<acct-A>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  2 :: account "<acct-B>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  3 :: (no rotation line)          <- already <acct-C>
lane  4 :: account "<acct-A>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  5 :: account "<acct-B>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  6 :: (no rotation line)
lane  7 :: account "<acct-A>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  8 :: account "<acct-B>" is cooling down - rotating to "<acct-C>"
lane  9 :: (no rotation line)

distinct rotation targets: 6 -> "<acct-C>"
```

**Result: 9/9 workers on one pool. Promised 3, delivered 1.**

And `fak accounts cooldown`, run in the same minute, already knew:

```
cooled accounts (2) - dropped from the servable pool until reset:
  uuid:06a1...860f  usage-limit  resets ...T20:35:26Z  - rehomed_seat
  uuid:5586...cca2  usage-limit  resets ...T20:28:35Z  - rehomed_seat
```

Those two UUIDs are byte-identical to the `pool=` values the allocator printed for lanes
1/2/4/5/7/8. The information needed to refuse those 8 slots was in the store the whole
time.

## Why it matters

- The wave's headline number (`distinct_pools=3`) is **advisory fiction** — it is computed
  from the roster, never re-checked against cooldown. An operator reads "3 pools" and gets
  serialization on 1.
- The under-fill is *silent*: no lane fails, no `REFUSE_*` fires. The plan is green, the
  spawns succeed, and the damage is only visible by grepping 9 separate stderr logs for a
  rotation line.
- It concentrates the entire wave's burn onto the one account still healthy, which is the
  fastest way to cool that account too and wedge the box for the next wave.

## Done condition

1. `fak fleet-accounts wave` filters cooled accounts out of the allocation set before
   granting slots (same store `fak accounts cooldown` reads).
2. When the post-filter pool is smaller than `--count`, the wave under-fills **honestly**
   and reports the shortfall with the cooldown reason + reset time, matching how the
   preflight already reports a seat/headroom shortfall.
3. `distinct_pools` in the plan reflects the post-cooldown-filter count, so the printed
   number is the number the wave will actually run on.
4. Regression test: a fixture cooldown store marking K of M accounts cooled, asserting the
   allocation contains none of the K and the reported shortfall names cooldown.

## Notes

- The guard-side rotation is **correct behavior** and should not change — it is the last
  line of defense. The defect is that the allocator makes it necessary N times over.
- Adjacent but distinct: #3523 (park-and-retry on `REFUSE_NO_ACCOUNT`) covers the
  *no account at all* case; this is the *account granted but already cooled* case, which
  never reaches a REFUSE.

records.title: fix(dispatch): launch_wave_detached.ps1 defaults are both broken — nonexistent -PointerFile and a -Workspace that fails preflight, so a bare wave spawns zero workers
records.body:
## What

`tools/launch_wave_detached.ps1` cannot be run with its own defaults. **Two** of its
default parameter values are broken, and each independently reduces a wave to zero
workers. A operator following the `.EXAMPLE` block in the script's own header gets
nothing.

## Defect 1 — the default `-PointerFile` does not exist

```
[string]$PointerFile = ".claude/goal-prompts/resolve-tickets-witnessed.md"   # line 49
```

That file is not in the tree:

```
$ ls .claude/goal-prompts/
ask-hard-questions.md            resolve-5025-engineroute.md
fix-reversibility-classifier.md  resolve-cache-value-issue-witnessed.md
port-python-to-go-witnessed.md   resolve-dispatch-program-issue-witnessed.md
questions-to-tickets.md          resolve-modeltier-issue-witnessed.md
resolve-5016-ultracode.md        resolve-top-issue-fable.md
resolve-5018-autonomy.md         resolve-top-issue-ultracode.md
                                 resolve-top-issue-witnessed.md      <- the near-miss name
                                 scout-and-study-witnessed.md
```

`launch_goal_detached.ps1:163` then throws `pointer file not found: <path>` on **every**
spawn. `launch_goal_detached.ps1:63` carries the identical broken default, so the
single-worker launcher is equally unrunnable bare.

## Defect 2 — the default `-Workspace` fails its own preflight

```
[string]$Workspace = "C:\work\fleet"    # line 50
```

The wave preflight runs `dispatch_preflight.py --workspace <Workspace>` (line 227), and
that workspace has no `tools/` tree, so the host guard is unreachable:

```
$ python tools/dispatch_preflight.py --json --workspace <default-workspace>
  "verdict": "REFUSE_INSPECT",
  "reason": "guard not found: <default-workspace>\tools\proc_resource_guard.py",
```

`Get-WaveAllocationCount` returns 0 for any verdict other than `SPAWN_OK` (line 251), so
`allocationCount` is 0, and line 407 throws:

```
wave preflight admitted zero lane(s) -- not dispatching.
```

Against the repo root the same call is clean — `SPAWN_OK`, `cap=24`, `headroom=24` — so
the refusal is purely the default pointing somewhere without the guard script.

## Why it matters

The refusal in defect 2 is *correctly worded as the no-DoS floor* ("recover, do not route
around it"), which actively misleads: the operator reads a capacity refusal and goes
hunting for exhausted seats or a hot host, when the real cause is a default path. Getting
this wrong in the other direction is worse — `-SkipPreflight` is right there, and it
removes the real no-DoS floor for the whole wave to work around a typo'd default.

Both defaults also mean every caller must pass `-PointerFile` and `-Workspace`
explicitly, which is undocumented in the `.EXAMPLE` blocks — both examples omit them and
therefore both examples fail.

## Done condition

1. `-PointerFile` defaults to a file that exists (`resolve-top-issue-witnessed.md` is the
   intended one), **or** the parameter becomes mandatory with no default.
2. `-Workspace` defaults to the repo root the script already computes as `$repoRoot`
   (line 75), rather than a hardcoded absolute path.
3. The two `.EXAMPLE` blocks run as written.
4. A preflight `REFUSE_INSPECT` whose reason is a missing guard script reports it as a
   *configuration* fault distinct from a capacity refusal, so the remedy text stops
   pointing at seats.
5. Regression: a dry-run plan invoked with defaults only asserts `granted > 0`.

## Notes

Both defects were hit in sequence launching a real wave today; the wave only ran after
both parameters were pinned by hand.

records.title: feat(guardaccuracy): choose a guard predicate by replaying admitted calls and counting false rejections
records.body:
## Axis

**Choose a gate's predicate by replaying the historical call corpus and counting *false rejections*, rather than picking the intuitive predicate and grading it against a hand-labeled set afterwards.**

A false rejection is defined structurally, not subjectively: a call that **completed successfully in production** and that the candidate predicate **would now block**. No human label is required — success in the journal *is* the ground truth.

## Prior art (INSPIRE only — see licence note)

`agnt-gg/agnt`, `backend/src/services/orchestrator/toolArgGuard.js:1-46` @ `66208c56`.

They shipped a guard for tool calls arriving with empty arguments (measured: 73 of 3,519 `edit_file` calls arrived as `{}`, which then resolved an absent path to the workspace root). Before enabling it they replayed **all 87,843 historical tool calls** through two candidate predicates:

| predicate | blocks | false rejections | real failures caught |
|---|---|---|---|
| any required param missing | 445 | **248** | 197 |
| ALL required params missing | 102 | **0** | 102 |

Their comment states the conclusion plainly: the predicate was *"forced by measurement, not chosen by taste."* The intuitive predicate would have blocked 248 calls that had worked.

**Their worldview:** AGNT is a local-first, single-tenant desktop agent whose users hit a blocked-but-legitimate call directly and immediately. An over-blocking gate is a support burden they personally absorb, so they pay up front to size the over-block before shipping. fak's fleet has the same exposure with worse feedback latency — a worker that gets over-blocked halts.

## fak seam

`internal/guardaccuracy/complaints.go:20` states the gap in fak's own words:

> a false-positive refusal is byte-identical in the decision journal to a correct one -- only the filing agent knows the call was legitimate

That is true for a **refused** call. It is *not* true for an **admitted** one: fak's journal records calls that ran and succeeded, and a candidate predicate can be evaluated against them offline with no labelling at all. Today fak grades the escalate boundary two ways, both of which need a human in the loop:

- `internal/guardaccuracy/guardaccuracy.go` — a **hand-labeled** corpus (`testdata/corpus.json`)
- `internal/guardaccuracy/complaints.go:26` — agent-filed appeals, explicitly **subjective** and surfaced as advisory-only

fak already has the replay technique in a neighbouring lane — `internal/agent/message_elide_corpus_replay_test.go:21` replays a corpus and measures exactly a false-positive rate. It has never been pointed at a **guard predicate**.

**Witness:** PARTIAL. The capability (grading a gate's accuracy) is present; the axis (counterfactual replay over *admitted* calls to select a predicate *before* it ships) is absent. Verified by reading the two `guardaccuracy` files and by `Grep` over `internal/` for `false.?reject|would.?have.?(refus|block)|shadow.?mode` — the only hits are the elision corpus replay and advisory-mode text, none on the guard predicate seam.

## Why this matters here specifically

Over-blocking is fak's most-recorded operational pathology: action rules matching prose in a commit message, `PUBLIC_LEAK` matching a host alias inside a Go comment, `DEAD_CODE` on a symbol used once module-wide. Each was discovered *in the field, by a blocked worker*. A replay harness converts that discovery loop from "a worker halts and files an appeal" into "the predicate is rejected before it ships".

## First checkable step

A test in `internal/guardaccuracy` that:
1. loads a fixture journal of **admitted, successful** calls,
2. evaluates two candidate predicates over it,
3. asserts the reported false-rejection count for each,

and fails if a predicate's false-rejection count exceeds a declared ceiling. Fixture-only — no live journal read, no network. The live-journal wiring is a follow-on.

## Licence

**INSPIRE, not INTEGRATE.** The source ships under the "AGNT Community Core License", a source-available fair-use licence that permits study (*"Study and learn from the codebase for educational purposes"*) and forbids redistribution or forking under another name. No bytes may be copied into this tree; the technique is reimplemented clean-room in Go. Cited for provenance only.

Study trail: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md`

records.title: feat(syspromptmmu): forbid presence-volatile gates on resident prompt blocks by construction (epic #3229)
records.body:
## Axis

**A resident prompt block's *presence* must be a monotone (append-only) function of conversation-stable inputs, enforced by construction — so a conditional section can turn on but never off.**

Not value-volatility (a timestamp inside a block). **Presence**-volatility: a block that appears on turn 3 because the user's message mentioned something, and is gone by turn 5. Every flicker rewrites the system block and therefore invalidates the cached copy of every message after it.

## Prior art (INSPIRE only — see licence note)

`agnt-gg/agnt`, `backend/src/services/orchestrator/system-prompts/promptElements.js:16-46` @ `66208c56`.

Their cost model, measured on one account over 7 days:

> cache reads are 96.4% of input tokens but only 57% of the input bill, while cache WRITES are 3.6% of tokens and 43% of the bill — a rewritten token costs 20x a read one, and a single prefix break on a 178k conversation runs about $1.89. So a gate that flickers is far more expensive than the block it removes.

Their rule, and — the part worth borrowing — how it is enforced:

> A resident block's gate MUST be a pure function of conversation-stable inputs. Never of the user's message. [...] `buildGateInputs` is deliberately given no access to the message so this cannot be written by accident.

The enforcement is **structural**: the gate function is not given the volatile input, so the mistake is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

**Their worldview:** AGNT is local-first and the operator pays the provider bill directly and visibly, so cache economics are a first-class product surface for them rather than an optimisation. That is why they wrote the rule as an invariant with a structural enforcement instead of a lint.

## fak seam

`internal/agent/anthropic_cachebp.go:33`:

> A candidate head span that carries a self-evidently per-request token — a sub-day timestamp or a UUID/nonce (`headValueIsVolatile`) — is NOT byte-stable across turns [...] We step DOWN from a volatile tools+system head to caching just the stable tools head

fak's handling is **detect-and-degrade at the wire**, and it covers **value** volatility only. It has no construction-side rule for **presence** volatility: nothing stops a resident block from being gated on a per-turn input, and `headValueIsVolatile` cannot see that class of change — a block that vanishes leaves no timestamp or UUID behind, just different bytes.

fak does declare `PrefixStable` on ablation concepts (`internal/ablate/registry.go:24`) and asserts non-tools byte-identity across A/B arms (`internal/ablate/defer_ab.go:131`), but both are **experiment-arm** properties, not a rule about how a resident block's gate may be written.

**Witness:** PARTIAL. fak is well ahead on wire-side prefix preservation (see `anthropic_compact.go`, `anthropic_elide.go` — both splice on original bytes and prove head byte-identity). The uncovered axis is the *construction* side: which inputs a resident block's gate is allowed to read.

## First checkable step

An architest-style test that enumerates fak's resident prompt-block builders and asserts each gate is a pure function of a declared conversation-stable input set — the cheapest form being: the gate-input struct simply does not carry the current user message, and a test pins that field set so adding one is a deliberate, reviewed act.

## Licence

**INSPIRE, not INTEGRATE.** Source-available under the "AGNT Community Core License" — study permitted, redistribution/forking forbidden. Clean-room reimplementation in Go; citation for provenance only.

Study trail: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md`
---

## Worker contract

### Parent context
Epic #3229 (context/token budget); clean-room follow-up from the August 8, 2026 AGNT concept study.

### Current state
`internal/agent/anthropic_cachebp.go` detects obvious value volatility at the wire, while `internal/syspromptmmu` authors the resident spine/policy plan from fixed literals. The construction API has no typed gate-input boundary or append-only presence latch for future conditional resident blocks.

### Why this is next
The current resident builder is the smallest seam where a future per-turn condition could make block presence flicker without leaving a timestamp or UUID for the wire detector to catch. Structural prevention belongs at authorship before more conditional blocks are added.

### Working spine
Declare resident block specs -> evaluate every gate through a conversation-stable input type -> latch admitted block IDs append-only -> emit the existing byte-identical base-context plan.

### Priority context
Working path: resident block registry -> stable gate inputs -> monotone builder -> system plan. Current blocker: gate predicates are unconstrained by type. Unblocks: safe conditional resident blocks. Not polish: prevents provider prefix rewrites that the wire detector cannot recognize.

### Work unit
leaf

### Expected steps
6

### Work scale
S1

### Assumptions
- `internal/syspromptmmu` remains the canonical fak-authored resident prompt-block builder.
- Existing base-context bytes, order, witnesses, and digest must remain unchanged.
- The implementation is clean-room and imports no AGNT source.

### Confusion risks
- This issue covers presence volatility, not timestamps/nonces inside a present block.
- Overlay/steering blocks are after the breakpoint and are not resident-block gates.
- The peer-held `internal/agent/**` tree is out of scope; the exact implementation is confined to `internal/syspromptmmu`.

### Coordination
- Holder `codex-issue-5897-headless` owns lease `issue-5897-syspromptmmu` only for the three likely files below.
- Do not touch peer-dirty or peer-leased `internal/agent/**` paths.

### Trigger
A uniquely assigned headless worker was directed to resolve #5897 completely after live issue, intent, and lease checks.

records.title: feat(adjudicator): scope action rules to sink-bearing arguments so prose describing an action is not refused
records.body:
## Axis

**Scope an *action* rule to the arguments that actually reach an execution sink, so an argument that merely *describes* a dangerous action is not refused. Rules about *data* (secrets, PII) stay unscoped and keep seeing every argument.**

The split is the whole point: action rules get narrowed, data rules never do.

## Prior art (INSPIRE only — see licence note)

`agnt-gg/agnt`, `backend/src/services/security/toolCapabilities.js:1-38` @ `66208c56`:

> Its matcher walks every string in every argument, so a rule that detects a dangerous *command* also fires on any argument that merely *describes* one. In practice that blocked a memory note about restarting the backend, a read-only search for a rule's own id, and a runbook file write — while the one call that genuinely restarted something was blocked for the same reason, indistinguishably.

Their model declares two things per tool:

- `capabilities` — what this tool can do at all
- `sink` — which arguments select an operation, destination, executable, query or path

and is **fail-closed by construction**: a tool with no declaration keeps the old full-argument scan, so narrowing is opt-in per tool and an undeclared tool never silently loosens. The companion selector is at `backend/src/services/security/nopeService.js:206` (`selectWorkflowSecurityArgs`), which also records the matched `field` on every audit line — *"a block on `params.content` reads very differently from one on `command`"*.

**Their worldview:** AGNT's users write automations whose payloads are prose — runbooks, memory notes, docs — flowing through the same tool surface as real commands. For them, conflating data with executable intent is not an edge case, it is the median call. fak's agents author commit messages, issue bodies and code comments about the very operations the guard polices, which is the same shape.

## fak seam

`internal/adjudicator/reversibility.go:435`:

```go
for _, key := range []string{"argv", "args"} {
    if joined, ok := stringSliceArg(args, key); ok {
        return joined
```

The joined string is then substring-matched (`reversibility.go:223`, `:228`). There is no declaration of which argument reaches a sink and which is payload — so an action rule matches identically whether the token appears in an executable position or inside prose being passed as data.

This is not hypothetical. fak's own guard-accuracy fixture carries it as a canonical over-block case (`internal/guardaccuracy/complaints_test.go`): a complaint summarised as **"commit message mentions rm"**. It also fired during the study pass that produced this ticket: a tool call was refused with `NEVER_AMEND_SHARED` because the *text being written to a file* discussed history rewriting — no such operation was being performed.

**Note the boundary.** `internal/hooks/gate_publicleak.go` is a **data** rule (it scans added lines for host aliases and credential shapes) and per the borrowed model must stay unscoped. Its known prose false-positives are a separate concern and are explicitly **out of scope for this ticket** — narrowing a DLP rule to a sink is the mistake this design exists to prevent.

**Witness:** PARTIAL. fak has fine-grained argument predicates (`internal/adjudicator/decide_argpredicates.go`, `ArgAllowGlob` containment) — but those constrain a *known* argument's value. There is no per-tool declaration of which arguments are sink-bearing at all. `Grep` over `internal/adjudicator` and `internal/hooks` for `sink|appliesTo` returns nothing.

## First checkable step

A per-tool capability/sink declaration table in `internal/adjudicator`, consulted by the reversibility classifier, with:
1. a test that a declared tool's action rules see only its sink arguments;
2. a test that an **undeclared** tool still scans every argument (fail-closed);
3. a test that a data/DLP rule is unaffected by any declaration.

Start with one declaration — the tool through which commit messages and issue bodies flow — which alone retires the recorded "commit message mentions rm" class.

## Licence

**INSPIRE, not INTEGRATE.** Source-available under the "AGNT Community Core License" — study permitted, redistribution/forking forbidden. Clean-room reimplementation in Go; citation for provenance only.

Study trail: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md`

records.title: feat(agent): learn a per-provider estimate-vs-billed correction ratio that cannot amplify itself (epic #3229)
records.body:
## Axis

**Persist a learned per-(provider, model) correction ratio between the *estimated* and *actually billed* input size, across sessions — designed so the correction can never amplify itself.**

fak already computes both numbers and already knows they disagree. It never closes the loop, and it forgets between sessions.

## Prior art (INSPIRE only — see licence note)

`agnt-gg/agnt`, `backend/src/services/orchestrator/calibrationStore.js:1-138` @ `66208c56`. Measured over 400 live executions:

| provider/model | fixed overhead (tokens) | spread |
|---|---|---|
| openai / gpt-4o | 57,455 | 1% |
| **Claude-Code / claude-opus-5** | **253,909** | **121%** |
| Kimi-Code / k3 | 385,102 | 134% |

Their explanation is the load-bearing part:

> CLI/OAuth-backed providers [...] inject their own preamble and built-in tool definitions into every request. AGNT never receives those bytes, so NO chars-per-token constant can ever account for them.

Design details worth taking:
- `MIN_SAMPLES_TO_TRUST = 3`, ratio clamped to `[0.5, 3]`, decaying weight `max(0.1, 1/(n+1))`, write-behind flush.
- `getCalibration` returns **null**, not `1`, when there is no data — *"deliberately not 1, so callers can tell 'no data' from 'no drift'"*.
- **Non-self-amplifying by construction:** the observation recorded is always `real / RAW-estimate`, never `real / corrected-estimate`, *"so seeding a conversation from this store cannot feed back into the number it learns."*

**Their worldview:** AGNT ships 15+ providers including CLI/OAuth-backed Claude Code and Codex, for a single operator who notices when a budget forecast is wrong. Heterogeneity forced them to learn the constant per provider instead of picking one.

## fak seam

`internal/agent/anthropic_footprint.go:21` already names both quantities and keeps them apart:

> house heuristic (`bytesPerTokenEstimate`), NOT the provider's OBSERVED usage counters

So fak has the estimate and the provider's real counters in the same process, and never derives a ratio from them. `Grep` over `internal/` for `calibrat` finds calibration in `internal/bench/tokenweightcal.go` (scheduler token weights, fitted offline on a sanctioned compute node into a versioned artifact) and `internal/dojocal` — **neither is a live estimate-vs-billed correction, and neither is per-provider**.

**Witness:** ABSENT on-axis. fak has offline, artifact-based calibration for a different quantity; it has no cross-session store of an estimator correction keyed by provider+model.

The CLI/OAuth finding lands directly on fak's flagship path: `fak guard -- claude` drives exactly the class of provider whose injected preamble the house 4-chars-per-token constant provably cannot model. A 121% spread on that provider means fak's footprint accounting for its own primary use case is the least trustworthy number it reports.

## First checkable step

A pure `internal/` package holding the ratio store as data:
- `Observe(provider, model, rawEstimate, realTokens)` and `Ratio(provider, model) (float64, bool)`;
- returns `false` (not `1.0`) below `MIN_SAMPLES`;
- a test asserting the recorded observation uses the **raw** estimate, so feeding a corrected estimate back in leaves the learned ratio unchanged — the non-amplification property, pinned.

No persistence, no wiring in step one; the store is a pure function of its observation sequence.

## Licence

**INSPIRE, not INTEGRATE.** Source-available under the "AGNT Community Core License" — study permitted, redistribution/forking forbidden. Clean-room reimplementation in Go; citation for provenance only.

Part of the context/token-budget track (epic #3229).

records.title: feat(agent): split the chars-per-token divisor for tool schemas from prose (epic #3229)
records.body:
## Axis

**Use a different chars-per-token ratio for dense JSON tool schemas than for prose. One shared ratio is wrong for both, and the error compounds into the eviction decision that consumes it.**

## Prior art (INSPIRE only — see licence note)

`agnt-gg/agnt`, `backend/src/utils/contextManager.js:16-32` @ `66208c56`, measured against `o200k_base` over their live 295-tool surface:

> whole array 4.75 chars/token [...] worst single tool 3.89. The shared prose estimator scored the same block at 3.125 chars/token — a 1.52x overcount (182,251 vs a real 120,021). That inflation drove `availableTokens` NEGATIVE [...] and made Strategy 4 delete the user's conversation on chats as short as two turns.

They now hold `CHARS_PER_TOKEN_JSON_SCHEMA = 4.0` separately from the prose constant.

The borrow is not the constant — it is the **finding that the two surfaces tokenize differently enough to matter, and that an estimator error does not stay an estimator error**: it propagated into a headroom calculation and became data loss.

**Their worldview:** a 295-tool surface is most of their prompt, so the tool array is the dominant term rather than a rounding error. fak's MCP surface plus deferral (#3231) puts it in the same regime.

## fak seam

fak applies **one** divisor everywhere:

- `internal/agent/anthropic_footprint.go:34` — `const bytesPerTokenEstimate = 4`, applied uniformly across every footprint bucket including the tools bucket (`:82`, `:154`, `:170`)
- `internal/bench/ctxadmission.go:115` — `const ctxCharsPerTokenHeuristic = 4`, the same "about four characters per token" rule

Against AGNT's measurements, `4` is close to right for **schemas** (they measured 4.75 whole-array) and materially wrong for **prose** (they measured ~3.125). fak's error therefore runs the opposite direction from theirs: fak **undercounts prose**, i.e. it believes it has more headroom than it does. That is the direction that fails *late* and *silently*.

**Witness:** PARTIAL. fak has a footprint estimator with per-bucket floors and it deliberately separates the heuristic from observed usage counters — the accounting structure is there. The uncovered axis is that the divisor is not a function of what is being measured.

Note `internal/bench/ctxadmission_test.go:102` already pins a case where the shared heuristic changes an admission decision, which is the same failure mode one step earlier.

## First checkable step

Split the constant by bucket kind in `internal/agent/anthropic_footprint.go` — a schema divisor for the tools bucket, a prose divisor for system/messages — and add a test that measures both against a checked-in fixture (a real tool array and a real prose block) and asserts each estimate lands within a declared tolerance of the fixture's recorded true token count. The tolerance assertion is what makes this falsifiable rather than a constant swap.

fak's divisor choice should be re-derived from fak's own tokenizer and fak's own surface — AGNT's numbers are the *reason to look*, not the values to copy.

## Licence

**INSPIRE, not INTEGRATE.** Source-available under the "AGNT Community Core License" — study permitted, redistribution/forking forbidden. Clean-room reimplementation in Go; citation for provenance only.

Part of the context/token-budget track (epic #3229).
