  clears state and resolves the gate instead of retrying. This is the race discipline that
  makes mid-stream abort safe, and it is the part most likely to be under-built if
  reimplemented from the idea alone.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — ABSENT (on-axis)

No mid-stream abort/substitute path exists. fak's guard decides at the `PreToolUse`
boundary; `internal/sessionsteer` injects at SessionStart and persists at Stop. Neither
can cancel a call that is still being written, and neither substitutes an action.

The *affordance-first* half is PRESENT as a scored discipline for prose
(`internal/negframe`, `fak score negframe`) but is **not** wired to any runtime injection
surface — the score grades documents, not the messages fak itself emits at runtime. That
gap is precisely what this leaf closes.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. A rule field for the **substitute action**. A rule without one is non-interrupting by
   construction — enforced at registration, not by convention.
2. The abort lifecycle: tool-call-id-scoped abort → discard the partial → inject → resume.
3. The injection template leads with the action. No `violation` token, no `reason=` blame
   field in the model-visible text.
4. The four staleness guards on the deferred retry, each independently tested.

## First checkable step

A test that drives a recorded stream through a rule carrying a substitute, and asserts:
the matched tool call is aborted, the sibling call receives a *distinct* reason, the
partial is discarded, and the injected text contains the substitute action and no
prohibition token.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A rule with no substitute action **cannot** be registered as interrupting; a test
      pins that it degrades rather than interrupts.
- [ ] Abort is scoped to the matched tool-call id; a sibling-call test proves the sibling
      is not killed with the same reason.
- [ ] The partial assistant output for the aborted call is discarded before resume (test).
- [ ] The injected message leads with the action to take. A test asserts the rendered text
      contains the substitute and matches **zero** `internal/negframe` findings — the
      existing classifier is the oracle, so this is a real gate and not a style opinion.
- [ ] All four staleness guards (retry token, prompt generation, abort-pending state,
      target-message identity) are implemented, and each has a test proving a stale retry
      clears state instead of firing.
- [ ] A failed resume resolves the gate rather than hanging the turn (test).
- [ ] Default-off behind an opt-in; with it off, behavior is byte-identical to today.
- [ ] `make ci` green; architest tier row present if a new leaf is added.

## Non-goals

- The anti-nag ledger (separate leaf) — this leaf may fire a rule repeatedly; bounding
  that is the next leaf's job.
- The non-interrupting tool-result reminder path (separate leaf).
- Any change to `PreToolUse` decisions.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(sessionsteer): bound repeat injections with a persisted once/after-gap ledger counted in completed turns (epic #5917)
records.body:
Bound how often a rule may inject: a persisted per-rule ledger with `once` and
`after-gap` repeat modes, where the gap is counted in **completed turns**, and the ledger
is restored on session resume.

## The axis

**Repetition pressure on the model's context.** Not "can fak inject" (it can — see
`internal/sessionsteer`) — the axis is whether a *repeated* injection is bounded. An
unbounded rule re-fires every turn it matches, which both burns context and trains the
model to ignore the channel.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/ttsr-injection-lifecycle.md` @ `896bf5f`, §5 and §7:

- `repeatMode: once` — a rule fires once after it has an injection record.
- `repeatMode: after-gap` — re-fires only when `messageCount - lastInjectedAt >= repeatGap`
  (default gap 10), and **`messageCount` increments on turn end**, so the gap is measured
  in completed turns, never in stream chunks. Counting chunks would make the gap depend on
  response length, which is meaningless as a nag budget.
- Persistence is a `ttsr_injection` entry; `restoreInjected(...)` rehydrates on resume.

The documented honest limitation, worth inheriting deliberately rather than rediscovering:
persistence stores **names, not ages**, so a restored rule restarts at message count zero
and becomes eligible after a full fresh gap. The source states this explicitly (§7). Copy
the simplification and document it, or fix it — but decide on purpose.

Also worth copying: the rollback asymmetry in §4's edge cases — when a turn ends aborted
or errored before the matched tool runs, the in-memory injection record is **not** rolled
back, but nothing was persisted, so a reload makes the rule eligible again. That is a real
divergence between live and resumed state and is the kind of thing that only shows up in a
soak test.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak has the injection channel and the persistence rails but not the bound:

- `internal/sessionsteer` injects a RULE at SessionStart and persists at the Stop hook —
  lifecycle-triggered, so "how often may this rule re-fire mid-session" never arises.
- `internal/goalpark` and `internal/seatpark` bound *waits* and *retries* with backoff,
  not *advice repetition*.

So the capability neighborhood is PRESENT and the axis is ABSENT: nothing counts per-rule
injections or suppresses a repeat. Filed as an enhancement to the existing steer seam
rather than a new capability.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

Ship-alone because it is useful to `internal/sessionsteer` on its own, independent of any
streaming work.

1. A per-rule ledger: `lastInjectedAt` keyed by rule name, plus a turn counter that
   increments on **turn end**.
2. `once` and `after-gap` modes with a configurable gap (default 10 completed turns).
3. Persist injected rule names; restore on resume.
4. An explicit, documented decision on the age-restoration semantics above.

## First checkable step

A table test that drives N synthetic completed turns through a rule in each mode and
asserts the exact turn indices at which injection is permitted — including that stream
chunks within one turn never advance the counter.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Per-rule ledger with `once` and `after-gap`; gap configurable, default 10.
- [ ] The counter advances on **turn end only**; a test proves multiple deltas/chunks
      inside one turn do not advance it.
- [ ] `once` suppresses every subsequent fire for the session's lifetime (test).
- [ ] `after-gap` permits a re-fire at exactly `gap` completed turns, not `gap-1` (test
      pins the boundary in both directions).
- [ ] Injected rule names persist and are restored on resume (round-trip test).
- [ ] The restored-age semantics are documented in the package header **and** pinned by a
      test, so the behavior is a decision rather than an accident.
- [ ] The abort/error path's rollback behavior is documented and tested: what happens to a
      rule marked in memory when the turn dies before delivery.
- [ ] Pure/table-testable — no clock or filesystem dependency in the counting logic.
- [ ] `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- Deciding *what* a rule injects (that is the affordance-first leaf).
- Streaming detection (separate leaf) — this ledger is transport-agnostic and works for
  boundary-triggered injections too, which is why it can ship first.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(secretgate): add reversible per-install HMAC secret placeholders — substitute-and-restore instead of remove (epic #5917)
records.body:
Add a **reversible** secret placeholder mode: substitute a credential with a stable
per-install HMAC placeholder on the way out to the provider, and restore it in
model-authored tool arguments before execution — instead of removing the bytes.

## The axis

**Whether the model can still *operate on* a credential it must never *see*.**

Not "does fak handle secrets" — it does, well. The axis is what survives the handling. Two
different answers:

- **Removal** (fak today): the credential is quarantined; the model sees an absence. It
  cannot reference the value, cannot pass it to a later tool call, and cannot reason about
  "the same token appeared in both files".
- **Substitution** (the borrow): the credential becomes a stable opaque handle. The model
  can carry it through a plan and hand it back in a tool argument, and the runtime restores
  the real bytes at the execution boundary. The model never sees the secret and never
  needs to.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/secrets.md` @ `896bf5f`. The mechanically load-bearing details:

- Placeholders are shaped `$$3P8W5JH1TK2Q:L$$`, optionally labeled
  `$$GITHUBTOKEN_3P8W5JH1TK2Q:L$$`.
- **The 12-char base is an HMAC of the secret under a per-install key** stored locally and
  **never sent to a model**. This is the security-load-bearing choice: a plain hash lets a
  transcript reader dictionary-attack a placeholder back to its secret; the keyed MAC
  defeats that.
- **Case-variants get independent bases**, so seeing one placeholder does not let a
  provider synthesize another by flipping the case hint. (Case hints `:U/:L/:C/:M` label
  the casing of the redacted value.)
- Restoration is a **deep walk of model-authored tool arguments before the tool executes**
  — the boundary that makes the whole scheme safe.
- A separate one-way `replace` mode exists for values that must never come back.
- An 8-character floor on obfuscate-mode matches, so ordinary short words are not redacted.
- The honest failure mode, documented: if the key cannot be persisted, the session warns
  and uses a process-ephemeral key — reversible within the process, not stable across
  restarts.

**License:** MIT (`LICENSE:1`) → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak's secret handling is real and arguably stronger on *detection*, and strictly weaker on
*reversibility*:

- `internal/secretgate/secretgate.go:1-16` — on discovery, a credential-bearing tool result
  is **quarantined** under a stable handle with a CAS-pin + PageIn-after-Clear witness. It
  explicitly delegates detection to `internal/canon` via the exported
  `canon.SecretPatterns` and "never forks the pattern list".
- The masking path is live in this very session: reading the source's own secrets doc
  tripped `SECRET_REDACTED`, masking the span rather than substituting it.

So: fak removes, the source substitutes-and-restores. fak already has the two hard
prerequisites — a single detector (`canon.SecretPatterns`) and a stable-handle discipline
(`secretgate`) — which is what makes this an enhancement to an existing seam rather than a
new subsystem.

Note `secretgate` is **default-inert** (opt-in via `FAK_SECRETGATE`,
`internal/secretgate/secretgate.go:14-16`); this leaf should inherit that posture.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. Per-install key: generate, persist with restrictive permissions, never log, never
   include in any provider-visible payload or any `-json` surface.
2. Placeholder mint: HMAC base + optional sanitized label + case hint. Independent bases
   for case variants.
3. Substitution on the outbound provider view, reusing `canon.SecretPatterns` — no second
   detector, matching `secretgate`'s stated discipline.
4. Restoration: deep-walk model-authored tool arguments, restore before execution.
5. Opt-in; default behavior unchanged.

## First checkable step

Round-trip test: a fixture secret is substituted in an outbound payload, the placeholder
appears in the provider-visible bytes, the model-authored tool argument containing that
placeholder restores to the exact original secret before execution, and the raw secret
appears nowhere in the outbound bytes.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Per-install key is generated, persisted with restrictive permissions, and a test
      asserts it appears in no outbound payload, no log line, and no `-json` output.
- [ ] Placeholder base is an HMAC under that key — a test proves two installs produce
      different placeholders for the same secret (this is the dictionary-attack defense
      and must be pinned, not assumed).
- [ ] Case variants of one secret produce independent bases (test).
- [ ] Detection reuses `canon.SecretPatterns`; a test or lint proves no second pattern list
      was introduced.
- [ ] Deep-walk restoration handles nested objects and arrays in tool arguments (test).
- [ ] Restoration happens strictly **before** execution; a test proves a tool receives the
      real secret and the transcript retains the placeholder.
- [ ] Sub-8-character matches are not obfuscated (test) — no redacting ordinary words.
- [ ] Key-unavailable path degrades to a process-ephemeral key with a warning, and never
      silently emits the raw secret (test).
- [ ] Default-inert / opt-in, consistent with `secretgate`; with the flag off, byte-identical
      to today.
- [ ] `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- Replacing `secretgate` quarantine — this is a second mode alongside it, not a rewrite.
- The one-way `replace` mode (add later if wanted).
- Any remote credential vault / broker.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(compactcohere): let a tool declare its own result prunable — the producer-side useless bit (epic #5917)
records.body:
Let a tool **declare its own output prunable** at production time, so compaction can evict
it without heuristics.

## The axis

**Who knows a tool result is worthless.** Compaction today infers value from position, age,
and size — all proxies. The tool itself knows: a grep that matched nothing, a status that
returned clean, a read of a file that was empty. That knowledge exists at production time
and is currently thrown away, forcing the compactor to re-derive it badly later.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/compaction.md` @ `896bf5f` — `AgentToolResult.useless`, a boolean the **tool sets on
its own result**. Compaction elides flagged results first, ahead of any heuristic pass.

The design virtue worth copying: it inverts the information flow. Instead of a central
compactor guessing, each tool contributes one bit it is uniquely qualified to supply. It
is also cheap to adopt incrementally — a tool that never sets the flag behaves exactly as
today.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak's compaction economics are real and in some ways ahead of the source:

- `internal/compactcohere/compactcohere.go:10` — `DefaultProviderCacheTTL = 5 * time.Minute`
  models the provider prompt-cache idle expiry, and `Classify`
  (`internal/compactcohere/compactcohere.go:127`) is a total, side-effect-free prefix-event
  classifier. fak reasons about *when* pruning is cache-safe.
- `internal/ctxmmu` / `internal/ctxresidency` page capability bodies out with a witnessed
  eviction.

What is absent on this axis: **no producer-supplied value signal anywhere**. Every eviction
decision is made by the consumer from external properties. Nothing in the tool-result path
carries a "this was worthless" bit.

So the capability is PRESENT and the axis is ABSENT — an enhancement to the existing
compaction seam.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. A `Useless bool` (or equivalent) on the tool-result type, defaulting false.
2. Set it in a small number of obviously-correct producers: zero-match search, clean
   status, empty read. Conservative — a false positive evicts real context.
3. Teach the eviction ordering to prefer flagged results, still subject to existing
   cache-safety classification.

Ship-alone value: even with zero consumers, the flag makes "how much of this transcript is
provably worthless?" measurable.

## First checkable step

A test that a zero-match search sets the flag, a matching search does not, and the
eviction ordering places a flagged result ahead of an unflagged one of identical size and
age.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Flag exists on the tool-result type, defaults false; absent flag = today's behavior.
- [ ] At least three producers set it, each with a positive **and** a negative test (the
      negative test is the one that matters — a flag set too eagerly silently destroys
      context).
- [ ] Eviction ordering prefers flagged results, and a test proves it still respects the
      existing cache-safety classification — the flag must not override `compactcohere`'s
      prefix-event decision.
- [ ] A counter/observability surface reports how many flagged results were evicted, so the
      value claim is measurable rather than asserted.
- [ ] No tool is *required* to set it; a survey test or lint confirms unflagged producers
      are unaffected.
- [ ] `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- The prune-size floor (separate leaf).
- Model-authored usefulness judgments — this is a mechanical, producer-side bit only.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(compactcohere): refuse a prune smaller than its placeholder — add the minimum-prune floor and structural cut validation (epic #5917)
records.body:
Refuse to prune a span smaller than the placeholder that replaces it — a minimum-prune
floor, plus the two adjacent cache-economics rules from the same source.

## The axis

**The arithmetic of an individual prune decision.** fak reasons well about *when* pruning
is cache-safe; this axis is whether a specific prune is *profitable at all*.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/compaction.md` @ `896bf5f`. Three rules, each a one-line invariant with a real
failure mode behind it:

1. **`MIN_PRUNE_TOKENS = 50`.** A pruned span is replaced by a placeholder costing roughly
   8 tokens. Pruning a span *below the floor* therefore **grows** the context while
   simultaneously churning the prompt cache — strictly worse on both axes at once. The
   floor is not a tuning knob; it is a correctness bound.
2. **Cache-aware prune timing** — prune only within a small suffix (≤8k) or once the
   prefix has idled past the cache lifetime. Pruning mid-prefix invalidates a cache entry
   worth more than the tokens reclaimed.
3. **Never cut at a `toolResult` boundary** — a tool result orphaned from its tool call is
   a malformed transcript for most providers, so the cut point must be structurally
   validated, not chosen by token offset alone.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak has the *timing* half of this and not the *arithmetic* half:

- `internal/compactcohere/compactcohere.go:10` — `DefaultProviderCacheTTL = 5 * time.Minute`,
  the assumed provider prompt-cache idle expiry.
- `internal/compactcohere/compactcohere.go:127` — `Classify(prev, cur, ttl)` is a total,
  side-effect-free prefix-event classifier; `DefaultBailStreakToYield` bounds thrash.

So rule 2 is substantially PRESENT — fak models cache lifetime explicitly, which is the
sophisticated part. Rules 1 and 3 are ABSENT: no minimum-prune floor exists, and no
structural cut-point validation was found.

Rule 1 is the cheapest correctness win in the whole study: a constant, a comparison, and a
test.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. A documented minimum-prune floor derived from fak's **own** placeholder cost — measure
   it, do not copy the source's 50. The source's constant is right for the source's
   placeholder; the *method* is what transfers.
2. A structural cut-point validator that refuses a cut orphaning a tool result from its
   call.
3. Wire both as guards on the existing prune path; keep `compactcohere`'s timing
   classification exactly as-is.

## First checkable step

A test that a span below the floor is **not** pruned, and that pruning it would have
increased total tokens — asserting the actual arithmetic, so the floor is justified by
measurement rather than by a borrowed magic number.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] fak's own placeholder cost is measured and recorded in the issue/code comment; the
      floor is derived from it and the derivation is written down.
- [ ] A span below the floor is never pruned (test), with the token arithmetic asserted in
      the test rather than the constant merely echoed.
- [ ] A cut that would orphan a tool result from its tool call is refused (test), including
      the boundary case where the tool result is the last element.
- [ ] `compactcohere`'s existing prefix-event classification is unchanged — a reviewer can
      confirm by diff that `Classify` was not modified.
- [ ] Guards are pure/table-testable, no clock dependency.
- [ ] A counter reports refused-prune decisions by reason (below-floor vs structural), so
      the floor's real-world hit rate is observable.
- [ ] `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- Changing the cache TTL model or the bail-streak yield.
- The producer-side useless flag (separate leaf).

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(accounts): preflight remaining quota and switch seats before the 429, not after (epic #5917)
records.body:
Switch seats **before** spending the request that trips the limit, by checking remaining
quota ahead of a provider call — instead of parsing the 429 after the loss.

## The axis

**When the rotation decision is made — before or after the failed request.**

fak's rotation is excellent and entirely *reactive*. Every path begins with a 429 that has
already cost a request, a round-trip, and (for a long generation) a partial turn. The axis
here is moving that decision one step earlier.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/non-compaction-retry-policy.md` @ `896bf5f` — the `retry.usageAware*` family:

- `retry.usageAwareFallback` (default `false`) — runs a **preflight before a provider
  request** for supported coding-plan usage reports.
- `retry.usageReservePct` (default `10`) — a remaining-quota reserve threshold.
- `retry.usageReservePolicy` (default `"confirm"`; also `"auto"`, `"fail-closed"`) —
  what to do at the threshold.

Two details worth copying deliberately:

- **Unknown/unmapped usage fails open.** A preflight that cannot read quota must not block
  the request. This is what makes the feature safe to enable by default later.
- The three-way policy separates *notice* from *action*: `confirm` asks an interactive
  session and keeps the current model when declined; sessions with no confirmation UI
  auto-apply an eligible fallback; `fail-closed` refuses to spend reserve at all. A fleet
  worker and an operator session genuinely want different answers here, and a single
  boolean cannot express that.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak's cooldown machinery is reactive by construction — the evidence is in the parser:

- `internal/accounts/cooldown.go:88` — `resetAtRE` matches `resets at <timestamp>` **out of
  a limit message**. Extracting a reset time from prose is only possible once the provider
  has already refused.
- `internal/accounts/cooldown.go:97` — `ParseReset(message string)` takes the refusal text
  as input. The signature itself is the proof: the input is the loss.
- `internal/accounts/cooldown.go:38` — `RateLimitCooldownWindow` is the post-429 window.

So the *capability* (multi-seat rotation, cooldown windows, rehome) is strongly PRESENT and
the *axis* (deciding before the spend) is ABSENT. Filed as an enhancement to the existing
accounts seam.

Adjacent and complementary, not duplicative: `internal/goalpark` parks long provider
Retry-After waits and `internal/seatpark` bounds `REFUSE_NO_ACCOUNT` backoff — both are
also post-refusal.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. A remaining-quota reading for the providers that report one, behind a narrow interface.
2. A reserve threshold + a three-way policy (`confirm` / `auto` / `fail-closed`).
3. A preflight hook on the outbound path that consults it and can select another seat.
4. **Fail-open** on unknown/unreadable usage, always.

## First checkable step

A table test over the policy matrix: (remaining quota × reserve threshold × policy) →
expected decision (proceed / switch seat / refuse), including the unknown-usage row
asserting proceed.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] Remaining-quota reading exists behind an interface with a fake for tests; no live
      provider call in unit tests.
- [ ] The policy matrix is a table test covering all three policies, including a
      **depleted** and a **reserve-boundary** row.
- [ ] Unknown/unreadable usage **fails open** — proven by test. This is the single most
      important row: a preflight that can wedge the fleet is worse than no preflight.
- [ ] The preflight can select a different seat before the request, and a test proves the
      original seat was never called.
- [ ] Default-off; with it off, behavior is byte-identical to today's reactive path, and
      `ParseReset` / `RateLimitCooldownWindow` semantics are untouched.
- [ ] The chosen decision is recorded (structured) so preflight saves vs 429s are
      measurable — the value claim of this leaf is that number.
- [ ] Interacts correctly with `seatpark`: a preflight-driven switch does not double-count
      against the backoff (test or documented reasoning).
- [ ] `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- Changing reactive 429 handling, `ParseReset`, or the cooldown windows.
- Provider-specific quota scraping for providers that publish no usage report.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(resume): gate auto-retry on a replay-safety predicate over the partial turn's emitted blocks (epic #5917)
records.body:
Gate auto-retry on whether the partial turn's already-emitted output is **provably
discardable**, so a retry can never silently duplicate a side effect.

Small leaf, high consequence.

## The axis

**Whether a retry is safe to replay** — a property of what the stream already emitted,
checked independently of *why* the request failed.

Error classification answers "is this error transient?". It does not answer "did the
aborted attempt already do something?". Those are orthogonal, and conflating them is how a
retry duplicates a tool call.

## Source (INSPIRE — clean-room)

`docs/non-compaction-retry-policy.md` @ `896bf5f`, "Retry classification":

> "The stale-replay and retryable-error branches additionally require that the stream did
> **not** already emit replay-unsafe output. Non-empty visible text, images, tool calls,
> and Anthropic server-tool blocks prevent replay. Thinking-only and whitespace-only
> partials are safe to discard and retry."

The precision is the borrow. It is a short, enumerable list of block kinds, split into two
buckets, with the *safe* bucket deliberately tiny: thinking-only and whitespace-only. Two
consequences worth keeping:

- **Thinking blocks are discardable.** A model that only reasoned before failing has done
  nothing observable — the most common partial, and it is safe.
- **Classifier refusals are subject to the same check.** A refusal is not a licence to
  replay; the source applies the gate to that branch too.

Related and separately valuable: an interrupted turn whose tool calls **already have
matching results** is continued rather than replayed — the failed assistant/tool-result
sequence is preserved so completed side effects are not re-run. Preserve-and-continue is
the correct answer for that case, not discard-and-retry.

**License:** MIT → Apache-2.0, compatible; **INSPIRE** (TypeScript → Go).

## Witness — PARTIAL (on-axis)

fak has substantial retry/resume machinery — `internal/attemptbudget` bounds attempts,
`internal/sessionreplay` handles replay, `internal/goalpark` parks Retry-After waits, and
`internal/accounts/cooldown.go:38` (`RateLimitCooldownWindow`) sizes the transient window.
Error classification is well developed, including a landed fix for misclassifying an
operator stop as transient (#3457).

What was not found is a **content-shaped replay-safety predicate**: a check over the
emitted block kinds of the partial turn, independent of the error class. Retry eligibility
appears to be decided from the error, not from what the stream already produced.

Because this is an ABSENT that would be embarrassing to file wrongly, treat the first task
below as a verification step: if such a predicate exists, close this as PRESENT-on-axis and
say so — that is a good outcome, not a wasted ticket.

## Scope of THIS leaf (ship-alone)

1. A pure predicate: `replaySafe(blocks) bool` over the partial turn's emitted blocks.
2. Unsafe: visible text, images, tool calls, server-tool blocks. Safe: thinking-only,
   whitespace-only, empty.
3. Apply it as an **additional** conjunct to existing retry eligibility — never as a
   replacement for error classification.
4. Apply it to the refusal branch too.

## First checkable step

Confirm no equivalent predicate exists (grep the retry/resume packages for a content-shaped
eligibility check). Then a table test over block-kind combinations asserting the
safe/unsafe verdict for each, including the empty and whitespace-only edges.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] The verification step is reported in the issue either way — if fak already has this,
      the ticket closes PRESENT-on-axis with the seam named.
- [ ] `replaySafe` is a pure function over emitted blocks with a table test covering every
      listed block kind plus empty and whitespace-only.
- [ ] It is applied as an **additional** condition to retry eligibility; a test proves a
      retryable error with unsafe emitted output does **not** auto-retry.
- [ ] A thinking-only partial with a retryable error **does** retry (test) — the gate must
      not be so conservative it disables the common case.
- [ ] Classifier refusals are subject to the same gate (test).
- [ ] An interrupted turn whose tool calls already have matching results is
      preserve-and-continued, not replayed (test) — no duplicated side effect.
- [ ] Refusal-to-retry is recorded with a reason so suppressed retries are observable.
- [ ] No change to error classification itself; `make ci` green.

## Non-goals

- Reworking backoff, jitter, or the attempt budget.
- Model-fallback chain behavior.

---

**Epic:** #5917 (oh-my-pi study). **Source pinned at** `896bf5f`. **Route:** INSPIRE (clean-room; MIT source, Apache-2.0 target).

records.title: feat(wip): put the reclaim worklist on the garden tick and re-describe reap --census (#5480 follow-on)
records.body:
## Parent context

Parent: #3871 (epic). Direct follow-on to #5480, which shipped the lever and left these two items.

## Current state

`65a343a970` landed the RECLAIM recovery worklist: `fak wip reconcile --reclaim` prints the RECLAIM rows ranked most-decayed-first by base drift and exits 3 when the queue is non-empty (`cmd/fak/wip_reconcile.go`, `internal/wiprecon/reclaim.go`). #5480 called that "the whole lever" and it is closed on it.

Two of that issue's five numbered asks are still open, and both are the ones that make the lever actually get pulled:

- **Ask 2 — put the driver on the garden tick.** `git grep -n reclaim HEAD -- cmd/fak/garden*.go` is empty. The worklist exists but nothing reads it on a cadence, so a RECLAIM row still decays to QUARANTINE unless an operator happens to type the command. That is the original "nothing pumps between the classifier and the lander" complaint moved one level out.
- **Ask 5 — re-describe the collector.** `fak wip reap --census` reports `landed 0 / unknown 0 / closed_dirty_recoverable 133` under a garbage-collection frame, which makes `0 reapable` read as good news when it means 133 unlanded deliverables are aging out.

## Why this is next

RECLAIM is a decaying state by construction — `Applies` is `git apply --check` against a working tree that keeps moving — so the queue's value is a function of how soon someone looks at it. An unscheduled worklist and a report that calls the backlog garbage are the two remaining reasons nobody looks.

## Working spine

The garden tick surfaces the reclaim queue on its own cadence, and `reap --census` names what is in the store.

## In scope

- A garden-tick step that runs the existing `--reclaim` worklist read-only and surfaces a non-empty queue (count + most-decayed row) in the tick's normal output, next to the sibling namespace's reaper. It must stay advisory — no auto-land into the shared tree, for the reason `cmd/fak/wip_reconcile.go:44-48` gives.
- Wording changes to the `reap --census` surface so the recoverable bucket is not framed as garbage, and `0 reapable` cannot be read as "nothing to do".
- Tests pinning both: the tick emits the queue when non-empty and is silent/zero when empty; the census wording is asserted by literal.

## Out of scope

- Auto-landing a reclaimed delta (deliberately refused in #5480).
- Ranking or classifier changes — `RankReclaim` and the `RECLAIM | QUARANTINE | DISCARD_WITNESSED` vocabulary are settled.
- `--file-ticket` roll-up, which is #5337.

## Done condition

A garden tick over a store with at least one RECLAIM row reports that queue without being asked, and `reap --census` describes a recoverable-but-unlanded store in terms that do not call it garbage. Both pinned by tests.

## Witness

`go test ./cmd/fak -run 'GardenTick|WipReap'` green, with the new cases named, plus a captured tick output showing the queue line.

## Acceptance gate

The tick must not mutate the checkpoint namespace and must not land anything — a test asserts refs are byte-identical across a tick over a non-empty reclaim queue.

## Work estimate

Estimate: 2 points.

## Completion standard

development

## Closure binding

Close via a commit whose body carries `Closes #<n>` and whose diff lands the witness above.

## Lane

cmd

records.title: region admission: a sub-lane passed to --lane resolves to no tree and collides with everything (regionadmit never adopted laneadmit's hierarchy)
records.body:
## Summary

`internal/laneadmit` now understands hierarchical lane names (`gateway/server`,
`gateway/server.go`), landed in d41f5605a8. `internal/regionadmit` — the *other* pure
admission twin, and the one every real surface actually calls — does not. The two twins
have diverged, and on the surface a user touches the divergence is not neutral: passing a
sub-lane to `--lane` today is **strictly worse** than passing its declared root.

## Reproduced from the code

`fak loop region` (`cmd/fak/loop_region.go:83,93-94`), `fak loop drive`, and the dispatch
tick all go through `regionadmit.Decide` / `regionadmit.ResolveTree`.

**1. A sub-lane resolves to NO tree, so it collides with everything.**

`regionadmit.ResolveTree` (`internal/regionadmit/regionadmit.go:94-102`) resolves a lane by
exact map lookup:

```go
if req.Lane != "" {
    return cleanGlobs(tax.Trees[req.Lane])   // :99
}
```

`tax.Trees` is keyed by declared lane name only, so `--lane gateway/server` misses and
returns `nil`. Rung 4 (`:287`, `dispatchorder.TreesOverlap`) reads an empty tree as unknown
blast radius and collides **conservatively against every live lease**. So the narrower name
a worker types to get *more* concurrency gets it *less*: `--lane gateway` is admitted
against a disjoint peer, `--lane gateway/server` is refused by any peer at all.

`laneadmit.Taxonomy.TreeFor` (`internal/laneadmit/lanetree.go:193`) is the fixed version —
it walks to the nearest declared ancestor and derives `internal/gateway/server/**`.

**2. Exclusivity does not inherit downward.**

Rung 1 (`internal/regionadmit/regionadmit.go:251`) is a direct lookup:

```go
if tax.Exclusive[req.Lane] && len(others) > 0 {
```

`tax.Exclusive["abi/registry.go"]` is false, so a sub-lane of an exclusive root does not
trip the runs-alone gate at rung 1. In practice defect 1 masks this (the empty tree refuses
at rung 4 anyway, and with nothing live an exclusive request admits regardless), so this is
a latent hole rather than a live escape — but it becomes a real one the moment defect 1 is
fixed without fixing this. `laneadmit.Taxonomy.IsExclusive`
(`internal/laneadmit/lanetree.go:169`) walks ancestors for exactly this reason.

**3. Same-lane comparison is string equality.**

`:268` `if req.Lane != "" && lane == req.Lane` never fires for a parent/child pair, so
`gateway` and `gateway/server` would not serialize against each other even though the
parent may edit anywhere beneath the child. `laneadmit` reports this as its own rung,
`ConflictLaneAncestry` (`internal/laneadmit/laneadmit.go:36,158`).

Note the two twins also carry **different `Taxonomy` types** — `regionadmit.Taxonomy` has no
`Loaded` field and its own `LoadTaxonomy` (`:317`), so this is not a one-line import.

## What would fix it

Either port the four helpers (`CanonicalLane`, `LaneContains`, `TreeFor`, `IsExclusive`) into
`regionadmit`, or — better, and the reason the algebra was kept pure and dependency-light —
have `regionadmit` build a `laneadmit.Taxonomy` and delegate the lane-name dimension to it,
leaving `regionadmit`'s narrowed-pair co-admit rung (`strictlyWithinLane`, `:149`) as the
geometry half. Prefer the second: two independent implementations of one contract is how
this drifted in the first place.

This changes the **live** admission path that `fak dispatch tick` and `fak loop drive`
already run, so it wants its own change, not a drive-by.

## Acceptance bar

- `--lane gateway/server` resolves to `internal/gateway/server/**`, not `nil`.
- `--lane abi/registry.go` trips `exclusive_lane_requested`.
- `gateway` vs `gateway/server` serialize; `gateway/server` vs `gateway/router` co-run.
- Every existing `internal/regionadmit` test passes unchanged — all 543 declared lanes are a
  single `[a-z0-9]+` segment, so flat verdicts must stay byte-identical (this is the property
  `laneadmit`'s `TestDecideFlatVerdictsUnchanged` pins on its side).

## Not this issue

This does **not** by itself raise fleet concurrency. No surface picks a sub-lane on its own —
`fak dispatch wave` still routes an issue to a declared leaf — and #5854 is the blocker for
that (the lease record conflates admission geometry with authorization geometry, so narrowing
only the pricer yields phantom concurrency). This issue is the prerequisite: the decision has
to understand a sub-lane before anything can usefully hand it one.

Docs state the gap today: `docs/region-admission.md` (`Sub-lanes` + `Honest boundary`).

records.title: commit-stamp lane vocabulary is flat: a (fak gateway/server) trailer matches no stamp shape at all, so a sub-lane cannot reach the ship path
records.body:
## Summary

A worker that holds a sub-lane cannot stamp a commit for it. The commit-stamp lane
vocabulary in `internal/hooks` is flat in two independent places, so a
`(fak gateway/server)` trailer fails twice — and the first failure is silent-ish in the
worst way: the stamp is not recognized as a stamp at all.

Blocks the sub-lane namespace landed in d41f5605a8 (`internal/laneadmit/lanetree.go`)
from ever reaching the ship path. Sibling of #5929 (the admission half).

## Reproduced from the code

**1. The trailer regex has no `/` in its alphabet.**

`internal/hooks/commitstamp.go:30`

```go
trailerLeafRE = regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)\((?:refs\s+)?fak[ :]+([A-Za-z0-9][\w.\-]*)\)\s*$`)
```

`[\w.\-]` is `[0-9A-Za-z_.\-]` — no `/`. So `(fak gateway/server)` does not match the
trailer shape at all. It is not an *off-lane* stamp, it is **no stamp**, which lands the
commit as un-gradeable / `NOT_SHIPPED` rather than as a legible refusal. `directLeafRE`
(`:31`) has the same alphabet.

**2. Leaf classification is an exact declared-lane lookup plus a depth-1 directory probe.**

`classifyLeaf` (`:486-502`):

```go
if tax.declared[ll] { return true, "", "" }
if leafIsRealDir(ll, root) { ... advisory ... }
...
return false, "", "off-lane stamp `(fak " + leaf + ")`: binds to a unit no lane declares"
```

`leafIsRealDir` (`:505-515`) only stats `internal/<leaf>` and `cmd/<leaf>` — one segment.
So even if the regex accepted `gateway/server`, classification would reject it as off-lane
and block, and `nearestLane`'s edit-distance hint (`:519`) would produce noise against a
543-entry flat vocabulary.

## The decision this needs, before the code

This is not purely mechanical — there is a real convention question, and it should be
answered deliberately rather than by whichever patch lands first:

- **(a) Keep trailers flat.** The `(fak <leaf>)` trailer binds `dos verify` to a *ship unit*,
  and the ship unit is arguably still the leaf even when the *lease* was narrower. Sub-lanes
  then buy concurrency during the work and collapse to the leaf at commit time. Cheapest,
  and nothing downstream changes.
- **(b) Accept a hierarchical trailer.** `(fak gateway/server)` binds precisely, and per-file
  attribution gets sharper. But every consumer of the leaf token — `dos verify`, the
  commit-audit referee, the scorecards, `tools/commit_stamp_doctor.py`, whatever keys on
  `leaf_recognized` — has to accept the wider alphabet too, or a correct trailer starts
  reading as a phantom unit somewhere downstream.

Recommend **(a)** unless someone can name a consumer that genuinely needs sub-leaf
attribution. If (a) is chosen this issue is still worth closing deliberately rather than
silently, because today's failure mode for a hierarchical trailer is "no stamp" — the least
legible of the three possible answers. At minimum, teach `classifyLeaf` to recognize a
slash-shaped leaf and refuse it with a *specific* message ("stamp the declared root
`(fak gateway)`; sub-lanes are an admission unit, not a ship unit") instead of letting the
regex drop it on the floor.

## Acceptance bar

- A `(fak gateway/server)` subject produces a **deterministic, legible** verdict — either
  recognized (b), or refused with a message naming the declared root to use (a).
- Whichever is chosen, `internal/hooks` and `tools/commit_stamp_doctor.py` agree, since the
  regexes there are documented as ported verbatim (`commitstamp.go:27-28`) and a divergence
  between the Go gate and the Python oracle is its own defect class.
- All 543 flat trailers keep their exact current verdict.

records.title: feat(hooks): scope attribution — deny only what THIS commit introduces, not the shared dirty tree
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/precommit/` — `stagedscope.go` + `doclintscope.go` (their #622).

## What it does there

Their pre-commit gate reads files off the checkout. That checkout is shared by ~20 agent sessions, so **a peer's unstaged working-tree edit is a tree-wide input to YOUR gate**. Measured 2026-07-29 in that repo: one session left `internal/ticket/` (5 untracked `.go` files) plus an uncommitted lane entry in their lane config. All three reachable states of that pair were red, so no edit to one's own diff could clear any of them. Every commit touching any `.md`, `llms.txt`, the lane config, their doclint tree or a root path was denied **fleet-wide for hours, citing a path in nobody's diff**. Go-only commits skipped the rule entirely and kept landing — which is why the outage was invisible from the lanes that were not blocked.

Their fix is a discriminator: **deny what THIS commit introduces**. Judge *HEAD with the staged paths overlaid* — exactly the tree a pathspec commit produces — rather than the disk the author happens to be standing on. Note the shape it catches is one a HEAD-baseline subtraction does *not*: the violation is absent from HEAD (not committed) and absent from your staged set (not staged), so a HEAD diff calls it "introduced by this commit" and denies.

## The generalizable kernel

A gate on a shared checkout has three candidate inputs — the working tree, the index, and `HEAD ⊕ index`. Only the third is the tree the commit actually lands. Reading either of the other two makes the gate's verdict a function of peer WIP.

## Why fak needs it

- `internal/hooks/filesource.go` states the seam plainly: `fileProbe` is "Exists + Size **over the working tree**", and both `*StagedDiff` and `*TrackedTree` satisfy it. So the staged gates resolve links, classify files and scan for dead refs against the *live shared tree*, not against the tree their commit produces.
- fak runs the same shared-checkout topology this failure needs; the `fak commit` lock is held 60–126s fleet-wide, so a false refusal costs the whole fleet.
- #5128 is already this exact class: *"a peer's STAGED-but-uncommitted file wedges the tree-wide DESKTOP_POPUP_REGRESSION gate for the whole fleet."* That ticket fixes one gate. This one fixes the seam all of them share.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A `hooks` change-set view backed by `HEAD ⊕ staged` — reads blobs via `git cat-file`/`ls-tree` for unstaged paths and from the index for staged paths — implementing the existing `fileProbe`/`fileReader` interfaces, so no gate body changes to adopt it.
- [ ] Every gate in `internal/hooks/gate_*.go` is classified in a committed table as `LANDS_TREE` (must use the new view), `WORKTREE_BY_DESIGN` (with a one-line written reason), or `TREE_TWIN` (the `--audit-tree` reporting mode, unaffected). No gate is left unclassified.
- [ ] At least `DOC_PLACEMENT`, `BROKEN_LINK`, `INDEX_SYNC`, `DEAD_CODE`, `UNTIERED_LEAF` and `DESKTOP_POPUP_REGRESSION` are moved to `LANDS_TREE`, or the table records why not.
- [ ] Regression test reproducing the failure: a fixture repo where an *untracked peer file* and a *modified-but-unstaged peer file* each trip a gate under the worktree view and are **silent** under the lands-tree view — asserted on the gate's `Finding` set, not just the exit code.
- [ ] Inverse test: a violation genuinely introduced by the staged set is still denied under the new view (no fail-open).
- [ ] `fak hooks pre-commit -json` reports, per finding, which view produced it, so a false refusal is diagnosable in one command without taking the lock.
- [ ] A table (in the ticket or a `docs/notes/` note) of gates whose verdict *changed* on the live tree at a named SHA, with counts — evidence the seam was real, not just theoretically wrong.

## Non-goals

- Changing what any individual gate *checks*.
- Removing the `--audit-tree` whole-tree mode; that mode's denominator is the tree on purpose.

records.title: feat(trunkverdict): a commit-keyed trunk-green record so nobody commits onto a red trunk unaware
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/trunkverdict/` (their #575) plus `tools/precommit/trunkred.go`.

## What it does there

Measured: their `main` was **red for 262 commits over ~28 hours and no gate noticed**. Their Definition of Done is `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test ./...`, and a `ci` verb runs exactly that — but that verb is *voluntary*. The enforced gate is a **content** gate: it reads the staged paths and blobs and type-checks the staged tree, and it never runs a test. On a shared checkout the failure is silent in the direction of "looks fine": a worker in one lane runs `go test ./internal/<its-lane>/...`, sees `ok`, and commits, never learning the tree underneath it is red in a package it does not own and would never run.

`trunkverdict` records, reads and interprets **the full-suite verdict for one commit** — the "is main green?" fact nothing in the repo wrote down. Two design choices are the transferable part:

1. **The property is deliberately weaker than "every commit is green."** That stronger one is unaffordable — a 15-minute suite on every commit from 30 agents would serialise the fleet worse than their busiest lane already does. The sufficient property is: *nobody commits onto a red trunk without being told.*
2. Because that is a **notification** property, the consumer (their `TRUNK_RED` rule) **warns rather than refuses by default**.

## The generalizable kernel

Trunk greenness is a *fact keyed to a commit*, with a recorded staleness — not a state you re-derive per commit. Record it once, read it many times, and let each reader pick its own severity and its own staleness tolerance.

## Why fak needs it

- `internal/trunkbuildprobe` diagnoses **why** the ci-fast subset is red (it archives HEAD, parses compiler errors, and finds the forgotten `git add`) — but there is no durable record of **whether** the trunk is green at commit C. The probe is a debugger, not a ledger.
- `internal/hooks` carries ~40 content gates and none of them is a suite verdict.
- fak's tree hits the pathology repeatedly: `cmd/fak`'s test build broken by peers, ci-fast red for long stretches, and per-lane `go test ./internal/<pkg>/...` as the standard worker green-gate — the exact "ok in my lane, red underneath" shape.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `internal/trunkverdict`: a record type carrying at minimum `{commit, verdict, suite command, started, finished, host, tool version}`, plus reader/interpreter functions that are pure and unit-testable with no git and no Go toolchain.
- [ ] The record is **keyed to a commit** and a reader can distinguish four outcomes, not two: `GREEN`, `RED`, `UNKNOWN` (never run), `STALE` (recorded for an ancestor N commits back).
- [ ] Staleness is reported as a *distance* (commits behind, wall-clock age); the package hard-codes no threshold, callers set tolerance.
- [ ] A `TRUNK_RED` advisory in `internal/hooks` that **warns by default**, is opt-in-refusing via config, and **never** refuses on `UNKNOWN`.
- [ ] Storage location is decided and the argument written down — a committed file churns a shared tree on every run, a git note or a `refs/fak/*` ref does not. (See the sibling `docpack` render-lock ticket for the same churn argument costed out.)
- [ ] A writer path exists and is wired to something that actually runs the full suite (cadence job or ci-fast), not left as an unwired port. If it must ship unwired, it carries the fires-on-success pin from the sibling `unwiredscore` ticket.
- [ ] Test: a red verdict recorded at commit C reads as `RED` at C and as `STALE` at C+5, from the same record.

## Non-goals

- Running the full suite on every commit.
- Refusing commits by default.

records.title: fix(corelocks): report the resolved lease root — an empty census must not be indistinguishable from reading the wrong journal
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/lanescan/` — `dosroot.go` (their #743 and #682, sharpening #640).

## What it does there

Their lease journal is found by a **positional walk**: the `dos` binary walks up from the caller's working directory and stops at the first `.dos/` it finds. Their lane wrapper never set `cmd.Dir`, and there are **shadow `.dos/` roots inside the repository**, so the walk lands on one without the caller ever leaving the tree. Measured at their HEAD 1ad4cadcc, one `lanes status` per directory, same moment, with **22 leases genuinely held**:

```
repo root (positive control)          22 live lease(s)
.claude/skills/fleet-wave/            no live leases — every lane is free.
results/.../lift-proveout/            no live leases — every lane is free.
/tmp (the #640 baseline)              no live leases — every lane is free.
```

The last three are **byte-identical**, which is the whole finding: #640's stated mitigation is "run every lanes verb from the repo root", and rows two and three satisfy it. The caller is inside the repository the entire time.

And it fails in the one direction that cannot be recovered from. An empty lease set means arbitration **admits every lane**, so the banner does not merely withhold the census — it affirmatively reports that the referee is a rubber stamp. Both readers are safety checks (status, reap) and both **fail open**: a close-out sweep sees "0 leases held" and releases a lane under a live worker; a reap finds nothing stale because it was handed nothing at all.

Finally, **no git-based enumeration can find the shadow roots**. An unanchored `.dos/` in `.gitignore` matches at every depth, so all three roots return 0 from `git ls-files`, `git status` cannot see them, and `ls-files --others --exclude-standard` excludes them by construction. Only a filesystem walk finds them.

## The generalizable kernel

Two rules for any positionally-resolved state store:

1. **An empty census must be distinguishable from "I read the wrong store."** Report the resolved root alongside the count, always.
2. **Fail closed when the census is empty and the root is not the canonical one** — because every consumer of a lease census is a safety check, and a safety check handed nothing admits everything.

Plus: an unanchored ignore pattern makes the shadow copies invisible to git, so discovery must be a filesystem walk, not a git subprocess.

## Why fak needs it

- fak carries `internal/corelocks`, `internal/leaseref`, `internal/laneadmit`, `internal/flock`, `internal/servicelease` and `internal/gpulease`, with `dos_arbitrate` as the fleet referee and a `.dos/` root in the tree.
- The consequence class is already fak's lived experience: stale-lease reaps in the experiments lane, and `fak sweep --apply` taking the whole lane including live peers. Both are "the census under-reported and something got released".
- The workspace has sibling checkouts and nested scratch trees under the same parent directory — exactly the shadow-root topology.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A resolver that returns the **resolved root path** with every lease/lane census, and a CLI surface that prints it — "which journal did I read?" must be answerable in one command.
- [ ] A `ShadowRoots` filesystem walk enumerating every nested state root inside the repo, **not** via `git ls-files`, with a test proving the git-based enumeration returns 0 for a root the walk finds.
- [ ] Callers that shell out to lease tooling set an explicit working directory or pass an explicit root; a test asserts no caller relies on the positional walk.
- [ ] **Fail-closed semantics**: an empty census resolved from a non-canonical root is an error, not `0 leases`. Test: one fixture, two cwds (canonical and shadow) — the shadow run must not return a bare `0`.
- [ ] Positive control in the suite: N leases held ⇒ census reports N from the canonical root, so a future `0` reads as a regression rather than as quiet.
- [ ] The ignore pattern for the state dir is anchored (`/.dos/`, not `.dos/`) so nested roots become visible to `git status`, or the ticket records why not.
- [ ] Every reader that acts destructively on an empty census (reap, sweep, release) is audited and listed; each either fails closed or documents why failing open is correct there.

## Non-goals

- Redesigning the lease format or the arbitration algebra.

records.title: feat(devindex): generate the verb surface from SOURCE with a REFUSES column and a printed gap count
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/verbsdoc/` — `main.go`, `surface.go`, `precondition.go`, `render.go` (their IDX-03 / #915).

## What it does there

Generates a verb-surface page: every verb and sub-verb, its purpose, the implementing package, the doc that governs it, and — **the column the tool exists for — what it REFUSES**.

The cost that bought it: someone needed a multi-camera batch-size sweep, wrote a bespoke script, and only afterwards found `tb bench batchsweep`, the verb for exactly that question — and then **could not use it anyway**, because it wants a dynamic engine and all five fielded models are static. Both facts were discoverable only by reading `--help` one verb at a time.

Two design constraints, both learned from failures rather than chosen:

1. **The tree is read from SOURCE, never scraped from `--help`.** A sub-verb missing from its own help text is precisely the drift the page exists to catch — eleven of them shipped that way — and a scraper would inherit the omission and call it complete.
2. **A blank preconditions cell is impossible by construction.** `PreState` is a closed five-state enum whose **zero value is `UNVERIFIED`**, and the count of unverified rows is **printed in the generated page itself**. A generated index that hides its own gaps reads as complete coverage, which is worse than no index.

Three modes: check (re-render and diff, non-zero on drift), `-write`, `-print`.

## The generalizable kernel

- **Source, not `--help`** — a generator's input must never be the downstream artefact whose drift it exists to catch.
- **A zero value that means UNVERIFIED** — so an unfilled cell is a loud state, not an empty string.
- **The artefact publishes its own gap count** — coverage becomes a number on the page rather than a claim about the page.
- The **refusal surface** is the column that makes a verb index usable. "Purpose" is the one everybody writes and nobody needs.

## Why fak needs it

- fak has a very large verb surface (`cmd/fak/`, `internal/devindex/verbs.go`, `internal/capindex`, the `fak_index_verbs` MCP verb) and the discoverability failure above is the daily one — "grep the local trunk before dispatching" and "`fak_feature_query` dumps the whole index" are both symptoms of *the index exists but does not answer the question*.
- fak's refusal vocabulary is large and load-bearing — `OFF_TRUNK`, `LOCK_BUSY`, `PRESTAGED_PATH_OVERLAP`, `CONCEPT_ADMISSION`, `IMPORT_OF_UNCOMMITTED_PACKAGE`, `UNTIERED_LEAF`, `DEAD_CODE`, `PUBLIC_LEAK`, `BARE_COMMIT_SWEEP` — and it is currently learned by hitting it. **Nothing renders "what will this verb refuse, and why" as a table.**
- `internal/unwiredscore` already measures an adjacent gap, so the "publish your own gap count" habit has a home.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A generator deriving the verb tree from **source** (`cmd/fak` command registration plus `internal/devindex`), with a test that either finds ≥1 verb/sub-verb absent from its own `--help` or asserts that set is empty at a named SHA.
- [ ] A **REFUSES** column: per verb, the refusal codes it can emit, derived from source rather than hand-listed.
- [ ] A closed precondition enum whose **zero value is `UNVERIFIED`**, and a generated page that prints `unverified rows: N / M`.
- [ ] Check mode: re-render and diff, non-zero exit on drift; wired into the same gate family as `INDEX_SYNC` / `CONCEPT_FRESHNESS`.
- [ ] `-write` and `-print` modes; `-print` touches nothing on disk.
- [ ] The generated page is reachable from `INDEX.md` / `llms.txt` and passes the existing doc gates.
- [ ] The page regenerates to a zero diff from a clean checkout at a named SHA, so the artefact is not stale the day it lands.

## Non-goals

- Hand-authored per-verb prose. Anything not derivable from source is out of scope for the generator.

records.title: feat(lint): closed-enum exhaustiveness over the Go AST — non-exhaustive switches and composite-literal holes
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/enumlint/` — `discover.go`, `rules.go`, `exempt.go`, `tree_test.go`, `realsite_test.go` (~1.8k LOC plus 733 lines of test).

## What it does there

Discovers **closed enumerations** from the Go AST — a defined type over a basic type, plus every package-level constant declared with it — and applies rules over the sites that consume them.

The scope decision is deliberately narrow and worth copying verbatim: the underlying-kind allowlist admits only `string`, `int`, `int8/16/32/64` and friends. *"A defined type over a struct or a slice is not a closed set of constants, and widening this would start reporting types that have no const block to be closed against."* Members carry `{Name, File, Line, Val}`, with `Val == ""` marking an iota member.

## The generalizable kernel

A closed vocabulary declared in Go is machine-discoverable, and the interesting defect is a **consumer that does not cover it**: a `switch` with no `default` missing a member, a map literal keyed by the enum with a hole, a validation function that admits a string the type does not name. The lint earns its keep because adding an enum member is the cheap half and finding every consumer is the expensive half.

## Why fak needs it

- fak is ~800 `internal/` packages and closed string vocabularies are its dominant modelling idiom: refusal codes, census classes, verdicts, lifecycle states.
- `internal/wipref/census.go` names one explicitly — *"CensusClass is the **closed vocabulary** a single checkpoint ref is classified into"* — and its `TestClassifyVocabulary` "walks every census class the classifier can emit". That is a hand-written, single-package version of exactly this lint, and it exists in only one package.
- The same shape recurs across `internal/branchrole`, `internal/turnkind`, `internal/policy`, `internal/adjudicator`, `internal/lifecycle`, and the `hooks` gate codes. Each re-implements coverage by hand, or not at all.
- Adjacent but not a duplicate: **#5649** ("derive closed vocabularies from source and detect drift") covers *discovery and drift of the vocabulary itself*. This ticket covers *exhaustiveness at the consumption sites*. They should share one discovery pass — land it once.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `internal/<name>`: AST discovery of closed enums (defined type over a basic kind, plus its package-level const block), returning `{Name, Members[{Name, File, Line, Val}]}` with iota members marked.
- [ ] The underlying-kind allowlist is explicitly narrow and the narrowness is argued in the package doc.
- [ ] Rule 1 — **non-exhaustive switch**: a `switch` on an enum-typed value with no `default` that omits ≥1 member is a finding, reporting file:line of both the switch and each missing member.
- [ ] Rule 2 — **composite-literal holes**: a map or array literal keyed by the enum type missing ≥1 member is a finding.
- [ ] An **exemption mechanism** requiring a written reason per exemption, plus a test that no exemption is stale (its target still exists and would still fire).
- [ ] A whole-tree run over `internal/**` at a named SHA with finding counts published, and a **counted baseline ratchet** (see the sibling `testq` ticket) so the tool is safe to land on a tree that still carries debt.
- [ ] A `realsite`-style test asserting ≥1 finding on a real in-tree enum, so the lint is proven non-vacuous rather than green-because-blind.
- [ ] Shares its discovery pass with #5649 rather than forking a second AST walker.

## Non-goals

- Reporting on open sets (structs, slices, interface implementations).
- Refusing on any finding at landing time. Ship as a ratchet.

records.title: feat(quality): a Go test-quality ratchet — assertion-free findings with a counted baseline floor
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/testq/` — `baseline.go`, `testq.go`, `main.go` (their #550).

## What it does there

Finds test-quality defects (assertion-free tests, tautological assertions, and friends) and gates them with a **ratchet**, not a refusal.

Two design arguments are the whole transfer.

**Why a ratchet and not a refusal.** #550 measured *roughly 1 in 4 candidates as a real defect*, and explicitly named three tests that must **not** be "fixed". A tool that denied on any candidate would be **wrong three times in four**. A ratchet is the strongest *true* statement available — "this class is not growing" — and it is what makes the tool safe to run on a tree that still has debt in it.

**Why a count and not a per-finding line.** Two findings of the same code in the same function have no stable distinguishing identity: the second one is only "the second one", and inserting an assertion above it would renumber it. Counting means fixing one of two still tightens the floor, and adding a third is still caught.

Baseline format is `CODE<TAB>path<TAB>TestFuncName<TAB>count`. Blank lines and `#` comments are skipped, and **anything else that does not parse is an ERROR, never a skipped line** — because a baseline that silently drops a malformed entry reads as a floor of zero for that key, so the tool's own bug presents as a fresh finding in someone else's diff.

## The generalizable kernel

The ratchet contract, in four clauses: (a) key findings by something *stable under editing*; (b) store counts, not line numbers; (c) **hard-fail on an unparseable baseline row**, because a lenient parser converts your bug into someone else's denial; (d) only ever claim "not growing", never "clean".

## Why fak needs it

- fak already runs exactly one ratchet of this shape and it is load-bearing: `internal/pythongate/baseline.go`. Its sharp edge is known operating lore — *a NEW `tools/*_test.py` cannot land, you must EXTEND one already in the baseline* — i.e. the ratchet works, and the **Go** side has no equivalent.
- fak has `internal/quality`, `internal/brittleness`, `internal/mutationefficacy`, `internal/mutationbudget`: scoring, but no landing-time floor on Go test quality.
- fak's known failure family is exactly what this catches: vacuous green-gates behind `//go:build ignore`, `go test -overlay` reporting a false `ok`, and green tests that never validated the header comment they were supposed to. A test that asserts nothing is that same failure with no build tag to give it away.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `internal/<name>`: findings over `*_test.go` ASTs covering at minimum — a test function with **zero reachable** `t.Fatal`/`t.Error`/assertion calls; an assertion comparing a value to itself; an `err` captured and never checked; a table-test expectation field that is never read.
- [ ] Each finding carries a `Key()` **stable under insertion** (code + file + test func), and the baseline stores a **count** per key.
- [ ] Baseline parser: `#` comments and blank lines skipped; **every other unparseable line is a hard error** naming the line number — covered by a test asserting the error, not a skip.
- [ ] The ratchet reports NEW findings only where a key's count **exceeds** its floor; fixing one of two tightens the floor on regeneration.
- [ ] A whole-tree run at a named SHA with per-code finding counts published in the ticket, and the seeded baseline committed.
- [ ] A precision spot-check: sample ≥20 findings, report how many are real defects versus deliberate, and record the deliberate ones as baseline entries with a reason comment.
- [ ] Wired as an advisory in the push/CI gate family. It **must not** refuse on a pre-existing finding.

## Non-goals

- Judging whether an assertion is *correct*. This gates presence and shape only.
- Auto-fixing.

records.title: feat(index): doc reachability census under NAMED resolver semantics, measured against HEAD not the worktree
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/indexgraph/` (their #878 / WK-03, sharpened by #907).

## What it does there

A **doc reachability census**: which tracked `*.md` files are reached by nothing else in the tree. It replaces a shell loop that lived inside the audit page itself.

Two findings make it worth porting rather than re-inventing.

**The audit's headline was unreproducible the day it landed.** At the commit that *published* the audit, the audit's own rule scored **63 of 576** — not the 76 of 582 it claimed for itself. Three plausible numbers had been produced by three unstated rules.

**So the tool reports under three NAMED matcher semantics, never one:**

- `R-AUDIT` — the audit's rule: a target is reached if any other tracked file contains the target's last two path components as a substring. Fail-**closed** on same-directory relative links, because a sibling linked as `[x](x.md)` carries no directory component.
- `R-LINK` — the doc linter's own resolver applied to markdown **link targets** only: resolve relative to the linking file's dir, then re-anchor at each ancestor accepting only a unique hit, then a uniqueness-gated basename match.
- `R-MENTION` — the same resolver over every path-shaped `*.md` token in the text, link or not, because a backticked path in prose or in a Go comment is how most of that tree cites.

`R-UNION = R-LINK ∪ R-MENTION`. **Nothing is summed across rules; each is reported with its own denominator, and every count carries the size of the domain it quantified over.**

And the corpus is **HEAD via `git cat-file`, never the working tree**: 115 paths were dirty from five live fleets, and a worktree census measures peer WIP.

## The generalizable kernel

- A reachability number is meaningless without its **named rule** and its **denominator**. Publish `{rule, numerator, denominator}` triples, never a bare percentage.
- Where rules disagree, **report all of them** rather than picking one — disagreement localises the ambiguity instead of hiding it.
- A census over a shared checkout must read **HEAD**, or it is measuring peer WIP.

## Why fak needs it

- fak has `INDEX.md`, `llms.txt`, a large `docs/` tree, `internal/devindex`, `internal/agentsindex`, and an `INDEX_SYNC` gate — plenty of index machinery, but no answer to "which docs are reachable from the front door, under which rule?"
- The HEAD-vs-worktree trap is *already* fak's known failure mode: live-tree gates read the worktree locally and HEAD in CI, and the concept-freshness regen counts peers' uncommitted symbols while the gate reads the index. Same bug, different gate.
- `internal/orphanscan` exists for code (#3167, #3169); the doc side has no equivalent.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `internal/<name>`: a reachability census over tracked `*.md`, reading blobs from **HEAD** via `git cat-file`, with the working tree explicitly not an input.
- [ ] **At least two named rules** implemented (a link-target resolver and a mention resolver), each reporting its own `{numerator, denominator}`; the union is reported separately and nothing is summed across rules.
- [ ] Every emitted count is accompanied by the size of the domain it quantified over — no bare percentages anywhere in the output or the generated page.
- [ ] Unresolvable link targets are counted and listed separately from unreached documents; the two are different defects.
- [ ] A published run at a named SHA, and a test that re-running at that SHA reproduces the numbers exactly.
- [ ] Zero-inbound documents are enumerated, not just counted, so the list is actionable.
- [ ] A verb (`fak index graph` or similar) rather than a `go run ./tools/...` prototype — the tb version is explicitly parked as unwired, and the port should not inherit that.

## Non-goals

- Deciding that a zero-inbound doc should be deleted. The census reports; a human or a separate policy decides.

records.title: feat(hooks): publish the doc gate DENOMINATOR — census the files the linter never sees
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/doclint/` — the corpus-coverage family: `ignoreddocs.go`, `rootignored.go`, `unscanneddocs.go`, `worktreedocs.go`, `trackedscopes.go`.

## What it does there

`doclint` is a 7.6k-LOC prose gate with ~14 checks. Five of those checks are not about prose at all — they are about **the linter's own denominator**. They answer: which documents exist that this linter never sees?

- `ignoreddocs` / `rootignored` — docs excluded by ignore rules, so the gate is silent on them and reads as passing.
- `unscanneddocs` — docs inside the corpus that no check happens to cover.
- `worktreedocs` — docs present on disk but not tracked, i.e. visible to a local run and invisible to CI.
- `trackedscopes` — which path scopes are actually in the corpus.

The argument, which they make repeatedly across that tree: **a checker that cannot enumerate its own blind spots reads as complete coverage, and that is worse than no checker.** The `verbsdoc` tool makes the same move with its printed count of unverified rows.

## The generalizable kernel

Every gate has a denominator. If the gate does not publish it, "0 findings" is unfalsifiable — it means either "clean" or "I looked at nothing", and those two are byte-identical in the output. The fix is a **coverage census emitted alongside the findings**: files in scope, files excluded and by which rule, files in scope that no check covered.

## Why fak needs it

- **This has already burned fak.** An unanchored `*scratchpad*` pattern in `.gitignore` silently swallowed real source files — empty `git status --porcelain` output, and the only way to see it was `git check-ignore -v`. That is the `rootignored` check, missing.
- The same class again: `check-ignore` false-positives on a trailing-slash directory pattern, so an untracked dir "matches" a blank line and exits 0.
- fak's doc gates (`DOC_PLACEMENT`, `BROKEN_LINK`, `INDEX_SYNC`, `CONCEPT_FRESHNESS`) each compute a scope internally and none of them reports it. A gate that goes quiet because its scope collapsed is indistinguishable from a gate that passed.
- fak's tree carries `_*` scratch directories, `.st_*` scratch families, sibling checkouts and gitignored artefacts — a large and moving exclusion surface.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A `Coverage` report emitted by the doc-gate family carrying, at minimum: `{in_scope: N, excluded_by_ignore: N, excluded_by_scope_rule: N, in_scope_but_no_check_applied: N}` with the file lists behind each count.
- [ ] **Ignore attribution**: for every excluded file, which rule (and which line of which ignore file) excluded it — the `git check-ignore -v` fact, computed once, not per-debug-session.
- [ ] A check that flags **source-shaped files** (`*.go`, `*.py`, `*.md` under `docs/`) caught by an ignore rule, since that is the class that has actually bitten this repo.
- [ ] A check that flags **untracked-but-on-disk** docs, so a locally-green run that would be red in CI (or vice versa) is visible — this is the local/CI split fak already knows it has.
- [ ] The coverage numbers are printed by `fak hooks pre-commit -json` and by the tree-audit mode, not hidden behind a debug flag.
- [ ] A test asserting the census is non-vacuous: a fixture with a deliberately ignored `docs/*.md` is reported as excluded-with-reason, and the gate does **not** report clean.
- [ ] A run at a named SHA publishing fak's current numbers, including any real blind spots found.

## Non-goals

- Changing any ignore rule. This ticket makes the exclusions *visible*; deciding they are wrong is separate work.
- Porting doclint's prose checks (see the sibling "in one breath" ticket).

records.title: feat(doclint): an in-one-breath contract gate for the measurable half — simplicity and brevity only
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/doclint/breath.go` (plus `framing.go` and `humility.go` for the same argument shape).

## What it does there

Every explainer page in that tree opens with an "In one breath" block, and the gate enforces the contract its README states for it: *"Two to four sentences, each 15 words or fewer, one idea per sentence, no em-dashes, no parentheses, no acronym that isn't spelled out on the spot."* The block exists because it has a **different audience** from the page beneath it — "someone, or something, with no background at all" — and it is deliberately cruder than the prose it introduces.

**Why it is a gate and not a memo.** All 64 pages carried the block, and every one got it by hand. A prose contract enforced by an author's diligence decays in exactly one direction: the next page gets written in the voice of the page *body* rather than the block, no existing check notices, and the README goes on describing a shape the tree stopped having. The decay is invisible **precisely because the block still reads well** — a 30-word sentence with two parentheticals is good technical writing, it is simply not the artefact the contract asked for, and nothing but a count can tell the two apart.

**The scope decision, and it is the load-bearing part.** The TREC PLABA track (arXiv 2507.14096, 2025) ran two years of expert manual evaluation over plain-language adaptations and scored four axes: accuracy, completeness, simplicity, brevity. Its headline: top systems *"rivaled human levels of factual accuracy and completeness, but not simplicity or brevity."* So the axes a machine already gets right are the ones this check cannot mechanically judge, and the two it fails are exactly the two that reduce to counting words and sentences. The check therefore gates **simplicity and brevity — the measurable half — and says nothing whatever about whether the block is true.**

**And the design it deliberately does NOT have**, which was the tempting one: comparing the block against the page body to prove the simple version follows from the precise one. PlainQAFact (arXiv 2503.08890, 2025) names why that fails — the *elaborative explanation phenomenon*. Good plain-language writing ADDS content absent from the source (definitions, background, an example) to make it comprehensible, so an entailment- or QA-style consistency check scores the **best-written** blocks as the **least faithful** ones.

## The generalizable kernel

For any prose contract: **gate the countable half, and refuse to gate the judgement half — explicitly, in writing, with the reason.** A prose gate that reaches for faithfulness inverts its own signal. A prose gate that counts is boring, correct, and cannot be gamed into rewarding worse writing.

## Why fak needs it

- fak's agent-facing prose surface is enormous and is a live budget problem: epic **#3229** (context/token budget), **#3535** (cut the ~10k turn-1 AGENTS.md forced read via a sectioned loader). A per-document "one breath" block with an enforced word ceiling is directly the artefact a sectioned loader wants to serve first.
- fak already has prose scorers — `internal/negframe`, `internal/answershape`, `internal/slop*`, `internal/promptlint`, the `slop-score` and `negframe-score` skills. None of them enforces a *stated* contract on a *named* block; they score free prose, which is the judgement half.
- The decay argument applies directly: fak's docs are written by many concurrent sessions, and "reads well but is not the artefact asked for" is undetectable by every gate fak has.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A named summary block is specified in `docs/` (delimiters, required position, the contract) before any code — the gate enforces a written contract, not the reverse.
- [ ] A gate enforcing only **countable** properties: sentence count range, per-sentence word ceiling, banned punctuation, and unexpanded-acronym detection against a spelled-out-on-the-spot rule.
- [ ] The package doc states, in writing, that faithfulness is **out of scope**, and cites the reason (elaborative explanation inverts the signal). A future contributor must not be able to add an entailment check without arguing past that paragraph.
- [ ] Ships as an **advisory with a counted ratchet** first (see the `testq` sibling ticket), not a refusal — fak's doc corpus predates the contract.
- [ ] A measured run: how many current fak docs carry a conforming block, how many carry a block that fails, how many carry none. Three numbers, with the denominator.
- [ ] The rendered contract is reachable from `INDEX.md` and passes the existing doc gates.
- [ ] Cross-link to #3229 / #3535 as the consumer: the block is what a budget-aware loader serves when it cannot afford the page.

## Non-goals

- Judging whether the summary is accurate or complete.
- Rewriting existing docs as part of this ticket.

records.title: feat(wipref): per-payload-file A/M/- classification — DIVERGED is its own state, and an orphan ref must not read as empty
records.body:
## Source

`tb/tensor-build-main/tools/holdcensus/` (their #605, correcting a salvage index written from a wrong answer in #495).

## What it does there
