That partition is what makes the paper's **rubric-category ablation** possible — dropping one category at a time and measuring the effect on task success is how they characterize *when and why* the method works. A taxonomy with one 84% bucket admits no such experiment.

## Why they built it that way

They needed to answer a reviewer question — *which* checks carry the win — so the categories had to be designed as independent, roughly-balanced axes up front. fak's vocabulary grew the other way: organically, one refusal at a time, each correctly typed as "an operator gate stopped this" at the moment it was added. Nobody chose an 84% bucket; it accreted. That is the same accretion pattern this study found in the source repo's own prompt corpus — recorded in the epic — and it is worth noting fak has decay machinery for skills and memory but none pointed at the reason vocabulary.

## First checkable step

Re-partition `OPERATOR_GATE` into attributable sub-categories along the lines the sample already suggests (contention / pathology / hygiene / architecture / cost / ledger-state / inventory-debt), keeping the existing `token` strings **stable** — the tokens are load-bearing across guards, skills, docs, and memory, so only the `category` field moves.

Checkable in one assertion: a test that **no single category holds more than ~⅓ of the reasons**, which converts "the taxonomy is balanced" from a judgement into a ratchet. That test is the whole ship-alone deliverable; per-category rollups and any ablation become possible once it passes.

Scoped to the reason vocabulary's `category` field only — no token renames, no behaviour change, no new refusals.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room, no text or bytes copied. The 7-section partition is cited as evidence of the pattern; fak's sub-categories should follow fak's own failure classes, not theirs.

records.title: feat(quality): score tool-argument values against the instruction, not just the tool schema (a fabricated legal value passes at 1.0)
records.body:
Borrow from the **RubricRefine** study (epic filed alongside; `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-RUBRICREFINE-2026-08-08.md`).

## The axis

**Is an argument's *value* grounded in the instruction — or merely legal against the tool's schema?**

These are different questions, and fak only asks the second one.

## The gap

fak checks tool arguments against the **tool's declared schema**, in two places, and both are schema-relative only:

- **Live kernel rung** — `internal/grammar/grammar.go:198-215` denies a call missing a required param before it spawns (`countMissing` counts required params absent from the arg map; present-or-not, never value-grounded).
- **Eval oracle** — `internal/quality/tool_call_fidelity.go` (#4565) scores tool selection plus argument presence / type / enum / range, and flags undeclared extras at `:104-110`:

```go
extra := 0
for _, name := range sortedKeys(call.Args) {
    if _, declared := spec.Args[name]; !declared {
        extra++
        faults = append(faults, fmt.Sprintf("argument %q is not in tool %q's schema", name, spec.Tool))
    }
}
```

The oracle's whole vocabulary for an argument is `toolArgSpec{Type, Required, Enum, Min, Max}` (`:55-61`) — every field is a property of the *schema*. And the judge never reads the task text:

```go
func (toolCallFidelity) Judge(_ Trace, eng Trace, c QualityCase) Verdict {
```

`c.Prompt` **exists on the case** (it is read by `internal/quality/instruction_following.go` and `request_fidelity.go:48`) — `tool_call_fidelity.go` simply never touches it. A grep for `Prompt` in that file returns **zero** hits in the implementation; only the test sets one.

**Consequence:** a model that fabricates a plausible value for a legitimately-declared argument scores a clean **1.0** and passes. Ask for a *3-day* forecast and let the model call `get_forecast(days=7)` — `7` is an integer inside `min 1 / max 10`, so every existing check passes. The wrong action executes downstream with a perfect score.

This is exactly the paper's failure family: contract violations that **run to completion without raising an error**.

## Why the neighbouring seams don't cover it

Checked and rejected as off-axis:

- `internal/ifc` gates on argument **provenance**, but its lattice is *taint* (trusted-local vs external) — a security axis. A literal the model invented itself is `Trusted` there, so it is orthogonal to this.
- `internal/toolseq` counts transition n-grams over a corpus (descriptive); `internal/toolproc/repeatclass` classifies mutability of repeated calls for cache reuse; `internal/callavoid` prices avoidance economics. None scores grounding.

## The source pattern

RubricRefine makes instruction-grounding a first-class check class, repeatedly and in both directions:

- *"Do not invent numeric literals such as rates, discounts, thresholds, or quantities that are absent from the instruction unless they are deterministically derived from prior grounded outputs"* — `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:28` @`2c082ad`
- *"If a tool returns multiple matching items and the instruction does not specify a selector criterion, do not invent one such as cheapest, highest-rated, earliest, shortest, or best. Preserve grounded item-selection provenance instead of adding unstated ranking logic"* — `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:11` @`2c082ad`
- *"Do not treat a rate/percentage literal as an already-computed amount unless the instruction explicitly says it is already calculated"* — `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:15` @`2c082ad`

Their rubric is conditioned on `{instructions}` **and** `{tool_docs}` together (`prompt_2_rubric_generation.txt:7-9`) precisely so the check set can span both.

## Why they built it that way

Their tasks hand the model a fresh registry plus an instruction carrying all the task-critical literals, and the benchmark grades the final numeric answer — so a fabricated-but-legal argument is the single highest-frequency way to fail while looking fine. They had to check values against the instruction because the schema alone never catches it. fak's oracle grew from the opposite direction (#4565 was about *routing* and *well-formedness*), so the schema axis got built and the grounding axis never did.

## First checkable step

One additive field, one case in the existing switch:

1. Extend `toolArgSpec` (`internal/quality/tool_call_fidelity.go:55`) with `Grounded bool \`json:"grounded,omitempty"\`` — "this argument's value must be supplied by the instruction".
2. In `Judge`'s per-argument switch (~`:89`), after the type check: when `as.Grounded` and the emitted value's canonical string form does not appear (case-insensitively) in `c.Prompt`, append fault `argument %q = %v is not supplied by the instruction` and do **not** increment `passed`.

**Witness test:** reuse the existing `toolFidelityCase` (Prompt: *"Fetch the 3-day Oslo forecast in celsius."*) and flip the faithful call's `"days":3` to `"days":7`. Today that passes at score **1.0**; after the change it must fail with the invented-literal fault.

Additive and default-off: absent/optional args stay vacuously conformant, so every existing case is unchanged — matching the package's stated posture. Sequence-minimality scoring (preferring the shortest grounded tool sequence) is a **separate follow-on** and must not be bundled here.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room Go, no prompt text or bytes copied. The rules above are cited as evidence of the pattern.

records.title: feat(trajctl): give rubric criteria a closed category so findings roll up by check kind (ids are positional and task-local)
records.body:
Borrow from the **RubricRefine** study (epic filed alongside; `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-RUBRICREFINE-2026-08-08.md`).

## The axis

**Can verification findings be rolled up by *kind of check*, so a category can be dropped and its contribution measured?**

## The gap

fak's actual LLM verifier — the trajctl rubric judge — attributes per **criterion**, never per **category**. `internal/trajctl/rubric.go:56-59`:

```go
// RubricCriterion is one concrete, checkable criterion of an issue-specific
// rubric. ID is the stable key per-criterion attribution cites.
type RubricCriterion struct {
    ID   string `json:"id"`
    Text string `json:"text"`
}
```

Two structural facts make category rollup impossible today:

1. **The ids are positional and task-local.** `normalizeRubric` synthesizes them at `rubric.go:143`:
   ```go
   id = fmt.Sprintf("c%d", len(out.Criteria)+1)
   ```
   So `c2` on one objective and `c2` on another are unrelated. There is no key that means the same thing across objectives.
2. **The pinned generation schema has no category field.** `rubricToolParameters` declares exactly `id` ("short stable criterion id, e.g. c1") and `text` ("one concrete, checkable criterion"). A grep for `categor` across `rubric.go` returns **zero** hits.

Consequence: per-criterion attribution (#2544, `judgescorer.go:156` — "so a row cites WHICH criteria moved, not just the aggregate") tells you *which criterion* moved on *this* objective, and nothing aggregable above that. **"Which kind of check earns its keep"** is unanswerable, and no kind can be ablated.

The four dimensions fak would want to label already exist — but only as **prose inside a system-prompt string**, never as an enum on the struct and never on the wire.

## Why this is PARTIAL, not ABSENT — fak has both halves, unjoined

fak runs this exact pattern well on adjacent seams:

- `internal/negframe/negframe.go:145` — a closed vocabulary explicitly for rollup: `var Categories = []Category{Prohibition, Absence, Refusal, Hedge, Exception}`, described as "used for per-category KPI folding", with `build.go:123` folding one KPI per category (`Key: "positive_" + string(cat)`).
- `internal/antipattern` — closed `Class` + `Group` vocabulary.
- `internal/abi/reasons.go` + `denyrules.go` — a closed two-level (class, rule-id) refusal vocabulary built so an operator can route on the category.

And fak has a real ablation harness: `internal/ablate` runs closed-token A/B with per-arm subprocess rungs. But its tokens are cache/wire/gate **operators** (`vdso`, `radix`, `gitgate`, `negframe_reframe`) and its arms measure cache effect / latency / cost — **never per-check-category verification yield**. So fak can ablate a whole check *operator* and price it; it cannot ablate a *category of check* and measure which category carried the discrimination.

The two halves — closed category vocabularies, and an ablation harness — are simply never joined at check-category granularity on the rubric seam.

## The source pattern

RubricRefine fixes a **7-section taxonomy** as the required rubric output format (`prompt_2_rubric_generation.txt:69-104` @`2c082ad`) — Intent, Ordering/dataflow, Argument/format, Type/shape contract, Execution-critical, Final-answer, Tool-choice — and mirrors it exactly in the scorer's response schema keys (`prompt_4_evaluation.txt:68` @`2c082ad`: `intent`, `ordering_dataflow`, `argument_format`, `type_shape_contract`, `execution_critical`, `final_answer`, `tool_choice`).

Because the taxonomy is fixed and on the wire, categories are droppable one at a time — which is what makes their **rubric-category ablation** possible, i.e. characterizing *which* check categories carry the win rather than only *that* the method wins.

## Why they built it that way

They had to answer a reviewer asking which part of the method actually does the work, with no ground truth at inference time — so the categories had to be designed as independent, stable, roughly-balanced axes up front and pinned into the schema. fak's rubric grew per-objective and task-local, which is right for *attribution within one objective* and structurally wrong for *rollup across objectives*. Nobody chose that; the positional id was the obvious thing at the time.

## First checkable step

One commit on `internal/trajctl/rubric.go`:

1. Add a closed `RubricCategory` enum, seeded from the four dimensions `rubricSystemPrompt` **already names in prose** (localization constraints, edit constraints, trajectory discipline, budget awareness) — so this pins existing intent rather than inventing a taxonomy.
2. Add `Category` to `RubricCriterion`.
3. Add it to `rubricToolParameters` as a JSON-Schema `enum` on a required key.
4. Make `validateRubric` reject an out-of-set category — **fail closed**, same as the existing duplicate-id check.

**Witness:** a table test asserting (a) a generated rubric carrying an unknown category returns an error and no rubric, and (b) `FormatRubricForPrompt` renders `[<category>/<id>]` so the judge's per-criterion findings become category-attributable.

Per-category evidence refs in `judgescorer` and a category-ablation arm in `internal/ablate` are **follow-ons, not this step**.

## Relationship to the sibling leaf

The refusal-taxonomy leaf filed alongside this one targets the *same axis* (per-category attribution) on a *different seam* (the DOS refusal vocabulary, where 76 of 91 reasons share one category). They are independently shippable and neither blocks the other.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room Go, no prompt text or bytes copied. fak's categories are seeded from fak's own existing prose, not from their 7 sections.

records.title: fix(selfquery): bound fak_feature_query with a default result cap so an intent-length query stops returning the whole index
records.body:
## The defect

`fak_feature_query` serves an **unbounded** result set. Three calls during the `study-repo`
pass on `agnt-gg/agnt`, phrased at three different axes, each returned the entire card index
(~1.0–1.2M characters, over the MCP response limit), so the whole capability-witness step had
to be redone with raw `Grep`. A capability lookup that cannot be called is a capability
lookup fak does not have.

**This is a boundedness bug, not a ranking bug.** The ranker is correctly wired and working
(see "What is NOT wrong" below) — it ranks all N cards and then serves all N of them.

## Root cause

`internal/selfquery/selfquery.go:254-256` @ HEAD:

```go
cards := rankCards(all, q)
if req.Limit > 0 && len(cards) > req.Limit {
    cards = cards[:req.Limit]
}
```

`Limit == 0` means *no cap*, and zero is what every default caller passes:

- `internal/gateway/mcp_index.go:260` — schema: *"0 or omitted means no cap"*
- `internal/gateway/mcp_index.go:279` — `Limit: req.Limit`, passed straight through
- `cmd/fak/feature.go:43` — `fs.Int("limit", 0, "cap the number of query cards (0 = all)")`

So the default invocation is "rank everything, return everything". Nothing downstream
truncates.

## The contributing cause: no stop-word floor

Membership in the result set is decided by a single test — `internal/selfquery/ranker.go:257`:

```go
if s > 0 { hits = append(hits, hit{c, s}) }
```

`s > 0` for a card that matched **any one** query token. And the IDF at
`internal/selfquery/ranker.go:188` is *deliberately* always positive:

```go
// BM25 IDF with the +1 inside the log so it is always >= 0: a term in
// every doc (d==n) yields a small positive weight, never negative.
idf[t] = math.Log(1 + (float64(n)-float64(d)+0.5)/(float64(d)+0.5))
```

That is a defensible BM25 choice. The consequence is that **no term can ever be scored out of
membership** — a term appearing in every single card still contributes a small positive
weight. `tokens()` (`internal/selfquery/selfquery.go:741-752`) applies no stop-word list and
no minimum token length, so every `the`/`a`/`to` in an intent-shaped query pulls in hundreds
of cards on its own:

| query | cards returned |
|---|---|
| `watermark` | 2 |
| `to` | 448 |
| `a` | 683 |
| `the` | 916 |
| a 13-token natural-language intent | **1342 cards / 1,502,804 bytes** |

Recall grows monotonically with query length, so the *more* precisely an agent phrases its
intent, the *more* of the index it gets back. That is the exact inversion an agent hits.

## What is NOT wrong (corrected during verification)

Three plausible-looking diagnoses were checked and are **false** — recording them so a fixer
does not chase them:

1. **"The ranker was never wired in."** It is wired: `internal/selfquery/selfquery.go:636`
   → `rankCards` → `rankHybrid`. Ordering is correct; the top card for a good query really is
   the right card. Only the tail is unbounded.
2. **"`ranker.go:210` (`if idf <= 0 { continue }`) is a regressed ubiquity cutoff."** It is
   mechanically dead given the `+1`-inside-the-log formula, but it reads as an ordinary
   defensive guard, not a cutoff that used to fire. Do not "restore" it — re-introducing a
   negative IDF changes scoring semantics, and the fix belongs at the result-set boundary.
3. **"Just pass `limit=-1` to opt out of the new cap."** Negatives are rejected at
   `internal/selfquery/selfquery.go:246` (*"feature query limit must be non-negative"*) and
   again at `internal/gateway/mcp_index.go:93` (`validateIndexLimit`). An explicit
   "give me everything" opt-out needs a **new** field (e.g. `all: true`), not a sentinel.

## Why it was never caught

`internal/selfquery/eval.go:48-51` grades the ranker on recall@K and MRR over the **top K**.
Those metrics are blind to how long the served tail is — the ranker scores well on exactly
the measurements that cannot see this bug.

## First checkable step

A table test in `internal/selfquery` asserting that a query of ≥8 common tokens returns at
most the default cap, and that `watermark` still returns its 2 precise hits (the cap must not
cost precision on a good query). It fails today at 1342.

Then: give `Response` a default cap in `Query` and surface an explicit opt-out field, keeping
`Limit: 0` accepted for wire compatibility.

## Scope fence

`internal/gateway/mcp_index.go:86` `capResults` is shared by **six** sibling handlers
(`:132, :146, :160, :171, :204, :240`), and "0 or omitted means no cap" is a house-wide
convention across the `fak_index_*` schemas (`:55, :219, :260, :301`). **Do not change the
shared convention.** Scope this to the feature-query path only and state in the change why
that one handler earns a default the siblings do not (its corpus is the whole card index and
its caller is an agent with a response-size limit).

## Not a duplicate of #5901

#5901 asks for set-based token containment as a **near-duplicate / ranking-quality** measure —
*which* cards should score highest. This ticket is about **how many** cards get serialized
regardless of score. #5901 could land in full and this bug persists verbatim: a better ranker
that still returns 1342 ranked cards is still over the response limit. They are independently
shippable and should be.

Study trail: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md` (dogfood note).

records.title: fix(tools): fold a paired-flag check into issue_lane_router so a bare --apply-labels-write cannot silently no-op
records.body:
## The defect

`tools/issue_lane_router.py --apply-labels-write`, passed **alone**, is silently accepted and
silently discarded. No warning, no backfill output, and the process returns the ordinary
routing payload. An operator reading "no errors, no pending changes reported" concludes the
class-label backfill ran. It never entered the branch.

Hit live during the `study-repo` AGNT pass: after `--apply-labels-write`, all eight of
#5896–#5903 were still unlabeled. They were backfilled by hand with `gh issue edit
--add-label`.

## Root cause

`tools/issue_lane_router.py:1653` @ HEAD gates the **entire** backfill block — plan, label
creation, `gh issue edit` writes, and all of its output (lines 1653-1671) — on the *arm* flag:

```python
if args.apply_labels:
    # The ONE write path. ...
    do_write = args.apply_labels_write
```

`args.apply_labels_write` (declared at `:1607`) is read **only inside** that block, at `:1657`.
There is no cross-flag validation after `args = ap.parse_args(argv)` (`:1611`), so an unpaired
write flag falls through to the plain report path at `:1673-1681`.

The three states, precisely:

| invocation | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `--apply-labels` | arm + **dry-run** plan: prints the add/remove diff, writes nothing |
| `--apply-labels --apply-labels-write` | the only combination that writes |
| `--apply-labels-write` alone | **never enters the branch**; flag discarded; no warning |

## This is a known trap, documented instead of fixed

`.github/workflows/issue-lane-router.yml:18-20` already carries a hand-written warning:

```
#   2. The write needs BOTH flags: `--apply-labels --apply-labels-write`.
#      `--apply-labels-write` ALONE is a silent no-op (the write branch is gated on
#      `if args.apply_labels:`).
```

A comment in a sibling workflow file is not reachable by the operator typing the command. The
help text at `:1608` also only *hints* ("with `--apply-labels`, actually WRITE…"); nothing
enforces it. `docs/work-class-axis.md:81-82` and `internal/issuehygiene/issuehygiene.go:417`
both print the correct two-flag remedy, so the paired form is unambiguously the intended
contract — it is just not defended in argparse.

## The cure — error, do not imply

One line after `args = ap.parse_args(argv)` (`:1611`):

```python
if args.apply_labels_write and not args.apply_labels:
    ap.error("--apply-labels-write requires --apply-labels")
```

**Choose `ap.error()` over having the write flag imply the arm flag.** The module docstring
(`:18-23`) promises the tool is read-only by default and writes to GitHub only under an
explicit operator-gated flag. Implying would silently convert a previously inert invocation
into a live GitHub write — trading a confusing no-op for an unexpected mutation. Refusing the
unpaired flag preserves the read-only-by-default contract.

(The parser variable is `ap`, not `parser`.)

## First checkable step

An offline case in `tools/issue_lane_router_test.py` — already in
`internal/pythongate/baseline.go`, so extending it lands where a **new** `tools/*_test.py`
could not:

```python
main(["--issues", tmp, "--apply-labels-write", "--json"])
```

Assert the payload carries no `label_backfill` and no `changes` key today, then flip the
assertion to the `SystemExit(2)` argparse raises after the fix. Prefer this over a CLI repro:
`collect()` shells out to `dos doctor` and git, so the in-process call is the deterministic
witness.

## Fold into the same change

- `.github/workflows/issue-lane-router.yml:18-20` — the warning is accurate **today** and
  becomes stale the moment the guard lands. Update it in the same commit.
- `tools/issue_lane_router.py:1608` help string — restate the requirement as enforced, not
  advisory.

## Scope fence

Argparse validation plus the two doc touch-ups. **Do not** touch the routing/classification
logic, the backfill planner, or the other gated flags. Also worth noting but out of scope:
the backfill branch `return`s at `:1671`, so `--apply-labels` *suppresses* the normal routing
payload entirely — a separate ergonomics question, not this bug.

One thing that is **not** the gap: documentation. The `--apply-labels` help at `:1605-1606`
already says *"Add --apply-labels-write to actually commit the writes."* The contract is
written down in three places and enforced in none.

Found during: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md`.

records.title: fix(gitgate): fold heredoc-body and backtick-span awareness into the shell lexer so prose about the trunk rules is not refused
records.body:
## The defect

Writing a file whose **text** documents the trunk-discipline rules is refused as if the rules
were being violated. Reproduced live on the current trunk during the `study-repo` AGNT pass: a
Bash call whose only effect was writing a markdown file into the session scratchpad — prose
quoting this repo's own rules, including a markdown code span around a force-push invocation —
was refused with:

```
NEVER_AMEND_SHARED: shared-history rewrite refused: never amend, rebase, or force-push on the
shared trunk. Make a new path-scoped commit (`git commit -- <paths>`, or `fak commit --path
<path>`), or fetch and merge the trunk in place. force-push refused: re-run `git push` WITHOUT
--force/-f. Constraint: Bash (POLICY_BLOCK/RETRYABLE)
```

No such operation was in flight. The refusal is **unappealable by rewording**, because the
payload's whole subject *is* the forbidden verb. Every agent writing a runbook, a doc, an
issue body, a commit-message file, or a bug report about these rules hits it.

## Root cause — gitgate, not the adjudicator

The refusal string is byte-identical to `internal/gitgate/gitgate.go:113`
(`neverAmendSharedLaw`) plus the hazard row at `:121`
(`{sub: "push", long: "--force", short: 'f', …}`). It is authored nowhere else.

`internal/gitgate/gitgate.go:579` `(*GitGate).classify` opens with:

```go
for _, src := range unwrapShellSources(cmd) {
    for _, seg := range tokenizeSegments(src) {
        if argv := gitArgv(seg); argv != nil {
```

Two independent paths turn payload text into a "recovered command":

1. **Backtick spans (the load-bearing one).** `commandSubstitutions`
   (`internal/gitgate/gitgate.go:1259`, backtick branch `:1290`), reached from
   `unwrapShellSources` (`:1225`), extracts backtick bodies from the **whole** command string
   *before* segmentation. An ordinary markdown code span in the payload is handed to the
   hazard table as a live command substitution.
2. **Heredoc bodies (secondary).** `tokenizeSegments` (`:1155`) has no heredoc concept —
   `grep '<<' internal/gitgate/*.go` returns nothing. `<` and `>` are treated as plain
   whitespace (`:1187`) and `\n` as a segment separator (`:1189`), so `<<` vanishes and every
   body line is lexed as its own shell command. This holds even under a quoted delimiter.

The recovered segment then reaches `gitArgv` (`:918`) → `inspectGitArgs` (`:617`) → the hazard
row → deny.

The package's own stated invariant covers the case next door but not this one
(`gitgate.go:1150-1154`): quote-stripping *"is what keeps a flag mentioned INSIDE a quoted
operand … from being read as a flag"*. True for quoted operands; silently false for heredoc
bodies and for backticked prose.

**Not `internal/adjudicator/reversibility.go:435`.** That classifier already builds a
quote-blanked `payloadScanView` (`reversibility.go:239-247`) so a trigger inside a quoted
argument is not a live token, and it never emits `NEVER_AMEND_SHARED` (no amend/force-push
family exists there).

## The cure already exists in-repo — gitgate just never received it

`internal/adjudicator/heredoc_inert.go:39` `stripInertHeredocBodies` solves exactly this, and
its doc comment names this exact failure. It is wired into `rce_pipe.go:160` and
`device_op.go:237`. gitgate is a separate rung and never got it.

Fix at the **head of `(*GitGate).classify` (`internal/gitgate/gitgate.go:579`), before the
`unwrapShellSources` loop** — subtract the inert body from the string, so both the
substitution scan and the tokenizer see a payload-free command. This is deliberately *not* a
`tokenizeSegments` change: the backtick path runs upstream of segmentation, so a tokenizer-only
fix leaves the dominant half of the bug standing.

## First checkable step

A table case in `internal/gitgate/gitgate_test.go` asserting `New().Classify(cmd)` returns
`ok == false` for a heredoc-writing command whose **body** contains a backticked force-push
span and a body line beginning with a git invocation.

**The fixture must use a backticked span or a body line that _starts_ with a git program
token.** Ordinary prose ("never run git push --force on the trunk") does **not** trip
`gitArgv` (`:918`) today, because it requires `isGitProgram` at the first non-env token — a
prose-only probe is a vacuous green.

Keep the existing positives green: a real force-push, and every laundering case
`gitgate_launder_test.go` pins (`bash -c`, `xargs`, `$(...)`, backticks **outside** a heredoc).

## Scope fences

- Do not weaken laundering coverage — a git call smuggled through `bash -c`, `$()`, a
  backtick, or `xargs` **outside** an inert body must still be refused.
- An **unquoted** heredoc delimiter does permit live `$(...)` expansion in the body, so
  blanket-dropping every body is a small real coverage loss. Prefer **defer**, never allow,
  for that case.
- The backtick half is separable and worth covering: a markdown code span in *any* unquoted
  payload position is read as a substitution, so a fix that only handles `<<` leaves
  `printf` -style writes of the same prose refused.

## Not a duplicate of #5898 — this is the load-bearing distinction

#5898 proposes a per-tool capability + **sink-argument** declaration table in
`internal/adjudicator`, seamed at `reversibility.go:435`. That design **cannot** cure this
bug: gitgate is a different rung, and it already reads only the single sink-bearing argument
(the Bash `command` string) — so argument scoping is not the miss. The defect is
*intra-argument*: the correct argument contains prose that is being lexed as shell.

#5898 cites this incident as motivating evidence under a misattributed root cause. Shipping
#5898 in full leaves this refusal intact. This ships independently — one function, one
package, one existing test file, no new abstraction.

Found during: `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-AGNT-2026-08-08.md`.

records.title: epic(puppetmaster-study): mine professorpalmer/Puppetmaster @5de5cd5 (honest-instrument discipline, passive quota harvest, relay-borrowed 401, lease write-boundary) for fak — witnessed borrows
records.body:
Umbrella for the witnessed borrows mined from **professorpalmer/Puppetmaster**, an MIT
Python supervisor that drives the agent CLIs/SDKs you already pay for.

**Source:** <https://github.com/professorpalmer/Puppetmaster>
**Pinned:** `5de5cd5858e891503a11df8303a619dcfb0a13f4` (v1.21.13, 2026-08-05)
**License:** MIT (© 2026 Cary). fak is Apache-2.0, so MIT→Apache vendoring would be
permitted with attribution — but **every child is routed INSPIRE (clean-room)**, because
the source is Python and the value is the technique, not the bytes. Each child cites its
source `path:line@5de5cd5`.

## Second pass — the first one is not re-litigated

`docs/notes/study-puppetmaster-borrow-scout-2026-07-10.md` pinned `9597e5b` (v1.18.0),
opened ~18 modules, and filed exactly one borrow (#3940, MMR redundancy suppression).
This pass deliberately mines the **v1.18.0 → v1.21.13 delta** plus the ~100 modules that
pass never opened. Everything the first pass resolved PRESENT — cache placement,
tool-offload + savings, budgeted skill injection, the egress/SSRF floor, fencing lease +
liveness, the preflight probe, mid-stream cancellation, forced-tool structured output,
multi-worker stitch — stays out of scope here and is not re-derived.

## Their worldview (reconstructed, with evidence)

- **A supervisor over vendor CLIs, not a framework for authoring an agent**
  (`docs/COMPARISON.md`). Their scarce resource is *subscription quota and money*; fak's is
  *trust and determinism*. That asymmetry predicts where they win.
- **"Agents should not share transcript history. They should share durable state."**
  (`docs/WHY.md`) — hence a WAL SQLite layer every process reads, rather than context
  passing. This is why their rate-limit knowledge survives a process boundary and fak's
  does not.
- **Their edge is mixed workloads and long horizons, explicitly not winning one hard
  implementation against a strong steered agent** (`AGENTS.md`); a swarm is a stated
  non-goal for "one coupled feature."
- **The load-bearing one:** they are single-author, they say so
  ("young and single-author (daily-driver beta)"), and they publish hard numbers with a
  `bench/` receipt per claim (`docs/CLAIMS.md`: 35.1% router savings, 40 follow-up queries
  at $0.00). A solo author who publishes numbers builds **mechanical anti-self-deception**
  into the tool: a KPI fenced at the write site so it cannot count itself, a savings report
  that debits its own overhead, a freshness probe that refuses to answer "fresh" when it
  could not afford to check, a citation verified by opening the file.

That last point is the whole thesis of this epic. fak's kernel is the part that **does not
believe the agents**. Puppetmaster's ledger is the part that **does not believe itself**.
Those are adjacent, not identical — and the second is where the witnessed gaps are.

## Children

Each is independently shippable and sized to a first checkable step. No monolith.

**Honest-instrument gaps (the thesis above)**
- freshness probes need a fifth verdict so an unaffordable or failed check cannot emit the
  reassuring answer — ABSENT-on-axis
- the savings report should debit the retrieval feature's own injection tokens — PARTIAL
  (fak's gross/marginal/net basis sweep re-prices the *savings*, never the *feature's cost*)
- mechanical source-verification of a cited `path:line` — ABSENT-on-axis
- finding-reuse keyed on working-tree bytes, fail-closed — PARTIAL (fak has the fingerprint
  idiom for KV prefixes, not for findings on a dirty checkout)

**Provider-economics plumbing**
- a durable passive rate-limit harvest ledger (the record side) — PARTIAL
- the admission predicate, carrying the rule that `Retry-After` alone must never preempt
  — PARTIAL. Complements #5926: that issue is the *policy* (sourced from an active
  usage-report probe); these two are the *substrate* (zero extra requests, cross-process).
- a relay's borrowed 401 must not sticky-deny a still-valid seat — PARTIAL

**Fleet safety**
- a displaced lease holder must suppress its own completed work at the write boundary
  — PARTIAL

## Earned dismissals (recorded, not filed)

- **Explicit-unknown / never a fabricated zero** (`puppetmaster/execution_provenance.py`) —
  **PRESENT-on-axis.** This is already a pervasive fak house rule
  (`internal/accountobs/accountobs.go:13`, `internal/assumecheck/registry.go:10`,
  `internal/answershape/oai_conformance.go:98`, `internal/balance/balance.go:140`, ~14 more).
- **Affected-test selection** (`puppetmaster/affected.py:4@5de5cd5`) — **DIVERGENT, and the
  tradeoff is real.** They *refuse* to infer which tests cover a change and require
  declarative glob rules, because they must serve a repo in any language. fak is Go-only
  and therefore owns the actual import graph including test imports
  (`cmd/fak/affected.go:1-27`), which is strictly more precise than any rule file. Adopting
  their design would trade a sound graph for a hand-maintained convention.

Full trail, including the candidate table and the fan-out coverage:
`docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-PUPPETMASTER-2026-08-08.md`.

records.title: fix(index): freshness probes need an `unknown` verdict — a check that could not run must not report `fresh` (fak devindex)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/codegraph.py:1480@5de5cd5`

Their index-staleness probe has a **fifth verdict, `unknown`**, returned whenever a bounded
scan runs out of file-count or wall-clock budget *before it has proven drift*. Only `stale`
drives a nudge or a self-heal. The probe is structurally incapable of returning the
reassuring answer for a check it could not afford to complete.

## The AXIS

A freshness probe must distinguish **"I checked and it is current"** from **"I could not
check."** Both are non-`stale`; only the first may be reported as fresh.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Puppetmaster is a supervisor over vendor CLIs whose author publishes hard benchmark numbers
with a per-claim receipt (`docs/CLAIMS.md`) while being openly single-author. Their code is
built to defend against *its own* dishonesty — a probe that says "fresh" because it timed
out would quietly corrupt the numbers they publish. fak's kernel is built to disbelieve the
*agents*; this is the adjacent discipline of a tool disbelieving *itself*.

## Witness against fak — ABSENT on-axis

Dogfooded `fak index freshness`, then read the code on the seam. fak has the capability
(several freshness gates), but no verdict for an unfinished check:

- `internal/devindex/freshness.go:74` — `CheckFreshness() []Drift` is binary. The doc at
  `:66` states "An empty slice means the index agrees with reality — the green state the
  gate exists to enforce," and `:71-73` explicitly documents that **a source it cannot read
  contributes no finding rather than an error**. An unreadable `main.go` therefore reads as
  green.
- `internal/conceptcatalog/freshness.go:108` initialises `result := FreshnessResult{Fresh: true, ...}`
  and at `:112` returns **that same value alongside the error** — the error path carries
  `Fresh: true`.
- `cmd/fak/concept.go:52` then encodes `res` to stdout **before** checking `e` at `:55`. So
  `fak concept freshness --check --json` on that path prints `{"fresh":true,...}` to stdout
  and exits 1. A consumer that parses stdout — which is what `--json` is for — reads the
  reassuring answer for a check that failed.

That third bullet is a concrete, present-tense defect, not a hypothetical.

## First checkable step

Add an `Unknown` verdict to `devindex.CheckFreshness` / `conceptcatalog.FreshnessResult`
(not-checked ≠ fresh), and fix `cmd/fak/concept.go:52` to check the error before emitting
JSON. Witness: a test that makes the generated-artifact read fail and asserts stdout does
**not** contain `"fresh":true`.

records.title: fix(accounts): a relay-borrowed 401 sticky-denies a still-valid seat — fence the 401 arm before writing durable health (fak accounts)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/failure.py:200@5de5cd5`

A 401 whose body names an **upstream-vendor** block is reclassified as a retryable
`server_error` *before* the status-code table runs, so it never reaches the
not-authenticated branch that would sticky-deny a still-valid subscription credential.

## The AXIS

Distinguishing a **relay's borrowed 401** (an intermediary passing through the upstream
vendor's refusal) from a **local-credential 401** — and doing it *before* any durable health
state is written.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Puppetmaster's whole shape is a supervisor driving vendor CLIs and relays the user already
pays for (`docs/COMPARISON.md`). Multi-key rotation across those relays is the product. A
borrowed 401 that durably marks a good key as dead does not degrade their tool, it removes
a seat the user is paying for — so the reclassification runs ahead of the status table
rather than as a special case inside it.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak has the capability (a closed `SeatHealth` vocabulary with genuinely careful fences) but
not this axis:

- `internal/accounts/orgwall.go:143` — `case status == http.StatusUnauthorized: return SeatHealthNeedsLogin`.
  Unconditional. **Zero body inspection.** The doc comment at `:122` states the intent
  outright: *"A 401 is always the credential (the `/login` case)."*
- The contrast is the point: the 403/402 arm immediately below (`:145-158`) runs two careful
  fences — `accountobs.UsageOverageRejection(h)` on headers, then a cap/reset text fence —
  before it will write a durable `org_auth_wall`. The 401 arm gets none of that, and it
  returns *first*.
- `SeatHealthNeedsLogin` is not advisory: it drives a `/login` prompt and seat exclusion.

And fak really does sit behind third-party relays — `internal/apihostprobe/apihostprobe.go:28-63`
enumerates `gateway.glama.ai`, `gen.pollinations.ai`, and Google's OpenAI-compatible
endpoint as supported hosts. A relay returning the upstream's 401 verbatim is a live
configuration, not a hypothetical one.

Distinct from the closed #1834, which was about the guard's own 3s 401 self-heal failing on
headless launch — not about *classifying* whose 401 it is.

## First checkable step

Add an upstream-vendor-block text fence to the 401 arm of
`internal/accounts/orgwall.go:143`, mirroring the existing fence-before-durable-state order
used by the 403 arm, and return a retryable/unknown state rather than `NeedsLogin` when the
body names the upstream. Witness: a table test in `internal/accounts` asserting a relay body
carrying an upstream refusal does **not** yield `SeatHealthNeedsLogin`, while a genuine
expired-token 401 still does.

records.title: epic(agent-runtime): fak-native ultracode as a harness-neutral orchestration profile
records.body:
## Outcome

Make **ultracode a fak-owned, harness-neutral orchestration profile**, not a Claude-only boolean that fak forwards. The profile should describe the desired behavior (high reasoning effort, decomposition, concurrent specialist workers, independent evidence, reconciliation, bounded stop) and compile through adapters for Claude Code, Codex, fak's own agent runtime, and future harnesses.

This is an integration epic under #3256. Reuse #3266 for the lease-gated task graph and #5025 for task-class engine selection; do not build a second scheduler or engine router.

## Research evidence (2026-08-08)

Local installed Claude Code `2.1.226` was inspected directly (`C:\Users\USER\.local\bin\claude.exe`), with the older decompiled local source checkout `C:\work\claude-code-source-code` (`2.1.88`) as a second source. The current binary shows that `ultracode` is a feature-gated settings posture, not a standalone model/API primitive:

- setting resolution is gated by `tengu_ultracode` / `tengu_ultracode_override`; managed settings and env override participate;
- enabling it raises the effective effort posture to `high` unless a stronger explicit posture wins;
- it enables Agent Teams and changes task/subagent policy and prompt affordances;
- the observable behavior is therefore a **bundle of policy + harness capabilities**, not semantics fak can preserve by relaying `{"ultracode":true}`;
- unsupported/disabled clients fall back rather than gaining portable orchestration semantics.

The older local source has Agent Teams, effort, Task/Team/SendMessage primitives but no literal `ultracode`, which is useful version-skew evidence: adapters need capability negotiation, not version-string guesses. Public Claude docs do not define `ultracode` as a stable cross-harness contract, so exact private implementation details are explicitly **not** a fak dependency.

fak today forwards the private setting in launch paths and fixed the multi-`--settings` last-wins hazard in #5510. #5016 made posture task-adaptive. Those are useful compatibility paths, but not native ownership.

## Architecture boundary

Define a canonical `OrchestrationProfile` and versioned `WorkflowPlan` in fak. Core types express intent and effects only; adapters own harness dialects. Suggested semantic axes:

- reasoning posture and planner policy;
- decomposition threshold and maximum fan-out;
- worker roles/capabilities and dependency DAG;
- concurrency, token/time/tool budgets, and cancellation;
- collision/lease requirements;
- evidence policy (self-check vs independent witness) and reconciliation strategy;
- interaction policy (attended questions vs autonomous defaults);
- fallback/degradation policy when a harness lacks a capability;
- provenance, decisions, and outcome telemetry.

The name `ultracode` can remain an operator preset/compatibility alias. It must resolve to explicit canonical fields so the system is inspectable and evolvable.

## Definition of done

- [ ] A minimal end-to-end spine accepts `--orchestration ultracode` (plus `auto|off`) and emits a versioned, explainable canonical plan before execution.
- [ ] The canonical schema contains no Claude/Codex command names or provider-specific JSON fields.
- [ ] Capability negotiation returns `native`, `emulated`, `degraded`, or `unsupported`, with machine-readable reasons; no silent fallback.
- [ ] Claude Code and Codex adapters can consume the same fixture plan and produce valid harness-specific launch/execution artifacts.
- [ ] The fak-native runtime executes one two-worker dependency graph through #3266's lease/task seam, independently witnesses the result, and reconciles it.
- [ ] Explicit operator pins beat auto routing; unsupported profiles fail closed or use the declared degradation policy.
- [ ] Traces and ledgers record requested/resolved profile, adapter, capabilities, fan-out, budgets, witness result, latency, and token/tool cost.
- [ ] A deterministic no-network conformance suite covers planning, adapter translation, cancellation, partial failure, budget exhaustion, and witness rejection.
- [ ] Documentation distinguishes Claude compatibility (`ultracode` setting) from fak-native semantics and includes a Codex example.
- [ ] A live comparative dogfood run reports outcome quality and net cost versus tuned single-agent and provider-native baselines; no efficiency claim without that witness.

## Non-goals

- Copying or depending on Anthropic private prompts/feature flags.
- Treating “spawn many agents” as success without collision control and independent evidence.
- Replacing #3266's task graph, #5025's engine router, or existing DOS/fak witness seams.

## Delivery slices

1. #5969 — Canonical profile + plan contract and conformance fixtures.
2. #5973 — Claude Code compatibility adapter with capability negotiation.
3. #5970 — Codex adapter over the same contract.
4. #5971 — Native plan/execute/witness/reconcile spine using #3266.
5. Comparative telemetry, adaptive policy, and rollback gate.

records.title: feat(quality): add a value-consumption oracle — a task-critical literal computed then discarded passes all 47 oracles
records.body:
Borrow from the **RubricRefine** study (epic filed alongside; `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-RUBRICREFINE-2026-08-08.md`).

## The axis

**Does a stated/required input actually influence the produced output — or is it computed and then discarded?**

Not "is this symbol unused" (ordinary linting, which fak already does). The question is whether a *task-critical value* lies on the path to the emitted answer.

## The source pattern

RubricRefine makes the dead intermediate an explicit check class, on both the scoring and generating sides:

- *"Ensure every task-critical numeric literal is on the computation path to the final emitted value; avoid dead intermediates that are computed but not consumed."* — `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:18` @`2c082ad`
- The scorer carries the matching rule at `prompt_3_rubric_scoring_system.txt:25` @`2c082ad`, and the numeric-consumption requirement appears again at `prompt_1_rubric_design_system.txt:58` @`2c082ad`.

It matters to them because a candidate can compute the right intermediate and still emit an answer that does not depend on it — producing a plausible final value that no longer reflects the task's inputs, with **no error raised**.

## Where fak stands — half-there, in two planes that never meet

**Plane 1 — config/runtime. fak does this well, but bespoke.** `cmd/fak/shrink_lever_wire.go:11-15,23-27` refuses a boot by name when an operator explicitly states a lever the built wire structurally cannot honor, splitting severity (explicitly-stated ⇒ REFUSAL, default-on ⇒ NOTICE). The reasoning is precisely this borrow's reasoning — `internal/gateway/shrink_lever_live.go:12-15`:

> *"All three mutate `req.Raw` and nothing else, and `req.Raw` is forwarded verbatim ONLY on that passthrough — the generic planner path rebuilds the upstream request from the decoded `req.Messages` and never reads `req.Raw` at all. So off the passthrough the levers are not merely unused, they are structurally unreachable: the bytes they edit are discarded."*

That is a dead-**value-path** argument, not an unused-variable argument. Same class elsewhere: `internal/gateway/defer_inert.go` (`DEFER_ENABLED_BUT_INERT`), `internal/cachevaluereport/inert.go:60` (`VerdictConfiguredButInert = "CONFIGURED_BUT_INERT"`), `guardvars.go:175` (`FindingShrinkLeverInertOnWire`).

But every one is a rule authored per ticket (#5493, #5538, #3621, #3649) over a **closed 3-item lever vocabulary inside one subsystem**. There is no registry pairing "declared input → witness that it reached the output", and no way to ask the question of anything the levers list does not name.

**Plane 2 — artifact judging, where this borrow lands. Nothing on the axis.** `internal/quality` is a real judging spine: an `Oracle` interface (`oracle.go:12-23`) with **47 registered oracles**. None checks value consumption. The nearest neighbours all measure something else:

- `report_omission.go:7-14` — material-omission scores *"the fraction present in the engine text"*: **substring presence**, not value path.
- `report_grounding.go:11-14` — claim-grounding *"checks the report asserts NOTHING the evidence does not back"*: the **reverse** direction (output→evidence).
- `tool_call_fidelity.go:24-28` — *"Score = passed argument checks / total argument checks"*: **schema conformance** only, no provenance, no downstream-consumption rule.

**A candidate that computes the task-critical intermediate and then emits an answer not depending on it passes all 47.**

And fak's actual named dead-code machinery is explicitly the **excluded** kind: `internal/hooks/gate_deadcode.go:9-10` scores *"an unexported top-level symbol that is defined but referenced nowhere else"* — ordinary unused-symbol linting, which this axis rules out.

## Verdict rationale

Not PRESENT: the capability-level hit ("fak detects inert things") is real but is neither general nor on the judging seam. Not ABSENT: the concept, the vocabulary (INERT / armed-but-did-nothing), and the enforcement posture all already exist in fak. Not DIVERGENT: nothing in `internal/quality` states a tradeoff against value-path checking. **PARTIAL — an enhancement to an existing seam.**

## First checkable step

Add one deterministic rubric oracle — `internal/quality/value_consumption.go` + `_test.go`, registered via `func init() { Register(...) }` next to `toolCallFidelity`, with **no edit to `oracle.go`** (the "child cohort registers more oracles against this same interface without editing this file" posture the registry already documents).

Scope the first cut to the **literal half**, checkable with no dataflow engine:

- The case declares task-critical literals in `Rubric.Required` (or a `VALUES: {...}` marker line, mirroring `instruction_following.go`'s `INSTRUCTIONS:` spec seam).
- The oracle parses the candidate's emitted program/trace text into assignment bindings plus the final emitted expression, and **FAILS when a declared literal is bound to a name that no chain of assignments reaches from the emitted final value**.
- `Score = consumed declared values / declared values`; `Pass` iff `Score >= Rubric.MinScore` (default 1).
- `Detail` names the **first** dead intermediate with its binding line, per the spine's localization contract.
- A case declaring no values passes with "nothing to consume", matching the existing no-op-case convention.

**Witness test** — the canonical failure:
```
units = 200; subtotal = units * price; print("done")
```
must fail naming `subtotal`, while the same program emitting `print(subtotal)` passes.

Generalizing plane 1's bespoke inert-lever rules into a shared registry is a **separate follow-on** and is not part of this step.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room Go, no prompt text or bytes copied.

records.title: fix(modelroute): refuse a cross-audit REFUTE grounded only in what the bundle deliberately elided
records.body:
Borrow from the **RubricRefine** study (epic filed alongside; `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-RUBRICREFINE-2026-08-08.md`).

## The axis

**A negative verdict must not be grounded in the absence of information the verifier was deliberately never given.**

This splits in two, and fak lands on opposite sides of the split:

| half | fak |
|---|---|
| bound *what the judge may consider* | **at or above the paper** |
| forbid a REFUTE grounded in *what the bundle deliberately elided* | **absent at this seam** |

## Half one — fak is ahead (recorded, not the ask)

The cross-audit envelope is a hard two-channel split (`IssueAuditTrustedRole` / `IssueAuditUntrustedRole`), the trusted channel is **byte-pinned and digest-verified** (`audit_bundle.go:831` refuses when `req.TrustedInstruction.Content != CrossAuditSystemPrompt`), and the instruction itself says *"Audit only against the supplied evidence bundle"* (`internal/modelroute/crossaudit.go:23`). `internal/assumecheck/assumecheck.go:210-213` goes further and makes admissible evidence **kind** a per-assumption declaration: *"WitnessKind is the ONLY evidence kind allowed to adjudicate this assumption. Evidence of any other kind yields OutcomeUnverifiable, never a cross-witness guess."* This is a real scope bound, not a capability-level match.

## Half two — the gap

**The bundle is deliberately incomplete, and it tells the auditor exactly what it withheld.** `internal/modelroute/audit_bundle.go:151-153`:

```go
Redactions    []IssueAuditBundleRedaction  `json:"redactions,omitempty"`
Truncations   []IssueAuditBundleTruncation `json:"truncations,omitempty"`
Omissions     []IssueAuditBundleOmission   `json:"omissions,omitempty"`
```

driven by `defaultAuditBundleMaxBlobBytes` / `MaxContentBytes` / `MaxComments` / `MaxPaths` (`:20-28`) plus credential redaction. Elision is the **normal** case, not the exception — `audit_bundle_test.go:218` (`TestIssueAuditBundleBoundedTruncationAndReviewTamperRefusal`) treats a bundle with *no* truncations and *no* omissions as a test failure.

That manifest is precisely *"information the verifier was never meant to see"*, and it is handed to the auditor inside the untrusted channel.

**Nothing stops the auditor grounding a REFUTE in it, and nothing downstream catches one.** The only post-hoc normalization is a closed-vocabulary check (`crossaudit.go:286-292`):

```go
review.Verdict = CrossAuditVerdict(strings.ToUpper(strings.TrimSpace(string(review.Verdict))))
if !review.Verdict.Valid() {
    review = IssueAuditReviewResult{Verdict: CrossAuditInconclusive, ...}
}
```

and the auditor's own citations are copied into the receipt **unresolved** (`crossaudit.go:333-337`):

```go
for _, ref := range review.EvidenceRefs {
    if ref = strings.TrimSpace(ref); ref != "" {
        refs = append(refs, EvidenceRef{Kind: "auditor", Ref: ref})
    }
}
```

A trim-and-nonempty check is the *entire* grounding of an auditor's evidence. So *"REFUTE — the diff for `internal/foo/bar.go` was truncated, so I cannot confirm the fix"* is accepted verbatim, digested into `EvidenceDigest` (`:380`), and appended to the durable ledger (`crossaudit_loop.go:458`) as a real refutation.

## Why the obvious PRESENT candidates don't cover it

fak does have genuine "absence must not become a verdict" rules — `internal/headlesslint/leftovers.go:246-248` (*"not refused (nothing proved they were not). Absence of evidence is not a zero."*), `internal/accountprobe/regdir.go:40`, `internal/modelroute/capability.go` rule 4 (missing the bar everywhere returns `UNMEASURED`, *"not T2"*).

But every one is about evidence that was **in the checker's remit and merely unknown**, and each resolves to a third blocking UNKNOWN state. None is a *scope declaration* that makes an absence **categorically illegitimate as a ground for a negative verdict**. Indeed fak's dominant posture on missing in-scope evidence is deliberately the opposite (`internal/bench/contamination.go:14` — *"INCONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE IS NEVER A PASS"*), which is correct there and is exactly why this distinct rule has to be stated separately rather than assumed.

**Note this refines a capability-level PRESENT recorded in the parent epic.** `internal/witness/settle.go:57` (*"unverifiable => ABSTAIN"*) genuinely covers the umbrella question "does 'couldn't check it' become a refusal?" — but it is the in-remit-but-unknown case. The elided-by-design case at the crossaudit seam is a different axis, and it is open.

## The source pattern

- *"Never produce a critical failure whose only basis is that something cannot be verified without execution."* — `prompt_4_evaluation.txt:64-65` @`2c082ad`
- *"Do not FAIL an item merely because the code was not executed."* — `prompt_3_rubric_scoring_system.txt:43-44` @`2c082ad`

Their verifier reads code it will never run, so *everything* dynamic is unseeable by construction. Without this rule the scorer refuses everything and the repair loop never terminates — they had to make the unseeable categorically inadmissible as grounds for failure, and decide the check on the visible call/contract text instead.

fak's bundle is bounded for cost and secret-hygiene rather than non-execution, but the structural situation is the same: **a judge that can see the outline of what it was denied, and no rule against using that outline as a reason to refuse.**

## First checkable step

Add one grounding check to the verdict normalization already at `crossaudit.go:286-292`:

- A `CrossAuditRefute` must carry **at least one** `review.EvidenceRefs` entry that resolves into evidence the bundle actually **included** (a `Blobs[].ID`, a `Closure.Commits[].ChangedPaths` entry, or an `Evidence.*` ref).
- A REFUTE citing only a `Manifest.Omissions` / `Truncations` / `Redactions` entry — or nothing resolvable at all — is rewritten to `CrossAuditInconclusive` with reason `"refutation not grounded in included bundle evidence"`.

**Witness:** a fixture reviewer that returns REFUTE citing a manifest omission; assert the receipt verdict is `INCONCLUSIVE`, so `crossaudit_loop.go:458` never appends it to the durable ledger.

Checkable in one test, **no prompt-version bump required** — the matching `CrossAuditSystemPrompt` clause telling the auditor the same rule can follow as a separate `issue-resolution-audit/v3` change. Downgrading to INCONCLUSIVE (not PASS) keeps the existing fail-safe posture intact.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room Go, no prompt text or bytes copied.

records.title: feat(accountobs): persist a passive rate-limit harvest ledger — the observer seam feeds a one-shot latch, so no quota fact outlives the process (fak accountobs)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/rate_limit_state.py:379@5de5cd5` (`record_from_headers`), schema at `:38`, coalescing upsert at `:223`

Every provider response is passed through a **best-effort harvest** that parses
`x-ratelimit-*` / `anthropic-ratelimit-*` into a durable WAL-SQLite row keyed by an
admission key. It costs **zero extra requests** — the quota is already on the response.
`record_from_headers` never raises into the hot path (`:409` swallows everything), and the
upsert **coalesces field-by-field over the prior row** (`:223`) so a response carrying only
`Retry-After` cannot erase a still-live tokens window, and a late-arriving older response
cannot clobber a newer one (`updated_at` guard at `:278`).

## The AXIS

Rate-limit knowledge **survives the process boundary** and accumulates, without spending a
single extra request to learn it.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

`docs/WHY.md` states the design law directly: *"Agents should not share transcript history.
They should share durable state."* Their users run several worker processes against one
paid subscription pool; a quota fact learned by worker A is worthless if it dies with
worker A. The header harvest is the cheapest possible way to make that fact durable, which
matters because their scarce resource is subscription quota.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak already owns the header **taxonomy** — it is the accumulator and the durability that
are missing:

- `internal/accountobs/accountobs.go` — `observedPrefixes = []string{"anthropic-ratelimit-", "x-ratelimit-"}`,
  with `Tracker` / `Observe` / `Snapshot` / `Unified()` / `Families()` / `PrometheusText()`.
  The parsing work is done and it is good.
- `cmd/fak/guard.go:895` assigns `UpstreamResponseObserver`, so the seam **is** wired at
  HEAD — but the closure at `:859-874` only calls `parkStore.RecordLongRetry(...)` and then
  latches `longRetryParked = true`. It is a **one-shot goalpark trigger**. No
  `accountobs.Tracker` is constructed anywhere in production, nothing accumulates, and
  nothing is persisted.
- `internal/agent/retry_limit.go:167` — `t := accountobs.New()` builds a **throwaway tracker
  per 429**, which is discarded immediately. Even the one production use is per-call.

Note for anyone reading the old finding: `docs/notes/2026-07-04-oauth-ratelimit-cache-read-finding.md:49`
claims `UpstreamResponseObserver` "is assigned only in a test" and that `accountobs` has
zero production callers. Re-verified against HEAD — **that is now stale**; the observer is
assigned at `cmd/fak/guard.go:895`. The accurate residual gap is narrower and is what this
issue files: the seam is wired, but only to a one-shot latch, so the `Tracker` accumulator
still has no production caller and no observation outlives the process.

## Relationship to #5926 — complementary, not duplicate

#5926 is the **policy**: preflight remaining quota and switch seats before the 429, sourced
from an *active usage-report probe*. This issue is the **substrate**: a zero-extra-request
*passive* harvest off responses fak already receives, persisted so peers share it. #5926 can
consume this; neither subsumes the other. The read-side predicate is filed separately so
each ships alone.

## First checkable step

Construct one process-level `accountobs.Tracker`, feed it from the existing
`UpstreamResponseObserver` closure at `cmd/fak/guard.go:859` **in addition to** (not instead
of) the goalpark latch, and persist a coalesced per-seat row. Witness: two sequential guard
invocations where the second reads a quota window recorded by the first — plus a test that a
`Retry-After`-only response does not erase a live tokens window.

records.title: feat(accountobs): a preemptive admission predicate over harvested remaining quota — every fak preemption today fires off a witnessed wall, never an advertised one (fak accountobs)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/rate_limit_headers.py:51@5de5cd5` (`blocking_reset_at`), consumed at `rate_limit_state.py:437` (`admit_or_raise`)

The admission predicate is a **pure function over a harvested snapshot**, and it is narrow
on purpose. Only a `remaining == 0` requests/tokens window with a **future** reset may
refuse a call. `Retry-After` is parsed and persisted for diagnostics but is *structurally
forbidden* from blocking admission. Their own comment states the reason:

> a bare 429 `Retry-After` is often **per-key**, and treating it as account-wide would
> defeat multi-key rotation.

The refusal it raises is a *recoverable* error (`:413`) carrying a fixed marker
(`rate_limit_quota_exhausted`) so downstream failover treats it as a routable failure rather
than a terminal one.

## The AXIS

**Which harvested signal is permitted to preemptively refuse a call**, on an account holding
several interchangeable credentials for the same provider. Getting this wrong does not fail
open — it fails *closed on a healthy seat*, which is worse, because it silently disables the
rotation that the multi-seat pool exists to provide.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their user pays for several subscriptions and expects the tool to use all of them
(`docs/COMPARISON.md`). A per-key `Retry-After` promoted to an account-wide block would idle
every seat because one seat was throttled — converting the product's main feature into a
liability. The narrowness is not conservatism; it is the rotation invariant expressed as a
predicate.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak rotates on **reactive** evidence and has no preemptive admission predicate over
harvested quota:

- `internal/accounts/cooldown.go` + `internal/accounts/orgwall.go` implement rotation and
  seat health *after* a rejection is observed.
- `internal/accounts/orgwall.go:141` — `case status == http.StatusTooManyRequests: return SeatHealthUsageLimited`
  is the reactive path: a 429 has already been spent.
- There is no function anywhere that takes a harvested quota snapshot and answers "should
  this seat be skipped *before* dialing," and therefore no place where the
  `Retry-After`-is-not-account-wide rule is expressed.

This is the **read side** of the substrate; the record side is filed separately under #5961.
It ships alone: a pure predicate plus a table test, inert until a caller consults it.

## Relationship to #5926

#5926 sources its preflight signal from an *active usage-report probe*. This predicate is
source-agnostic — it grades a snapshot whatever produced it — and carries the multi-seat
correctness rule that #5926 does not currently state. #5926 can consume it directly.

## First checkable step

Add a pure `func Admit(snapshot, now) (skip bool, until time.Time)` to `internal/accountobs`
(or a sibling leaf) implementing exactly the narrow rule: block only on a zero-remaining
window with a future reset; never block on `Retry-After` alone; never block on a healthy
remaining count that happens to carry a spurious `Retry-After` on a 2xx. Witness: a table
test with those three cases, including the 200-with-`Retry-After` case that must not block.

records.title: feat(agent-runtime): define portable orchestration profile and workflow-plan contract
records.body:
## Parent

Part of #5964. This is the contract-first spine; adapters and execution must depend on it rather than inventing their own meanings for “ultracode”.

## Problem

fak currently has a provider-specific boolean and several adjacent seams (work classes, launch profiles, engine routes, task graphs), but no single portable object that says what orchestration behavior was requested or resolved. Without that contract, Claude, Codex, and fak-native implementations will drift and telemetry cannot compare like with like.

## Deliverable

Add a small versioned core package for:

- `OrchestrationProfile` (requested policy);
- `HarnessCapabilities` and typed support level (`native|emulated|degraded|unsupported`);
- `WorkflowPlan` (roles, DAG, budgets, leases, witness/reconcile and interaction policies);
- `Resolution` (requested → resolved fields, defaults, overrides, degradation reasons, provenance).

Keep provider/harness dialects outside this package. `ultracode` is a named preset resolving into fields, alongside `off` and `auto`; it is not a magic execution branch.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `fak orchestration plan --profile ultracode --task <fixture> --json` emits a stable schema-versioned plan and human explanation without launching a model or worker.
- [ ] The package has no imports from Claude/Codex/CLI adapter packages and no provider-specific field names.
- [ ] Precedence is tested: explicit operator fields > declared task/work class > preset defaults > conservative base defaults.
- [ ] Capability negotiation is pure and table-tested, including missing concurrency, task messaging, cancellation, leases, and independent-witness support.
- [ ] Every degradation is explicit in JSON and text; strict mode rejects any degradation.
- [ ] Fixture corpus covers off, auto-grind, auto-rigor, forced ultracode, attended/unattended, budget caps, and unsupported harnesses.
- [ ] JSON round-trip and unknown-field/version behavior are tested so adapters can evolve independently.
- [ ] One captured CLI selfcheck proves the canonical plan can be generated offline.

## Integration constraints

Consume #3266's task/lease concepts rather than creating a second scheduler. Leave engine choice as a reference resolved by #5025. Use existing witness terminology and effects; do not encode Claude Agent Teams tool names.

records.title: feat(agent-runtime): adapt canonical ultracode plans to Codex workers
