## Parent

Part of #5964; depends on #5969. This is the portability proof: the same orchestration request must work without Claude's `ultracode` setting.

## Problem

Codex has different primitives and may not expose provider-native Agent Teams. A portable fak profile therefore needs an adapter that maps semantic intent onto Codex capabilities (or fak/DOS-launched Codex workers) without leaking Claude vocabulary into the core.

## Deliverable

Implement a Codex adapter over the canonical profile/plan. Prefer native Codex worker/subagent facilities when discoverable; otherwise use fak's controlled worker launcher and witness seams. The adapter owns prompt/tool dialect translation, while task graph, leases, budgets, and evidence remain canonical.

## Definition of done

- [ ] The exact same #5969 fixture plan used by the Claude adapter compiles for Codex with no schema mutation.
- [ ] Adapter reports native/emulated/degraded/unsupported capability per semantic axis, not one blanket “Codex supported” bit.
- [ ] Explicit model/effort/engine pins win; auto engine decisions delegate to #5025 rather than duplicating its table.
- [ ] Two independent workers execute disjoint tasks, exchange only declared artifacts, and fold through an independent witness.
- [ ] File-tree collisions are denied before launch through the existing lease/arbitration seam.
- [ ] Cancellation, worker timeout, partial failure, budget exhaustion, and orphan cleanup have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Tool names, message shapes, and prompt framing are isolated in the adapter and covered by golden fixtures.
- [ ] A live Codex dogfood witness records plan ID, worker IDs, commits/effects, witness verdict, tokens/tools, and elapsed time.
- [ ] Documentation gives one command to run the same profile through Claude, Codex, and fak-native execution and explains declared differences.

## Non-goal

Do not claim behavioral parity from argv generation alone. The proof is a checkable multi-worker effect plus independent read-back.

records.title: feat(agent-runtime): execute and independently witness a native multi-harness workflow
records.body:
## Parent

Part of #5964; builds on #5969 and the lease-gated task graph in #3266.

## Problem

Provider adapters can translate a plan, but fak-native ultracode requires an owned control loop: plan, lease, launch, supervise, gather effects, independently witness them, reconcile conflicts, and stop within budget. Existing DOS/fak primitives cover pieces; this issue composes them into one minimal runtime spine rather than adding another fleet framework.

## Minimal spine

A single command takes a canonical plan with two disjoint worker nodes and one reconcile node, executes it through the selected adapters, and emits a witnessed run record. At least one worker may be Claude and one Codex to prove model/harness modularity.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Planner emits immutable node IDs, dependencies, declared read/write effects, budgets, and witness requirements.
- [ ] Executor acquires leases before spawn and refuses colliding effects; #3266 remains the scheduling/lease authority.
- [ ] Supervisor handles start, heartbeat, timeout, cancellation, retry policy, and orphan reap with idempotent state transitions.
- [ ] Worker narration is never folded as fact: checkable effects route through the existing witness seam before reconciliation.
- [ ] Reconciler distinguishes confirmed, contradicted, missing, and conflicting effects and cannot mark the run successful with unresolved required effects.
- [ ] Crash/resume from the run ledger does not duplicate an already-confirmed effect.
- [ ] Deterministic integration tests cover happy path, collision deny, worker lie, witness rejection, timeout, partial completion, cancellation, and resume.
- [ ] One offline/selfcheck demo runs scripted workers through the real state machine.
- [ ] One live mixed-harness run produces a scrubbed artifact with plan, capability resolution, event timeline, confirmed effects, cost, and terminal verdict.
- [ ] `fak guard`/policy applies to every child tool call; adapters cannot bypass the security floor.

## Boundaries

This issue integrates #3266, #5025 and witness primitives. It does not duplicate their registries or routing tables. The first spine is intentionally two workers plus reconciliation; adaptive fan-out belongs in a measured follow-up.

records.title: feat(hooks): order the pre-commit fix list blocking-first and mark each finding's disposition (registry order is oracle-parity, not impact)
records.body:
Borrow from the **RubricRefine** study (epic filed alongside; `docs/notes/CONCEPT-STUDY-RUBRICREFINE-2026-08-08.md`).

## The axis

**When a verifier hands an agent a multi-item fix list, is that list ordered highest-impact-first — and is each item marked binding vs cosmetic?**

The axis has two halves. fak is split across them.

## Half one — binding vs advisory: PRESENT, and stronger than the source

Not a borrow. fak mechanizes what RubricRefine only exhorts (*"Treat verifier feedback as binding requirements, not optional suggestions"*, `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:4` @`2c082ad`):

- `internal/hooks/commitstamp.go:41,58-60` — `CommitLintReport` splits `Issues` (blocking, drives exit 1) from `Notes` (advisory, never touches the exit code), with `OK = len(Issues)==0`.
- `internal/hooks/hooks.go:70-77` — `Finding.Advisory` = *"visible but non-blocking in this push"*.
- `cmd/fak/hygiene.go:128-141` — partitions each gate's findings into `hard` / `advisory`, prints hard first.
- `cmd/fak/commit_poison_audit.go:335` — derives `f.Blocking = severityRank(f.Severity) >= severityRank("high")`.

## Half two — highest-impact-first ordering: the gap

**The pre-commit stack — fak's canonical multi-item fix list handed to a committing agent — is emitted in gate-registry order, and the registry says so explicitly.** `internal/hooks/hooks.go:94`:

```go
// PreCommitGates returns the pre-commit gates in the SAME order tools/githooks/pre-commit
// invoked them, with their mode/escape env vars. Order is preserved so operator output and any
// first-failure behavior match the Python path.
```

That ordering decision was made deliberately — for **oracle parity with the retired Python hook**, not for impact. Findings are then appended flat at `cmd/fak/hooks.go:414`:

```go
allFindings = append(allFindings, findings...)
if mode == "block" {
    blocked = true
    ...
```

`mode` is consulted **only to pick a stderr label** — it never marks or ranks the finding that goes into the JSON. There is no sort anywhere on the path to `emitFindingsJSON` (the one `sort.Slice` in the file, at `:651`, operates on `named`, an unrelated slice).

**And the graded magnitude fak already computes is inert.** `internal/hooks/hooks.go:70-77`:

```go
Severity int `json:"severity,omitempty"` // 0 = ungraded; DUPLICATION: copied-coverage percent (0-100)
```

`Finding.Severity` is written by **exactly one** gate (`gate_duplication.go:157`) and read by **nothing** — every remaining `.Severity` reference in the package is a comment about it. fak computes a 0–100 impact score and then throws it away.

**The blocking-before-advisory ordering that de facto holds today is an accident of registration order, not an invariant.** Soften `PUBLIC_LEAK` to warn and set `FLEET_DUP_GUARD=block`, and the advisory finding prints and serializes *first* — the agent's fix list leads with the thing that does not block.

## Why this is PARTIAL, not ABSENT

`internal/codelint/codelint.go:195` + `internal/swebench/fleet.go:304` already do the **entire** technique — errors-first ordering, cosmetic findings dropped rather than deprioritized, framed as *"fix them before continuing"*:

```go
// Summary renders findings as a compact, model-facing block: one line per finding,
// errors first. Used to feed a coding agent its own diagnostics.
```

But that is one narrow seam (one file, two severity levels, inside the SWE-bench harness fleet loop), not the general remedy path. Its existence is what makes this a PARTIAL rather than an ABSENT — and it is the in-repo template for the borrow.

Also checked and rejected as off-axis: `issuecontractrepair` has a `kindRank` and collapses to a single most-important `NextAction` per issue, but emits rows in **issue-number** order (`issuecontractrepair.go:357`) — the rank orders the summary table, never the work list.

## The source pattern

- *"Order `revision_instructions` highest-impact-first."* — `prompt_4_evaluation.txt:45` @`2c082ad`
- *"Fix every listed critical failure before making cosmetic or secondary changes."* — `prompt_5_generator_system.txt:6` @`2c082ad`

Their repair loop is budget-bounded and may stop early, so an unordered list risks spending the whole budget on cosmetics while a critical failure survives. fak's pre-commit path has the same property whenever a fix list is truncated, skimmed, or partially applied by an agent under context pressure.

## First checkable step

In `cmd/fak/hooks.go`'s gate loop, set the per-finding disposition and rank the hand-off list before it is serialized:

1. Replace `allFindings = append(allFindings, findings...)` (`:414`) with a copy that sets `f.Advisory = (mode != "block")` on each finding.
2. `sort.SliceStable(allFindings, ...)` blocking-before-advisory just before `emitFindingsJSON` — tie-break on existing gate order, then `File`, then `Line`, so the ordering stays deterministic.

**Witness:** a test that softens `PUBLIC_LEAK` to warn (`FLEET_SCRUB_GUARD=warn`) and blocks `DUPLICATION` (`FLEET_DUP_GUARD=block`) over a staged set tripping both, then asserts `-json` `findings[0]` is the DUPLICATION finding with `"advisory": false`, and the PUBLIC_LEAK finding carries `"advisory": true`.

Purely additive to the JSON (`advisory` is already `omitempty` on the type). **No gate verdict changes, exit code untouched** — this orders and marks the hand-off, it does not re-decide anything.

Wiring `Finding.Severity` into the sort as a secondary rank is a **follow-on**, not this step: only one gate populates it, so ranking on it today would be arbitrary across gates.

## License

Source is **all-rights-reserved** (no LICENSE file at the pin) ⇒ **`inspire` only**: clean-room Go, no prompt text or bytes copied.

records.title: feat(agent-runtime): adapt canonical ultracode plans to Claude Code capabilities
records.body:
## Parent

Part of #5964; depends on the canonical profile/plan contract in #5969.

## Problem

Claude Code's private `ultracode` setting is useful as a compatibility fast path, but it is feature-gated, version-skewed, and bundles effort plus Agent Teams policy. Forwarding the boolean does not prove that requested fak semantics are available, and #5510 demonstrated that naïve settings injection can erase hook settings.

## Deliverable

Implement a Claude Code adapter that probes effective capabilities and chooses one of:

1. **native compatibility** — safely merge the private setting into the one effective settings document when available and policy-allowed;
2. **explicit emulation** — compile the canonical DAG/roles into stable public Claude primitives (Task/Team/message operations) where the declared semantics can be met;
3. **degraded/unsupported** — report exactly which semantics cannot be preserved, honoring strict/fallback policy.

No Anthropic private prompt text or binary implementation detail is copied into fak.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Adapter consumes only the canonical #5969 contract and returns launch artifacts plus a typed capability report.
- [ ] Probe fixtures cover a pre-ultracode client (local `2.1.88` shape), a current feature-capable client (`2.1.226` shape), feature-disabled policy, Agent Teams disabled, and unknown future output.
- [ ] Exactly one merged `--settings` argument reaches Claude; regression test preserves guard hooks from #5510.
- [ ] Explicit effort/operator settings win according to the canonical precedence rules; adapter records what it changed.
- [ ] Native, emulated, degraded, and strict-refusal paths each have deterministic no-network tests.
- [ ] Version strings alone never select capability; probe/effective-setting evidence does.
- [ ] Dry-run output redacts paths/secrets and shows requested/resolved semantics and generated argv/settings.
- [ ] One live smoke witness (no private prompt capture) shows tasks/workers are actually available when native support is reported.

## Safety

Unknown probe output is unsupported, not optimistic. Managed settings and organization policy override local convenience settings. Cancellation and worker cleanup are mandatory capabilities for an unattended run.

records.title: fix(safesync): a displaced lease holder still writes its results — the lost-lease branch stops the heartbeat and tells nobody (fak safesync)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/worker_runtime.py:102@5de5cd5`

A worker that discovers it **lost its task lease mid-run discards its own finished
artifacts** rather than persisting them, emitting `worker.lease_lost`. The suppression
happens in the displaced worker, at the moment it would have written.

## The AXIS

Preemption safety at the **write boundary of a completed unit of work**. This is distinct
from — and strictly stronger than — a store that rejects a stale terminal status update:
the store-side check assumes the displaced writer reaches the store and that every write
path is guarded. The worker-side check needs neither assumption.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their model is durable shared state rather than shared transcripts (`docs/WHY.md`), so
several processes legitimately hold work for the same task across a reclaim. A displaced
worker that writes anyway does not merely waste effort — it publishes a result derived from
a world it no longer owns, into the exact store the successor is reading.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak has lease **detection** and correctly refuses to fight a reclaiming peer, but there is
no write-boundary suppression:

- `internal/safesync/writer_lease.go:104-108` — `ErrWriterLeaseLost` exists and is precise:
  "a Refresh on a lease this holder no longer owns."
- `internal/safesync/writer_lease.go:289-291` — on `ErrWriterLeaseLost` the heartbeat
  goroutine **simply `return`s**. The doc at `:270` confirms the intent: "A lost lease ends
  the heartbeat — the reclaiming peer must not be fought."
- That is the whole handling. The heartbeat stops, but **nothing signals the work-producing
  caller**, and nothing suppresses its output. The displaced holder keeps working and will
  still write whatever it produces.

The deference to the reclaiming peer is right. The missing half is telling the producer it
has been displaced, so it can drop its results instead of publishing them.

## First checkable step

Give `WriterLease` an observable lost-lease signal (a closed channel or a `Lost() bool` the
producer can consult) fed from the `:289` branch, and have at least one production write
path consult it before persisting. Witness: a test where a peer reclaims a lease mid-run and
the displaced holder's completed output is **not** present in the store afterwards.

records.title: feat(cachevaluereport): debit recall injection tokens in the savings report — the basis sweep reprices the numerator, never the feature cost (fak cachevaluereport)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/memory_cost_log.py:5@5de5cd5`

Every memory-injection dispatch writes one numbers-only ledger entry (record count,
estimated tokens, estimated USD), and the savings report renders it as an **explicit debit
line inside the same MEASURED block that reports the savings**. The retrieval feature pays
for itself in public.

A sibling rule at `puppetmaster/reads_log.py:31` fences the reuse counter to a frozen
allowlist of user-facing result-read kinds **at the write site**, so the savings command's
own reads and the orchestrator's internal store reads cannot inflate the headline the tool
publishes about itself.

## The AXIS

A retrieval/memory feature's **own prompt-token overhead is metered per injection and
appears as spend in the same report that claims the savings** — rather than being invisible
to the ledger.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

`docs/CLAIMS.md` publishes hard numbers with a `bench/` receipt per claim (35.1% router
savings; 40 follow-up queries at $0.00), from an author who says plainly that the project is
single-author. When you publish a savings percentage under your own name, the cost of the
thing producing the savings has to be in the denominator or the number is marketing. The
debit line is what makes their claim falsifiable.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis (and this one nearly read as PRESENT)

fak's savings accounting is genuinely sophisticated, which is exactly why the coarse read is
wrong here:

- `internal/cachevaluereport/fleet_benefit.go:113-124` computes a **basis sweep** — the fleet
  `fak_share` repriced three ways, `Gross(1.0x) ≥ Net(observed) ≥ Marginal(0.1x)` — and the
  comment states the intent: *"the Gross−Net gap is the overstatement made visible"* (#2807).
  It renders that gap explicitly at `:633`.

That is honest **re-pricing of the savings**. It is not the axis. The basis sweep varies how
the *shed tokens* are valued; it never books the **cost of running the feature** — the prompt
tokens spent injecting recalled context — as a debit against the benefit.

Second-phrasing witness to guard a false ABSENT: grepped `internal/cachevaluereport`,
`internal/recall`, and `internal/claimcheck` for `own cost` / `overhead` / `subtract` /
`amortiz` / `net_savings` — no hit books the feature's own injection cost.
`internal/recall/journal_index.go:124-185` tokenizes for the inverted index but records no
per-injection token or cost ledger.

So fak measures the numerator three ways and never measures this term of the denominator.

## First checkable step

Emit one numbers-only ledger record per recall injection (record count + estimated injected
tokens; no content), and render it as a debit row inside the existing MEASURED block in
`internal/cachevaluereport/markdown.go`. Witness: a report over a fixture where a recall
injection occurred shows a non-zero debit row and a net figure strictly below the current
gross.

records.title: feat(citeverify): mechanically verify a cited path:line against source — an out-of-range anchor is a fabrication fak cannot currently detect (fak citeverify)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/claim_conflicts.py:400@5de5cd5` (`source_verify_claim`), out-of-range check at `:433`

A worker's `path:line` citation is **machine-verified by opening that file and reading that
exact line**, returning `supports | contradicts | unknown | mixed`. The load-bearing case:

```python
if line_no < 1 or line_no > len(lines):
    statuses.add("contradicts")
```

A fabricated or out-of-range anchor is caught **mechanically**, with no model in the loop.

The asymmetry is the careful part: only an unambiguously resolved file with a **non-empty**
line that lacks the claimed symbol may be called a lie (`:454`). Every other failure mode —
an unresolvable path, a basename matching two files, a non-code extension, a dotfile or
secret-shaped name, a file over 1 MiB, a decode failure — returns `unknown`, never
`contradicts`. Resolution is fenced under `cwd` with symlink-escape and sensitive-name checks
(`:325-349`).

## The AXIS

**Adjudicating an evidence citation when the citation itself may be fabricated** — and doing
it so that ambiguity can never be mistaken for dishonesty.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their swarm stitches findings from several workers into one report the user acts on
(`docs/WHY.md`: share durable state, not transcripts). A confident finding citing a line
that does not exist is the highest-cost failure in that pipeline, and it is invisible to any
amount of rhetorical grading. So they check the file. The `unknown`-biased asymmetry is the
same instinct as their freshness probe: never emit the strong answer you did not earn.

## Witness against fak — ABSENT on-axis

Dogfooded with varied phrasing, then grepped raw:

- `internal/claimcheck/claimcheck.go` grades a claim's **rhetoric** — six net-true-value
  questions (Q1–Q6). It never opens a cited file and never binds a claim to source bytes.
- `mcp__dos__dos_citation_resolve` verifies **legal cases** exist in a third-party reporter.
  Different domain entirely; it does not resolve a code anchor.
- Raw grep across `internal/` and `cmd/` for `path:line` / `cited line` / `verify.*citation`
  / `anchor.*resolve` returns only *parsers and matchers*, never a verifier:
  `internal/codelint/packs.go:229` parses POSIX/Windows compiler diagnostic formats;
  `internal/dispatchaudit/signatures.go:131` matches a ripgrep-style prefix to detect a
  worker echoing repo files. Neither opens the cited file to check the anchor.

fak generates `path:line` citations constantly — in dispatch audits, in findings, in issue
bodies (including this one) — and has no mechanical way to catch a fabricated one. This is
also the gap behind the existing operational note that citation lanes cannot verify their
own links.

## First checkable step

A pure `internal/citeverify` leaf: `Verify(claim string, evidence []string, root string) Status`
implementing exactly the asymmetry above — out-of-range line ⇒ `contradicts`; ambiguous
basename, unresolvable path, oversized/binary/sensitive file ⇒ `unknown`; resolved non-empty
line lacking every claimed symbol ⇒ `contradicts`. Witness: a table test whose out-of-range
case returns `contradicts` and whose two-files-match-basename case returns `unknown`.

records.title: feat(claimcheck): key finding reuse on working-tree bytes and fail closed — an uncommitted edit must invalidate a reused finding (fak claimcheck)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/validation.py:297@5de5cd5` (`compute_validation_fingerprint`)

Reuse of a completed finding is keyed on a fingerprint binding **four** inputs: the `HEAD`
sha (or the literal `"uncommitted"`), a per-scoped-path sha256 of the **working-tree bytes**
— dirty and untracked included, not committed content — the rules digest, and the evaluator
digest. Statuses are `fresh | reused | stale | superseded`, and only
`REUSABLE_VALIDATION_STATUSES = {"fresh", "reused"}` may be reused.

`strict=True` raises `ValidationFingerprintError` when any input is incomplete — the
fingerprint **fails closed** rather than producing a key that under-specifies what it
covers.

## The AXIS

What a *"this finding is still valid, reuse it"* key must bind **so the reuse decision is
honest on a dirty checkout**. Hashing committed content is the intuitive choice and it is
wrong: an edited-but-uncommitted scoped file must invalidate reuse, because that is the
state the finding was actually computed against.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their users hand work to several agent processes over a working tree that is being edited
the whole time (`docs/WHY.md` — durable shared state, not shared transcripts). A finding
reused because "HEAD didn't move" while the file underneath it did is a stale answer
presented as a current one. Same instinct as their freshness probe and their citation
verifier: refuse to assert what you did not actually check.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak already has the fingerprinted-reuse idiom, applied to a different object:

- `internal/cachemeta/sysprompt_fingerprint.go:65` — a `Combined` fingerprint is "the single
  authoritative fingerprint the reuse decision compares," with `PrefixReuse` /
  `PrefixInvalidated` verdicts (`:94`, `:97`) and `DecideReuse` at `:117`. The comment at
  `:26` even frames the scope fence in the right terms — "This changes WHAT invalidates a
  prefix." But the object is a **KV prompt-prefix**, keyed on system-prompt identity.
- `internal/bench/fanrun.go:177` reuses a prior measurement "under a matching grid
  fingerprint" — again the idiom, again a different object.
- Nothing binds a **finding** to the working-tree bytes of the paths it was computed over,
  and nothing fails closed on an incomplete key.

So this is an extension of an idiom fak already understands, not a new concept — which is
what makes it small.

## First checkable step

Add a `Fingerprint(headSHA string, scopedPaths []string, rulesDigest, evaluatorDigest string) (string, error)`
to a pure leaf, hashing **working-tree** bytes for each scoped path (untracked included) and
returning an error rather than a key when any input is missing or a path is unreadable.
Witness: a test asserting the fingerprint changes when a scoped file is edited **without
committing**, and that a missing `rulesDigest` returns an error instead of a key.

records.title: doctor mcp: resolve plugin-provided Codex servers
records.body:
## Problem

`codex mcp list/get` reports plugin-provided MCP servers such as `dos`, and Codex can initialize them, but `fak doctor mcp --server dos` returns `CONFIG_INVALID: mcp_servers.dos command not found` because the probe only reads literal `[mcp_servers.*]` entries from `config.toml`. This makes the documented startup diagnostic fail on the exact plugin MCP startup warning it should diagnose.

## Repro

1. Enable a Codex plugin whose `.mcp.json` declares `dos`.
2. Confirm `codex mcp get dos --json` returns stdio command `dos-mcp`.
3. Run `fak doctor mcp --server dos --json`.
4. Observe `CONFIG_INVALID` despite the registered, healthy server.

## Done condition

- `fak doctor mcp --server NAME` resolves a plugin-provided stdio MCP registration through Codex's effective configuration when no literal TOML table exists.
- The diagnostic remains read-only and never prints environment values.
- A test captures plugin-only resolution and the real initialize probe reaches `initialize_response: pass` (or an isolated resolver witness plus existing protocol probe coverage).
- Literal `[mcp_servers.NAME]` behavior remains unchanged.

records.title: fix(safecommit): an unparseable review verdict is filed as `unavailable` and passes — a judge that ran badly must not read as a judge that never ran (fak safecommit)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/gates.py:600@5de5cd5`

Their `ReviewVerdict` carries an **`available` flag separate from `passed`**, giving the
oracle-backed gate three states rather than two:

- the judge **never ran** (unconfigured, no credential) ⇒ gate no-op, work passes;
- the judge **ran and answered unreadably** ⇒ `available=True, passed=False` ⇒ work is
  **rejected**;
- the judge ran and answered ⇒ its verdict stands.

## The AXIS

Distinguishing **"the oracle was absent"** from **"the oracle answered unreadably."** Only
the second may block. Collapsing them in the *other* direction — treating an unreadable
answer as absence — turns every malformed judge response into a silent pass.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their gate runs against whatever vendor CLI the user has configured that day, so "no judge
today" is a normal, expected state that must not brick a laptop workflow. But an
unconfigured environment and a judge that returned garbage are different facts, and the
second one is evidence something is wrong — a solo author publishing quality numbers
(`docs/CLAIMS.md`) cannot let it read as approval.

## Witness against fak — PARTIAL on-axis

fak has the three-verdict vocabulary but collapses the two cases into the permissive one:

- `internal/modelroute` defines `ReviewPass` / `ReviewRefute` / `ReviewUnavailable` — the
  tri-state exists.
- `internal/safecommit/safecommit.go:889-890` — when the reviewer returns a verdict that is
  neither `ReviewPass` nor `ReviewRefute`, fak calls
  `unavailableReview(model, diff, fmt.Sprintf("reviewer returned verdict %q", res.Verdict))`.
  An **unparseable answer from a judge that demonstrably ran** is filed as *unavailable* —
  the same state as a judge that was never invoked.
- `unavailableReview` at `:894` constructs `Verdict: modelroute.ReviewUnavailable`, which the
  gate treats as a no-op.

So a reviewer that runs and emits malformed output currently produces a pass. The reason
string is preserved, which is good, but nothing downstream can act on the distinction because
the verdict is identical.

## First checkable step

Split the unavailable path: keep `ReviewUnavailable` for "the judge never ran" and introduce
a distinct state (or an `Available bool` alongside the verdict) for "ran, answer unusable,"
routed to refuse. Witness: a test where the reviewer returns a garbage verdict string and the
commit gate **refuses**, while a test with no reviewer configured still passes.

records.title: feat(fleetaccounts): rank plan-billed seats by nominal price, bill them at $0 — routeRank has no cost term, so a flat-rate pool orders arbitrarily (fak fleetaccounts)
records.body:
Part of #5961 (Puppetmaster study @ `5de5cd5`). **INSPIRE** — clean-room Go, MIT source, no bytes copied.

## The borrow

**Source:** `puppetmaster/model_registry.py:134@5de5cd5`

Two costs on one model spec, as two separate methods:

- `routing_cost_usd` — the model's **nominal per-MTok price**, used *only for ranking*;
- `marginal_cost_usd` — what the user is **actually billed**, which for a plan-billed
  (subscription) model is **$0**.

A plan-billed pool therefore still has a meaningful cheapest-sufficient ordering, because
the nominal price is a proxy for how much of the **finite shared pool** a call consumes,
even though every candidate costs the same out of pocket: nothing.

## The AXIS

Cheapest-sufficient selection **inside a single flat-rate plan pool** — ranked by finite
shared-pool consumption rather than by out-of-pocket dollars, which are identically zero and
therefore rank nothing.

## Why *their* users made them build it that way

Their entire product is "drive the CLIs you already pay for" (`docs/COMPARISON.md`), so the
common case is a pool where *every* option is already paid for. Ranking by real dollars
collapses to a tie and picks arbitrarily; ranking by nominal price is what actually makes
their headline 35.1% router-savings claim (`docs/CLAIMS.md`) mean anything inside a
subscription.

## Witness against fak — ABSENT on-axis

fak's fleet is overwhelmingly a subscription-seat pool — precisely the world this technique
is for — and the route ranking has **no price term at all**:

- `internal/fleetaccounts/route.go:106` — `routeRank` returns
  `(-RouteWeight, LiveSessions, ActiveSessions, Product, tag)`. `RouteWeight` is a
  hand-set weight; the other terms are load and identity. Nothing expresses what a call
  costs the pool.
- There is consequently no notion anywhere that two seats identical in out-of-pocket cost
  ($0, both plan-billed) can differ in how much finite pool capacity they burn.

Related but distinct from #5416 (three-zone device/fleet/vendor placement), which is about
*where* a call runs, not about ranking inside one flat-rate pool.

## First checkable step

Add a nominal `RoutingCostPerMTok` to the model spec, separate from any billed-cost field,
and make it a rank term in `routeRank` **below** the existing hard constraints. Witness: a
table test where two plan-billed seats with equal `RouteWeight` and equal load order by
nominal price, while the billed cost reported for the chosen call stays $0.

records.title: fix(sessiondiag): type recent Codex/fak session crash evidence and log-store pressure
records.body:
## Problem

Multiple recent Codex/fak-backed sessions on the shared Windows control point terminated or became unusable without a typed fak diagnosis. Current local evidence shows a concrete pressure signature that fak does not surface:

- Codex 0.147.0 has 43 concurrent `codex` processes.
- `~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite` is 1.67 GiB with 359,146/428,601 pages on SQLite's freelist (~1.37 GiB reclaimable), plus a ~382 MiB WAL during the observed round.
- The same structured log contains 996 `codex_app_server_client` `consumer queue is full` event drops on 2026-08-08, including bursts in active sessions, and repeated slow log INSERT warnings.
- SQLite `quick_check` is `ok`; Windows Application Error has no matching Codex/fak process fault, so corruption or a native application crash is not yet established.

The missing product behavior is an evidence-preserving, read-only diagnosis that distinguishes host pressure / Codex log-store contention / in-process event loss from a real fak child crash, instead of making operators infer a cause from a dead session.

## Definition of done

- Add a first-class Go `fak` diagnostic leaf/verb for recent Codex/fak session crashes or abrupt exits; no new Python tooling.
- Read Codex's local structured log and relevant process/store metadata read-only, with bounded queries and no requirement to stop live sessions.
- Emit stable typed findings for at least: oversized/reclaimable log store, large WAL or slow log writes, in-process consumer-queue event loss, matching explicit panic/fatal/child-exit evidence, and insufficient evidence/no fault.
- Do **not** label queue loss or store bloat as the crash root cause without temporal corroboration; report observed correlation and the missing witness explicitly.
- Human and JSON output must redact prompt/tool bodies, paths outside a safe basename, arguments, environment, tokens, and server payloads.
- Add captured fixtures covering the observed 0.147.0 pressure signature, a clean store, an explicit fak/Codex child failure, malformed/missing/unreadable DB, and secret-bearing rows.
- Add a behavior regression test that fails before the change and proves the pressure signature receives an actionable typed verdict after it.
- Document triage and safe remediation, including backup/checkpoint/compact guidance that never mutates a live Codex DB; any mutation must be a separate explicit operator-confirmed action or ready-to-run shutdown-time command.
- Capture a live read-only witness on this host and record database byte hashes before/after to prove diagnosis did not mutate the store.
- Validate with `fak validate --mine <all changed paths>` (tests under WSL per repo policy), then land one signed-off issue commit and push.

## Initial evidence / hypothesis boundary

Observed: severe freelist/WAL amplification, concurrent writers, slow INSERTs, and app-server consumer-queue drops. Not yet proved: that any one signal caused the recent session terminations. The implementation must preserve that distinction and make the next crash independently diagnosable.

## Proof artifact

A captured diagnostic report over a sanitized fixture plus a live before/after file-hash/read-only run. The report must name the typed pressure/event-loss findings while refusing an unsupported causal crash claim.

records.title: feat(commitlifecycle): default end-to-end commit, park, reclaim, land, and push queue
records.body:
## Parent context

Parent: #3871.

## Problem

The repository has the individual safety mechanisms for agent-authored work, but no single default-on lifecycle contract joins them:

- `fak commit` safely commits an explicit path set in the shared trunk.
- `fak guard` checkpoints dirty work on blocked exits and hard stops.
- `fak wip reconcile --reclaim` inventories recoverable checkpoints.
- `fak wip land` restores a selected checkpoint but intentionally does **not** commit it.
- `fak worktree worker land` serializes detached-worker diffs onto `main`.
- `fak dispatch status` reports live workers, while garden now surfaces the reclaim queue.

These are working commands, not yet one working system. A normal worker can still finish in an ambiguous state: committed locally but not pushed, parked with no durable queue item, reclaimed but not routed to a lander, or applied to the shared tree with no path-scoped commit/push continuation. Operators must know which namespace and verb to inspect next.

## Working spine

Add one typed, read-only `fak commit lifecycle` (name may vary if an existing noun is more canonical) that folds the current repository into an end-to-end queue with mutually exclusive states and one executable next action per unit:

`EDITING -> COMMIT_READY -> COMMITTED_UNPUSHED -> PARKED -> RECLAIM -> LAND_READY -> LANDED_UNPUSHED -> SHIPPED`

The spine reads existing facts; it does not invent a second checkpoint, lease, or worker registry. With no flags it is enabled and reports the current state. An explicit `--apply` pumps only mechanically safe edges through the existing verbs; ambiguous restore/commit decisions remain operator-gated.

## In scope

1. Define a typed lifecycle row keyed by issue/session/worker identity where available, with source namespace and current witness (`HEAD`, WIP ref, worker worktree, remote ancestry).
2. Fold at least the shared-tree commit path, guard checkpoint path, reclaim queue, and detached-worker landing path into one queue.
3. Emit exactly one `next_action` command for every non-terminal row; the command must use the existing safe verbs (`fak commit`, `fak wip reconcile|land`, `fak worktree worker land`, push reconciliation), never raw `git add -A` or a hand-rolled worktree.
4. Make the read-only fold default-on in the normal operator surface (`fak dispatch status` or garden tick) so parked/landing debt cannot disappear unless an operator knows the new verb.
5. Add an explicit apply mode for safe, deterministic edges only. It must refuse auto-commit when the checkpoint's intended path set/message/issue binding is absent or when the shared tree has unrelated dirt.
6. Preserve peer safety: no auto-apply into a dirty shared tree; no deletion of the only checkpoint copy; no force push; no completion claim without remote ancestry.

## Out of scope

- Replacing `fak commit`, `fak wip`, or `fak worktree worker`.
- Automatically resolving merge conflicts.
- Treating a local commit or worker narration as shipped.
- Remote checkpoint deletion policy, tracked separately in #5556.

## Done condition

A fixture covering one unit through edit, checkpoint/park, reclaim, land, path-scoped commit, and push ancestry produces the expected state transitions and executable next actions. A default operator command surfaces a parked/reclaim/land-ready row without any opt-in flag. Apply mode advances only safe edges and leaves an independently dirty peer path byte-identical.

## Witness

- Unit tests for the pure lifecycle fold and next-action rendering.
- A throwaway bare-remote end-to-end test proving `SHIPPED` only after the landed commit is reachable from the configured remote branch.
- A captured default `fak dispatch status --json` (or garden JSON) containing a parked/reclaim row and its next action.

## Acceptance gate

The end-to-end test snapshots refs, index, and unrelated working-tree bytes before apply. A refused or partially completed lifecycle tick must leave all three unchanged except for the explicitly selected unit's witnessed safe edge.

## Relationship

Parent: #3871. Builds on #5928 and #5480. Coordinates rather than duplicates #5556 and #5940.

## Lane

Prefer a new additive `internal/commitlifecycle` leaf with thin `cmd/fak` wiring; the default operator-surface integration is a second path only if needed in the same atomic issue.

## Completion standard

development

## Work estimate
Estimate: 8 points. Uncertainty: operator-supplied estimate; revise through the parent denominator when evidence changes.

## Overall completion contribution
Contribution: 8/100 points.

## Parent context
Parent objective: harden advanced fak landing/storage so crashes leave recoverable, guarded, observable work. Follow-on to #5990 and existing remote checkpoint mirror #5479.

## Problem
`fak worktree worker land` now anchors every off-branch candidate locally under `refs/fak/worker-land/*` before trunk CAS (#5990), but those refs are machine-local. If the host/disk dies after `commit-tree` and before trunk reaches the candidate, the local recovery ref and detached worktree can disappear together. records.title: feat(wiprecon): claim and resume crashed checkpoints through witnessed adoption
records.body:
## Parent context
Parent objective: harden advanced fak landing/storage so crashed sessions can be picked up without trusting narration. Complements #5990 (worker-land candidate refs), #5994 (land-ready inventory), and existing `fak wip reconcile`.

## Problem
`fak wip reconcile --reclaim` correctly classifies a crashed owner's checkpoint and prints `fak wip reclaim --session <id>`, but the operator still has to discover/run the path and no durable successor-ownership receipt proves who picked it up. Recovery can remain indefinitely actionable yet untended, or two sessions can race to reclaim the same checkpoint. The original objective requires work to be picked back up or landed after a session crash, not merely listed.

## Done condition
- Reclaim uses a compare-and-swap ownership/adoption receipt bound to checkpoint ref+SHA and successor session; exactly one successor wins.
- A default lifecycle/garden queue surfaces unowned RECLAIM checkpoints with exact argv, age/drift, remote-mirror freshness, and attempt history.
- An opt-in dispatcher may launch the reclaim command, but never auto-applies QUARANTINE and never drops a checkpoint.
- The successor materializes into an isolated worker path or explicit patch target, verifies bytes against checkpoint SHA, journals the adoption before mutation, and preserves the original ref until a witnessed trunk landing.
- Crash during reclaim is resumable from the adoption receipt; stale adoption can be taken over only through a liveness/TTL/CAS rule with an audit event.
- Tests simulate original-owner crash, two reclaimers, successor crash mid-materialization, restart/resume, successful landing, and quarantine refusal.

## Scope
`wiprecon`/`wip reclaim`, lifecycle queue integration, ownership receipt, observability, and crash-matrix tests. Existing classification semantics remain fail-safe.

## Work estimate
Estimate: 8 points. Uncertainty: operator-supplied estimate; revise through the parent denominator when evidence changes.

## Overall completion contribution
Contribution: 8/16 points.

## Completion standard
development

records.title: Stale tools/.bin/fak.exe predates the changed: core-lock witness verb, so a correct claim abstains
records.body:
## What happens

`fak commit --core-lock-maintenance-witness changed:<path>` is refused with
`CORE_SELF_MODIFY ... resolved abstain` when run through the checked-in
`tools/.bin/fak.exe`, even for a claim that is exactly correct.

The binary predates the `changed:` verb. `internal/corelockgate/changedwitness.go`
introduced it; the checked-in binary was built before that. An unrecognized claim
kind falls through to the shared resolver, whose grammar has no `changed:` — and an
unrecognized kind ABSTAINS. Abstain is not clearance, so the lock stays closed.

## Why it misdirects

`CoreLockRemedyCommit` in current source is two sentences; the second one names the
cure:

> A file this change ADDS is not tracked yet, so `committed:<path>` is refuted for
> it — name it with `changed:<path>`, which confirms only for a path this very
> commit carries.

The stale binary prints only the first sentence. So a maintainer adding a
core-locked file is told to supply a witness, is given no verb that can work for an
added file, and the one verb that would work is both absent from the binary and
absent from its remedy text. Verified: `grep -c 'name it with changed:<path>'`
returns 0 against `tools/.bin/fak.exe` and 2 against a binary built from current
source.

## Impact

Any worker that shells out to `tools/.bin/fak.exe` (the in-repo default) cannot land
a commit that ADDS a file under a hard-self core-lock path. The refusal looks like a
bad claim rather than a stale tool, which is the expensive part — the maintainer
re-spells the claim instead of rebuilding.

Hit while landing #5933, which adds two files under `internal/corelocks/`.

## Done condition

Either the checked-in `tools/.bin/fak.exe` is rebuilt from a source revision that
contains the `changed:` verb, or the wrapper refuses/warns when the binary's
core-lock grammar is older than `internal/corelockgate`, so the failure names
staleness instead of presenting as an abstaining witness. A regression test should
pin that a `changed:<path>` claim naming a path in the changed set resolves
CONFIRMED through whatever binary the repo tells workers to use.

records.title: fak commit's COMMITTED_RED build gate fails open on archive timeout and the skip is absent from --json
records.body:
## What happens

`fak commit`'s `COMMITTED_RED` prospective-tree compile gate fails **open** when its
archive step times out. Observed on stderr during a real commit:

```
fak commit: build-check skipped: archive timed out after 2m0s (failing open): context deadline exceeded
```

The commit then proceeded and landed. No `--no-build-check` was passed.

## Why it matters

`COMMITTED_RED` is the gate the headless-worker contract leans on — the checkpoint
bar is "it COMPILES, and `fak commit`'s gate enforces this; never pass
`--no-build-check`". A worker is told the gate is what makes a checkpoint safe. But
the gate is skippable without the operator asking for it: any condition that makes
the archive slow (a large tree, a loaded host, several fleet workers committing at
once) silently converts the enforcing gate into no gate, and the only signal is one
stderr line that no exit code reflects. The commit is graded A.

The timeout is also more likely exactly when the risk is highest: a busy shared
trunk with many concurrent workers is both the slow case and the case where a red
commit costs the most.

## Impact

A commit that would red the trunk can land while the tooling reports the gate ran.
Workers that parse `--json` see no indication at all — the skip is stderr-only and
absent from the result object.

Seen while landing #5933.

## Done condition

A timed-out build check is not reported as a passed one. Concretely: the `--json`
result carries the build-check outcome as a distinct state (`passed` /
`skipped-timeout` / `failed`) rather than being invisible, and a timeout either
refuses the commit or requires the caller to have opted into fail-open explicitly.
Whichever is chosen, a regression test should pin that a timed-out gate cannot
produce a result indistinguishable from a gate that ran and passed.

records.title: docs(wip): reconcile --reclaim help still steers to 'fak wip land', not the adopt argv the queue prints
records.body:
## What

`fak wip reconcile --reclaim` now prints, per row, the exact argv that advances it —
`fak wip reconcile adopt <session>` for an unclaimed row, `... resume <session>` for one
this session already holds, and nothing for a row a live peer holds (#5998, landed in
196d597bd + 0a1103020).

The verb's own help text in `cmd/fak/wip.go` (~line 197) still says:

> RECLAIM decays into QUARANTINE as the tree moves, so the drift column is that
> verdict's remaining life — act on the top row first, with `fak wip land <session>`.

So the same command gives an operator two different instructions for the same row: the
help says `wip land`, the queue underneath says `wip reconcile adopt`.

## Why it matters

`wip land` is a real verb, so this misdirects rather than errors — which is worse. An
operator following the help lands the delta with **no adoption receipt**, which is exactly
the race #5998 closed: two successors reading one queue can both act on the same
checkpoint because neither took a witnessed claim first. The help text is the surface that
tells them it's fine to do that.

## Fix

Update the `--reclaim` paragraph to name `fak wip reconcile adopt <session>` (and mention

records.title: fix(cmd): runTestQuality call in prepush_build.go passes a repo root positionally and reds trunk
records.body:
`cmd/fak/prepush_build.go:277` calls `runTestQuality(r, io.Discard, stderr, nil)`, but the function is `func runTestQuality(stdout, stderr io.Writer, argv []string) int` (`cmd/fak/testquality.go:36`). The repo root was passed as a positional first argument to a function that takes its root through a `--root` flag in `argv`.

`cmd/fak` therefore does not compile at trunk HEAD:

```
$ go vet ./cmd/fak/
vet: cmd/fak/prepush_build.go:277:53: too many arguments in call to runTestQuality
	have (string, io.Writer, io.Writer, nil)
	want (io.Writer, io.Writer, []string)
```

Witnessed against a pristine `git archive HEAD` extraction at `51731125e9`, so this is committed trunk state and not a peer's uncommitted work-in-progress. The advisory test-quality call arrived with #5936 (`29f20b6315` / `2318bc270b`).

Because `cmd/fak` is the package `fak hooks pre-push` itself lives in, this red also disarms the very gate that is supposed to catch a red trunk.

### Done-condition

- `go vet ./cmd/fak/` is clean at HEAD.
- The call still scans the resolved repo root `r` rather than falling back to the process CWD, i.e. the root travels as `[]string{"--root", r}`.
- The call stays advisory: a non-zero `tqCode` still only prints the WARNING and never changes the push decision.

records.title: push: two untiered leaves already on trunk (citeverify, usagepreflight) wedge TIER_DECLARED for every pusher
records.body:
`fak sync push` refuses with `TIER_DECLARED (blocked): architest tier table drift would
red the trunk`, and the drift is **already published on `origin/main`** — so every agent
that tries to push is blocked by two leaves that neither they nor their commit touch.

## Evidence

```
$ fak sync push
[REFUSED] not pushed (PUSH_ERROR): TIER_DECLARED (blocked): architest tier table drift would red the trunk.

$ fak hygiene
TIER_DECLARED (advisory; outside this push): 2 finding(s):
  internal/citeverify/:     ... has no tier declaration ... This push does not touch that leaf; its owner must declare it.
  internal/usagepreflight/: ... has no tier declaration ... This push does not touch that leaf; its owner must declare it.
```

Both leaves are already ancestors of `origin/main`:

| leaf | introduced by | on origin |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/usagepreflight` | `3a06969191 feat(preflight): implement remaining-quota admission (#5926) (fak usagepreflight)` | yes |
| `internal/citeverify` | `ebb98675e2 feat(citeverify): add mechanical source-line verification (#5976) (fak citeverify)` | yes |

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a drive-by fix

`gateTierDeclaredTree` in `internal/hooks/gate_tierdeclared.go` is a **whole-tree** gate:
it flags every `internal/<leaf>` holding a tracked non-test `.go` file that is missing
from the `tier` map in `internal/architest/architest_test.go`. It does not scope to the
paths being pushed. So the refusal is correct about the trunk being red, but it is served
to whoever pushes next rather than to the leaf's owner.

`fak hygiene` already knows this and says so — it renders these two as
`advisory; outside this push` with `its owner must declare it`. The push path treats the
same finding as blocking. That asymmetry is the actionable part: a finding the gate itself
labels "outside this push" should not wedge an unrelated pusher.

Declaring the tiers for someone else is not a safe drive-by: the tier a leaf lands in
binds its `(fak <leaf>)` ship-stamp to an architectural layer, and the gate's own guidance
is to pick "the LOWEST tier whose role it fits" — a judgment call belonging to the author.

## Done when

- [ ] `internal/citeverify` and `internal/usagepreflight` have rows in the `tier` map in
      `internal/architest/architest_test.go` (or `fak new-leaf <leaf> --tier <tier>`),
      chosen by their authors.
- [ ] `fak hygiene` reports no `TIER_DECLARED` findings.
- [ ] Decide the policy question: should the push gate demote a `TIER_DECLARED` finding
      the gate has already classified as `outside this push` to advisory, so pre-existing
      published drift cannot wedge an unrelated pusher? (If yes, a regression test where
      a tree carries an untiered leaf the push does not touch, and the push proceeds.)

Found while shipping #5998 (`0a11030204`), whose paths are `cmd/fak/` and
`internal/commitlifecycle/` — both already declared. That commit reached `origin/main`
only because a peer's later push carried it; the refusal never cleared on its own.

records.title: epic(arch): build the serving/guard kernel separately from development tooling
records.body:
# Epic: make the serving/guard kernel independently buildable from repository-development tooling

## Problem

The released `cmd/fak` package currently owns both product runtime and development control-plane commands. The existing `fak dev` namespace is a discoverability boundary only: it routes back into the same `main` switch, while `go list -deps ./cmd/fak` currently reaches 703 packages, including 456 `internal/*` packages. A production image that needs the serving/security checkpoint (`serve`, `guard`, policy/preflight, and their runtime support) therefore compiles and carries repository mutation, issue orchestration, CI, fleet, benchmark, and maintainer-only packages.

Issue #5465 documented this coupling and chose to explain the one-binary shape. This epic deliberately changes that decision: development commands and their packages should be separately buildable, and the core serving/guard artifact must not link them.

## Product boundary

- **Core/runtime artifact (`fak`)**: the agent-kernel product surface required to serve models, guard/adjudicate tool calls, evaluate policy/preflight, run the supported agent/runtime entry points, and inspect those runtime effects.
- **Development artifact (`fak-dev`)**: commands whose subject is developing, testing, releasing, benchmarking, operating the shared fak repository, dispatching contributors/workers, managing GitHub work, or maintaining lab/fleet infrastructure.
- **Shared libraries**: narrow, side-effect-free contracts genuinely required by both artifacts. Shared must not become a dumping ground that lets dev packages leak back into the runtime graph.

The exact verb inventory is an acceptance artifact of the first child, not an implicit consequence of which source file happens to contain a case today.

## Architecture direction

1. Establish a machine-readable command ownership inventory (`runtime`, `dev`, or explicitly justified `shared`) and gate complete classification.
2. Extract dispatch/bootstrap seams so two `main` packages can be built without source duplication or importing a `main` package.
3. Move development dispatch and its package graph behind `cmd/fak-dev`; remove it from `cmd/fak` linkage.
4. Enforce import direction and a measured runtime dependency budget in architecture tests.
5. Publish/install the artifacts independently, with an explicit compatibility and migration policy for legacy `fak dev ...` invocations.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `go build ./cmd/fak` and `go build ./cmd/fak-dev` succeed independently from a clean committed tip.
- [ ] `fak help` and runtime dispatch expose only the approved runtime inventory; invoking a dev-only verb through `fak` cannot reach dev implementation code.
- [ ] `fak-dev help` exposes the approved development inventory and representative repository workflows retain behavior and exit-code compatibility.
- [ ] A source/import-graph witness proves `cmd/fak` has no dependency path to every package classified dev-only; the check fails on an intentional forbidden import.
- [ ] Core packages do not import dev packages. Any shared package is named in the ownership manifest with a rationale and has no repository/GitHub/fleet side effects unless the runtime contract explicitly requires them.
- [ ] Release and install automation can build/package the runtime artifact without building or shipping `fak-dev`; maintainer installation of both artifacts remains documented and tested.
- [ ] Compatibility behavior for `fak dev ...` is explicit, time-bounded, and tested (thin handoff when `fak-dev` is installed or a clear migration error; never linked dev implementations).
- [ ] Baseline and final witnesses record runtime package count, binary size, and clean build time with provenance. These are boundary witnesses, not an unmeasured performance claim.
- [ ] Runtime smoke tests cover at least `serve`/`guard` or their no-hardware self-check seams, policy/preflight, and help; dev smoke tests cover help plus representative read-only and mutating repository commands in isolated fixtures.
- [ ] README, INSTALL, CLI reference, release docs, and architectural rationale describe the two artifacts and do not claim one binary/one surface.
- [ ] Every child issue is closed by a diff-witnessed commit and the final epic audit maps each checkbox above to authoritative current-state evidence.

## Non-goals

- Renaming arbitrary internal packages without reducing the runtime dependency graph.
- Hiding dev commands only in help while continuing to link them into `fak`.
- Build tags that make the default source graph ambiguous; two explicit build targets are preferred.
- Removing developer workflows or weakening their guards.
- Claiming latency or size gains without a net-true witness.

## Delivery order

1. Inventory, ownership contract, and failing architecture witness.
2. Minimal two-binary end-to-end spine.
3. Dev dispatch/package migration and runtime graph ratchet.
4. Compatibility shim and command parity.
5. Release/install split and documentation.
6. Final graph/runtime/release audit.

## Prior evidence and supersession

- #5465 correctly observed that repository-development verbs were bundled into the public binary and documented the then-current one-binary decision.
- This epic supersedes that architectural choice while preserving the useful `fak dev` taxonomy as input to the ownership inventory.


## Child issues

- [ ] #6020 — exhaustive command ownership inventory, baseline, and graph leak witness
- [ ] #6021 — minimal independently buildable `fak-dev` end-to-end spine
- [ ] #6022 — migrate dev-only dispatch/packages and ratchet the runtime graph
- [ ] #6023 — thin, tested compatibility handoff for legacy `fak dev ...`
- [ ] #6024 — independent CI/release/install/container artifacts
- [ ] #6025 — two-artifact architecture and user/developer documentation
- [ ] #6026 — independent final audit against this epic DoD

Dependency order: #6020 → #6021 → #6022 → #6023/#6024 → #6025 → #6026.

records.title: refactor(cmd): migrate dev-only dispatch and enforce a runtime dependency ratchet
records.body:
## Problem

A second binary is not meaningful while dev implementations remain reachable from `cmd/fak`. The classified dev command families and their package dependencies must move behind `fak-dev`, with a ratchet that prevents recurrence.

records.title: fix(accounts): a corrupt cooldown store silently disables the whole cooldown gate
records.body:
## Problem

A **corrupt** `account-cooldown.json` silently disables the entire account-cooldown
gate fleet-wide. Every seat resolution and launch then runs cooldown-blind and
re-offers capped accounts, which is the exact failure this store exists to prevent.

`loadCooldownStoreFailOpen` (`cmd/fak/accounts_cooldown.go:56`) returns **nil** on any
read/parse error, and that nil is the "cooldown-blind fold":

- `cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go:354` — `reg.ServeAt(name, loadCooldownStoreFailOpen(), time.Now())`
- `cmd/fak/accounts.go:667` — `accountsResolveServe(..., loadCooldownStoreFailOpen(), ...)`

Fail-open is deliberate (#4675: bad cooldown state must never block a resolve, launch
or preflight) and that part is right. The defect is that it is **silent** — nothing on
any of these paths tells the operator the gate is off. A one-byte corruption
downgrades a fleet safety gate to a no-op with no signal at all, and the fleet keeps
dispatching into walls until somebody happens to run `fak accounts cooldown`.

## Witness

Observed on a maintainer box 2026-08-09. The store was a complete, valid JSON object
of 3611 bytes followed by a stray `}\n` (3613 bytes total):

```
$ fak accounts cooldown
fak accounts cooldown: cooldown store unreadable (<local>/Fleet/account-cooldown.json):
  invalid character '}' after top-level value
```

`json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode` consumes a valid `{schema, entries}` dict ending at
byte 3611 of 3613; the remaining bytes are exactly `\n}`. The 11 entries parsed
cleanly once the stray brace was dropped.

While in that state `fak accounts cooldown` errored, but **`fak accounts launch` and
seat resolution did not warn at all** — they silently took the nil-store branch.

Provenance of the corruption is NOT established and is a second question:
`CooldownStore.Save` (`internal/accounts/cooldown.go:300`) marshals with
`json.MarshalIndent` and writes temp-then-`os.Rename`, so it cannot emit a trailing
brace, and it is the only writer of this path in the tree. An external or crashed
writer is the likely source. Filing the blindness, not the provenance.

## Definition of done

- [ ] An unreadable/corrupt cooldown store emits a visible operator warning on the
      resolve and launch paths, not only in the `cooldown`/`status` verbs.
- [ ] The nil-store (cooldown-blind) fold remains fail-open — no resolve, launch or
      preflight may be blocked by bad cooldown state (#4675 stays true).
- [ ] A test seeds a corrupt store and asserts both halves at once: the launch/resolve
      path still succeeds AND the warning naming the store is emitted.
- [ ] Consider quarantining the corrupt file (rename aside) so the next `Save` restores
      a working store instead of leaving the gate off indefinitely — or explain in a
      comment why silent overwrite is preferred.

## Witness for the fix

A test with a deliberately corrupt fixture, asserting the warning text and the
non-blocking exit status on the launch path.

## Notes

Severity is "safety gate silently off", not "crash": the blast radius is every spawn
made while the store is unreadable, each of which may be pinned to a capped account.

## Parent ref

Standalone safety-gate repair tracked by #6027; no parent epic is required.

## Current state

`loadCooldownStoreFailOpen` converts every cooldown-store read or parse failure to a nil store. Resolve and launch remain available, but neither path emits an operator-visible warning, so a corrupt store disables cooldown filtering without a signal.

## Why now

This is priority/P1 because the live fleet is actively rotating capped seats. Silent loss of cooldown filtering causes repeated launches against unavailable accounts and directly reduces the 12-hour issue-resolution campaign's productive capacity.

## Working spine

Seed a corrupt cooldown store, execute the real account resolve and launch seams, preserve their successful fail-open result, and capture one warning that names the unreadable store.

## Work unit

One coherent accounts-lane logic fix plus its behavior witness; do not split warning emission and fail-open preservation across commits.

## Expected steps

4

## Assumptions

- The fail-open requirement from #4675 remains authoritative.
- Warning output can be injected or captured without changing the public account-selection result.
- Corruption provenance is not required to close this issue.

## Confusion risks

- Do not turn corruption into a launch refusal.
- Do not claim the unknown writer of the trailing brace has been identified.
- Do not test only `accounts cooldown`; the witness must drive resolve or launch.

## Coordination

Own only the accounts lane and explicitly named account command files. Preserve peer changes in the shared trunk and commit only the issue's paths.

## Trigger

Dispatch when #6027 is open, priority/P1, and the accounts lane is unleased.

## Batch policy

One issue and one commit for key `accounts-corrupt-cooldown-warning`; dedupe against an existing #6027 worker or closing commit before every rerun.

## In scope

- Operator-visible warning on real account resolve and launch paths when cooldown state is unreadable.
- Continued successful fail-open behavior.
- A corrupt-store behavior test asserting both properties.
- Optional quarantine only if it is needed for safe recovery and is covered by the same witness.

## Out of scope

- Discovering or fixing the unidentified external writer that appended the stray brace.
- Changing cooldown policy, reset times, account routing, or provider retry behavior.
- Blocking resolve, launch, or preflight because cooldown state is corrupt.

## Done condition

A corrupt cooldown fixture leaves resolve and launch successful while producing a captured warning naming the store, with the regression test committed and pushed in the same #6027 change.

## Acceptance gate

`fak validate --mine cmd/fak/accounts_cooldown.go --mine cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go --mine cmd/fak/accounts.go` plus the focused corrupt-store test under WSL/CI; the exact path list may be narrowed to the files actually changed.

## Closure binding

The closing commit subject contains `#6027` and the matching `(fak accounts)` leaf trailer; GitHub closure is accepted only after the commit diff and test witness are independently read back.

## Lane

accounts

## Likely files

- `cmd/fak/accounts_cooldown.go`
- `cmd/fak/accounts_launch.go`
- `cmd/fak/accounts.go`
- focused `_test.go` siblings in `cmd/fak/`


## Model tier

JUDGE — this safety-gate change must preserve fail-open semantics while independently proving an operator-visible warning on the real launch/resolve seam.

## Problem

The runtime/dev ownership inventory answers which binary owns a command, but it collapses two materially different kinds of development work: portable agent-development patterns that fak can dogfood and teach (leases, isolated workers, scoped commits, dispatch, validation), and tooling that exists only to maintain or operate this repository and its lab. Without a second axis, extraction can either hide useful patterns as maintainer internals or accidentally present fak-specific machinery as supported product API.

## Scope

- Define an orthogonal reuse classification for dev-owned commands: portable pattern, fak-maintainer specific, or lab-operations specific; runtime commands remain not applicable.
- Add that classification to the machine-readable ownership inventory and require every dev-owned command to have exactly one class and a rationale.
- Seed and test representative portable work-pattern families, including lease/coordination, isolated worker, scoped commit, validation, issue-contract, and dispatch concepts.
- Document the contract: portable means the pattern is suitable for examples/dogfood and possible later extraction, not that today's repository-bound command is a stable end-user API.
- Explain promotion criteria from an internal implementation to an adopter-facing example or product capability.

## Definition of done

- [ ] `fak index ownership --json` classifies every dev command on the reuse axis and validation rejects missing/invalid combinations.

- [ ] Current ownership/devindex tests pass and the committed-tip build witness remains green.

## Parent context
Part of epic #3256, the bring-your-own-tools/all-in-one runtime program.

## Current state
`fak init` emits a typed, fail-closed `fak.toml`, and `internal/deploymanifest` documents the precedence contract `explicit flags > manifest > built-in defaults`. Current runtime evidence contradicts that promise: no serve/up path calls `deploymanifest.Load`; only `cmd/fak/init.go` imports the package. Users therefore cannot customize a real serve with the reviewable file fak already presents as its deployment surface.

## Why now
fak should be opinionated by default without forcing every user to share every built-in opinion. Wiring the existing manifest into the most-used runtime gives users auditable control while preserving zero-config behavior and avoids adding more environment variables or a second config format.

## Working spine
`fak serve --config fak.toml` loads the existing typed manifest before parsing flags, maps the supported deployment fields onto serve defaults, and lets every explicit CLI flag win.

## In scope
- Add an explicit `--config FILE` serve input (no implicit ambient file lookup).
- Apply manifest policy floor, auth key env, default token budget, and observability bind as serve defaults.
- Preserve explicit flag precedence, including explicit values equal to built-in defaults.
- Fail closed with the existing named deploymanifest reason for unknown/invalid config.
- Add `--print-effective-config` JSON provenance output so users can see each effective value and whether it came from built-in, manifest, or flag.
- Document zero-config defaults and precedence.

## Out of scope
Starting the full multi-runtime `fak up` supervisor, inline policy materialization, tenant/template orchestration, and secret values in configuration.

## Done condition
A captured CLI test proves: no-config serve behavior is unchanged; a manifest changes supported values; explicit flags override it; typo'd keys refuse; and effective-config output names value provenance without starting a server.

records.title: epic(coordination): coordinate cache, compute, harness, and serve as one agent kernel
records.body:
## Thesis

fak's central product idea is not merely that it has a cache, can choose a computer, can drive a harness, or can serve a model. The leverage comes from coordinating those layers at one checkpoint. Cache state informs placement; placement and serving pressure constrain harness fan-out; harness intent gives serving and cache policy meaning; observed outcomes close the loop.

**Central mantra: coordinate the whole agent path, not isolated components.**

A stack of individually tuned components still makes locally rational, globally expensive decisions. fak should make the cross-layer decision explicit, explainable, enforceable, and measurable.

## Scope

Treat these as one coordinated system while preserving their existing ownership seams:

1. **Cache/context** — prefix/KV/object residency, reuse horizon, context pressure, compaction and transfer cost.
2. **Compute/placement** — device, fleet, vendor, topology, capacity, locality, price and failure domain.
3. **Harness/runtime** — task DAG, fan-out, leases, budgets, capabilities, interaction and witness policy.
4. **Serve/engine** — queue pressure, batching, model route, admission, prefill/decode state and backpressure.
5. **Trust/operations** — policy authority, decision provenance, trace, replay, recovery and measured outcome.

This epic coordinates existing programs rather than replacing them: agent orchestration #5964, model placement #5416, agentic scheduling #1911, tracing #5629, meaningful control #2208, and shared task/lease semantics #3266.

## End-state contract

For each agent-work unit, fak can consume a versioned snapshot from all participating layers, resolve one plan under explicit operator policy, apply actions through layer adapters, and emit a correlated decision record containing inputs, alternatives, reasons, actions, effects and independent witness. Layer-local optimization remains possible, but cannot silently contradict the global plan.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Public product and architecture language lead with cross-layer coordination and define the five layers consistently.
- [ ] A minimal offline spine accepts a fixture snapshot spanning cache + compute + harness + serve and emits a deterministic, explainable coordinated plan.
- [ ] Live adapters contribute typed observations and apply typed actions without importing each other's implementations.
- [ ] One correlation identity follows a work unit through harness planning, cache lookup/transfer, compute placement, serve admission and result/witness.
- [ ] Backpressure, cancellation, retry and recovery are coordinated across layer boundaries rather than handled as unrelated local events.
- [ ] Security and operator pins form hard constraints; optimization cannot negotiate them away.
- [ ] A replayable decision ledger explains both the chosen plan and rejected alternatives.
- [ ] A tuned-baseline A/B demonstrates net value over independently tuned components; no cross-layer performance claim ships before that witness.
- [ ] Kill switches allow each coordination policy to degrade to declared layer-local behavior without corrupting active work.

## Non-goals

- Building a second scheduler, cache, harness, or serving engine.
- A god object that bypasses the existing leaf boundaries.
- Renaming generic orchestration as coordination without sharing observations or decisions across layers.
- Claiming benefit from a modeled or naive baseline.

## Program shape

The first child is the contract/offline spine. Parallel follow-ons cover layer adapters, closed-loop control, observability/replay, failure semantics, policy boundaries, operator UX, documentation, conformance, and the live net-true benchmark.
## Filed delivery map

### Spine and layer contracts (G0)

- #6046 — neutral snapshot/constraint/plan/decision-record contract + offline spine.
- #6047 — cache/context observation and action adapter.
- #6048 — compute/model-placement adapter, integrated with #5416.
- #6049 — harness intent/capability adapter, consuming #5964/#5969.
- #6050 — serve admission/backpressure adapter.
- #6056 — canonical product language, architecture map and glossary.

### Closed loop, trust and proof (G1+)

- #6051 — bounded live observe/resolve/apply/verify controller.
- #6052 — cross-layer failure, compensation and restart recovery.
- #6053 — correlated trace, explain and deterministic replay, integrated with #5629.
- #6054 — authority, hard constraints, pins and kill switches, integrated with #2208.
- #6055 — unified operator status/preview/control surface.
- #6057 — deterministic conformance and fault corpus.
- #6058 — net-true A/B/C against tuned independent components (claim gate).
- #6059 — shadow/canary/default rollout and rollback gate.

### Existing adjacent programs (dependencies, not duplicates)

- #5964/#5969 — portable harness orchestration intent.
- #5416 — device/fleet/vendor model placement.
- #1911 — agentic scheduling and cross-agent compute sharing.
- #5629 — end-to-end trace context and OTLP backbone.
- #2208 — meaningful operator-control plane.
- #3266 — shared task and lease semantics.

records.title: Implement durable REQUIRE_WITNESS held-call spine
records.body:
## Problem

`abi.VerdictRequireWitness` and the gateway wire projection exist, but today the verdict only routes outward with `disposition: ESCALATE`. The kernel does not yet persist the exact held call, publish a typed witness request, verify a bound attestation, revalidate policy, execute at most once, and resume the parked continuation.

## Minimal working spine

Implement one end-to-end fake `money_transfer` flow:

1. proposal adjudicates to `REQUIRE_WITNESS` and returns a durable `held_id` without executing;
2. a second principal reads the bounded witness request and submits an approval bound to `held_id`, canonical call digest, witness contract, identity, and expiry;
3. the kernel verifies and revalidates the call, takes a compare-and-swap execution lease, and executes exactly once;
4. duplicate/replayed attestations do not duplicate the effect;
5. the parked session receives exactly one admitted result; cancellation/expiry makes late attestations inert.

## Done condition / witness

A test drives the real held-call store and executor through hold -> attest -> revalidate -> execute -> admit -> resume, captures the state/event sequence, and proves no execution before attestation plus at-most-once execution after duplicate delivery. Expose the smallest status/attestation/cancel surface needed to run one captured local demo.

## Constraints

- Persist a continuation reference, not a live context window.
- Witness providers submit attestations; they never mark a call READY directly.
- Re-adjudicate after transforms and revalidate immediately before execution.
- Result admission/QUARANTINE remains independent.
- Keep plugin loading/marketplace work out of this spine; use typed interfaces that can support it later.

Design: `docs/notes/REQUIRE-WITNESS-TOOL-CALL-CONTINUATIONS-2026-08-09.md` (lands separately).

## Parent context

Parent: #2721 (agent-kernel concept and proof program).

## Work estimate
Estimate: 8 points. Uncertainty: operator-supplied estimate; revise through the parent denominator when evidence changes.

## Overall completion contribution
Contribution: 8/8 points.

## Completion standard

records.title: Define typed tool-call plugin stages and user preference layering
records.body:
## Problem

The stable verdict ABI exposes `TRANSFORM`, restrictive registered verdict kinds, `REQUIRE_WITNESS`, and result `QUARANTINE`, but there is no explicit plugin host contract separating typed extension stages from authority. Without one, `TRANSFORM` can be mistaken for the plugin entry point itself, and user-selected plugins can accidentally imply authority widening.

## Scope

Define and implement the minimal typed plugin profile and host interfaces around these stages:

- proposal canonicalizer/transform producer;
- adjudicator;
- witness request adapter and attestation verifier;
- result-admission filter;
- audit/notification observer.

A profile pins plugin identity/version/digest, stage, permissions/data egress, timeout, fail-closed fallback, and precedence. Folding must be monotone: plugins can narrow, transform subject to re-adjudication, require a witness, quarantine, or defer; they cannot override the kernel capability floor or execute tools directly.

## User preference boundary

Prove layered resolution of kernel floor + organization + project + user + per-call narrowing. Include preferences for witness route, wait/background mode, transform auto-apply versus preview, disclosure, timeout, and resume notification. A user preference must not weaken an organization denial.

## Done condition / witness

A real plugin-host test loads two pinned test plugins, captures the proposal -> transform -> re-adjudicate -> execute -> result-admit trace, rejects a transform loop and an attempted authority widening, and proves a user preference can add a witness requirement but cannot remove a mandatory one.

Design: `docs/notes/REQUIRE-WITNESS-TOOL-CALL-CONTINUATIONS-2026-08-09.md` (lands separately).
